Introduction:
This This book is a collection of closely related articles. Each was written to stand on its own,
but none should be taken as the whole. The arc begins with the question of whether “philosophy”
can be reborn within a revealed horizon and then moves through method, metaphysics,
knowledge, science, and public order before ending in adversarial and applied tests. The opening
essay, “Wisdom and Philosophy in the Bahá’í Faith: On the Divine Horizon of Ḥikmat and the
Boundaries of Speculative Reason,” states the keynote: philosophy is neither absorbed into
theology nor emancipated from it; rather, reason is disciplined by Revelation’s horizon and
judged by its capacity to integrate and elevate practice. This first essay frames everything after it;
it provides the rationale that the next two pieces supply with evidence and scope. Thus “2: Why
Thinkers Become Bahá’ís – Intellectual Conversions and Admiration” offers historical and
contemporary trajectories in which intellectuals re-configure prior commitments under the
pressure of Revelation; it concretizes the claim that philosophy here is transformative rather than
merely apologetic and prepares the reader to see the project as lived, not only argued. “3. The
Philosophical Horizon of the Bahá’í Writings” then inventories the questions the corpus itself
provokes—ontology, epistemology, language, law, civilizational purpose—so that subsequent
essays answer to an internal agenda rather than to borrowed frameworks; it sets the table for the
rest of the volume.
With that table set, “4: The Typology of Philosophers in Bahá’í Thought: Revelation, Reason,
and the Ethics of True Knowledge” supplies evaluative criteria: it distinguishes sanctified
knowing from merely clever erudition and establishes why the relation to truth, transformation,
and ethical purification matters. These criteria become the standards by which later claims are
measured. “5. Hermeneutics, Interpretation, and the Limits of Understanding in the Bahá’í Faith”
then secures the constitutional grammar of reading—canon, authorization, legislation when the
text is silent, and the moral grammar (adab) of disagreement—so that the book’s constructive
theses are neither esoteric free play nor authoritarian closure. This hermeneutic framework is the
hinge between the opening program and the rest: everything that follows presupposes it, and the
later case studies will, in turn, test it.


From this hinge, the collection moves to first philosophy. “The Unity-Function: Translating
Qāʿidat al-Wāḥid into Phenomenology and Deconstruction” reformulates the classical “from the
One only one proceeds” as a transcendental operation: not a hypostatic emitter of effects but the
minimal act of gathering a manifold “as one,” which formally constrains how plurality lawfully
appears (the same-respect clause). This piece depends on the opening essay’s relocation of
philosophy within Revelation’s horizon and immediately feeds the next two essays, which state
the consequences for metaphysics. “The End of Theology: Bahá’í Metaphysics and the Limits of
Speculative Reason” argues that the ‘end’ of theology is not negation but transformation:
speculative cosmography gives way to a metaphysics disciplined by unknowability,
manifestation, and praxis. “The End of Theology II: The Metaphysical Status of Cosmos and the
Resolution of Kant’s Antinomies in Bahá’í Metaphysics” extends that transformation, showing
how the unity-function plus the Bahá’í doctrines of manifestation and capacity re-frame
cosmology and relieve classic antinomies; it stands to the first “End of Theology” as
demonstration to thesis and carries forward the unity-function’s formal insight into a concrete
philosophical terrain.
“ The Baháʼí Praxis: Translating Theology into Social Action” is the natural sequel: if
metaphysics is truly re-formed, it must cash out in the order of action, institutions, and
consultation. This essay operationalizes what the hermeneutic piece authorized and what the end-
of-theology papers demanded, connecting doctrine to policy and pedagogy. At the same time,
“Thresholds of Just-Being: Deficiency, Demise, and the Ontology of Belonging” treats
anthropology at the edges—defect, loss, marginality—to test whether the unity-function and the
new metaphysic can sustain a non-triumphal account of human limits; it prepares the conceptual
ground for the pair on faith and alterity. “What Is Faith? And Who Is a Believer?” identifies faith
not as private assent but as a rational-ethical orientation within the revealed horizon; this directly
undergirds “Beyond Totality: Bahá’í Ethics and the Prophetic Epistemology of the Other,” which
brings a Levinasian challenge into conversation with the unity-function and consultation to argue
that unity-in-diversity is not a slogan but an ethic of attending to alterity within order.
Having moved from ontology to ethics, the volume turns to knowledge. “The Spectrum of
Knowledge in the Bahá’í Faith: Material, Conceptual, Existential, Moral, and Divine Forms of
Knowing” offers a five-fold taxonomy that later pieces use as their metric. “Bahá’í Epistemology


and the Modern Landscape of Knowledge: From Scientific Realism to Discourse Theory and
Virtue Epistemology” then stages direct confrontations with contemporary epistemologies,
showing where alignment and divergence obtain when Revelation is the orienting horizon. This
is intentionally followed by “Superstition and the Structure of True Knowledge: A Bahá’í
Critique of Khurāfāt and Epistemic Deviation,” which marks the boundary conditions: by
purging pseudo-knowledge and esoteric spectacle, it protects the very epistemic field that the
previous two essays sought to integrate. The capstone of this cluster, “Toward a Unified Bahá’í
Paradigm of Science: Integrating the Seven Modes of Knowledge through Complexity,
Revelation, and Praxis,” operationalizes the taxonomy and the engagements into a working
paradigm—complexity-aware, normatively guided by Revelation, and practically testable—
thereby returning us to the praxis motif and forward to first principles.
“Presupposition of Revealed Truth: On First Principles, Revelation, and the Ground of
Rationality” collects the results: it argues that what counts as a rational starting point is itself
framed by a horizon one cannot derive from below. This essay closes the loop with the opener
(“Wisdom and Philosophy…”) and with the unity-function piece, and it prepares the reader to
see political theology and institutional order not as external appendices but as entailments.
Accordingly, “Toward a Bahá’í Political Philosophy: Manifestation, Authority, and the Form of
Civilizational Unity” articulates how ontological unity becomes the architecture of governance,
law, and global order—explicitly depending on the hermeneutic constraints and on consultation’s
procedural truth. The next three essays are stress-tests of that political philosophy across concrete
fractures in community life and authority. “Managing the Fold: Punishment, Marginality, and
Apostasy as Tools of Communal Governance—Religions Compared, Bahá’í Focused” asks
whether discipline and inclusion can co-inhere without panoptical overreach; it relies on the
earlier anthropology of marginality and the ethic of consultation. “After Shoghi Effendi:
Guardianship, Lineage, and the Limits of Claim” takes up succession and legitimacy, applying
the earlier constitutional grammar of interpretation; it also supplies historical and doctrinal
constraints that the following piece uses. “The Possibility and Consequences of the Lack of a
Final Interpretation after the Age of the Interpreter in the Bahá’í Faith” then articulates openness
and closure in definitive form: binding canon without private coercion, legislative authority


without hermeneutic violence, revision without relativism—precisely the balance the book set
out to defend.
Two concluding essays extend this balance into philosophical dialogue and a targeted doctrinal
case. “The Present Absent: Bahá’í Authority and Derridean Motifs” revisits the genealogy of
meaning and the motif of trace, showing how a prophetic horizon can accept the discipline of
différance without collapsing into indeterminacy; it folds back to the early engagement with
modern theory, secures the hermeneutic middle, and re-confirms the unity-function’s resistance
to hypostatization. “Women’s Membership in the Universal House of Justice: Equality, Equity,
and the Logic of a Singular Exception” serves as a hard case that forces the whole architecture—
hermeneutics, consultation, political philosophy, and epistemic taxonomy—to work together: it
asks whether a covenantal system can reconcile an apparent doctrinal exception with its moral
commitments without special pleading. The logic of resolution on offer here depends on every
earlier component being in place.
Read sequentially, then, the collection moves from program (why philosophy in a revealed
horizon), to method (who counts as a knower; how reading is governed), to first philosophy
(unity-function and the end of speculative cosmography), to praxis (action, anthropology, ethics
of alterity), to knowledge and science (taxonomy, confrontation, purge, integration), to first
principles (the ground of rationality), to political order (authority, law, governance), and finally
to adversarial and applied tests. Read non-linearly, each essay still names its debts and
consequences. In either path, no single paper may be taken as proxy for the rest: the unity-
function without the hermeneutic grammar risks abstraction; the political philosophy without the
anthropology risks severity; the epistemic taxonomy without the superstition critique risks
inflation; the Derridean dialogue without the canonical anchor risks dissolution. The parts are
designed to answer to one another.
A brief note about count and editorial fit: the draft you shared presently has twenty-three stand-
alone essays. If you prefer a canonical twenty-one, two natural mergers preserve the architecture:
(i) the pair “The End of Theology” and “The End of Theology II” can be issued as one long
essay with two movements; (ii) the authority cluster can present “The Present Absent” as an


internal dialogue section within “The Possibility and Consequences of the Lack of a Final
Interpretation…”. Either merger leaves every cross-dependence above intact.












Iman Motlagh Arani


Wisdom and Philosophy in the Bahá’í Faith: On the Divine Horizon of Ḥikmat and the
Boundaries of Speculative Reason
Abstract
This article examines the emergence of a distinct philosophical paradigm within the Bahá’í Faith,
one that reconfigures the nature, purpose, and authority of philosophy itself. Rather than framing
philosophy as an autonomous rational enterprise or as subordinate to dogmatic theology, the
Bahá’í Writings present a prophetic ontology in which wisdom (ḥikmat) is both divinely sourced
and civilizational in purpose. Through a genealogical engagement with classical, Islamic, and
modern philosophical traditions, the article analyzes how the Bahá’í Revelation both affirms and
transforms philosophical categories such as being (wujūd), causality, knowledge, and
interpretation. Central to this transformation is the Manifestation of God, not merely as a
religious figure but as the ontological fulcrum of truth, whose utterance reorders the hierarchy of
knowledge from Revelation to reason, from action to understanding. The article also introduces a
new typology of philosophers, distinguishes legitimate from false uses of reason, and explores
the structural function of interpretation within a post-metaphysical covenantal order. Ultimately,
the Bahá’í model challenges secular and theological dichotomies by proposing a unity of thought
and Revelation that is dialogical, ethically oriented, and historically responsive—a metaphysical
vision of philosophy not as speculation, but as world-shaping praxis.
Introduction: The Question of a Bahá’í Philosophy
Is there such a thing as a Bahá’í philosophy? At first glance, the question may seem
contradictory, or at least ambiguous. Philosophy has often been understood as the autonomous
exercise of reason—an enterprise whose very legitimacy rests on its independence from religious
dogma or revealed authority. To posit a “Bahá’í philosophy” thus appears to confront two
powerful critiques simultaneously: from rationalists who reject the mingling of Revelation and
Reason, and from religionists who see philosophy as a source of skepticism, relativism, or
secular dilution. And yet, the Bahá’í Writings explicitly affirm the value of reason, uphold the
unity of science and religion, and identify ḥikmat (wisdom) as a cardinal virtue. The question,
then, is not whether philosophy can be reconciled with Revelation, but rather: what new
philosophical configuration emerges when Revelation itself defines the horizon of thought?


To explore this question, we must begin with the meaning and origin of philosophy. The term
philosophy, from the Greek philosophia, denotes the “love of wisdom.” But the seemingly
simple etymology conceals a long and fractured history. In classical antiquity, philosophy was
not merely a theoretical enterprise. For Plato, it was the soul’s ascent toward intelligible realities
and moral purification through dialectical reflection. For Aristotle, it was the systematic
investigation of first principles and the nature of being. Yet even these founding figures stood in
the midst of older traditions—pre-Socratic fragments, Pythagorean theologies, Eleatic paradoxes.
As Derrida reminds us, the beginning of philosophy is itself a metaphysical illusion. There is no
absolute point of departure. “The beginning and the end,” he writes, “are traces and traces of
traces.”
Indeed, philosophy has never been wholly separate from religion. In its earliest forms,
philosophical inquiry was often inseparable from myth, prophecy, and divine cosmology. The
very founders of Greek philosophy—Thales, Pythagoras, Heraclitus—were shaped by
theological, cosmological, and esoteric traditions. Bahá’u’lláh affirms this integration of sacred
and rational knowledge when He writes: “The sages aforetime acquired their knowledge from
the Prophets, inasmuch as the latter were the Exponents of divine philosophy and the Revealers
of heavenly mysteries.” He further notes that “Empedocles, who distinguished himself in
philosophy, was a contemporary of David, while Pythagoras lived in the days of Solomon… and
acquired Wisdom from the treasury of prophethood.” The fundamental insights of philosophy, in
this light, did not emerge in isolation from religion, but were “emanated from the Prophets.”
The myth of autonomous reason as the true origin of philosophy finds its strongest articulation in
Enlightenment rationalism. Here, reason is elevated above all else, and philosophy is purified of
theological influence. From this perspective, philosophy’s task is to critique, not confirm,
religious claims. As Gilson notes, such a view leads inevitably to the conclusion that a “Christian
philosophy” is absurd, since reason and Revelation must be categorically separated.
But Gilson challenges this dichotomy. In his view, Christian philosophy is not a contradiction but
a new mode of philosophizing—one in which reason is illuminated by faith, and Revelation does
not abolish but transforms philosophical inquiry. This perspective is most clearly embodied in
the thought of St. Thomas Aquinas, who, while drawing deeply from Aristotle, reorients his
metaphysics around the doctrine of creation ex nihilo, a concept rooted not in reason alone but in


the revealed truths of the Bible. Theology, in this account, is not merely content for philosophy
but an “indispensable auxiliary to reason.”
The concept of Ego sum qui sum (“I am that I am”), revealed in Exodus, becomes the
cornerstone of a new understanding of Being itself. It is this biblical insight, Gilson argues, that
gives rise to the “existential notion of being” that marks a fundamental transformation in
metaphysics. Likewise, the Augustinian motto nisi credideritis, non intelligetis—“unless you
believe, you shall not understand”—suggests that faith is not the enemy of reason, but its
precondition. The philosophical tradition shaped by Christian Revelation does not negate reason;
it expands it.
This historical pattern extends beyond the Middle Ages. Even modern philosophers who sought
to distance themselves from theology—Descartes, Pascal, Malebranche, Leibniz, Kant, Hegel—
remained deeply indebted to religious concepts and theological frameworks. Descartes’s cogito,
his proofs for God, and his doctrine of occasionalism are all unintelligible without reference to
the Christian metaphysical tradition. Malebranche's occasionalism and Pascal’s turn from
rationalism to Christian mysticism testify to a continued intertwining of faith and thought.
Leibniz’s pre-established harmony and doctrine of the Necessary Being echo theological
principles from Aquinas and Avicenna. Kant, often regarded as the architect of modern
philosophical autonomy, nonetheless affirmed that he had to “deny knowledge in order to make
room for faith.” When read in conjunction with the Critique of Practical Reason, the Critique of
Pure Reason reveals not the expulsion of theology, but its reconfiguration—placing moral law,
freedom, and God at the heart of reason’s practical vocation. Hegel, too, developed his dialectic
of Spirit in ways that retained deep affinities with theological patterns of history and eschatology.
What these examples reveal is that philosophy has never been truly autonomous. Its concepts,
categories, and problems are historically and structurally entangled with religious thought. The
“death of metaphysics,” lamented by Gilson, occurs precisely when philosophy attempts to sever
these ties. The recovery of philosophy, he argues, depends on a return to its theological roots—
not to subordinate reason, but to restore its capacity for truth.
The Bahá’í perspective continues and completes this restoration. It affirms the necessity of
reason while grounding it in the Revelation of the Manifestation of God. As Bahá’u’lláh
declares, “The beginning of wisdom and the origin thereof is to acknowledge whatsoever God


hath clearly set forth.” Reason without Revelation is blind; Revelation without reason is mute.
Their union is not a compromise but a fulfillment.
In the sections that follow, we will trace how this union unfolds in the lives of intellectual
converts to the Bahá’í Faith; we will articulate a working definition of Bahá’í philosophy; and
we will explore the structures of reason, Revelation, and interpretation in Bahá’í thought. Our
aim is not to imitate Christian or Islamic models, but to ask whether Bahá’í philosophy marks the
emergence of a new paradigm: one in which the love of wisdom is reborn as a covenantal
responsibility—a responsibility to think, to act, and to understand within the horizon of divine
truth.
2: Why Thinkers Become Bahá’ís – Intellectual Conversions and Admiration
The possibility of a Bahá’í philosophy is not a speculative idea invented by later commentators.
It is, rather, a historical phenomenon with identifiable figures—philosophers, theologians,
scientists, and poets—who encountered the Bahá’í teachings and found in them not only spiritual
truth but also philosophical depth. The emergence of the Bahá’í Faith was not met solely with
emotional or religious allegiance, but with a profound recognition that its principles, concepts,
and cosmology offered new ways of thinking about ontology, epistemology, ethics, and
civilization. In short, many of its earliest and most articulate proponents were thinkers who either
converted to the Bahá’í Faith or were intellectually transformed by it.
Among the Western intellectuals are such figures as Auguste Forel, the Swiss neuroanatomist,
psychologist, and moral philosopher who, after a lifetime of scientific work and ethical
reflection, embraced the Bahá’í Faith in 1921. Forel found in the Bahá’í teachings a unified
vision that harmonized the empirical rigor of science with the moral demands of spiritual life. He
praised its rational ethical system, its call for universal peace, and its foundational affirmation of
the oneness of humanity as principles long sought in his humanist and scientific work. Similarly,
Dr. J.E. Esslemont, a Scottish physician and author of Bahá’u’lláh and the New Era, described
the Faith as a "spiritual revolution" rooted in reason and divine law. Later thinkers such as
William S. Hatcher, a mathematician and logician trained in analytic philosophy, devoted much
of his scholarly output to formalizing Bahá’í teachings using symbolic logic and axiomatic
reasoning. His book Logic and Logos is a direct attempt to construct a philosophical theology


based on Bahá’í epistemology. Figures like H.M. Balyuzi, John Esslemont, George
Townshend, and Udo Schaefer further exemplify this pattern: intellectuals who were drawn to
the Faith not in spite of their rational training, but because they found its truths resonant with
their highest intellectual ideals.
In addition to Western converts, some of the most important Persian and Islamic thinkers of
the 19th and 20th centuries embraced or developed Bahá’í philosophical thought from within the
Islamic intellectual tradition. These figures are foundational to any serious understanding of
Bahá’í philosophy. Mírzá Muḥammad Qá’iní (Nabíl-i-Akbar) was one of the most erudite
scholars of his generation—a mujtahid, philosopher, and theologian who had studied under Ḥajj
Mullā Hādī Sabzavārī, the preeminent exponent of post-Sadrian metaphysics. Bahá’u’lláh
Himself described Nabíl-i-Akbar as “the most erudite of the divines” and affirmed that he had
subordinated his formidable philosophical acumen to the Revelation.
Mírzá Abu’l-Faḍl-i-Gulpáygání, perhaps the most celebrated Bahá’í scholar of modern times,
was a polymath proficient in Islamic jurisprudence, Qur’anic exegesis, classical Arabic and
Persian literature, logic, theology, and comparative religion. His works, such as Burhán-i-Lámiʿ
and Fara’id, defend the Bahá’í Revelation using rational, philosophical, and hermeneutic
methods that blend classical Islamic scholarship with universalist Bahá’í reasoning. He taught at
al-Azhar University, wrote extensively in Arabic, and was recognized for his intellectual
integrity and methodical argumentation.
Mírzá Asadu’lláh Fádil Mázandarání authored monumental historical and doctrinal works,
most notably Zuhúru’l-Ḥaqq, which blends historiography, theology, and interpretive insight.
His writings reflect a deep engagement with Islamic philosophy and mystical thought, yet they
are entirely oriented around the implications of Bahá’u’lláh’s Revelation. Likewise, ʻAbdu’l-
Ḥamíd Ishráq-Khávarí, compiler of Raḥíq-i-Makhtúm and Qámús-i-Íqán, synthesized vast
textual traditions, drawing on kalām, tafsīr, and mysticism to clarify Bahá’í doctrines through an
encyclopedic, philosophical lens.
Finally, Dr. ʿAlī-Murād Dāvūdī, a leading professor of Islamic philosophy at Tehran University
and head of its department of philosophy, stood as a singular figure in modern Iranian


intellectual history. Deeply trained in Avicennan and Sadrian traditions, Dāvūdī wrote
extensively on metaphysics, epistemology, and ethics. His Bahá’í writings explore topics such as
being (wujūd), unity (tawḥīd), the station of the Manifestation, and the nature of divine law. He
saw in Bahá’í Revelation the realization of the metaphysical unity sought by centuries of Islamic
philosophers. His disappearance and presumed martyrdom in the wake of the 1979 Iranian
Revolution marked the tragic silencing of one of the Bahá’í world’s most sophisticated
philosophical voices.
These Persian Bahá’í scholars did not merely adapt inherited categories; they reconceptualized
them in light of Revelation. Their philosophical activity was not apologetic, but constructive—
grounding a new metaphysics, ethics, and theology based on Bahá’í teachings, while maintaining
fidelity to reasoned inquiry and classical method. In their works, reason is not abolished but
sanctified, and philosophy becomes an act of spiritual discernment. Their lives are the
strongest refutation of the idea that Bahá’í thought is too abstract, too scriptural, or too
theological to be philosophical. It is precisely in these thinkers that Bahá’í philosophy proves its
vitality.
What unites all these figures—East and West—is not a uniform method or school, but an
encounter: an encounter with a Revelation that challenged and elevated their intellectual
commitments. In their lives, we see that Bahá’í philosophy is not merely possible; it is already in
motion. It unfolds in the crossing of traditions, the transformation of rational categories, and the
spiritualization of intellectual life. It does not negate philosophy’s past, but offers a new future:
one in which the love of wisdom is reborn within the light of divine unity.
3. The Philosophical Horizon of the Bahá’í Writings
To speak of a Bahá’í philosophy is not merely to ask whether philosophical questions are present
in the Bahá’í Faith, but to ask whether the very structure of Bahá’í Revelation engenders a
philosophical activity of a new kind. The answer must begin with the content of the Bahá’í
sacred texts themselves. The writings of Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá do not merely include
occasional references to philosophers or abstract metaphysical themes. They constitute, when
read as a totality, a sustained and comprehensive engagement with the foundational questions of
philosophy: ontology, epistemology, cosmology, ethics, anthropology, political order, aesthetics,


and the philosophy of language and interpretation. To read them philosophically is not to impose
a foreign framework, but to recognize their inherent philosophical architecture.
Philosophy, traditionally defined as the love of wisdom, in the Bahá’í Writings appears not as an
autonomous speculation but as a response to the divine impulse embedded within creation.
Bahá’u’lláh repeatedly affirms that “the essence and the fundamentals of philosophy have
emanated from the Prophets,” grounding wisdom (ḥikmat) in Revelation itself. What follows
from this is a redefinition of philosophy—not as the abstract construction of human reason
isolated from divine aid, but as the unfolding of reason within the orbit of divine illumination.
This structure is neither Augustinian nor Thomistic. It neither fully integrates philosophy into
theology, nor insists on their separation. Instead, it constitutes a new dispensation of wisdom,
one in which philosophy becomes the reflective face of Revelation, and Revelation the animating
soul of philosophy.
This vision is not a rhetorical embellishment. It is embodied in the immense corpus of
Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, whose writings together amount to a comprehensive system of
metaphysical, ethical, and civilizational discourse. The writings of Bahá’u’lláh—such as the
Kitáb-i-Íqán, Lawḥ-i-Ḥikmat, Lawḥ-i-Basīṭ al-Ḩaqīqah, Lawḥ-i-Maqṣūd, Hidden Words, Seven
Valleys, Four Valleys, and the Súiriy-i-Haykal—engage directly with metaphysical concepts
such as being, essence, causality, the unknowable God, the divine Will, emanation,
manifestation, creation, nature, and the purpose of existence. In these works, He articulates a
cosmology in which God is utterly transcendent, His Essence (dhāt) beyond all knowing, and yet
His attributes reflected in the entire cosmos through the Manifestations of God. The reality of
being (vojūd) is continually presented as an act—the bestowal of existence by God—rather than
a static essence (ḥaqīqat or dhāt). This view undercuts the metaphysics of substance in favor of a
metaphysics of manifestation (ẓuhūr) and relation.
In Lawḥ-i-Ḥikmat, Bahá’u’lláh affirms the dignity of the philosophers and sages of the past—
naming Socrates, Empedocles, Pythagoras—and yet insists that their wisdom was drawn from
the treasury of the Prophets. This repositions the philosophical tradition not as the source of
ultimate truth but as the echo of divine insight. In the Kitáb-i-Íqán, Bahá’u’lláh elaborates a
profound hermeneutics, distinguishing between the outer form and inner meaning of sacred texts,
and calling for a mode of reading that is detached from literalism, guided by spiritual purity, and


attuned to the symbolic nature of Revelation. This is not merely a theological admonition; it is a
metaphilosophical claim about the nature of meaning, truth, and interpretation.
The Seven Valleys and Four Valleys develop a mystical epistemology, presenting stages of
knowledge, love, and unity as existential transformations rather than logical deductions. The
structure of the journey is neither merely Sufi nor Neoplatonic, but reframed in a Bahá’í
metaphysical anthropology in which the soul’s purpose is to reflect divine attributes through
stages of search, love, knowledge, unity, contentment, wonder, and true poverty. The
epistemology implied here is performative and spiritual: knowledge is acquired not solely by
syllogism but by the soul’s transfiguration.
In texts such as Lawḥ-i-Maqṣūd and Lawḥ-i-Madīnat al-Tawḥīd, Bahá’u’lláh sets forth ethical
and ontological principles that ground unity not merely as a moral imperative but as the
ontological structure of reality. Unity (tawḥīd) is not only the singularity of God, but the inner
coherence of all being. It is the metaphysical principle that binds cosmology, ethics, and social
order. In this sense, philosophy is no longer an abstraction; it is civilization-building. Every
metaphysical concept in these texts is inseparable from its ethical and historical implications.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s writings deepen and systematize these insights. In Some Answered Questions,
He addresses questions of metaphysics, anthropology, logic, psychology, political theory,
evolution, and the nature of science. He distinguishes between the essence and the attributes of
God, affirms the eternity of creation, and argues that nature is the expression of divine Will. His
discussions of the soul, mind, and spirit distinguish faculties and levels of existence with a
precision that maps closely to classical philosophical debates, yet always redirected through the
lens of Revelation. In His addresses at the Metaphysical Club and the Hotel Plaza, He explicitly
affirms the unity of religion and science, defining true philosophy as that which is animated by
spiritual insight.
His other works—such as Treatise on Politics, Secret of Divine Civilization, Risāla-yi-
Madanīyyih, Tafsīr du‘ā’-yi ṣaḥar, and various tablets—offer philosophical reflections on
political order, civilization, law, ethics, causality, and eschatology. He reaffirms the rational
basis of belief, redefines causality in light of divine purpose, and offers a model of civilization
that is both metaphysical and developmental. Philosophy, for ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, is never separate
from the renewal of society.


From these texts emerges a unified philosophical framework that is both metaphysical and
prophetic. The concept of the Manifestation of God serves as the central axis around which all
philosophical themes revolve. It is through the Manifestation that humanity comes to know the
unknowable God, to reflect divine attributes, to acquire true knowledge, and to build just
societies. In contrast to Thomistic or Augustinian models, Bahá’í philosophy does not seek to
merge philosophy into theology, nor to grant reason an independent dominion. Rather, it
introduces a new metaphysical paradigm rooted in Mazhar (manifestation)—a principle more
dynamic than essence, more relational than being, and more unifying than causality.
In this paradigm, the unknowable Divine Essence (dhāt) is not reduced to abstract concepts or
rational inference, but acknowledged through its manifestations—the kalimāt (Words) of God
that structure existence, history, and meaning. These kalimāt are not mere utterances but
ontological events, bridging the infinite and the finite, the eternal and the temporal. Revelation is
not a static deposit of dogma but a dynamic process of unveiling. Metaphysics is no longer the
study of fixed substances, but of living relations, divine signs, and civilizational purpose.
This view critiques inherited metaphysical systems—Greek ontology’s emphasis on presence
and substance, Augustinian theology’s fixation on exemplarism, and Enlightenment
rationalism’s detachment from divine telos—not by discarding their insights, but by transcending
their limitations. It affirms the legacy of Plato and Aristotle, yet insists that true philosophy must
be animated by the spirit of the age. The Bahá’í paradigm is not philosophy as speculation, but
philosophy as transformation—an ethics of becoming, a metaphysics of manifestation, and a
civilization-building wisdom rooted in ḥikmat.
Thus, Bahá’í philosophy is not a theology in disguise, nor a diluted rationalism. It is a post-
metaphysical unity of reason and Revelation—grounded in the radical unknowability of God, the
ontological function of the Manifestation, the symbolic nature of language, and the teleological
unfolding of unity in diversity. The Bahá’í philosopher, therefore, is not one who “explains” the
Faith, but one who thinks within its horizon—who, moved by love of wisdom, seeks to know in
order to serve, and understands in order to act. As such, Bahá’í philosophy is not a contradiction
but the redefinition of philosophy itself.


4: The Typology of Philosophers in Bahá'í Thought: Revelation, Reason, and the Ethics of True
Knowledge
What emerges from the Bahá’í Writings is a multi-layered typology of philosophers, sages, and
men of knowledge, grounded in a metaphysical and ethical framework wholly distinct from
inherited Greek and scholastic paradigms. This typology is not merely historical or classificatory;
it is ontological and eschatological. It reflects the degrees of access to divine reality, the ethical
purification of the soul, and the proper ordering of knowledge in relation to Revelation. At the
summit of this hierarchy stand the Manifestations of God, but the typology also includes
Prophets (Nabīs), Imams (A’immah), the Guardian and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, righteous scholars, mystic
knowers, and errant philosophers—each evaluated according to their relation to divine light.
At the highest level are the Manifestations of God, who are not philosophers in the classical
sense, but divine educators whose knowledge is innate, infallible, and immediate. Bahá’u’lláh
writes: “The sages aforetime acquired their knowledge from the Prophets, inasmuch as the latter
were the Exponents of divine philosophy and the Revealers of heavenly mysteries” (Lawḥ-i-
Ḥikmat, as cited in The Centrality of Philosophy and Wisdom in the Bahá’í Faith, Source 282).
Their utterances are described as “the crystal, living waters,” while all other knowledge is but
“the dregs.” Unlike human philosophers who acquire knowledge discursively, the Manifestations
are direct emanations of divine will, endowed with inherent infallibility. Their metaphysical
station is the metaphysics of ẓuhūr—manifestation—as the bridge between the unknowable dhāt
(Essence) and the world of vojūd (existence).
Immediately beneath them stand the Prophets (Nabīs) and the Imams (A’immah), figures who are
not originators of new dispensations but are divinely inspired and protected from error in their
interpretive and spiritual authority. They possess what theologians term “endowed infallibility.”
In the Bahá’í Faith, this role is uniquely fulfilled by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and the Guardian of the
Cause. Though not Manifestations themselves, they are described as “the Center of the
Covenant” and “the infallible Interpreter of the Word.” Their station affirms the continuity of
divine guidance through time and the legitimacy of authoritative, non-speculative interpretation.
Descending further in the hierarchy, we encounter the category of true sages and righteous men
of learning. These are individuals whose knowledge is sanctified by spiritual purity and
detachment from selfish ambition. As Bahá’u’lláh declares: “Righteous men of learning... are, in


the sight of Him Who is the Desire of the world, stars of the heaven of true knowledge” (Lawḥ-i-
Dunyá, Source 273). These individuals are fountains of wisdom not because of academic
credentials but because of their moral alignment with divine purposes. Their knowledge is
transformative, not speculative; ethical, not merely intellectual.
Complementing this category are the mystic knowers and seekers—those who have traversed the
Seven Valleys or Four Valleys, who attain knowledge not through syllogism but through the
purification of the heart. As Bahá’u’lláh writes: “Knowledge is a light which God casteth into the
heart of whomsoever He willeth” (Chihár-Vádí, Source 16). Their epistemology is performative:
to know is to become, and true understanding arises from inward transfiguration. These mystics
do not reject reason, but surpass it through spiritual unveiling (kashf) and proximity to the
Source.
In stark contrast, the Writings critique various types of false or vain philosophers. First among
them are materialists, who restrict knowledge to sensory data and deny the soul’s spiritual
reality. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, in Some Answered Questions, laments: “Certain philosophers of America
and Europe are content to gradually approach the animal world and so to go backward.” He
critiques their belief that man is simply a species of animal with no immortal soul. In Tablets of
the Divine Plan, he adds: “No matter how much man gains wealth... he will not become as
independent as a cow.” This metaphor highlights the futility of materialistic ambition without
spiritual purpose.
Next are those who possess knowledge divorced from humility—what Bahá’u’lláh calls “satanic
knowledge.” These are the philosophers whose pride, self-love, and addiction to disputation
blind them to divine light. “Knowledge is the most grievous veil between man and his Creator,”
He warns (Kitáb-i-Íqán, Source 124). Such scholars may be prolific in logic or metaphysics, but
their knowledge is sterile, a reflection of “vain and obscure thoughts.” Their hearts, unpurified,
become obstacles to the truth they claim to seek.
The Writings also critique religious leaders and scholars who oppose the Manifestation due to
self-interest or dogmatic rigidity. These figures, though outwardly learned, become “the wolves
in shepherd’s clothing” (Lawḥ-i-Ibn-i-Dhib, Source 298), leading people astray with their
literalism and veiled ambition. Bahá’u’lláh states that “by their sanction and authority, every
Prophet of God hath drunk from the chalice of sacrifice” (Kitáb-i-Íqán, Source 98).


Bahá’í metaphysics, therefore, does not begin with being as presence (ousia), nor with being as
act (esse), but with ẓuhūr—manifestation—as the dynamic interface between divine
unknowability (dhāt) and cosmic reality (vojūd). The hierarchy of knowledge flows from the
Essence, to the Manifestation, to the infallible Interpreter, to the righteous knower, to the mystic
seeker. The true philosopher is not one who claims autonomous reason, but one who aligns
knowledge with the ethical telos of transformation—what the Writings call ḥikmat. As
Bahá’u’lláh states, “The beginning of wisdom and the origin thereof is to acknowledge
whatsoever God hath clearly set forth.”
Bahá’í philosophy, then, redefines the very meaning of philosophy. It does not seek to isolate
reason from Revelation, nor subordinate philosophy to theology. It critiques classical ontologies
of substance, existentialisms of despair, and logicisms of abstraction, while honoring their
historical contributions. In its place, it offers a post-metaphysical, prophetic ontology: one rooted
in manifestation, guided by unity-in-diversity, and oriented toward the civilizational renewal of
the world.
To think philosophically in the Bahá’í sense is not to speculate endlessly on first principles, but
to respond to the Revelation with ethical and intellectual integrity. The Bahá’í philosopher does
not speak about Revelation but from within it—transformed by its light, and committed to
manifesting its truth in action.
5. Hermeneutics, Interpretation, and the Limits of Understanding in the Bahá’í Faith
5.1. Genealogy, Language, and the Crisis of Meaning
Nietzsche’s On the Genealogy of Morality shattered the illusion that moral or metaphysical
concepts possess an essential, unchanging core. For Nietzsche, concepts such as “truth,” “good,”
and “spirit” are not fixed reference points but historical artifacts—expressions of power
relations, psychological reversals, and cultural transformations. Interpretation is not a neutral act
of unveiling meaning, but a will to power: a re-inscription of forces through language. In his
genealogical method, Nietzsche traces moral values not to divine command or rational
deduction, but to instincts, resentment, and socio-political stratagems. The 'origin' is therefore
always already a site of violence, and etymology becomes an archaeological excavation of buried
conflicts.


This insight calls into question any claim to a pristine beginning, including the idea of “pure
reason” or “revealed truth.” Nietzsche’s suspicion reverberates through post-structuralist thought,
with Derrida’s différance continuing the assault on origin and stability. If words are the sediment
of conflicting historical intentions, can any theological or philosophical discourse remain
immune? Can we still speak of ‘wisdom’ or ‘divine knowledge’ without falling into the traps of
conceptual idolatry?
A genealogical analysis of key terms further complicates our task. The Arabic term ḥikmat
(wisdom/philosophy) originally connoted ‘judicious action’ or ‘putting something in its proper
place,’ eventually acquiring metaphysical weight through its assimilation into Aristotelian and
Neoplatonic thought in Islamic philosophy. Ta’wīl, meaning ‘to return to the origin,’ once
denoted hermeneutic interpretation in search of an inner truth, yet it became associated with
arbitrary esotericism and doctrinal deviation. Tafsīr, from the root f-s-r, implies clarification or
exposition, typically employed for exegesis of Qurʼanic text. Sharīʿa, meaning ‘path to water,’
initially referred to divine law but gradually became a symbol of codified legalism. Dīn, often
translated as ‘religion,’ stems from notions of judgment, debt, and reciprocal submission. The
Greek logos began as ‘speech’ or ‘account’ and eventually evolved into the cosmic reason in
Stoic and Christian metaphysics. Nomos, or ‘law,’ originally referred to custom or distribution,
and ʿaql, reason, derives from the verb ʿaqala, ‘to bind’—suggesting that reason is a restraining,
ordering force. Each of these terms has undergone conceptual distortions across historical shifts,
theological disputes, and political regimes.
However, the Baháʼí Writings offer a radical alternative to the genealogical suspicion. While
acknowledging the instability of human language and the inadequacy of metaphor, Bahá’u’lláh
and the Báb speak of words not as ideological residues but as theophanic events. Language, in
this vision, is not a prison of deferred meaning, but a vessel of divine effulgence. “Every word is
endowed with a spirit,” Bahá’u’lláh affirms, and its impact depends on purity of heart and
intention. The revealed Word is not merely signification but ontological actualization: it calls
realities into being. Divine Names are not contingent labels; they are metaphysical forces with
creative efficacy.
In this contrast, the Bahá’í perspective reframes the question: genealogy may show the
degradation of meanings over time, but Revelation inaugurates a new linguistic beginning. While


Nietzsche teaches us to deconstruct the origin, Bahá’u’lláh offers a restored Origin—a renewal
of language that purifies the “choice Wine” and liberates the Word from its historical
entanglements. In this light, one may still trace etymologies and remain cautious of inherited
categories, yet without surrendering to relativism. For although all human interpretation is
situated and partial, divine Revelation is the irruption of a language not of this world, though
spoken through it. The challenge is not to escape history, but to recognize when the Word breaks
history open and reconfigures it from within.
If Nietzsche’s genealogical method seeks to unearth the contingent power formations hidden
beneath seemingly eternal truths, then Foucault’s archaeological and genealogical projects
deepen this suspicion by demonstrating how discursive formations—institutionalized regimes of
knowledge and authority—constitute what can be said, known, and interpreted at any given
historical moment. In this light, authority over interpretation is not a neutral transmission of
meaning but a historically and theologically constituted function. The act of interpretation
becomes itself a political act: an intervention into the space where power and meaning meet.
From this perspective, the Bahá’í Faith’s structure of interpretive authority may be seen not as a
diffuse field of interpretation open to democratic negotiation, but rather as an explicitly bounded
transmission of ta’wīl—authorized, infallible exposition—restricted to a divinely designated
lineage. In the genealogy of the Bahá’í Dispensation, authority over meaning has not simply
emerged through historical convention or institutional power, but is asserted to descend directly
from the ontological Will of Revelation. As Bahá’u’lláh declares in the Kitáb-i-Aqdas:
"When the ocean of My presence hath ebbed and the Book of My Revelation is ended, turn your
faces toward Him Whom God hath purposed, Who hath branched from this Ancient Root."
(Kitáb-i-Aqdas, par. 121)
This passage—reaffirmed in Kitáb-i-‘Ahd, the Book of the Covenant—makes the line of
succession clear: interpretation is not to be diffused across the community, but concentrated in
the being of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, "He Whom God hath purposed," whose ontological function is to
explicate the Word with divine authority. This authority is not merely institutional but is
expressed as metaphysical: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is not just a chosen successor but a being ontologically
branched from the Primal Revelation.


The same principle continues in the Will and Testament of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá:
"After the disappearance of this wronged one, it is incumbent upon... all... to turn unto the
Branch from the two Lote-Trees... Shoghi Effendi... He is the Expounder of the verses of God."
(Will and Testament of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá)
Here, Shoghi Effendi is named not only the Guardian of the Cause but explicitly “the Expounder
of the verses of God.” Interpretation, in this schema, is not a historical evolution of hermeneutic
engagement but a continuation of divine infallibility under human stewardship. This breaks with
both Nietzsche’s and Foucault’s views of interpretive authority as emergent, contingent, and
power-laden: in the Bahá’í view, interpretive authority is given, not constructed—a delegation of
divine omniscience to human agency through Revelation.
And yet, we arrive at a critical genealogical rupture: after Shoghi Effendi, the line of Guardians
ends—no further appointed Guardian exists. The interpretive authority is no longer embodied in
a living person but is transmitted through a textual corpus. The writings of Bahá’u’lláh, ‘Abdu’l-
Bahá, and Shoghi Effendi form a sealed canon. The interpretive function—if it remains—must
now be negotiated in the absence of an infallible interpreter.
Here, Nietzsche and Foucault re-emerge: what happens when authority dissolves into text? The
interpretive vacuum opens a field of contestation. Even when the canon is complete, its meanings
are not. Every engagement with the text is already situated—historically, linguistically,
ideologically. And if, as Foucault argues, knowledge is constructed through historically
contingent rules of formation, then every act of understanding now must be situated within
discursive limitations—no longer under a single Sovereign Interpreter, but within the diverse
community of readers. The Bahá’í paradigm finds itself faced with the paradox of authoritative
Revelation and interpretive multiplicity.
One cannot ignore the Derridean problem: does the withdrawal of the Author open the infinite
play of signification? Can the meanings of Bahá’í texts—however divinely revealed—be frozen
in time when interpretation is inevitable? To read is already to interpret. Every act of
understanding is marked by différance. As Nietzsche would say, “there are no facts, only
interpretations”—but here, in the Bahá’í system, there were facts: the interpretations of the


Guardian, the voice of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, the Speech of the Manifestation. What now remains are
traces.
Indeed, even these authoritative interpretations are themselves texts, subject to temporality,
language, and understanding. Every new generation must engage them anew, not merely
preserve them. This invites a shift: from authority as vertical power to understanding as
horizontal dialogue. And here, perhaps, the Bahá’í community may lean toward a Gadamerian
horizon—toward dialogue between readers, between text and community, between past and
present.
But such dialogue requires more than pluralism—it requires fidelity. A fidelity not only to the
textual signifiers, but to the ontological referents they signify: the Manifestation, the Covenant,
the divine order. This is not relativism, but hermeneutic accountability. The Bahá’í writings do
not sanction esoteric readings that distort the “outward sense” (ẓāhir), nor private gnosis that
would displace the authority of the Manifestation. As Bahá’u’lláh warns, those who “claim an
inner meaning” contrary to the apparent Word “have been and will be hypocrites and liars.”
Nevertheless, the act of understanding cannot be silenced. The dialectic of speech and meaning
continues. Even if interpretation is not publicly authorized, it is existentially unavoidable. And
thus, in the absence of the Guardian, the Bahá’í community must live in what we might call a
post-hermeneutic vigilance: not engaging in formal ta’wīl, but seeking understanding in a spirit
of humility, coherence, and reverence.
5.2. Dialogue, Revelation, and the Possibility of Understanding
The absence of an interpretive authority after Shoghi Effendi does not merely represent an
institutional discontinuity; it poses a deeper epistemological and hermeneutic crisis for the Bahá'í
community. If, as Derrida insists, all meaning is deferred (différance), and if, as Gadamer argues,
understanding is always historically situated and prejudiced (Vorurteil), how can the Bahá'í
community continue to understand and act upon its sacred texts in the absence of a divinely
authorized explainer? Does interpretation collapse into relativism, or is there a sacred structure
that persists beyond the institutional voice of authority?


To approach this question, one must first revisit Gadamer's notion of the "fusion of horizons"
(Horizontverschmelzung), in which the horizon of the interpreter and the horizon of the text must
enter into dialogue. In Gadamer's view, tradition is not a burden to be overcome but a medium
through which understanding takes place. The text speaks, not because it possesses an immutable
meaning, but because the interpreter brings their own historically shaped understanding into a
dynamic encounter with it. This does not mean that interpretation is arbitrary. Rather, the
interpreter is called to listen, to allow the text to question them, to be transformed in the
dialogue.
Gadamer's hermeneutics thus affirms the dignity of the reader while preserving the authority of
the text. In this light, the Bahá'í paradigm may be seen not as a collapse of meaning after the
Guardian, but as a shift: from authoritative explication to dialogical responsibility. The Bahá'ís
are now called to engage the sacred Writings, and their authorized interpretations, through the
"consultative" process that governs the functioning of the Universal House of Justice and the
community at large. Understanding, therefore, becomes a communal act of reading and response.
Derrida's contribution to this discussion is more radical. In deconstruction, there is no
transcendental signified; meaning is always already postponed, caught in the play of signs. But
Derrida also insists that this infinite deferral does not lead to nihilism. Rather, it grounds an
ethics of responsibility: the reader must respond to the text without ever mastering it. There is no
final interpretation, only the trace of meanings, the excess that escapes systematization. Applied
to Bahá'í hermeneutics, this implies that while the Guardian provided an authoritative
interpretive frame, the discontinuity of that authority does not nullify interpretation. Instead, it
calls forth an interpretive humility—a willingness to read without claiming mastery.
From this perspective, the Bahá'í model after Shoghi Effendi may be seen as structurally open to
dialogical and differential understanding. There is no individual interpreter, but a textual
constellation that includes the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh, the interpretive voice of 'Abdu'l-Bahá and
the Guardian, and the consultative authority of the Universal House of Justice. Interpretation thus
becomes a layered activity: textual fidelity is upheld by anchoring oneself in the explicit
statements of the authoritative figures, while the ongoing application of principles is conducted
through collective consultation.


But this collective consultation does not resolve the ontological instability of meaning; it merely
governs its expression. Therefore, Bahá'í hermeneutics must confront a paradox: the Writings
claim clarity and sufficiency, yet understanding them continues to be an act of interpretation
conditioned by history, culture, language, and intention. The claim that "the seal of choice wine
has been broken" suggests an eschatological unveiling—a moment where interpretation is no
longer hidden but clear. Yet even the wine, once poured, must be tasted, and every tongue will
taste differently.
In this sense, Bahá'í hermeneutics cannot escape the hermeneutic circle. It must acknowledge
that the clarity of the Writings does not eliminate the contingency of the reader. But it proposes
that this contingency be met not by solitary judgment, but by the covenantal structure of
consultation, deference to authoritative texts, and a moral commitment to unity.
This tension mirrors Gadamer’s insight that understanding is not method but encounter. To read
Bah’í texts is not to decode a manual; it is to enter a sacred conversation. Derrida would call this
a responsibility to the Other—to the trace of the divine that speaks through language but is never
fully captured by it.
Thus, the crisis of interpretation is not a crisis of relativism, but of ethical maturity. In the
absence of a living interpreter, the Bahá'í community must become interpreters: not in the
authoritative sense, but as co-respondents to the divine Word. The death of the interpreter may
then be, paradoxically, the birth of dialogical responsibility. As the Guardian once wrote,
philosophy need not begin and end in words. Nor should hermeneutics. It must end in
transformation.
5.3. Covenant, Complexity, and the Ethos of Unified Interpretation
The challenge of interpretation within the Bahá'í Faith, particularly in the post-Guardianship era,
brings into view the dialectical relationship between unity and complexity. The Bahá'í Covenant,
unlike creedal systems that rely on theological assent to fixed dogma, is rooted in the principle of
organic continuity and evolving understanding. It does not dissolve the need for interpretation;
rather, it demands that interpretation be conducted in the spirit of covenantal fidelity—not to any
one personal authority after the Guardian, but to the collective corpus of authoritative texts and


the institutions that guard their integrity. This covenantal hermeneutics resists the twin dangers
of dogmatism and relativism.
The principle of interpretation in the Bahá'í context thus centers not merely on textual exegesis
(tafsīr) but on a covenantal ethos of integrative coherence. Any act of understanding must strive
to do justice to the whole of Revelation, not to a curated fragment chosen to justify a
preconceived position. In this respect, Bahá'í hermeneutics implicitly affirms a principle akin to
what Derrida called "justice as that which is undeconstructible": an orientation toward the totality
of the revealed Word, not as a closed totality, but as a demand of infinite responsibility.
To interpret a single verse about, for example, the role of women, the Universal House of Justice,
or the nature of the soul, is not to isolate that verse, but to draw into its horizon every other verse,
commentary, and authorized interpretation that touches on it. This task presumes a hermeneutics
of complexity: to avoid simplistic readings, to detect tensions and harmonies across time, and to
recognize the historical context in which utterances were made—their immediate audience,
exigency, and temporality. This does not relativize the truth of the Revelation, but rather guards
its universal claim by discerning which utterances were context-specific and which were meant
as perennial.
Here, the philosophical tension between historical criticism and textual fidelity becomes a central
concern. In contrast to a naive historicism that would reduce meaning entirely to context, the
Bahá'í approach affirms the possibility of timeless truth articulated through time-bound
expressions. The faithful interpreter must thus learn to distinguish the transient from the
essential, the time-bound from the eternal. This distinction cannot be made arbitrarily; it must be
grounded in the totality of the Writings and the guidance of the Covenant.
This approach aligns with the Gadamerian view of interpretation as a "fusion of horizons"—not
the subordination of one meaning to another, but the dialogical transformation of both interpreter
and interpreted. But unlike Gadamer, who sees the text as open to perpetual reinterpretation in
conversation with tradition, the Bahá'í model insists that the foundational Revelation of
Bahá'u'lláh represents the final and complete divine grammar for this dispensation. Thus,


interpretation must remain loyal to its telos: the full disclosure of the Manifestation's intention, as
unveiled across all authoritative texts.
The Bahá'í Writings themselves demand this multi-dimensional interpretive ethic. For example,
the Kitáb-i-Aqdas offers concise imperatives, but it is only through its intertextual web—the
Tablets of Bahá'u'lláh, the authoritative explanations of 'Abdu'l-Bahá, the interpretations of the
Guardian, and the elucidations of the Universal House of Justice—that a fuller understanding of
any one principle emerges. This cumulative structure forms a matrix of meaning, not a free-for-
all of interpretive creativity.
Thus, complexity in the Bahá'í paradigm is not chaos, but an ordered interrelation of meanings
grounded in Revelation. The interpreter must be faithful not only to the text, but to its
embeddedness in history, language, and the chain of authorized explanation. As Bahá'u'lláh
writes, "The essence of understanding is that one should not contradict the Text, nor advance a
meaning contrary to what hath been made manifest."
Such a hermeneutics demands both humility and total intellectual engagement. It guards against
selective quoting, against reducing Bahá'u'lláh’s Revelation to moral platitudes or personal
preferences. In accordance with ʿAbdu’l-Bahá’s explicit directive, “if two souls dispute and
contend over a divine question… both are in error” (Will and Testament 15). The wisdom of this
decree is that unity must never be compromised in the search for meaning. Dialogue in the
Bahá’í paradigm is not a contest of interpretations, but a sacred process of consultation animated
by reverence, love, and mutual silence when divergence arises. When no consensus is reached, it
is enjoined that one “should ask the Expounder for the truth of the situation,” thereby preserving
both the dignity of the Revelation and the harmony of the community. Interpretation, in this
light, is not the invention of new meaning, but the conscientious reception of insight through the
disciplined synthesis of the Sacred Writings under the shadow of unity. The Covenant, therefore,
is not merely institutional; it is an epistemological safeguard. It affirms that understanding must
proceed within the bounds of authorized guidance, and that all interpretation is an act of
fidelity—to the Word, to the community, and to the divine Will that transcends all individual
reasoning.


5.4 The Dialogical Nature of Understanding and Unity
The Bahá'í writings frame the act of understanding not as a solitary encounter with fixed
meanings, but as a deeply dialogical, consultative, and spiritual undertaking. At its heart, the
pursuit of interpretation is inseparable from the moral imperative of unity, both
epistemologically and socially. This perspective offers an alternative to hermeneutic paradigms
that emphasize fragmentation, suspicion, or infinite deferral. Instead, it places language,
meaning, and truth within the relational dynamics of divine purpose, human humility, and mutual
consultation.
Bahá'u'lláh writes, "Be united in counsel, be one in thought. Let each morn be better than its eve
and each morrow richer than its yesterday. Man’s merit lieth in service and virtue and not in the
pageantry of wealth and riches" (Tablets of Bahá'u'lláh 138). This imperative to unity is not
merely ethical but epistemic: the realization of truth is conditioned by the quality of interaction
among human minds, the consultation of diverse perspectives, and the purging of speech from
"idle fancies and worldly desires." As Bahá'u'lláh further states, "Take heed that your words be
purged from idle fancies and worldly desires and your deeds be cleansed from craftiness and
suspicion" (Tablets 138).
This dialogical imperative finds institutional expression in the concept of consultation
(mashvarat), which is not a method of voting or debate, but a sacred act that generates insight
through sincere participation. The Universal House of Justice underscores that consultation "is
the lamp of guidance which leadeth the way, and is the bestower of understanding"
(Consultation: A Compilation 6). Understanding, in this view, emerges not from individual
mastery of text, but from the collaborative effort to approach truth through humility, reverence,
and shared search.
Consultation functions as the epistemological foundation of peace itself. In the Most Holy Book
(Kitáb-i-Aqdas), Bahá'u'lláh commands the rulers of the world to gather and "take counsel
together" in order to lay the foundations of the world’s "Great Peace." He writes: "Should any
king take up arms against another, all should unitedly arise and prevent him. If this be done, the
nations of the world will no longer require any armaments" (Tablets 165). The imagery here is


not just political but philosophical: unity in action must be preceded by unity in counsel. Justice,
understanding, and enduring peace are generated through cooperative deliberation.
From a hermeneutic standpoint, this reveals a unique integration of epistemology, ethics, and
social order. Understanding is not isolated cognition but participatory transformation. One does
not merely interpret the text but is shaped by it, in community with others. The act of
interpretation thus becomes a vehicle for collective growth.
Bahá'u'lláh's own vision of human development points toward this ideal: "Every thing must
needs have an origin and every building a builder. Verily, the Word of God is the Cause which
hath preceded the contingent world... yet is being renewed and regenerated at all times" (Tablets
141). Revelation is not static. The text is always becoming, always being reinterpreted in new
contexts. But such re-interpretation must be faithful to the foundational purpose: "to promote the
unity of the human race, and to foster the spirit of love and fellowship amongst men" (Gleanings
215).
Unity in hermeneutics thus echoes unity in ontology. The same Word of God that orders the
cosmos calls humanity to order its understanding through dialogue. This does not mean erasing
differences or enforcing uniformity, but rather approaching interpretive diversity with the
consciousness that we are bound by a higher moral horizon. It means that every act of reading
must be tempered by the responsibility to seek justice, preserve unity, and "manifest My
wisdom... to banish ignorance from the earth" (Tablets 138).
Therefore, the Bahá'í paradigm of understanding is both eschatological and ethical. It is
eschatological because it views interpretive maturity as a sign of the "coming of age" of
humanity. Shoghi Effendi connects this to the emergence of a new world order, in which "the
unification of the whole of mankind" will stimulate "the intellectual, the moral and spiritual life
of the entire human race" (World Order of Bahá'u'lláh 163). And it is ethical because it requires
the virtues of humility, trust, sincerity, and consultation to make any knowledge possible.
In this sense, Bahá'í hermeneutics transcends the dichotomy between the solitary reader and the
authoritative interpreter. It replaces both with a model of dialogical unity—a covenantal
epistemology rooted in Revelation, animated by community, and sustained through consultation.


Here, understanding is not the private property of the scholar, nor the dictate of the ruler, but the
fruit of hearts turned in collective sincerity toward the Word and Will of God.
Philosophy, Interpretation, and the Limits of Reason in the Bahá'í Faith
The Bahá'í Faith articulates a nuanced position on philosophy and reason, affirming the value of
sound intellectual inquiry while establishing strict boundaries around metaphysical speculation
and interpretive authority. This position stems not from anti-intellectualism, but from a
theological epistemology grounded in divine Revelation as the ultimate arbiter of truth. Reason,
in this view, is a noble faculty, divinely bestowed and essential for human progress, but one that
must operate in harmony with Revelation, rather than in defiance or isolation from it.
A core theme in the Bahá'í writings is the distinction between philosophy that leads to truth and
mere intellectual exercise that leads nowhere. Bahá'u'lláh categorically rejects "academic
pursuits that begin and end in words alone," stating, "Such academic pursuits as begin and end in
words alone have never been and will never be of any worth. The majority of Persia's learned
doctors devote all their lives to the study of a philosophy the ultimate yield of which is nothing
but words" (Tablets of Bahá'u'lláh 169). This criticism is not a wholesale rejection of philosophy,
but a warning against metaphysical hairsplitting and barren dialectics that yield no actionable
insight or moral transformation. As Shoghi Effendi clarified in a letter written on his behalf,
"Philosophy, as you will study it and later teach it, is certainly not one of the sciences that begins
and ends in words. Fruitless excursions into metaphysical hair-splittings is meant, not a sound
branch of learning like philosophy" (Messages from the Universal House of Justice).
The proper aim of philosophy, according to Bahá'í thought, is aligned with the pursuit of truth,
justice, and moral refinement. Bahá'u'lláh emphasizes that "the purpose of knowledge is the
recognition of the Truth. Whoso is veiled from this by even the subtlest of veils is among the
dead" (Epistle to the Son of the Wolf 23). Knowledge divorced from spiritual recognition
becomes an illusion of understanding. Thus, one who "encompassed all the sciences of the earth
yet paused at the Word 'Yea'" would, in the sight of God, "be unworthy of mention and counted
among the most ignorant of people" (23).
This epistemological orientation supports the Bahá'í principle of the harmony of religion and
reason. As 'Abdu'l-Bahá explains, "Religion must conform to science and reason; otherwise, it is


superstition. God has created man in order that he may perceive the verity of existence and
endowed him with mind or reason to discover truth" (Promulgation of Universal Peace 63).
Reason, therefore, is essential and honored, but its scope is limited: it cannot, on its own,
penetrate the full reality of divine mysteries without the aid of Revelation. As 'Abdu'l-Bahá
continues, "The greatest philosophers without this Spirit are powerless, their souls lifeless, their
hearts dead! Unless the Holy Spirit breathes into their souls, they can do no good work" (Some
Answered Questions 226).
In this light, the Bahá'í Faith offers a redefinition of what constitutes a true philosopher or wise
person (ḥakīm). A ḥakīm is not merely one who reasons well or is versed in dialectics but one
who marries insight with action, reason with submission, and speech with transformative power.
"A true philosopher would never deny God nor His evidences, rather would he acknowledge His
glory and overpowering majesty which overshadow all created things" (Tablets of Bahá'u'lláh
169). Furthermore, "The beginning of Wisdom and the origin thereof is to acknowledge
whatsoever God hath clearly set forth, for through its potency the foundation of statesmanship...
hath been firmly established" (169).
Interpretation (ta’wīl), when divorced from the apparent text and undertaken by unauthorized
individuals, is explicitly prohibited in Bahá'í teachings. Bahá'u'lláh writes, "Whoso interpreteth
what hath been sent down from the heaven of Revelation, and altereth its evident meaning, verily
he is of them that have perverted the Most Exalted Word of God" (Kitáb-i-Aqdas verse 105).
Interpretation, if it alters the evident sense or imposes a hidden meaning that contradicts the
outward word, is viewed as both heretical and destructive. As 'Abdu'l-Bahá warns, "Bahá'ís
neither consider themselves among those firmly grounded in knowledge who can engage in
interpretation (ta'wīl), nor do they believe that anyone other than God has the right to interpret
(ta'wīl)" (Makátīb-i-'Abdu'l-Bahá, vol. 1, 317).
In contrast, explanation (tafsīr) is permitted when it remains in accord with the manifest text and
does not claim access to an esoteric layer that supersedes the literal command. Bahá'u'lláh
asserts, "The people of Bahá are souls who consider anything contrary to the apparent command
of God to be false. The inner and the inner of the inner revolve around this outward" (Lawḥ-i-
Burhān).


This disciplined hermeneutics mirrors the Faith's broader commitment to spiritual clarity and
ethical transformation. "The head of wisdom is the fear of God," Bahá'u'lláh proclaims, affirming
that reverence for divine law is the foundation of true understanding. This fear "prevents
humanity from that which causes humiliation and degradation... and assists him in that which
causes elevation and sublimity" (Tablets of Bahá'u'lláh 169). Thus, philosophy in the Bahá'í
sense is inseparable from piety, and wisdom cannot be abstracted from justice, consultation, and
compassion—the "two luminaries" that illumine its heaven (169).
Ultimately, the Bahá'í model of reason and interpretation affirms that philosophy, when guided
by Revelation and animated by virtue, becomes a creative force for civilization-building.
Detached from divine purpose, it devolves into the "chilling of spirits" and the "idle imaginings"
of a speech without fruit. The Bahá'í philosopher is thus a new figure—a lover of wisdom who
recognizes its Source, a practitioner of truth who honors its Form, and an interpreter who speaks
only when illuminated by the light of the Manifest Word.
Conclusion
This article has sought to answer a deceptively simple question: is there such a thing as a Bahá’í
philosophy? Not in the sense of a system imposed from outside, but as a mode of thought native
to the Revelation itself—one in which reason, wisdom, and spiritual insight coalesce. We began
by showing that philosophy and wisdom (ḥikmat) are not marginal to the Bahá’í Faith, but
central to its structure, purpose, and metaphysical vision. Drawing on a wide range of thinkers—
Muslim, Christian, and Bahá’í—we explored how philosophical inquiry can emerge within
Revelation without reducing itself to theology or losing its reflective autonomy.
Section 2 affirmed that Bahá’í thought has inspired and attracted philosophers, scholars, and
scientists from both East and West. The lives of intellectual believers—from Mírzá Abu’l-Faḍl to
Auguste Forel, from Nabil-i-Akbar to Ali-Murad Davudi—demonstrate that Bahá’í philosophy is
not an abstract theory but a lived intellectual and spiritual horizon. Section 3 then traced the deep
philosophical content within the writings of Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, showing how themes
such as ontology, epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics are radically reconfigured within a
prophetic metaphysics grounded in ẓuhūr (manifestation), the unknowability of the Divine


Essence (dhāt), and the centrality of the Word (kalimah) as both ontological bridge and
hermeneutical key.
In Section 4, we explored the relationship between philosophy and theology, situating Bahá’í
metaphysics in continuity and contrast with figures such as Aquinas, Augustine, and Avicenna.
We argued that Bahá’u’lláh does not offer a theology of esse (pure being), but a metaphysics of
ẓuhūr—a dynamic, non-totalizing model that affirms hierarchy, causality, and cyclical history
without collapsing into either classical ontology or fideistic submission. Philosophy is not
subordinated to dogma, nor does it function in abstraction; rather, it is reborn in the act of
Revelation, becoming a mode of world-building guided by ethical transformation.
Section 5, finally, addressed the interpretive foundations of Bahá’í thought. Here we saw that
hermeneutics—understood as the search for meaning through Revelation—is central to Bahá’í
philosophy. Unlike theological traditions that privilege either rigid exegesis (tafsīr) or esoteric
symbolism (taʾwīl), the Bahá’í Writings affirm a mode of interpretation that is both disciplined
and open, rooted in the coherence of the Revelation as a whole and guided by authorized
interpreters: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and the Guardian. Drawing from both Western hermeneutics
(Gadamer, Ricoeur) and Islamic traditions of meaning, Bahá’í hermeneutics insists on three
principles: the centrality of the Manifestation, the unity of meaning and practice, and the
humility of the interpreter. Interpretation, in this model, is not the assertion of personal authority,
but a covenantal responsibility to understand truth within the bounds of revealed guidance.
Together, these five sections articulate the lineaments of a Bahá’í philosophy: not a school, but a
paradigm; not a synthesis of the past, but the emergence of a new structure of thought. It is a
philosophy in which metaphysics is inseparable from ethics, where knowledge is a function of
purity, and where interpretation is never detached from action. In contrast to postmodern
skepticism or religious literalism, Bahá’í thought offers a vision of philosophy as both
intellectually rigorous and spiritually anchored—a vision grounded in the Manifestation of God,
animated by the love of wisdom, and committed to the transformation of self and society.

The Unity-Function: Translating Qāʿidat al-Wāḥid into Phenomenology and Deconstruction
Abstract
This article proposes a translational re-reading of qāʿidat al-wāḥid—“al-wāḥidu lā yaṣduru
minhu illā al-wāḥid” (“from the One only one proceeds”)—as a transcendental unity-function
rather than an ontic embargo on plurality. Moving the maxim from efficient causation to
conditions of constitution, it argues that any genesis of sense, object, or world presupposes a
minimal, non-hypostatized operation that gathers a manifold “as one.”1 Read through Husserl
(constitutive synthesis and horizonal identity), Heidegger (Grund as gathering under Ab-grund),
and Derrida (iterability, trace, an-archic beginning), the classical same-respect clause is
reformulated with precision: one undivided horizon cannot, as such and at once, ground
heterogeneous effects; plurality appears lawfully where respects or horizons multiply, or across
succession.2 Reassessing kalām critiques (omnipotence, scriptural immediacy) and internal
tensions (attribute plurality, sequence objection), the paper shows that the principle constrains
form, not outcomes, thereby preserving both freedom and transcendence while dispensing with
obsolete cosmography and henological reification. Stress-tests across mathematics (rule-
iteration), language (performatives and citational force), and agency (intention–deed articulation)
exhibit cross-disciplinary fecundity. An epilogue situates the result within Bahá’í doctrinal
architecture—emanation without identification (Primal Will/First Word), unity-in-diversity
governed by capacity—indicating resonances and limits. The upshot is a principle of unity-of-
genesis: no intelligible beginning without a minimal iterable one; no plurality “as such and at
once” from one undivided respect; no relapse into onto-theology, since “ground” here names a
mode of gathering rather than a highest entity.
Keywords
qāʿidat al-wāḥid; unity-function; phenomenology; deconstruction; constitutive synthesis; same-
respect clause (ḥaythiyya); Grund / Ab-grund; iterability and trace; Avicenna; Mullā Ṣadrā;
Bahá’í theology (Primal Will/First Word); unity-in-diversity.

1 On the formal role of “gathering-as-one” see App. X: T1 (Functional Uniqueness) grounded in U1 (Determinacy)
and AP1 (Identity/Leibniz); cf. App. Y (Uniq, Immed).
2 Formalized by U1–U3 (Determinacy; Same-respect coherence; Temporal succession) and proven in App. X: T2–
T4 (no simultaneous heterogeneity; non-branching; lawful plurality by succession); cf. App. Y (Same, X/Next).


Introduction: Aim and Thesis
This article argues that qāʿidat al-wāḥid—the classical maxim “al-wāḥidu lā yaṣduru minhu illā
al-wāḥid” (“from the One only one proceeds”)—can and should be reformulated as a
transcendental unity-function: a minimal, non-hypostatized condition without which no
genesis—of meaning, objectivity, discourse, or world—can so much as begin. In this register,
“the One” does not name a supreme being or highest cause, but an operative form of gathering
that lets a manifold appear as one under a determinate horizon. The move is deliberately anti-
henological: it relocates the principle from ontic efficient causation to conditions of
constitution, preserving what the rule insightfully grasped (the indispensability of unity for
issuance) while releasing it from commitments that provoked perennial objections in kalām,
falsafa, and ʿirfān.3
Three modern interlocutors discipline and specify this translation. Husserl clarifies the operative
core as unifying synthesis—from the “collective combination” that makes a many as one to the
horizonal identifications and passive–active syntheses presupposed by any appearance.
Heidegger retrieves ground beyond onto-theology: ground as gathering (legein) that discloses,
and as Ab-grund (withholding) that prevents reification—thus modeling a unity that enables
without becoming a thing. Derrida secures the result against nostalgia for pure origins by
insisting on iterability and the an-archic contamination of every beginning: there is no
immaculate first, yet genesis still requires a repeatable unit of form. Read together, these
