perspectives convert “only one from the One” into a precise constraint on heterogeneity under
the same respect/horizon of constitution: one and the same undivided horizon cannot, as such
and at once, ground incompatible effects without incoherence.
Finally, an epilogue situates this reformulated principle in relation to Bahá’í theology. Without
collapsing theology into phenomenology, it sketches resonances and limits between the unity-
function and Bahá’í teachings on the unknowable Essence, the mediating office of the
Manifestation of God, and unity-in-diversity as a civilizational norm—clarifying how a non-

3 Conservativity and non-hypostatization: App. X: T5 (Conservativity of Aḥad); U5 (transcendence—no
object-constant for Aḥad); cf. App. Y (Aḥad vs. Mashiyyat).


henological account of unity can illuminate (and be disciplined by) Bahá’í conceptions of
oneness, revelation, and institutional form.
Classical Dossier: Text and Scope of qāʿidat al-wāḥid
Definition. The rule states: al-wāḥidu lā yaṣduru minhu illā al-wāḥid—“from the One only
one proceeds.” On the philosophical reading, ṣudūr (“issuance”) means efficient causation:
from a single (simple) cause only a single effect comes to be. On a mystical reading—where
efficient causation is not fundamental and ẓuhūr/tajallī (“manifestation/epiphany”) takes its
place—the content becomes unity at the level of manifestation.
What is “the One” (al-wāḥid)? In the rule, wāḥid denotes that which lacks any internal part
or composition, a being “simple from every aspect” (basīṭ min jamīʿ al-wujūh). Mullā Ṣadrā
explicitly restricts the principle to a simple agent that is free of conditions, relations, and
instruments. Because philosophers aim to account for the existence of multiplicity without
compromising this simplicity, they add the unity of the respect/aspect of issuance: so long as
the respect (jiha/ḥaythiyya) of issuance is one, no more than one effect will be produced by the
one cause; if multiple respects are considered, a plurality of effects from the same cause becomes
possible.4
Clarifying example (of wāḥid): Think of an absolutely simple source as a single, undivided
breath. So long as the same breath in the same articulation is at issue, it cannot be two
heterogeneous utterances at once. If distinct articulations (distinct ḥaythiyyāt) are introduced, a
sequence of different words is possible—without denying that each word issues from one breath
under a different respect.
What is ṣudūr? Where does the rule apply? Among the Peripatetics, ṣudūr is the term used for
issuance as efficient causation—the giving of existence by an efficient cause—and the rule is
discussed under the efficient cause, not under final or material causality. Hence, at least for Ibn
Sīnā and on the basis of his arguments, the rule properly governs efficient causation (the giver
of existence) and does not extend to the other causal types. (Some later passages hint at
analogues for other causes, but the core scope is efficient causality.)

4 Same-respect restriction and plurality: U1–U3 with App. X: T2 (no simultaneous heterogeneity) and T7
(sequence/respect differentiation).


Clarifying example (of ṣudūr): Issuance is like the relation of a word to a speaker—the word
exists from the speaker’s act of voicing. A single, undivided act of voicing (one respect) cannot
be simultaneously two incompatible words.
How does ẓuhūr differ from ṣudūr? In ʿirfān, efficient causation is displaced by
manifestation/epiphany (ẓuhūr/tajallī). The principle is then read as unity at the level of
manifestation: the Divine Essence (named as sheer hiddenness, ghayb maḥḍ) is beyond all
conceptual determinations (iʿtibārāt), and the first manifestation is identified with the Breath of
the All-Merciful (al-nafas al-raḥmānī) or diffused/unfolded existence (al-wujūd al-munbasit),
which possesses a pervasive (siryānī) unity—what the ʿurafā call the unity of multiplicity
(aḥadiyyat al-kathra) as distinct from the Aḥadiyya (absolute oneness) of the Essence.
Clarifying example (of ẓuhūr): Manifestation is like the relation of a seed to a tree—the tree is
a developmental disclosure of what the seed contains. Here the emphasis is on
appearing/unfolding rather than on an act of efficient production.
Philosophers typically take the “one” on the side of the cause to be the Necessary Existent
(God) and the second “one” on the side of what proceeds to be the First Intellect. I propose that,
to avoid conflating the first wāḥid with the second, we should formulate the rule as: From al-
Aḥad nothing issues except al-wāḥid. God directly brings into being a single creature; because
of the multiple respects within the First Intellect, several beings then proceed (e.g., the
Second Intellect, the soul of the first heaven, and its body), and so on. By contrast, ʿirfān links
the Divine Essence and the Breath of the All-Merciful/unfolded existence, which contains
multiplicity compatibly with unity (pervasive unity), thereby avoiding a worry raised against the
philosophical version: while the philosophical Necessary Existent is said to admit conceptual
multiplicity of attributes (though identical with the Essence in reality), the mystical Divine
Essence is without determination and thus supplies a true instance of absolute simplicity at the
level of sheer hiddenness.
Clarifying example (two registers).
– Philosophical: from a single voicing (one respect) there is one word; later plurality comes
when the respects multiply (different articulations).
– Mystical: the seed manifests the tree without the seed’s essence becoming composite;
multiplicity is contained within the mode of manifestation.


A classical difficulty, sharpened—and resolved
A familiar/similarity objection presses the sequence implicit in the rule: If from the One only one
proceeds, why does this prohibition on plurality not propagate down the line?5 If the First Cause
is basīṭ min jamīʿ al-wujūh (absolutely simple), then—so the objection runs—its first issuance
must itself be basīṭ; and if the first issued is basīṭ, it too should issue only one, and so on without
end. Since the Avicennian presentation correlates these issuances with Ptolemaic heavens, what
remains of the account once that cosmography is set aside?
Two distinctions, consistently observed in the tradition, defuse the worry.
(1) Absolute simplicity vs. qualified simplicity.
Only the Necessary Existent is basīṭ min jamīʿ al-wujūh: free of composition, relation, and
instrument, and therefore the sole strict instance of the “One” to which the rule applies as cause.
The First Intellect, though immaterial and “simple” in lacking material composition, is not
simple “from every aspect.” It is necessary through another (not necessary in itself) and bears
conceptual and relational respects—its consideration of the First, its consideration of itself, and
its relation to possibles that proceed through it. Thus the First Intellect is one (numerically, and
simple in certain respects) but not the wāḥid of the rule. Accordingly, the ‘one’ (al-wāḥid) that
is other than al-Aḥad differs in several technical respects that register its inferiority relative
to al-Aḥad: al-Aḥad is wājib bi-dhātihi and qadīm dhātan; the first ‘one’ after it is wājib bi-
ghayrihi and ḥādith bi-dhātihi (while, on the Peripatetic account, its procession is without
temporal beginning, i.e., qadīm zamānan). For al-Aḥad, any plurality in issuance would
count as a defect; hence there is only one immediate issuance. For the derivative ‘one,’ by
contrast, plurality of issuances is not a flaw but precisely its function, arising from its
plurality of respects.
(2) The same-respect clause vs. plurality by distinct respects.
The rule bars two heterogeneous effects from one and the same ḥaythiyya (undivided respect) of
a simple cause. But if a cause bears multiple, formally distinct ḥaythiyyāt, each respect can

5 Resolved via App. X: T7 (sequence objection) and T8 (attribute plurality via distinct respects); later causes can
bear multiple ḥaythiyyāt.


ground its own effect without breach—plurality then tracks the plurality of respects. Example:
the First Intellect, qua related to the First, yields one effect; qua reflexively considering itself,
another; qua related to possibles, a third. What is excluded is one undivided respect issuing two
heterogeneous effects simultaneously; what is permitted is multiplicity distributed over distinct
respects.
With these in view, the sequence objection loses its force:
•
First step (the One). From the absolutely simple Necessary Existent, one immediate
effect issues—the First Intellect.6 This satisfies the rule: one effect from the One, under
one respect.
•
Second step (the first issued). The First Intellect is not “simple from every aspect.”
Precisely because it harbors multiple ḥaythiyyāt, plurality may proceed from it—never
from one undivided respect, but by distinct respects. Hence there is no violation: the
rule restrains a simple agent “under the same respect,” not an agent already articulated by
a plurality of aspects.
•
Cosmographic clothing. Correlating these respects with Ptolemaic spheres is a
historical application that can be abandoned without touching the doctrine’s form: (i) an
absolutely one cause has one immediate issuance; (ii) later plurality is intelligible
because later causes are not absolutely simple but carry multiple ḥaythiyyāt.
Two compact models make the logic vivid:
•
Issuance (ṣudūr): word–speaker. A single, undivided articulation (one respect) cannot
be two incompatible words at once. Yet the same speaker, since speech admits
different articulations (distinct respects), can utter many words. The rule constrains the
one articulation; it does not forbid plurality where articulations (respects) multiply.
•
Manifestation (ẓuhūr/tajallī): seed–tree. The seed is not composite as the tree is, yet it
contains multiplicity in the mode of manifestation—the ʿirfānī waḥda siryānīyya

6 App. X: T1 (Functional Uniqueness) under U1 (Determinacy).


(pervasive unity). Here plurality does not contradict unity; it is the manner of appearing
proper to what is no longer basīṭ min jamīʿ al-wujūh.
Result. “From the One only one proceeds” binds uniquely the Necessary Existent. The first
issuance need only be one as an effect; it need not be absolutely simple—and on the
philosophical analysis it cannot be, since it is necessary through another and bears distinct
respects. Plurality downstream is therefore not a breach but the very mechanism by which the
rule preserves intelligibility: one from the absolutely One; many from what is no longer one in
every respect—always under the governance of the same-respect clause. Discarding the
Ptolemaic scaffold changes the scenery, not the logic.
Demonstrations and Their Logic
At the heart of the rule lies a single constraint: simplicity forbids concurrent heterogeneous
effects under one and the same respect.7 Let a simple cause (ʿilla basīṭa) be one that is basīṭ
min jamīʿ al-wujūh—without parts, conditions, instruments, or internal respects—and let a
respect/aspect (ḥaythiyya/jiha) be any formally distinct ground from which an effect proceeds.
Then the same-respect restriction states: if a cause is one and the respect of issuance is one, it
cannot, as such and at once, issue two heterogeneous effects (i.e., effects different in formal
content or order). This already leaves room for plurality by distinct respects and for plurality by
succession (when the operative respect varies); neither violates the rule.
Ibn Sīnā’s classic argument makes the point with maximal economy. Suppose a single, simple
cause were to produce both a and b. Then the true predications “being-cause-of-a” and “being-
cause-of-b” would be non-synonymous; but true, non-synonymous causal predicates track
distinct grounds. Distinct grounds, whether construed as constituents or accidents, entail
composition; hence the cause would not be simple—contradiction. Therefore, from the one
(under one respect) only one proceeds. A compact formalization sometimes used is: (1)
“cause-of-a” ≠ “cause-of-b”; (2) if two non-synonymous causal predicates are truly said of one
thing as such, they correspond to distinct grounds in that thing; (3) distinct grounds entail
composition; therefore a simple cause cannot as such and at once be cause of both a and b. Two

7 App. X: T2 (No simultaneous heterogeneity) using AP2 (reflexivity of equality) + U1; cf. App. Y (Uniq, Immed).


clarifications are standard. First, the clause “as such and at once” blocks trivial counter-examples
(e.g., reproducing the same effect many times, or producing at different times). Second, the
argument does not deny that one cause may relate to many effects per accidens (by extrinsic
conditions) or by distinct ḥaythiyyāt; it denies only the co-issuance of heterogeneous effects from
one undivided respect.
Later demonstrations—mereological, modal, epistemic—proliferate in the literature, yet they
largely collapse into cause–effect commensurability (sunkhiyya/munāsaba): a cause can give
only what is formally in measure with it. A simple cause has one formal measure. To posit two
heterogeneous effects together from that one measure is simply to smuggle in more than one
measure, i.e., internal plurality. Read this way, the same-respect restriction is the logical face of
sunkhiyya: one measure → one effect; plurality requires plural respects.
Further clarifications.
(i) Two “identical” outputs. If a=ba=ba=b strictly, there are not two effects; numerical
multiplicity collapses and the case is trivial. If, instead, there are two numerically distinct yet
qualitatively indiscernible effects, their distinctness must be grounded by individuating
conditions (thisnesses)—place, time, recipient, or some relation. Either those individuations are
in the cause (multiplying ḥaythiyyāt and violating simplicity) or outside the cause (in
media/recipients), in which case the plurality is not immediate as such and at once from one
respect but arises per accidens through distinct conditions. In both readings, the same-respect
restriction stands.
(ii) An “incomplete” immediate effect. By sunkhiyya/munāsaba, the immediate effect of a pure
respect must be the maximally proportionate (the most perfect compossible) effect of that
respect. To posit a first outcome that is defective or lesser introduces a limiter. If the limiter is
intrinsic, simplicity is broken (a further delimiting respect has been smuggled into the cause). If
the limiter is extrinsic, immediacy is lost (the result depends on conditions outside the cause). A
third option—tarjīḥ bilā murajjiḥ (preference without a preferer)—is excluded by the very logic
of causation in this tradition. Hence the first immediate proceeds as the noblest possible
(Avicenna: the First Intellect), while lesser or “incomplete” outcomes arise only downstream,
where delimitation and receptivity already diversify respects. Thus the “incompleteness” option


either inserts an intrinsic delimiter (pluralizing respects) or makes the outcome depend on
extrinsic conditions (removing immediacy); neither describes the first issuance.
(iii) The sun’s many effects (light, heat, burning). The sun is not basīṭ min jamīʿ al-wujūh. It
acts through multiple respects and instruments/relations: diverse emission spectra, distances,
media, thresholds in recipients. “Light,” “heat,” and “burning” are different effects because
distinct ḥaythiyyāt and conditions are operative—e.g., burning requires fuel, oxygen, and
reaching an ignition temperature; heating varies with absorption coefficients; illumination
depends on line-of-sight and reflectance. Hence the sun’s plurality is by multiplied respects and
recipient conditions, not from one undivided respect; the rule targets only the latter. By
contrast, the Necessary Existent acts without instrument or relation; under one undivided
respect it bestows one immediate effect. Plurality appears at subsequent tiers precisely when
respects have multiplied (in intermediaries) or conditions vary on the side of recipients—just as
the sun’s one radiance ramifies into unlike outcomes only once media and recipients are
introduced.
Two corollaries are commonly drawn. First, the rule’s primary scope is efficient causation,
since ṣudūr is treated by the Peripatetics as the giving of existence; their simultaneous
acceptance of one final cause for many effects coheres with this delimitation. Second, the
paradigm case follows immediately: only the Necessary Existent is basīṭ min jamīʿ al-wujūh;
hence one immediate effect (the First Intellect) proceeds, and plurality then arises from the
multiple ḥaythiyyāt of what is no longer absolutely simple.
Mullā Ṣadrā preserves this Avicennian core while recasting its ontology through the primacy of
existence (aṣālat al-wujūd) and the gradation/modulation of being (tashkīk al-wujūd). Here,
“simplicity” names non-delimited being and “composition” names ontic delimitation. From
Pure Simple Being—without internal delimitations—only one can proceed immediately;
allowing two heterogeneous immediacies would inscribe distinct delimitations into what was
posited as non-delimited. Plurality is therefore placed downstream, in determinate modes of
being that already bear distinct ḥaythiyyāt and can ground multiple effects by those respects. The
logical kernel is unchanged: no two heterogeneous determinations issue from one
undelimited respect.


For later use, the section’s content can be summarized schematically: Premise (simplicity): the
cause is one and simple (no plurality of ḥaythiyyāt). Premise (commensurability): effect-forms
must be in measure with the cause’s respect. Conclusion: at most one heterogeneous effect can
issue as such and at once. License for plurality: once respects multiply (or delimitation
intervenes, as in graded being), plurality is intelligible—not from one respect, but by distinct
respects.8 This positive logic sets the stage for the next section on objections and internal
tensions, where these same constraints will answer logical and theological challenges without
reliance on obsolete cosmography.
Opposition and Internal Tensions
The maxim al-wāḥidu lā yaṣduru minhu illā al-wāḥid (“from the One, only one proceeds”)
safeguards the absolute unity and simplicity of the First Principle. Kalām theologians—pre-
eminently al-Ghazālī and Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī—contest it on theological and logical grounds.
The theological charge is twofold. First, the rule is said to compromise divine omnipotence and
to contradict scriptural immediacy: the Qurʾānic “Be! (kun)” presents creatorship as direct and
unmediated, whereas the emanationist picture interposes a cascade of intermediaries. Second, the
rule seems ill-equipped to square divine simplicity with the conceptual plurality of attributes
(knowing, willing, powerful). In different strands of kalām, either attributes are reduced to the
essence to secure unity, or a plurality of real attributes is affirmed at the cost (philosophers
allege) of smuggling multiplicity into the divine. A further kalām contention is that once a thing
comes to be, its need for its cause ceases—a thesis Avicennans expressly reject in favor of
sustained ontological dependence.
Philosophers relocate the rule from a timeline to an order of dependence and intelligibility. The
procession schema marks what depends on what, not a schedule of fabrication. The First’s act is
atemporal; time accrues only where motion and matter do. Thus scriptural affirmations of
immediacy are read as teaching that all creatures depend directly on God as the ultimate giver of
existence—without denying mediate orders of intelligibility in virtue of which multiplicity
becomes thinkable. At the same time, the rule’s scope is precise: it binds only a simple agent
under one and the same respect. The contradiction does not lie in the bare pair “issuing a /

8 Plurality by respect differentiation: App. X: T8; coherence by U2.


issuing non-a”; it appears only when one undivided respect in a simple cause is made the
simultaneous ground of heterogeneous effects. Divine power is not curtailed; the rule is a
formality constraint on how effects are attributed to a cause qua simple.9
A minimal PPP–QQQ model (no function symbols). Let Q be the set of respects/aspects
(ḥaythiyyāt) available to a cause, and P the set of admissible effect-forms. Think of the cause as
coming with a rule that assigns to each respect in Q exactly one effect in P.
• Simplicity under one respect. When Q has exactly one element (one undivided respect), the
rule can return only one effect. This is exactly the principle: from one undivided respect only one
(heterogeneous) effect proceeds.
• Plurality by distinct respects. When Q has more than one element, different inputs (different
respects) can be assigned different effects without violating the rule; the plurality lies in the
domain of respects, not in “one” respect doing many things at once.
• Plurality by succession or conditions. To model conditions and time, add sets M
(media/recipients) and T (times). The cause’s assignment now takes triples (q,m,t)(q,m,t)(q,m,t)
as inputs and returns an effect in P. The same-respect restriction says: for a fixed triple
(q,m,t)(q,m,t)(q,m,t) you cannot get two heterogeneous outputs “as such and at once”. If the
medium or time changes, the input has changed—so there is no contradiction.
Read this way, the First’s giving of existence is an assignment with no temporal parameter;
“immediacy” means all effects depend on the First without creaturely instruments, while
intelligible plurality enters wherever the inputs are no longer one—i.e., when respects or
conditions multiply in intermediaries. Two practical morals follow. (1) The contradiction appears
only if the same input (q,m,t)(q,m,t)(q,m,t) is said to yield both a and non-a simultaneously;
change respect, condition, or time, and no contradiction arises. (2) Divine omnipotence is
untouched: the rule is a type/formality constraint. A simple cause qua simple behaves like an
assignment defined on a single respect, not on several respects at once, and it does not output a
composite “bundle” of heterogeneous effects in one go—doing so would smuggle plurality either
into the inputs (several respects) or into the output type (a composite), contradicting the
hypothesis of simplicity.

9 Constructive scope and synthesis: AP3 (witnessed ∃) with App. X: T10 (final synthesis of AP/U results).


Concrete example (the sun). The sun, as a natural cause, is not simple in the strict sense and
operates through multiple respects and recipient-conditions. Let
P = {illumination, heating, burning, …},
Q = {wavelength band, intensity profile, angle of incidence, …},
M = {medium, surface albedo, fuel/oxygen, ignition threshold, …}.
Different combinations of respect and condition yield different effects: illumination (visible band
with line-of-sight), heating (IR absorption given albedo), burning (fuel/oxygen plus ignition
threshold). The plurality of effects comes from distinct inputs—different respects and
conditions—not from “one undivided respect” producing many at once. By contrast, the
Necessary Existent, being absolutely simple, has just one respect and no creaturely conditions;
its immediate issuance is therefore one. Plurality arises downstream, precisely where respects
and conditions multiply (in intermediaries and recipients).
Rāzī’s logical critique sharpens the point. Framed one way, it alleges that the philosophers
equivocate between “issuance of a” and “non-issuance of a”, which are contradictories, and
“issuance of non-a”, which is merely different, not contradictory. The reply is exact: the
contradiction at issue is not sentential negation; it arises only when one and the same undivided
causal respect is made to ground two heterogeneous effects at once. If distinct respects are
present, plurality follows without breach; if the respect is one, heterogeneous co-issuance
collapses simplicity.
A second Rāzian pressure point concerns being: if “being” (wujūd) is truly predicated of God
and creatures, then either (i) it is univocal, risking accidentality of being in God and thus
composition, or (ii) it is equivocal, destroying the bridge that lets one reason from creaturely
being to divine being. A softer variant says: to explain diverse effects, philosophers will be
forced to posit multiplicity in God—different grounds for different effects—and so compromise
simplicity. Avicennian clarifications answer in three steps. (1) Wujūd is a first intelligible said in
many ways; it is neither a genus nor an accident added to God. In the Necessary Existent,
essence = existence; in contingents, existence is received and thus really distinct from essence.
The conceptual unity of “being” (ishtirāk maʿnawī) does not entail a common accident in re. (2)
Divine attributes (knowledge, power, life) are really identical with the essence; their distinctions
are iʿtibārī (conceptual/relational), arising from different considerations or relations to effects,


not from ontic parts in God. (3) God knows particulars by knowing Himself as their cause; no
conceptual “bits” are added to the essence, so no internal composition follows from omniscience.
Mullā Ṣadrā radicalizes the reply by relocating the debate from concepts to reality (aṣālat al-
wujūd + tashkīk). Wujūd alone is ontologically primary; essences are delimitations of being.
Being is one reality, but graded (modulated) in intensity and delimitation. The First is Pure
Simple Being—non-delimited unity with no internal respects. From such non-delimited unity
only one can proceed immediately; to allow two heterogeneous immediacies would write distinct
delimitations back into the source and deny its very non-delimitation. Plurality is placed
downstream, in determinate modes of being that already carry distinct ḥaythiyyāt; many effects
arise by those respects, not from “one undivided respect” in the source. On this picture, divine
attributes are identical with the essence as maximal intensity of being; differences in naming
track our conceptual vantage or relations to what proceeds, not intra-divine composition. Thus
Rāzī’s fork—either univocity that makes “being” accidental in God or multiplicity in God to
explain many effects—is dissolved: the concept of being is shared enough to underwrite
demonstration, yet being is not a genus/accident and so cannot introduce composition in the
Necessary Existent; diversity belongs to graded, delimited being on the effect-side.
Finally, on scriptural immediacy, verses such as “He says to it ‘Be!’ and it is” proclaim unshared
dependence and the absence of impediment, not a prohibition of intelligible order in
manifestation. The maxim “only one from the One” functions as a restriction on heterogeneous
co-effects under the same respect; it is not a denial that God originates plurality through what is
no longer basīṭ min jamīʿ al-wujūh. In short: omnipotence is untouched, the immediacy of
creatorship is preserved at the level of source, and the logical core of the principle is
maintained—one respect → one effect; plurality → plural respects.
Method Switch: From Ontic Causation to Transcendental Constitution
Cause ≠ ground ≠ constitution. Ontic names the level of particular beings and happenings—the
inventory of events and efficient productions (e.g., “fire burns cotton,” “A heats B”).
Transcendental names the enabling conditions that must already be in place for any sequence to
be intelligible as a genesis at all (a unifying rule, a determinate respect under which the many is


gathered, the possibility of stable repetition). On the merely ontic picture (Aristotle’s efficient
aitia, later powers-and-liabilities, necessity/sufficiency tests), causation is event-to-event
production. Hume’s challenge bites here: experience shows only constant conjunction and the
habit of expectation, not a felt necessary tie. The reformulation therefore shifts register: instead
of hunting an unseen bond, it asks what structure must be present for a run of happenings to
count as a lawful beginning rather than mere succession. In this register, ground is the
metaphysical enabler of such lawfulness; constitution is the unifying synthesis by which a
manifold is apprehended “as one.” The inherited rule is thus not a new description of God’s
efficient act but a constraint on the form of genesis as such: one undivided respect → one
immediate effect; plurality only where respects (or horizons) multiply.10
Example: A single pen-stroke is just ink on paper at the ontic level. It becomes a “1” (rather than
a stray mark) only when a schema selects and unifies it under the numeral’s rule. Without that
schema, there is no constituted “beginning” of counting at all.
Kant (Second Analogy, made concrete). “Transcendental” for Kant means conditions
supplied by the understanding that make experience possible. In the Second Analogy,
causality is such a rule: it organizes the sensible flow so that B must follow A (not merely
happens to). Call constitution the minimal unifying act that lets a scattered “many” appear as
one object or event (e.g., hearing successive notes as one melody requires a binding rule). Read
this way, the classical clause “not two heterogeneous effects under the same respect” becomes a
constraint internal to constitution: within one and the same unifying horizon, incompatible
outcomes cannot be founded at once without shattering the very synthesis that makes them
intelligible. Two guardrails keep “origin” talk disciplined: (i) Appearances vs. things-in-
themselves—our causal rules legislate only for appearances; (ii) Understanding vs. reason—
the understanding provides categories that constitute experience, while reason projects an idea
of the unconditioned that guides inquiry; to hypostatize that guiding idea is to confuse a
condition of intelligibility with a piece of ontology.
Example: The same ink-stroke cannot count simultaneously (under one schema) as the

10 App. X: T1–T4, T10; axioms U1–U3.


numeral “1” and the letter “I.” To obtain both readings one must switch the respect—
precisely the “same-respect” clause at work.
Heidegger radicalizes this turn by recasting categories as temporal schemata of disclosure and
centering productive imagination as the formative power that gathers a manifold into unity.
Ground (Grund) is retrieved as letting-be, a gathering that opens a clearing, not a highest
item; Ab-grund (abyss) names the withholding that keeps “ground” from hardening into a thing.
Along this path the maxim ceases to be about what an absolutely simple cause can produce and
becomes a formal condition of disclosure: genesis of sense requires a unifying gathering;
within one undivided gathering (one respect), heterogeneous co-effects are excluded. This is
not a limit on power; it is the rule by which anything can first show up as intelligible.
Example: Think of a traffic signal. Under the ordinary driving rule, a red light as such founds
exactly one outcome: stop. You can’t take that same, unchanged red—under the same rule—to
found go at the same time. To get “go,” you must switch the respect: either the light itself turns
green (the input changes), or you adopt a different rule-set (e.g., you’re a pedestrian reading a
WALK sign, not the drivers’ light). That’s the “same-respect” clause in everyday terms: one
unifying rule → one determinate outcome; different outcomes require a different rule or
input.
On both the Kantian and Heideggerian readings, the classical maxim is transcendentalized: it
states a condition of intelligibility rather than a tally of what a first cause “can” or “cannot”
make. One unifying respect → one immediate outcome; plurality requires a switch or
plurality of respects. This is how a “first” can be first for experience at all: by a unity-function
that gathers a manifold as one while forbidding, under the same respect, the simultaneous
institution of incompatible outcomes.
Husserl I — Unity as Constitutive Synthesis
Husserl’s early inquiry into number shows that multiplicity becomes a many only through an act
of collecting (Zusammenfassung) that gathers distinct items together-in-one. The operative
connector—our ordinary “and”—is not a further item added to the heap; it is the act-form that
binds items into a single intentional whole. On this basis he distinguishes a unit (Einheit, a mere
“something” eligible to be counted) from the number one (a technical marker in the cardinal


series). Likewise zero and one are not “numbers” in the same sense as two, three, etc., because
they lack the very collective operation that constitutes a many-as-one: with zero, there is nothing
to collect; with one, nothing is collected. From the start, then, unity is an operation rather than
an object11—a constituting act that confers a counted-whole upon disparate items (e.g., five
scattered coins become “this-five” only when gathered by the collecting act; successive tones
become “one melody” only when listening binds them under a rule).
In Husserl’s mature phenomenology this operational unity generalizes beyond arithmetic to
any appearing. An object is given through changing adumbrations (profiles, sides) that must
be recognized as the same across perspectives. Such identity-through-change is secured by a
harmonious synthesis that binds successive givennesses—retaining the just-past look,
anticipating the next, and integrating bodily movement (kinaesthesis) that explains why the looks
shift. Example: walking around a cube presents ever-new facets and edges, yet the profiles are
synthesized as one self-same cube; should a profile arrive that cannot fit (a sudden perfectly
round “edge”), the synthesis falters and the object is reidentified.
Every appearance also stands within a horizon of anticipations and co-givennesses that regulate
how further profiles may fulfill what is now merely intended. Anticipations are those empty
intentions (the cup’s unseen interior, expected weight) that become determinately given if one
turns or lifts the object; co-givennesses are features implied by the style of the thing (a handle
affords grasping; a door implies hinges). As new profiles arrive they either concord with these
horizons, stabilizing the synthesis, or discord, forcing a revision. Example: from the front, a rim
and handle suggest a hollow vessel; if turning reveals a solid block with a painted handle, the
violated horizon compels a different identification.
Two clarifications make the transcendental upshot precise. First, the unifying function is
formal: it adds no content but organizes a manifold under a single respect so that a “this” can
be intended as one and the same through variation. Second, heterogeneous outcomes cannot be
founded simultaneously under that one undivided respect.12 Where one and the same
synthesis remains unbroken, it yields one coherent sense; plurality and difference arise only
when respects are distinct (different modes of synthesis, different horizons) or when sense

11 Operational unity: App. X: T1; prohibition of concurrent heterogeneity: T2.
12 App. X: T2 (No simultaneous heterogeneity).


unfolds in succession. A simple illustration: when counting ⟨book, cup, key⟩, the act that reduces
each to a mere “one” and then collects them makes three; if that same undivided collecting were
to yield both “three” and “blue” at once, the synthesis would already be bifurcated by different
respects (numerical vs. qualitative).
Husserl’s contribution, then, is not a new ontic cause but a transcendental account of unity:
any genesis of sense presupposes a unifying synthesis that (i) gathers a manifold as one and (ii)
disciplines what can co-occur “under the same respect.” This provides the needed unity-
function—a minimal, constitutive operation without which there is no many-as-one, no identity
across profiles, and hence no intelligible appearing at all.
Husserl II — Genetic Phenomenology and the Beginning
Husserl’s genetic turn relocates “beginning” from a point-like origin to a structured becoming.
Static descriptions had traced how something is given—modes of appearance, intention and
fulfillment—by taking a cross-section of experience “at rest.” Genetic description asks how
those very structures arise in time: how sense is pre-constituted, how attention is drawn, how
habits form, and how a style of experiencing gets built up. What looks static turns out to be a
slice through a deeper history in which consciousness steadily arises out of consciousness.
At the base of this history lies passivity: a lawful, pre-predicative synthesis in which the ego is
not yet choosing. Here objects first make a claim on us through affection; something stands out
and “calls” to be noticed. This is not physical causation but a binding pull—like your name
suddenly popping out of café noise, or a red blemish on a page drawing your eye. That pull
motivates a first, minimal activity, a turning-toward that answers the solicitation—leaning closer
to the page, shifting your gaze to the flashing light. From there, association does quiet work.
Long before concepts, the stream knits itself together by similarities, contrasts, recurrences, and
part–whole linkages. Smelling coffee primes warmth and mug; the feel of a handle primes grasp;
hearing two notes predisposes a third. These are not mere habits tacked onto bare givens; they
are the lawful fabric of passive constitution.
Time-constitution gives this fabric its thread. Each now is held as just-past (retention) and leans
into a structured expectation of nexts (protention). Identity and alteration are registered as


concordance or discordance across this flow. A melody is one melody only because retentions
keep prior notes in play and protentions prepare the likely continuations; a wrong note breaks the
synthesis. Likewise, as you walk around a parked car, each profile differs, yet the temporal
synthesis binds them as one and the same car; if a profile arrives that cannot fit—say the “car”
suddenly shows a perfectly round edge with no transition—the identity is reworked.
Embodiment anchors and articulates these unities. The lived body is the zero-point of
orientation; through kinaestheses—the “I can move”—near and far, hidden and shown, left and
right are constituted. You turn your head and the cup’s handle comes into view; two trains lurch
and your felt sway tells which one moves. Even “objective rest” and “objective motion” are
constituted against this bodily background. Over time, acts leave deposits. Beliefs, attentional
styles, and practical grips sediment into a habitual “how” that operates pre-reflectively: fluent
reading, driving by feel, reaching for a switch in the dark. Meanings also sediment culturally.
Numbers, lines, points, even “objectivity” itself, are once-achieved senses that enter traditions;
they can be forgotten under later methods and reactivated by a teleological-historical reflection
that retraces how their sense was instituted.
Across these layers runs a single through-line: a minimal unifying synthesis that gathers a
manifold as one under a determinate respect. Affective awakenings motivate a turn; associative
regularities knit phases; kinaesthetic orientations stabilize a horizon; retentions and protentions
hold an identity in flight; sediments carry forward a style of sense-making. Where the same
synthesis remains in force, it yields one coherent sense; to get plurality you must change the
respect—switch horizon, task, or mode of synthesis—or let sense unfold in succession. That is
why incompatible outcomes cannot be founded simultaneously within one undivided synthesis.
A simple example makes this visible: the printed string “lead” cannot, under one and the same
reading horizon, mean both the metal and the verb “to guide.” The ink marks are identical, but
the anticipations, co-givennesses, and practical interests that frame them differ; to obtain the
other meaning you must shift respect (chemistry note versus instructions), and the synthesis
reorganizes accordingly.
On this view, a “beginning” is never a bare first instant; it is a structured inception already
exhibiting order: motivated continuity, horizonal coherence, and lawful unifications that make


the sequence count as the beginning of something. And because this unification works “under
one respect,” it quietly instantiates the same constraint that governs your wider thesis: within one
undivided synthesis, heterogeneous co-effects are excluded; plurality arrives where respects (or
horizons) multiply or where the sequence lawfully unfolds.
Kant → Husserl Interlude: A Priori Synthesis
For Kant, experience is possible only by an a priori synthesis that gathers a manifold into unity:
the forms of intuition (space, time) and the categories of the understanding jointly effect a
unification in which, paradigmatically, number is “the unity of a synthesis of the manifold of a
homogeneous intuition.” The “one” of a number is not a thing waiting in advance; it is a
unifying act that collects successive items as one count. “Synthesis” is double: both the unity of
parts in a whole and the spontaneous activity that produces that unity (Transcendental Deduction,
A- and B-versions), with the schematism of the imagination mediating between pure concepts
and temporal intuition.
Husserl radicalizes this insight by relocating the a priori from fixed faculties to intentional life
and its eidetic structures. Through the phenomenological reduction and free imaginative
variation, necessity is secured not by appeal to innate forms but by exhibiting the invariant
structures of consciousness itself. “Unity” becomes an operation of constitution, visible in
Evidenz: what is intended as identical shows itself as such by lawful syntheses that can be seen,
repeated, and verified in intuition.
This relocation also reframes logic. Apophantics—the theory of ideal forms of meaning—
studies the a priori structures of judgment independently of psychological episodes. Arithmetic
belongs with formal logic not because numbers are empirical, but because their sense is
constituted through categorial forms (“and,” “something,” “multiplicity”) that can themselves
be intuited. Against Kant’s narrow analytic/synthetic boundary, Husserl insists that many
“formal” necessities are grounded in the empty essences of these forms and are accessible in
categorial intuition no less than in sensible intuition.
Where Kant’s productive synthesis names an indispensable yet elusive mediation, Husserl lays
it bare as passive synthesis: a lawful, pre-predicative stratum—association, the temporal flow
of impression–retention–protention, kinaesthetic orientation—in which a manifold is already


bound into unity before any judging. This is a new transcendental aesthetic: aesthesis
(passivity) grounds logos (activity). Active objectivation—judgment, proof, theory—builds upon
this subsoil; it does not replace it. Accordingly, Evidenz becomes the measure of foundation: not
a feeling of certainty but the intuitive fulfillment in which what is intended shows itself “itself.”
In this sense, foundation precedes proof: what Heidegger aptly glosses in Kant as principles
that “first make possible their ground of proof” finds phenomenological articulation in Husserl’s
account of constitution. The initiality of a foundation is not a temporal first, but a form of
genesis—a synthesis by which a manifold is gathered “as one” and within which heterogeneous
outcomes cannot be founded simultaneously under the same respect. Read this way, the
“principle of the One” is already at work as a unity-function: the minimal, iterable operation
without which no beginning of sense is thinkable at all.
Heidegger — Ground, Abyss, and Gathering
Rehearing Der Satz vom Grund “in a different key,” Heidegger loosens Grund from any appeal
to a highest entity and from the metaphysical reflex that treats ground as a reason possessed by
one being over others. Throughout metaphysics, he notes, Grund tacitly signifies the same as
Being, yet Being—everywhere presupposed—“remains without ground”: it has no cause,
principle, or explanation within the onto-theological habit that mistakes beings for Being. To
hear the principle as Satz vom Grund rather than “principle of reason” is to let Grund be thought
as the way Being grants a togetherness of beings, not as a deductible ratio. This shift runs with
Heidegger’s retrieval of logos from legein: not a logical form but a “laying that gathers,” a
saying that lets things lie before us together. Logos is a temporal happening, a gathering-letting
that discloses what is present in its presencing; language is this unique gathering of beings.
Correlative to Grund so understood is Ab-grund—abyss—not a thing underneath things but a
withholding that lets ground be ground. Ab-grund names the “remaining-away” of ground, the
groundless ground: the earth’s self-concealing support that sustains precisely by withdrawing.
The point is not nihilism but safeguard: abyss prevents the fixation of ground into a final
substrate and so keeps disclosure open. Hence inceptual thinking is abyssal thinking; it resists
reifying ground into some ultimate “stuff” and lets the granting/showing of Being remain an
event rather than a possession.


With this comes a systematic re-posing of the Greek cluster archē / aitia and the Latin principium
beside the German Grund. Archē means at once “beginning” and “rule.” Metaphysics habitually
heard the beginning as a first item and the rule as mastery by a supreme being; Heidegger re-
opens archē as the originary emergent that sets a region into its sway without becoming a highest
entity within it. Likewise principium—classically divided as principium fiendi (principle of
coming-to-be), essendi (principle of being), and cognoscendi (principle of knowing)—is
detoured from a catalogue of explanatory grounds toward a letting of beings be present,
intelligible, and knowable. Even aitia (so often equated with efficient cause) is re-heard in its
Greek sense as “because” or “responsibility for,” nearer to letting-be than to mechanical
production. In each case, what seems a fixed “foundation” becomes a mode of granting. Grund is
the gathered field within which archē as inception takes hold; Ab-grund holds this field open by
refusing any closure into a last cause; principium names the operative sway that first sets
measure; and aitia shades back from causal push to the more originary “on account of which”
that lets appearance come to presence. Thus cause, principle, beginning, and ground are not
collapsed but re-articulated: they interrelate as ways Being bestows a region’s order, not as rungs
on a ladder to a supreme entity.
This gathering shows itself phenomenologically as Lichtung, the clearing in which beings stand.
The clearing is not empty sameness; it is the strife (Kampf) of world and earth, the rift (Riss) that
sketches a ground-plan and holds opponents together without collapse. In this sense the “Same”
(das Selbe) is not identity that erases difference, but the unity in which difference appears as
difference. Heidegger’s account of the fourfold (Geviert)—earth, sky, mortals, divinities—makes
this visible: things gather the four in a unity of mutual mirroring, a held-together of distinctions
rather than a leveling. A bridge, for example, does not add four elements together; it gathers them
into a place where they belong together, each bearing the others’ presencing. This is legein as
event: the letting-lie-before that grants a world.
Seen in this light, the classical “same-respect” clause receives a phenomenological register. A
horizon that gathers—logos as legein, the clearing in which beings stand—cannot, as such and at
once, disclose two heterogeneous configurations under one and the same gathering without
tearing its own integrity. What is barred is not plurality as such, but the simultaneity of
incompatible disclosures from one undivided gathering as such. Where the gathering


multiplies—where rifts articulate distinct “respects” within the horizon—plurality is lawful;
where the gathering is one and undivided, incompatible showings cannot co-occur “under the
same respect.” The rule, translated, now marks the integrity of a clearing’s operation rather than
a limit imposed by a highest cause.13
think of a stage during a performance. The same set, lighting, and blocking—the same
“gathering”—can present the scene as a sunlit garden or as a stormy night, but not both at once
under the very same arrangement. To get the other showing you must change the respect: re-
light, re-set, re-block. The prohibition is not “no variety”; it is “no mutually exclusive stagings
from one and the same undivided setup.” That is what the “same-respect” clause protects at the
level of disclosure.
The upshot is that the “One” here is not a hypostasis but a mode of gathering: the way a horizon
unifies without totalizing, holds apart without sundering, grants measure and limit without
installing a supreme ens. Grund as gathering lets beings appear together; Ab-grund safeguards
this letting by withholding any final foundation. Archē is re-heard as inception that both begins
and governs without becoming a first thing; principium names the operative sway by which a
domain is first measured; aitia turns from pushing-cause to the “on account of which” proper to
letting-appear. Read this way, the classical maxim is recast rather than denied: unity signifies a
gathering operation, and the “same-respect” is the horizon’s own integrity-condition—what one
gathered showing can or cannot disclose at once—while abyss keeps unity from congealing into
a thing.
the “One” is like a curator’s organizing theme in a museum room—it makes very different works
hang together, sets the lighting and sight-lines, and gives measure to what belongs there. The
“abyss” is the curator’s refusal to turn that theme into a total rule that swallows every possible
display; it keeps an open center so new showings remain possible. The maxim “from the one,
one” then says: given one undivided curatorial setup, you cannot present two incompatible
installations at the same time in that room; to host plural displays, you introduce distinct
sections, change the lighting, or move to another room—that is, you multiply respects rather than
violate the integrity of a single gathering.

13 Same-respect coherence and succession: U2; App. X: T4.


Two clarifications make the connection to the overarching thesis precise. First, the prohibition is
situational, not ontic: it tells you what a given gathering can disclose “as such and at once.” A
clearing can articulate multiple respects—paths, regions, focal points—and so sustain manifold
showings in sequence or in differentiated registers; what it cannot do is be, in one undivided
regard, the scene of mutually exclusive configurations. Second, this blocks any relapse into onto-
theology. Because Being “remains without ground,” there is no supreme cause whose simplicity
must be protected by rationing effects. The integrity to be protected is that of the gathering
itself—the logos that grants a world. Thus the One that matters here is the operative One of
gathering, and the abyss that accompanies it is not a deficit but the very generosity by which
beginnings, principles, causes, and grounds are kept open to their task: letting beings appear
together.
translate this into a city square. The square gathers traffic, markets, festivals, and protests by
offering paths, sightlines, thresholds. At any moment the same undivided setup cannot be a silent
memorial and a loud concert “as such and at once”; to manage plurality you re-zone the square,
schedule events, or reconfigure its paths—i.e., you multiply respects. And because there is no
hidden “highest building” that rules the square, what governs is the square’s own way of
gathering. Its open center—the “abyss”—keeps it from hardening into one fixed use and is
precisely what lets new beginnings take place there.
Derrida — An-arche, Trace, Iterability
Derrida denies any pure origin and at the same time insists that meaning occurs only as iterable
form—a repeatable unit of inscription whose every repetition differs. The “beginning” is
therefore an-archic (without an arche-point), yet never formless: genesis presupposes minimal
repeatability, a “one” not as hypostasis but as the operator of iteration. Read this way, there is no
simple, self-identical source that could ground signification once for all; there is only the
differential machinery by which something counts as the same enough to be repeated and thus to
signify, even as repetition dislocates it.
Why is any “beginning” contaminated? Because what would make a beginning count as a
beginning—its legibility, recognizability, binding force—already presupposes repeatability,
spacing, and retention that exceed any punctual origin. Derrida’s point is not psychological or
historical but structural: a pure arche would have to be self-present, self-identical, and self-


grounding, yet signification only occurs as iterable form. A mark, word, signature, promise, or
law must be repeatable as “the same” across contexts, and that very iterability inserts difference,
delay, and alterability into the first moment. The inaugural is therefore an-archic (without an
arche-point) and yet never formless: genesis requires a minimal iterable one—not a hypostasis,
but the operator that lets something be taken again as “this.”
This condition is named in Of Grammatology as trace and archi-writing. The trace is instituted
and “unmotivated” in any naturalist sense: not a thing lurking before speech, but the structural
spacing and retention without which presence could not present. It is “prior” only in structure, as
the condition for temporalization and reference. Archi-writing names this irreducible archi-
synthesis that opens time, relation to the other, and language. Hence the decisive formula: if “all
begins with the trace,” there is precisely no originary trace—the very concept destroys its name.
What shows up as first is already marked by remainder and delay; the living present is inhabited
by “dead time,” the past-and-to-come folded into any “now” as its very possibility.
“Structure, Sign, and Play” translates the same logic into the register of systems. Classical
thought secures meaning by a center (origin, presence, ground) that would anchor substitutions.
Derrida shows that a structure lives by substitutions around a non-place: play without a final
fulcrum. This is not relativism but a rule of legibility. Iterability articulates that rule: to function,
a mark must be repeatable as “the same,” and the same repeatability opens it to graft, drift, and
alteration. A signature binds only because it can be cited and recognized; the possibility of
forgery is not an accident that happens later but the internal condition of its efficacy. Likewise a
first “yes” (promise, vow, consent) binds only as an iterable affirmation; its force is at once pre-
performative and citational. There is no pure first yes; the inaugural affirmation is structurally
doubled by the possibility—and necessity—of being said again.
Derrida’s vocabulary tightens this diagnosis. The trace marks the “before” of presence as
retention and spacing; différance names the double movement of temporal deferral and spatial
differing by which identity is constituted; supplement (already in the reading of Rousseau) names
the add-on that both completes and exposes an originary lack, showing that the “origin” needs
what comes after to be itself; pharmakon and parergon display how the border or remedy that
seems external is internal to what it frames or cures. None of these introduce a contingent stain


on an otherwise pure source; they name the very economy that lets something begin to count as
the same.
Sometimes Derrida figures the pre-originary “place” of this economy with Plato’s khôra: neither
sensible nor intelligible, not a substrate, but the spacing that lets anything take place. In that
sense khôra is “undeconstructible” not as a hard core but as the minimal non-place that resists
capture while enabling places, inscriptions, and events. The same holds for life/death/survival:
“life” functions only by archive and repetition; what “remains” is not a substance above time but
the iterable remainder that exceeds any present ontology. The trace “remains”—yet not as a
being, but as the condition for beings to be countable, sayable, memorable at all.
Read through this lens, there is no simple, self-identical source that could ground signification
once for all; there is only the differential machinery by which something is counted as the same
enough to be repeated and thus to signify—even as repetition dislocates it. The “beginning” is
contaminated because its possibility already includes its repeatability, and repeatability already
includes difference. But the beginning is not therefore void: genesis presupposes a minimal
iterable one (unit of inscription, act-type, form of citation). That “one” is not a highest entity; it is
the operative unity of iteration.14
Transposed into the register of our overarching maxim, the reformulated principle reads: no
genesis or signification without a minimal iterable one; and because iterability entails
difference, unity and difference are co-originary. There is no arche-point that precedes this
structure, but there is a least form without which nothing could so much as begin to count as the
same. The classical “same-respect” clause now takes a phenomenological-semiotic inflection:
within one operative iteration—one gathered horizon of legibility—the mark cannot, as such and
at once, ground two heterogeneous configurations without tearing the conditions of its
recognition; multiplicity arises lawfully across reinscriptions, re-framings, and shifted horizons.
Thus the “One” survives not as a hypostasis but as the mode of gathering in and as iterability: a
minimal, iterable unit that both founds and fractures any origin, making possible the only
beginnings we ever have—those that begin again.

14 Iterability and synthesis: App. X: T9 (iteration over W) + T10 (formal scope).


The Reformulated Principle (Numbered Theses)
(T1) Any genesis of sense presupposes a unity-function that gathers multiplicity “as one.”
Unity names the minimal act of collection under which a manifold first counts as a manifold
(word–stream gathered as a sentence; items gathered as a number).15
(T2) This unity is an operator, not an entity; it is formal/transcendental rather than
ontic/metaphysical.16
It does not add a new thing to what appears; it is the condition under which anything appears as
one at all (a form of constitution, not a highest cause).
(T3) Unity and difference are co-originary: iterability entails both repeatability and alteration.
What is “the same” is only so as repeatable across contexts, and repeatability structurally
includes difference (every citation re-inscribes and shifts).17
(T4) The classical “same-respect” clause translates as: a single gathered horizon cannot ground
simultaneous heterogeneous effects as such.
One undivided act of gathering cannot, at once and as one act, disclose incompatible
configurations; plurality arises by distinct respects or successive reinscriptions.18
(T5) “Ground” is abyssal (Heidegger): enabling without becoming a highest cause.
Grund as gathering lets things appear together, while Ab-grund (withholding) keeps this enabling
from hardening into a hypostasis.
(T6) The operator is compatible with freedom/contingency: it constrains coherence, not
outcomes.
It fixes the form of genesis (how anything can begin as intelligible) without predetermining what
begins.
(T7) Scriptural immediacy of creatorship concerns order of manifestation; this principle
concerns order of intelligibility.

15 Foundational unity-function: AP1, U1; App. X: T1.
16 Unity as operator not entity: App. X: T5 (conservativity of Aḥad); U5.
17 Co-originary unity/difference: App. X: T9 (iterability across W-stages).
18 Same-respect clause: U1–U3; App. X: T2–T4.


“Be!” names immediacy in appearing; the unity-function names the condition under which such
appearing is thinkable as one.
(T8) The classical demonstrations track a genuine necessity—not of emanation, but of
constitution.
Their force is: from one undivided respect, only one heterogeneous effect can issue as such;
plurality requires distinct respects or mediations.19
(T9) The mystical waḥda siryānīyya offers a phenomenological analogue of pervasive unity
without hypostasis.
Unity pervades and holds differences without becoming a separate “One-thing”—a gathered
flowing, not a freestanding entity.
(T10) The principle’s scope is formal: it disciplines claims about genesis across mathematics,
language, and agency.
Wherever a beginning is at stake (number, text, resolve), intelligibility requires a minimal
iterable one and the integrity of its “same-respect” gathering.20
Stress-Tests
a) Mathematics / Number. Early Husserl shows that number arises from collective
combination: you start with a manifold (just “many items”: pebbles on a table, strokes on a
page) and perform a unifying act—the mental “and”-operation that collects them together-as-
one counted whole. In that setting (i.e., within this Husserlian analysis), a unit means simply “a
something eligible to be counted” (this pebble, that pebble), not “the number one.” The numeral
“1” is a later technical sign that we use in calculations (e.g., as the multiplicative identity or as
the base for the successor operation); it is not itself the product of collecting several things.
Likewise “0” names the limit-case where there is nothing to collect, and “1” the case where
there is nothing to combine—hence 0/1 are not ‘numbers’ in the same sense as pluralities
like 2, 3, 4, which arise only when the collecting act really binds several items into one
plurality.21

19 One undivided respect → one effect; plurality requires distinct respects: App. X: T2, T7, T8.
20 Formal scope and synthesis: App. X: T10. once from one undivided respec
21 Single operation cannot bear incompatible axioms at once: App. X: T1 (functional), T2–T3 (non-branching within
a respect/class).


Modern symbolic mathematics pushes far beyond what we can survey intuitively—that is,
beyond what we can grasp “in one look” or keep clearly present at once (think huge numerals,
long proofs, nested quantifiers). It achieves this because its unities of operation—successor, +,
×, function application, quantifier scope—stay stable under iteration: the same rule is re-
applicable, step after step, and its outputs remain legible as belonging to one ongoing
construction. This is exactly our principle at work: mathematics needs repeatable unifying
forms so that a sprawling manifold of steps counts as one rule-governed progression.
The same principle also explains why a single formal horizon cannot carry heterogeneous
constraints—i.e., incompatible rule-sets—at once under the same respect. One deductive
setup cannot be simultaneously classical and intuitionistic inferences (they disagree, for
example, about unrestricted excluded middle); one and the same “plane” of geometry cannot
satisfy Euclid’s parallel postulate (“through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel”)
and the hyperbolic version (infinitely many such lines); one binary operation on a given domain
cannot be both commutative (a+b=b+a) and anti-commutative (a+b=−(b+a)) without
collapsing into triviality. To run both, you must change the respect (switch logics, switch
geometries, switch operations)—which is precisely to move to a different unifying horizon, not
to ask one undivided horizon to ground incompatible outcomes.
Example. Counting pebbles: each pebble is a unit (a mere “something”); two appears only when
two such “somethings” are collected as one plurality. By contrast, the symbol “1” serves as a
neutral element in multiplication or as the successor base—an operator-role whose usefulness
presupposes that the collecting and iterating rules themselves remain fixed and re-applicable
throughout the calculation.
b) Language / Performatives. Derrida’s “yes” (oath, vow, promise, consent) names an iterable
unit of form because binding speech acts must be recognizable again: they need to be citable,
recordable, and appealable later (minutes, contracts, audio, logs). Without that repeatable
recognizability, there’s no stable criterion that a commitment was undertaken, so nothing to hold
parties to. Hence the “yes” must be repeatable as the same—not identical in every feature, but
stable enough in type (the force-bearing form “yes/agree/promise”) that different tokens count
as that same act when recalled, quoted, or enforced.


Denying a pure origin doesn’t abolish unity-conditions; it shows that unity is citational and so
context-impregnated. Every performative draws on prior conventions (formats, formulas,
signatures); that’s its unity. But each occurrence sits in new circumstances (speaker, time,
medium, audience, legal forum), so every repetition differs. Iterability means exactly this: the
form can be carried across contexts and must be alterable to travel, yet it remains legible
enough—through minimal markers like conventional wording (“I promise…,” “Yes”),
authorized positions (officiant–respondent, offeror–offeree), and felicity conditions (proper
procedure, uptake)—to bear the same commitment.
Same-respect clause. Under one undivided felicity horizon (same context, same time, same
convention), a single utterance cannot be both a promise and its refusal: that would collapse the
act’s unity. To cancel, hedge, or ironize is to introduce another respect (a second act, a shifted
frame, or a later time). Our principle thus reads: some minimal one-ness of form is required
for any speech act to arise as such, and difference is co-given with its iterable life.
Example. “I do” at a wedding—or ticking “I agree” on a consent screen—binds because the
form persists across media (spoken, written, digital) and can be re-produced and cited
(certificate, log, recording). Each token is situated and thus non-identical (different voices, times,
devices), yet the act counts as the same performative under the relevant convention; trying to
make the very same utterance, in that very moment, both “I do” and “I don’t” would fracture the
single felicity horizon rather than fulfill it.22
c) Agency / Causation. Relocating the principle from necessitated efficient causality to
conditions of coherent action removes the free-will worry. The rule now functions as a formal
constraint on intelligibility, not a force that predetermines outcomes. It says: if there is one
undivided respect—one live project or intention (Heidegger’s Entwurf, the projection that opens
a field of significance)—then one deed issues as such from that respect. Freedom selects which
deed to perform; the unity-operator secures that what is done counts as one intelligible act rather
than a blur of incompatible doings.

22 Performatives under one felicity horizon: App. X: T2; temporal relief via T4 (succession).


Applied to agency, the same-respect clause reads: a single, indivisible intention cannot at once
ground heterogeneous acts. Plurality remains perfectly compatible, but it arrives either (i) by
distinct respects (sub-projects, roles, layered descriptions) or (ii) by succession (before/after). In
both cases the input has changed—either the horizon under which the act is undertaken or the
time at which it is done—so no breach occurs.
Example. With the one intention “sign the contract now,” I cannot, in the very same stroke and
under that very intention, both sign and refuse. To “sign while refusing” either splits the intention
(two respects: compliance vs. protest) or staggers it in time (sign now, rescind later). Likewise,
the single instruction “turn left now” cannot, under that same instruction, yield both a left-turn
and a right-turn; to include the right-turn one must adopt a different respect (e.g., “ignore the
GPS; follow the detour”) or change the temporal ordering (“left now, right immediately after”).
The grammar of agency is thus: one undivided respect → one deed; multiple deeds → distinct
respects or times.23
Objections and Replies
What this section is doing.
It defends the reformulated principle—any genesis of sense needs a unity-function (“one”) that
gathers a manifold as one, and the same gathered horizon cannot, as such and at once, ground
heterogeneous effects—against four predictable challenges. The replies stay at the level of
conditions of intelligibility (formal/phenomenological), not ontic stories about what particular
beings do.
Objection (Heideggerian): “You’ve smuggled a Highest One back in (henology).”
Reply. The “one” here is not a being at all. It names an operation of gathering—the way a field
of appearing is held together as one horizon. “Ground” is taken as Ab-grund
(withholding/letting), not as a supreme entity that explains others. The principle’s “same-respect”
clause protects the integrity of one gathering: one undivided horizon cannot disclose, at once and
as such, incompatible configurations (e.g., presenting the same item as square and round). This is
a constraint on disclosure, not a thesis about a highest thing.24

23 Indivisible intention vs incompatible acts: App. X: T2; diachronic allowance: T7.
24 App. X: T5/U5 — Aḥad excluded from object-language; preserves transcendence without hypostatization.


Objection (Derridean): “There is no pure origin—every beginning is contaminated.”25
Reply. Agreed. “Contaminated” beginnings still require a minimal iterable form to begin at all.
Call it the iterable one: a repeatable unit (a mark, rule, “yes,” or schema) that lets recognition
persist across differences. Without that repeatable minimum, there is nothing to iterate or
contaminate. The principle does not restore purity; it states the least unity without which iteration
(and so signification) cannot occur. Unity and difference are co-originary: the repeatability that
founds meaning also exposes it to alteration.
Objection (Theological): “Scripture ascribes immediate creatorship; mediation violates
that.”26
Reply. The claim here concerns the order of intelligibility, not the revealed order of
manifestation. Saying that one undivided respect of disclosure cannot ground heterogeneous
outcomes at once is a formal point about what makes any event intelligible as this event. It does
not deny that God creates immediately; it says only that even the intelligibility of “Let there be
X” presupposes one determinate horizon per act of disclosure (not X and non-X from the same
act as such). Theology can speak to how God acts; the principle specifies a condition on how any
act can be understood.
Objection (Classical-internal): “There is no clean philosophical ‘instance’ (e.g., the
Necessary Existent) to carry your rule.”
Reply. The reformulation changes registers. It no longer hunts for an ontic carrier inside a
cosmology; it articulates a transcendental constraint operative whenever anything shows up as
one: if a manifold is gathered into one horizon H, then H cannot, as such and simultaneously,
ground heterogeneous outcomes. This is compatible with (but not dependent on) emanationist
schemes; it survives the fall of any cosmography because it disciplines form, not celestial
mechanics.
Why these matters (one clear line).
Formally: if a manifold M appears under a single, unbroken respect H, then H can ground at
most one heterogeneous outcome at once; plurality lawfully arises either by (i) distinct respects

25 App. X: T9 — iterability maintains unity while enabling lawful difference.
26 U5 + T5 — transcendence of Aḥad; immediacy realized via Mashiyyat (see T6).


(a different horizon H′) or (ii) iteration over time (re-inscription). That is the whole point of the
section.
Bahá’í Perspective — Emanation without Identification
From Bahá’í sources the classical rule qāʿidat al-wāḥid—that from the One only one proceeds
“under the same respect”—is affirmed in spirit but recast with two guardrails: (i) the divine
Essence (the “real Existence” in ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s diction) remains absolutely transcendent,
sanctified above descent, composition, and limitation; and (ii) what proceeds immediately is not
the Essence itself resolving into forms, but the first emanation—the Primal Will/First Word
(also glossed as the First Intellect)—through which all things are realized and diversified
according to capacity.
1. Unity of existence—clarified and corrected.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes a popular, imitative waḥdat al-wujūd (which treats
“existence” as a generic accident inhering in things) from the “real Existence… sanctified
and exalted above all expression—that by which all things are realized.” The former
collapses Creator into creation; the latter preserves a single source for all that is, without
making the many identical with the One. Hence His refrain: superior realities do not
descend; the Pre-existent does not resolve into originated forms. The favored image is
sun and rays: the sun remains in its height; rays emanate, illuminating all things without
the sun’s descent or division. This repudiates the sea-wave identity thesis (Creator =
waves), while keeping its grain of truth: everything that is shines with derivative light.
2. Emanation vs. manifestation (ẓuhūr).
On this point ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is explicit: “The Sufis maintain that the realities of things are
the manifestation of the One; the Prophets say that they emanate therefrom. And great
indeed is the difference.” Manifestation here would mean the One becoming the many
(like ink turning into letters); emanation means a bestowal from a source that remains
wholly transcendent. Thus the Bahá’í stance refuses any hypostasis of unity within the
plane of the originated, even while affirming a pervasive sign-revelation: “within every
atom are enshrined the signs… of that most great Light.”


3. “Basīṭ al-ḥaqīqa” carefully read.
When philosophers say basīṭ al-ḥaqīqa kull al-ashyāʾ wa laysa bi-shayʾ minhā,
Bahá’u’lláh glosses “al-ashyāʾ” as the perfections of existence qua existence (kamālāt
al-wujūd min ḥaythu huwa wujūd), not as discrete entities. The Simple Reality
comprehends all perfections in an uncompounded way; it does not unravel into
innumerable existents. “The lights of the Simple Reality are seen in all things,” yet “God
hath ever been and shall ever remain sanctified from ascent and descent, limits,
conjunction, and attachment.” This preserves the One as beyond beings, while explaining
why its light is legible in beings.
4. The first procession: the Primal Will (al-mashīʾa al-ūlā).
Because “the Unseen is exalted above all names,” Bahá’u’lláh says, all names and
attributes return to the First Word/Primal Will—the locus where divine names gather
and from which creation begins. In this register: from the absolutely One, one immediate
proceeds—the Primal Will/First Intellect—and multiplicity then “is specified and
individuated according to [the recipients’] capacity, receptivity, and essence.” This is
precisely qāʿidat al-wāḥid in a Bahá’í idiom: one direct effusion from the aspectless
Source; plurality downstream by mediated respects.
5. Divine knowledge and the a‘yān-thābita claim.
Against the theosophical proof that God’s pre-existent knowledge requires pre-existent
“objects” (hence the a‘yān fixed in the Essence), ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers: the divine
knowledge is independent of its objects; to require them would assimilate it to
creaturely knowing. Were individuations “identical” with the Essence, pre-existences
would multiply and the Essence would become a seat of plurality. Thus the “objects of
knowledge” are not co-eternal constituents of God; rather, all distinctions arise on the
side of emanation.
6. Two modes of tawḥīd: existential and noetic.
Bahá’u’lláh marks a tawḥīd-i wujūdī—“all is perishing save His Face”: before the Real,
otherness is null—and a tawḥīd-i shuhūdī: in every thing the signs of the One are
witnessed. The first safeguards transcendence (no being stands before God as a second);


the second licenses a universal theophanic reading of the world (everything bears Names
and Attributes) without identity of Essence and world.
7. Nature, will, and lawful plurality.
“Nature is God’s Will and its expression in and through the contingent world… Its
manifestations are diversified by varying causes.” The unity is in the source (one Will,
one effulgence); the plurality issues by law from differences of site, capacity, and
relation. This is the Bahá’í analogue of the classical same-respect restriction: one
undivided effulgence does not, as such and at once, yield incompatible effects;
heterogeneity appears where respects multiply—on the side of recipients and mediations.
8. Re-reading the rule in Bahá’í terms.
•
The One to which the rule strictly applies is the transcendent Essence—“glorying in
holiness,” unenterable by names and beyond all descent.
•
The one immediate proceeding is the Primal Will/First Word (“the first radiance of
Thy revelation”), the “source of unity and the dawning-point of oneness,” to which “all
names and attributes return.”
•
Multiplicity unfolds through the Kingdom (malakūt) into creation (khalq), as the one
light refracts according to receptive capacities; “nothing whatsoever can exist without the
revelation of the splendor of God,” yet “the sun… remains transcendent in the heights of
its sanctity.”
9. What this accepts—and what it disallows.
It accepts that “the cause through which all things are realized is but one,” that the One’s
light is legible everywhere (“until none shall contemplate anything but that he shall see
God therein”), and that a minimal unity-function is necessary for any genesis. It
disallows taking that ubiquity as identity (Creator = creation), or treating divine
knowledge as needy of its objects, or positing a descent of the Essence into forms. In
Bahá’í terms, the One names neither a highest being among beings nor a formless, all-
absorbing substance; it names the absolutely transcendent Real and, for the order of
emanation, the Primal Will by which the many are coherently given.


Up-shot for qāʿidat al-wāḥid.
Read along these lines, the principle survives with clarified scope: from the absolutely One
only one immediate procession—the Primal Will; plurality then lawfully issues because later
causes and recipients are no longer “simple from every aspect” but vary in ḥaythiyyāt (respects)
and istiʿdād (capacity). Thus unity governs the form of giving (one undivided effulgence), while
difference governs the mode of receiving (many measures). Emanation without identification;
transcendence without distance; universality of sign without collapse of source and sign.27
Conclusion — From Emanation Rule to Unity-of-Genesis
Recast as a transcendental operator, qāʿidat al-wāḥid survives its traditional objections and
acquires a determinate task. At its core lies a disciplined necessity: no genesis of sense, object,
or world occurs without a minimal unity-function that gathers a manifold “as one,” and
this unity co-originates with difference. Husserl secures the first clause by showing that every
appearing depends on constitutive synthesis (identification across adumbrations, retention–
protention, associative binding); Heidegger prevents reification by freeing Grund from any
supreme entity and hearing it as a gathering (legein) sheltered by Ab-grund (withholding);
Derrida prevents nostalgia for pure origins by demonstrating that every beginning is iterable—
repeatable only as altered. In this register, the classical “same-respect” clause translates
