What Is Faith? And Who Is a Believer?
Introduction
This article advances a thesis: faith is best construed as a graded, practice-bound disposition
integrating assent, trust, and enactment, rather than as mere belief or ineffable feeling.
Methodologically, the argument triangulates (i) historical-linguistic analysis of Semitic ʾ-m-
n/īmān and Latin fides, (ii) close readings of authorized scriptural corpora (Bible, Qurʾān, Bábí
and Bahá’í writings), and (iii) targeted engagements with al-Ashʿarī’s kalām, Kierkegaard’s
existential account, Tillich’s “ultimate concern,” and Wittgenstein’s grammatical elucidations.
On this basis the paper proposes analytic criteria for identifying degrees and kinds of faith and
addressing the boundary question—who counts as a believer?—without collapsing diverse
religious language-games into a single metric. The lexical section cautions, in particular, against
conflating yamīn/yumn (y-m-n, “right/auspice”) with ʾ-m-n (“security/assurance”), marking
“right-hand” associations as symbolic or homiletic unless a demonstrable lexicographic chain is
shown. Scriptural soundings (e.g., Heb 11; key Qurʾānic loci) display faith as assurance enacted
in resilient obedience; the Bábí/Bahá’í materials further specify recognition of the Manifestation,
detachment and fear of God, and deeds exceeding words as conjoint proofs. Philosophically,
Ashʿarī definitions anchor īmān in taṣdīq warranted by dalīl (with islām as outward compliance),
while Wittgensteinian considerations discipline talk of “faith” by mapping its communal uses
rather than positing private inner objects. The resulting triadic model—assent, trust, enactment—
supplies operational indicators (dispositional stability under trial; behavioral uptake over time)
for comparative analysis across traditions. Finally, the article is explicitly tethered to the author’s
companion study, “Thresholds of Just-Being,” which elaborates a spectrum of belonging from
maximal nearness to “nur noch” deficiency; together, the two essays correlate degree-theoretic
metrics of faith with an ontology of religious presence and suspension.
Lexical–Etymological Discussion
Īmān (إیمان) is the verbal noun of Form IV ʾāmana (“to believe; to give security”), built on the
Semitic root ʾ-m-n, whose core sense is security/firmness/assurance. Form I ʾamina means “to
be safe/secure,” with yaʾmanu as its imperfect and ʾamn/ʾamān as the verbal noun
(“security/safety”); Form IV ʾāmana with bi- ordinarily means “to believe in; to assent to,” and


with a direct object can mean “to give security to; to make safe.” Standard lexica gloss īmān as
taṣdīq (assent/verification grounded in assurance) (Ibn Fāris, 1979; Ibn Manẓūr, 1955–1956;
Lane, 1863–1893; Wehr, 1979). Some interpreters draw a conceptual link between īmān and
“right(-hand)” (yamīn/yumn), a motif reinforced by Qurʾānic eschatology in which those given
their record in their right hand are vindicated (Qurʾān 17:71; 69:19–24; 84:7–9) and by the
emblem of the ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm (“straight path”). This yields a symbolic association between
“rightness/auspice” and the disposition of faith. However, on strict lexical grounds yamīn/yumn
derives from the distinct root y-m-n and should not be conflated with ʾ-m-n; Persian glosses
such as “coming from the right(-hand) side” are therefore best treated as theological or homiletic
associations, not as an etymology of īmān, unless a specific historical lexicographic chain is
demonstrated (Ibn Fāris, 1979; Lane, 1863–1893).
The English word faith enters Middle English in the mid-thirteenth century (attested as feith, fei,
fai), via Anglo-/Old French feid/foi “faith, belief, trust, confidence, pledge,” traceable to the
eleventh century. Its ultimate source is Latin fīdēs “trust, faith, reliability, pledge,” from fīdere
“to trust,” conventionally derived from the Proto-Indo-European root bheidh- (“to trust/confide;
to persuade”). In English it participates in the morphology of abstract nouns in -th (cf. truth,
health), and its semantic field historically ranges over (i) trust/loyalty, (ii) religious belief, and
(iii) in scholastic and post-scholastic theological usage, assent where demonstrative evidence is
unavailable. By the early fourteenth century, uses marking propositional assent in religious
contexts are well attested, with subsequent extensions to interpersonal trust (reliability, good
faith) and to marital fidelity (OED, n.d.; de Vaan, 2008).
Taken together, the Semitic and Indo-European evidence suggests a stable semantic nucleus of
assured trust rather than bare cognition. To avoid over-reach, we do not claim that faith
originates in reason; rather, reason constrains and often mediates the formation of faith, while
reliance and practice disclose its lived depth. For the purposes of this article we adopt the
following working definition: faith is a graded integration of assent (taṣdīq), trust/reliance,
and enactment, whose degree is indicated by dispositional stability (e.g., resilience under
counter-evidence and adversity) and by behavioral uptake.
Descriptions of a “highest form” of faith (e.g., intuitive or affective certitude) or putative moral
correlates (e.g., necessary purity/rectitude) are tradition-relative theses. We therefore bracket


such claims here and, in later sections, test the triadic model comparatively against authorized
scriptural corpora (Bible, Qurʾān, Bábí and Bahá’í writings) and against selected theorists (al-
Ashʿarī, Kierkegaard, Tillich, Wittgenstein). This keeps the analysis responsive to texts while
preventing the importation of devotional conclusions as if they were linguistic facts.
Faith in the Bible
In Hebrews, chapter 11, we read: “Faith is the assurance of things we hope for and the proof of
what we do not yet see. It was by faith that the ancients received commendation. By faith we
understand that the universe was formed by the word of God, so that what is seen did not come
from visible things. By faith Abel offered to God a better sacrifice than Cain, and because of this
faith it was testified about him that he was righteous, for God bore witness concerning his gifts.
And so, though he has passed from this world, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken from
this world so that he did not taste death and was not found, because God took him; for before he
was taken it was testified of him that he pleased God. And without faith it is impossible to please
God, for whoever draws near to Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who
diligently seek Him. By faith Noah, when warned by God about things not yet seen, took heed
with godly fear and built an ark to save his household. By his faith he condemned the world and
became an heir of the righteousness that is according to faith. By faith Abraham, when called,
obeyed and was ready to go to a place he would later receive as an inheritance; and although he
did not know where he was going, he set out. By faith he sojourned in the promised land as in a
foreign country, dwelling in tents, like Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same
promise; for he was looking forward to a city with foundations, whose architect and builder is
God. By faith Abraham received the power to beget offspring, though Sarah was barren and he
himself was old; for he considered the One who promised to be faithful. Thus from one man—
indeed, from one as good as dead—descended a multitude as numerous as the stars of the sky
and as countless as the sand on the seashore. All of these died in faith without having received
the promises, but they saw them from afar and welcomed them. They confessed that they were
strangers and exiles on the earth…. By faith Abraham, when tested, offered up Isaac; and he who
had received the promises was ready to sacrifice his only son, the very one of whom it had been
said, ‘Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.’ Abraham reasoned that God was able even
to raise the dead, and in a manner of speaking he did receive Isaac back from death. By faith
Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed


each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped while leaning on the top of his staff. By faith Joseph, as he
neared the end of his life, spoke of the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions concerning
his bones. By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after his birth, for they saw that he
was an extraordinary child, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when
grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. He chose to suffer affliction with the
people of God rather than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He regarded disgrace for the sake
of Christ as of greater value than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to the reward.
By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s wrath, for he persevered as seeing the Invisible One.
By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood so that the destroyer of the firstborn
would not touch the firstborn of Israel. By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry
land; but when the Egyptians attempted to do so, they were drowned. By faith the walls of
Jericho fell after the people had marched around them for seven days. By faith Rahab the
prostitute did not perish with the disobedient, because she had welcomed the spies in peace.”
(Heb 11:1–31, NRSV; specific loci: 11:1–7, 8–16, 17–22, 23–31)
Likewise, in John 20:29 we read: “Jesus said to him, ‘Because you have seen me, you have
believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.’” (NRSV)
In light of these verses one may say that faith appears as a deep and multidimensional reality
rooted in trust, conviction, and unwavering belief in the unseen and the sacred. Faith is described
as assurance and certainty concerning hoped-for things and as evidence of realities not
immediately accessible to the senses. It transcends the empirical realm and provides an
apprehension of truth grounded not in physical proof but in intuitive insight.
The narratives in these passages show that faith is not a passive belief but an active power that
prompts decisive actions. Abel’s offering and Noah’s building of the ark, for example, are
attributed to their faith, which moved them to act in ways aligned with the will of God.
Abraham’s willingness to sacrifice Isaac—(and, in the Islamic version, Ishmael)—and Sarah’s
trust in God’s promise are further instances of how faith shapes human conduct even amid
adversity and uncertainty.


Moreover, faith is portrayed as essential to relationship with God, for without it one cannot
please Him. Believers are depicted as those who not only believe in God’s existence but trust in
His promises and earnestly seek Him. Such trust issues in righteousness, as evidenced by those
who, though they did not receive complete fulfillment of the promises in their lifetimes,
remained steadfast in their conviction.
Within this same biblical horizon, classical Christian theology articulates faith with greater
precision. Drawing directly on Hebrews 11:1, Thomas Aquinas treats faith as ordered to realities
not seen and as intrinsically oriented to hope’s object, “the substance of things hoped for and the
evidence of things not seen,” a description he receives as paradigmatic of faith’s structure
(Aquinas, ST II–II, q.1, a.4; q.4, a.1). On the Thomistic account—presented in modern terms by
Étienne Gilson—faith is a properly theological virtue whose efficient cause and formal object is
God Himself, prima veritas (Gilson, 1993, 2000). It is, formally, an assent of the intellect to
what God reveals because God speaks; materially it concerns propositions taught by revelation;
and efficiently it is produced in us by grace as a divine gift (Aquinas, ST II–II, q.1, a.1–2; q.2,
a.9–10; q.6, a.1). The act is intellectual, but it is commanded by the will under grace (“an act of
mind assenting to divine truth by virtue of the command of the will as moved by God”), so that
the believer’s adhesion is grounded not in demonstrative vision but in the authority of the One
believed (Aquinas, ST II–II, q.1, a.1; q.2, a.9). In the Franciscan stream, St. Bonaventure (as read
by Gilson) emphasizes the adhesion of the believer to what revelation teaches, highlighting the
personalist contour of credal assent (Gilson, 1965).
These definitions carry characteristic claims that resonate with the epideictic catalogue of
Hebrews 11. First, faith rests on divine authority and revelation—credere Deo, Deum, in
Deum—and is thus distinct in formal object from scientia or purely philosophical demonstration,
even while “preambles of faith” may be accessible to reason (Aquinas, ST II–II, q.1, a.4; q.2,
a.10). Second, because its ground is divine truth, faith yields a distinctive certitude—a firmness
of adhesion stronger than many merely probable opinions—yet remains faith precisely insofar as
its object is non visum (II–II, q.4, a.8). Third, faith is fides quaerens intellectum: it seeks
understanding without ceasing to be faith, in the Augustinian and Anselmian line (“unless you
believe, you will not understand”; “faith seeking understanding”) (Augustine, 1997; Anselm,
1995). Fourth, believing what is unseen is meritorious insofar as it proceeds from a will moved


by grace, and faith endures until it is superseded by the beatific vision, when belief gives way to
sight (Aquinas, ST II–II, q.2, a.2; q.5, a.1). Finally, charity is the form of faith (caritas as forma
fidei): acts of faith not yet informed by love are imperfect, whereas perfected faith is animated by
charity (II–II, q.4, a.3–4). None of this entails “blind faith”: classical theology allows motives of
credibility—signs, testimony, miracles—as rationally relevant dispositions toward assent, even
though they do not cause the act of faith itself (II–II, q.2, a.9–10).
Contemporary analytic distinctions complement (and sometimes recast) these theses. Apologetic
writers often differentiate “belief that” (evidential assent to propositions) from “belief in”
(personal trust), arguing that the former frequently provides rational grounding for the latter
(Geisler, 1998; Geisler & Turek, 2004). On this view, all worldviews—including atheism and
agnosticism—advance truth-claims that require some fiduciary posture; neutrality is not
exemption from belief. Responsible belief proportionates assent to the probability and evidence
actually available, recognizing that many central commitments concern “things not seen” (Heb
11:1; John 20:29) and so cannot be assimilated to empirical science without remainder (Geisler,
1998; Geisler & Turek, 2004; cf. Aquinas, ST II–II, q.1, a.4). Methodologically, evangelical
scholarship also warns that a priori preunderstandings can distort historical judgments (e.g.,
some reconstructions of the “historical Jesus”); hence the call for methodological self-awareness
in belief-formation (Farnell, Geisler, & Holden, 2016). At the same time, some scholars caution
against “bibliolatry,” the over-identification of Scripture as an end rather than the divinely given
means to the knowledge of God (Wallace, 2011).
When attention shifts from the believer to the belief as a propositional content in the biblical–
theological register, additional claims appear. For Aquinas, the formal object of faith is First
Truth, presented “by way of a proposition” to which the intellect assents; in this sense, “nothing
false can come under faith” properly so called, since faith adheres to divine truth (Aquinas, ST
II–II, q.1, a.1; q.1, a.3, ad 3). Augustine’s maxim that we should not attribute error to Scripture
locates apparent contradictions in copyists, translators, or readers rather than in the divine Author
(Augustine, 1992, Serm. 43; 1997). Hermeneutically, the International Council on Biblical
Inerrancy (ICBI) argues that the meaning expressed by each biblical text is “single, definite, and
fixed,” to be sought by grammatico-historical exegesis attentive to literary form, with Scripture
interpreting Scripture; authorial intent and historical claims are to be received where the text


presents them as factual (ICBI, 1978; 1982). Logical norms such as the law of non-
contradiction govern interpretation, and functional accounts of Scripture (e.g., “wise unto
salvation”) may not be used to nullify its truth-claims or to subordinate them to external
scientific hypotheses about origins in a way that overturns the text’s teaching (ICBI, 1978;
1982).
In sum, faith is presented as a dynamic and transformative force that connects individuals to the
divine, guides their actions, shapes their identity, and sustains them through life’s trials. It is both
the foundation of religious experience and the means by which believers align themselves with
divine purpose even when faced with challenges that strain the limits of human understanding.
Faith in Islam
In Islam, faith is a many-sided concept that includes belief in the unseen, complete trust in God,
and commitment to live according to His commandments. It is not merely intellectual assent to
certain teachings; rather, it is a dynamic and transformative state that touches every dimension of
a believer’s life.
The Qurʾān presents faith as a fundamental quality that defines the relationship between the
believer and God. In Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:177, it states: “Righteousness is not that you turn your
faces toward the east or the west, but true righteousness is this: to believe in God and the Last
Day and the angels and the Book and the prophets, and to give wealth—despite love for it—to
relatives, orphans, the needy, the wayfarer, beggars, and for freeing slaves; and to establish
prayer and give alms; and those who fulfill their covenants when they make them; and those who
are patient in hardship and adversity and in times of conflict. Such are the truthful, and such are
the God-fearing.” This verse underscores that true faith includes belief in God, the Last Day, the
angels, the Book, and the prophets, inseparably bound to righteous deeds such as charity, prayer,
and patience in tribulation. Faith, therefore, is not confined to verbal profession; it must be
manifested through actions corresponding to divine commands.
Faith in Islam also requires unwavering commitment even in the face of personal or social
opposition. Sūrat al-Mujādalah 58:22 expresses this as follows: “You will not find a people who
believe in God and the Last Day loving those who oppose God and His Messenger, even if they


be their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their clan. In their hearts He has inscribed faith and
supported them with a spirit from Himself, and He will admit them into gardens beneath which
rivers flow, to abide therein forever. God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him.
These are the party of God—indeed, it is the party of God who are the successful.”
Further, the Qurʾān presents faith as a source of spiritual strength and tranquility. Sūrat al-Fatḥ
48:4 states: “It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers, that they might
increase in faith upon their faith; and to God belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth, and
God is ever Knowing, Wise.”
And in Sūrat al-Nūr 24:62: “The true believers are only those who have believed in God and His
Messenger and who, when they gather with him for a matter of common concern, do not depart
until seeking his permission. Indeed, those who ask your permission—such are they who believe
in God and His Messenger. So when they ask you leave for some of their affairs, grant leave to
whom you will of them, and ask God’s forgiveness for them; surely God is All-forgiving, All-
merciful.”
Islamic ḥadīth and the interpretations of Muslim scholars also provide definitions of faith; a few
are noted here by way of indication:
The Prophet of Islam is reported to have said that faith is “affirmation with the heart, confession
with the tongue, and action with the limbs and members.” (Biḥār al-Anwār, vol. 66, p. 68).
From Imām ʿAlī: “The root of faith is to submit well to the command of God.” (Sharḥ Ghurar
al-Ḥikam, Āmidī, vol. 2, p. 416, University of Tehran).
Also from him: “Faith is a tree whose root is certitude, whose branch is piety, whose light is
modesty, and whose fruit is generosity.” (Sharḥ Ghurar al-Ḥikam, Āmidī, vol. 2, p. 47).
Shaykh Ṭabrisī, author of the Qurʾānic exegesis Majmaʿ al-Bayān, defines faith as: “assenting to
all those things whose assent God has made obligatory.” (Majmaʿ al-Bayān, vol. 10, p. 238).
Within this Qurʾānic horizon, classical Islamic doctrine defines īmān as firm assent to God
(Allāh), His oneness and perfect attributes, and confirmation of all that the Messenger conveys


about unseen realities. In the Ḥadīth of Jibrīl, faith is “to believe in God, His angels, His books,
His messengers, the Last Day, and in the divine decree (al-qadar), its good and its bad,” while
islām is the outward pillars and iḥsān is worshiping God as though one sees Him (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim,
Kitāb al-Īmān). This six-article content coheres with Qurʾānic summons to comprehensive assent
(e.g., Q 4:136) and with 2:177’s inseparability of conviction and righteous action (Abdel
Haleem, 2004). Classical Sunnī statements and widely transmitted maxims add that faith is
word and deed; it increases and decreases (cf. Q 8:2; 48:4), and its motive is seeking God’s
pleasure. In Imāmī sources, īmān is taṣdīq in what God has made obligatory to affirm (al-
Ṭabrisī, Majmaʿ al-Bayān, 10:238), while reports from ʿAlī link faith to submission to the divine
command and portray it as a tree with certitude as root and generosity as fruit (al-Āmidī,
Ghurar al-Ḥikam).
Doctrinally, tawḥīd functions as the spirit and foundation of the religion. Later systematic
theology often expounds its scope under three interlocking aspects: lordship (tawḥīd al-
rubūbiyya), that God alone creates, sustains, and disposes (e.g., Q 7:54; 39:62; 51:58); worship
(tawḥīd al-ulūhiyya), that worship is God’s exclusive right (Q 1:5; 39:3); and names and
attributes (tawḥīd al-asmāʾ wa-l-ṣifāt), affirming what God and His Messenger affirm “without
alteration, negation, asking how, or likening,” while maintaining transcendence (Q 59:22–24;
42:11). This tripartite taxonomy is a systematic exposition rather than a Qurʾānic lexical
division, but it encapsulates the scriptural insistence that God be known, worshiped, and
described aright.
From doctrine to habitus, the believer (muʾmin) is marked not only by assent but by embodied
fidelity. The Prophet is reported to have said that faith comprises affirmation with the heart,
confession by the tongue, and action by the limbs (al-Majlisī, Biḥār al-Anwār, 66:68).
Canonical ḥadīth map the branches of faith: “Faith has over seventy branches, the lowest
removing harm from the road and the highest the statement ‘Lā ilāha illā Allāh,’” and “modesty
is part of faith” (al-Bukhārī, Īmān; Muslim, Īmān). They also delineate interior affect: the
sweetness of faith is tasted when God and His Messenger are dearer than all else, when love is
for God’s sake, and when one would sooner face fire than return to unbelief (al-Bukhārī, Īmān;
Muslim, Īmān). Ethical and communal dispositions are integral: “The Muslim is the one from
whose tongue and hand people are safe,” “Whoever believes in God and the Last Day should


speak good or remain silent,” “honor the neighbor,” “honor the guest,” and “spread peace
(salām) among you”—explicitly linked to mutual love and entry into Paradise (Muslim, Īmān;
Birr wa-l-ṣila). Conversely, the signs of hypocrisy include betrayal, lying, breach of covenant,
and abusive disputation (al-Bukhārī, Īmān; Muslim, Īmān). In the register of praxis,
“purification is half of faith”; prayer is light, charity proof, patience illumination, and the
Qurʾān a witness for or against one (Muslim, Ṭahāra; Ṣalāh). Asked about the best deed, the
Prophet prioritized belief in God and His Messenger—placing faith as the fountainhead of the
virtues (al-Bukhārī, Īmān; Muslim, Īmān).
At the same time, the tradition specifies minimums and margins: the believer resists evil with
hand, tongue, or heart—“and beyond that there is not a mustard-seed of faith” (Muslim, Īmān);
grave sins diminish faith but do not, in classical jurisprudence, ipso facto expel one from Islam,
with repentance always open (al-Bukhārī, Hudūd; Muslim, Īmān). Soteriologically, even “a
speck of faith” bears consequence—God brings forth from the Fire those who possess it (al-
Bukhārī, Tawḥīd; Muslim, Īmān). Finally, belief in divine decree (qadar)—that “what struck
could not have missed and what missed could not have struck”—is integral to faith’s tranquility
and resilience (Muslim, Īmān; al-Tirmidhī, Qadar). Warnings against innovation in religion,
paired with the maxim that the best guidance is that of Muḥammad, reinforce the imperative to
hold fast to the Qurʾān and the Prophetic Sunnah—alongside, in Imāmī teaching, the guidance of
the Imams—especially when truth and falsehood are mingled (Muslim, Ḥajj; al-Tirmidhī, ʿIlm;
al-Ṭabrisī, Majmaʿ al-Bayān).
Philosophically, classical logic and kalām describe assent (taṣdīq) as a state of the intellect
produced through syllogistic or equivalent reasoning (qiyās/burhān)—for example, assenting
that the world has a Creator—while accepted reports (khabar) yield belief by virtue of the
perceived truthfulness of the speaker, a structure that grounds reception of prophetic and
imamic teaching. In this register, faith is not reducible to bare propositional assent; rather, it is
assent shaped by trust, enacted in worship and character, and increased by obedience (Q 49:14–
15; 48:4).
Faith in the Bábí/Bahá’í Dispensation
In the Bayān, the Báb frames faith as recognition and steadfast assent to “the Point of the Bayān”
and to the verses revealed in His Day. Faith is not a merely inward state but an ontological


reconstitution of the self: “For the creatures I have created, no paradise is higher than to stand in
the presence of My Self and to believe in My verses; and no fire is more intense than that these
creatures should be veiled from the Manifestation of My Self and fail to believe in My verses”
(The Báb, Bayān-i Fārsī, Vāḥid II, bāb 1). The image of the mirror turning to the sun captures
the epistemic and ethical consequence of such recognition: orientation confers illumination;
estrangement leaves one “rising and setting” in vain. Faith’s scope is explicitly inter-
dispensational: those truly within the Qurʾānic and Gospel economies must, by the logic of
recognition, acknowledge the subsequent Manifestation; failure to do so discloses a defect in the
prior assent itself (Vāḥid II, bāb 16). Degrees of faith appear both noetically and
performatively: some believe at hearing, some at beholding, others linger “upon the Path,” their
progress measured not by duration but by responsiveness to revealed verses (Vāḥid II, bāb 12).
Crucially, recognition in one Theophany normatively entails recognition of the next: “Whoever
believes in ‘He Whom God shall make manifest’ … has believed in God from the One of Whom
there is no first” (Vāḥid III, bāb 15).
The Báb distinguishes four maqāmāt and corresponding classes of adherents, indexing
ascending comprehension of His station: those who regarded Him as Bāb to the Qāʾim (awlu’l-
ajsād), as the Qāʾim (awlu’l-anfus), as Messenger and Pen of Revelation (awlu’l-arwāḥ), and
as the Primal Will (mashīʾat-i Ūlā) (awlu’l-afʾidah)—“the first degree of faith.” Each class
adduces proofs appropriate to its horizon (cited in the paraphrase you provided). The taxonomy
makes “faith” intrinsically graded and oriented to recognition of divine maqām.
Bahá’u’lláh: recognition, purification, enactment. In the Bahá’í dispensation, faith retains this
recognitive core while being cast as an integrated disposition binding assent, trust, and
enactment. “The first effulgence … was the knowledge of God,” yet “knowledge of the Ancient
King is not attained save by knowledge of the Greatest Name”; thus, “faith in God and
knowledge of Him are not complete save by confessing what hath issued forth from Him and by
acting in accordance with what He hath commanded” (Bahá’u’lláh, Lawḥ-i-ʿAbdu’r-Razzáq).
Bahá’u’lláh repeatedly defines the essence of faith as “fewness of words and abundance of
deeds,” and enjoins purification and detachment as prerequisites for certitude: “cleanse the eye
of thine heart from the things of the world … [so that] thou wilt need no proof” (Bahá’u’lláh,
Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh, pp. 156–59; The Seven Valleys and the Four Valleys, pp. 3–18). Faith is


an ascetic of the will no less than an epistemic adherence: “The fear of God is the fountainhead
of all goodly deeds and virtues,” the “commander of the hosts of justice,” guarding against moral
and civic disintegration when the “lamp of religion” is obscured (Bahá’u’lláh, Tablets of
Bahá’u’lláh, pp. 120–22; Gleanings, pp. 205–210).
At the same time, recognition of the Manifestation remains definitive: “The true Faith hath laid
fast hold, in this day, on the hem of Our bounty, and circleth about Our Person” (Bahá’u’lláh,
Gleanings, p. 136). To refuse what God declares—even if it overturns inherited categories—is to
fall outside faith: “All have been—and shall be—adorned with the robe of faith through
confessing God … apart from this, they are unmentioned” (Bahá’u’lláh, Lawḥ-i-ʿAbdu’r-
Razzáq). This logic underwrites Bahá’u’lláh’s own self-disclosure: “He Who now voiceth the
Word of God is none other except the Primal Point Who hath once again been made manifest”
(Gleanings, p. 104).
‘Abdu’l-Bahá: two kinds of faith; the eternal ethical core. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá sharply distinguishes
(without separating) confessional faith (“recognition expressed by the tongue”) and operative
faith (“expressed through deeds”)—each necessary for integrity of īmān (Selections from the
Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá [SWAB], §227). The ethical content of faith is perennial and
unabrogated: “spiritual virtues and divine qualities … faith, knowledge, certitude, justice, piety,
righteousness, trustworthiness, love of God, benevolence, purity, detachment, humility,
meekness, patience and constancy” (Some Answered Questions [SAQ], pp. 148, 302). Faith is
“life eternal” and the sign of bounty—graced attraction more than human technique (SAQ, p.
215); it is also a mediated epistemic access through which one “believe[s] in God” by reasoning,
observation, and the revealing power of faith (Tablet to Auguste Forel, pp. 11–12 [numbering
varies by edition]).
Who is a believer? In Bábí–Bahá’í terms, a believer is one who has recognized the
Manifestation of God, adhered to His Covenant, and enacted His law with purified intention.
For the Báb, “no paradise is higher” than belief in the verses of the Manifestation; for
Bahá’u’lláh, the “first and foremost testimony” is His own Self, then His Revelation, then His
Words (Bahá’u’lláh, Gleanings, pp. 106–07). ‘Abdu’l-Bahá universalizes the mark of true
discipleship: deeds conformed to inner life, fortitude, daily communion, justice, courtesy,
trustworthiness, generosity, and the refusal of backbiting (SWAB §§1, 73, 139, 202). The


believer seeks with “the lamp of search … and fervid love,” detaches from “idle sayings” and
“acquired knowledge” that occlude vision, and consorts with all “in a spirit of friendliness and
fellowship” (Seven Valleys, pp. 4–7; Gleanings, pp. 95–97). Spiritually, those “born of the Spirit”
in every dispensation attain “life” and “resurrection,” while the obdurate incur the metaphorical
“death” of unbelief (Gleanings, pp. 140–42).
Belief, authority, and interpretation. In the Bahá’í order, belief is tethered to authenticated
Text and authorized interpretation. Only Tablets bearing the seal or signature of Bahá’u’lláh
or ‘Abdu’l-Bahá have binding authority; pilgrims’ notes and unauthenticated reports are non-
authoritative. The Centre of the Covenant (‘Abdu’l-Bahá) and, subsequently, the Guardian
(Shoghi Effendi) hold interpretive authority; “no other interpreters whatsoever” exist (Shoghi
Effendi, The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh [WOB], pp. 3–5, 97–104; Lights of Guidance, nos.
144–147). Divine truth is relative in the sense of progressive disclosure; individual interpretation
is commendable as a personal aid to understanding, provided it neither claims authority nor
foments contention (WOB, pp. 58–62). Core beliefs include the existence and oneness of a
personal God (unknowable Essence), the unity of the Prophets and continuity of Revelation,
the non-incarnation of the divine Essence, and the infallibility of the Manifestations as the
educative link with God (Bahá’u’lláh, Gleanings, pp. 46–55; Shoghi Effendi, The Dispensation
of Bahá’u’lláh in WOB, pp. 97–157).
The Báb’s Covenant anticipates belief in “Him Whom God shall make manifest”; the Bahá’í
Covenant centers on Bahá’u’lláh, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, and the institutions they establish. To be a true
believer, Shoghi Effendi specifies, requires full recognition of the Forerunner, Author, and
True Exemplar, loyal adherence to their Writings, and close association with the Bahá’í
Administrative Order, which “derives its authority” from ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s Will and Testament
and rests on provisions of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas (Shoghi Effendi, World Order, pp. 134–41, 143–46;
Bahá’í Administration, pp. 62–64). The Order is an instrument—not a substitute—for the Faith;
to sunder them is to mutilate the Cause (WOB, pp. 144–46). Practical corollaries follow: non-
interference in partisan politics, obligatory consultation with Spiritual Assemblies on Cause-
related steps, disciplined study of the Text, and universal responsibility to teach (Shoghi Effendi,
The Advent of Divine Justice, pp. 23–41; WOB, pp. 64–67).


The Bahá’í doctrine of progressive revelation maintains that all major religions are divine in
origin, harmonious in principles, and successive in mission; it repudiates finality for any single
dispensation and aims at the unification of their followers (Shoghi Effendi, The Promised Day Is
Come, pp. x–xii; WOB, pp. 57–61). Accordingly, the Faith enjoins unfettered search for truth,
harmony of religion and science, equality of women and men, compulsory education, elimination
of extremes of wealth and poverty, abolition of priesthood and slavery, monogamy, obedience to
government, work as worship, an auxiliary international language, and institutions for collective
security (Shoghi Effendi, World Order, pp. 41–52, 202–210; Gleanings, pp. 249–270). These are
not optional addenda but the ethical entailments of faith’s recognition-trust-enactment triad.
Both Bábí and Bahá’í texts insist that the touchstone of true belief is the Manifestation—self,
revelation, and verses as conjoint proofs. Divine pedagogy includes tests that sift sincerity;
moral transformation (fear of God, justice, steadfastness, purity of heart) evidences authentic
faith (Bahá’u’lláh, Gleanings, pp. 197–205; Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh, pp. 47–50). Conversely,
superstition—occult numerologies, demonologies, pyramid-prophecies—is excluded from the
economy of belief; Scriptural narratives (e.g., Adam, the Flood) bear symbolic meanings, and in
illness the Text enjoins recourse to competent physicians (Shoghi Effendi, Lights of Guidance,
nos. 1477, 1518, 1523; Bahá’u’lláh, The Kitáb-i-Aqdas, ¶113).
Read together, the Bábí/Bahá’í sources construe faith as a graded, practice-bound disposition:
a truth-indexed assent to the Manifestation (recognition), a volitional trust (detachment, fear of
God, covenantal loyalty), and an enactment (deeds exceeding words) ordered to the
Manifestation’s law and aims. Degrees of faith map to degrees of recognition and obedience;
the believer’s identity—kaynūniyyat—is transfigured by orientation to the Sun of Truth. In this
dispensation, therefore, “all knowledge and all faith is this: that a person should look and derive
the fruit of his existence … and in the presence of any Manifestation be nothing but pure ‘death’
[self-effacement]” (The Báb, Bayān-i Fārsī, Vāḥid III, bāb 12).
The Question of Faith in Abū’l-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī
Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī frames īmān as taṣdīq—an inward assent or affirmation—and thus a
believer is the one who assents. In his kalām writings, assent concerns the truth of God’s
existence, His attributes, His messengers, and the binding character of His commands and
prohibitions. The act of taṣdīq is not identical with ʿilm (knowledge) in the logical sense, nor


with taṣawwur (mere conception); rather, knowledge is that by which assent is achieved. Put
differently, maʿrifa (cognition) is a necessary prelude and instrument to faith but is not, as such,
faith itself (al-Ashʿarī, 1953; al-Juwaynī, 2000).
On Ashʿarī principles, faith must be warranted by evidence (dalīl). Reflection or inquiry
(naẓar) is religiously obligatory for arriving at knowledge of God; prophetic revelation furnishes
the primary data and the norm for such inquiry. Hence, taqlīd—merely holding what others say
without proof—does not meet the ideal of theological faith, even if it imitates its conclusions.
Within the Ashʿarī school there arose a well-known intra-school debate about the status of the
muqallid (the imitator): some authorities (e.g., early readings of al-Bāqillānī) held that a belief
formed without one’s own dalīl fails to attain the technical reality of īmān; other Ashʿarīs
conceded that such belief may suffice for legal and communal purposes while remaining
theologically deficient. What is common, however, is the normative requirement that faith be
grounded—by rational argument, by soundly transmitted proof, or by both (al-Bāqillānī, 1966;
al-Juwaynī, 2000; Gardet & Anawati, 1986).
Al-Ashʿarī also distinguishes īmān from islām. Islām designates outward submission and
compliance, whereas īmān names inward assent rooted in the heart. The relation is thus part–
whole: genuine assent entails submission, but submission—taken as outward profession and
performance—need not rise to the level of inward assent. The Qurʾān itself articulates this
evaluative contrast: “The desert Arabs say, ‘We have believed.’ Say, ‘You have not believed;
rather say, “We have submitted,” for faith has not yet entered your hearts’” (Q 49:14; cf. 49:17),
a locus classicus for Ashʿarī exegesis of the distinction (Abdel Haleem, 2004). In the same spirit,
al-Bāqillānī—expounding Ashʿarī doctrine—formulates a two-tier summary: faith is to believe
in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day; islām is to testify to divine
unity and Muḥammad’s messengership and to perform the pillars (profession, prayer,
almsgiving, fasting, pilgrimage). This maps theological assent (īmān) and ritual submission
(islām) onto the complementary agencies of heart and limbs, without collapsing one into the
other (al-Bāqillānī, 1966, pp. 24–28; cf. al-Juwaynī, 2000, pp. 106–113).
Two further clarifications, standard in the Ashʿarī tradition, refine this profile:
Increase and decrease of faith. Because īmān is defined technically as taṣdīq, many Ashʿarīs
deny quantitative increase/decrease in its essence: assent is either realized or not. They


nonetheless allow talk of “strengthening” faith—by broadened evidences, repeated affirmation,
removal of countervailing doubts, or augmentation of obedience—without thereby treating the
reality of taṣdīq as a scalar quantity. Later Ashʿarīs (e.g., al-Ghazālī) acknowledge that certitude
admits intensification phenomenologically while preserving the juridical–theological identity of
īmān as assent (al-Juwaynī, 2000; al-Ghazālī, 2013).
The contrary of faith. On Ashʿarī definitions, the opposite of taṣdīq is takdhīb/inkār
(denial/rejection), not mere ignorance. Thus unbelief (kufr) is essentially the negation of assent to
what God and His Messenger have brought; culpability then tracks access to proof and refusal of
it (al-Ashʿarī, 1953; Winter, 2008).
In sum, the Ashʿarī position construes īmān as inward assent (taṣdīq) to revealed truth,
normatively acquired through inquiry and proof; islām as outward compliance; and imitative
acceptance without dalīl as falling short of the doctrinal ideal, even where juristic status and
communal belonging may be recognized. This preserves both the primacy of the heart in faith
and the indispensability of reasoned warrant and transmitted authority in its formation.
Faith in the Philosophy of Søren Kierkegaard
Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855), conceives faith not as the bare assent of the intellect but as an
existential stance: a passionate appropriation of a paradox that places the single individual in an
absolute relation to God. In his pseudonymous writings (Johannes de Silentio in Fear and
Trembling; Johannes Climacus in Philosophical Fragments and Concluding Unscientific
Postscript), faith is described as a venture undertaken at the boundary where objective
demonstration ends. “Truth is subjectivity” names not the abolition of logical or scientific truth
but the claim that, in religious matters, what ultimately matters is how one exists in relation to
what is believed—whether one attains to inwardness, earnestness, and obedient trust when the
object of faith is objectively uncertain (Kierkegaard, 1992). Hence the “leap” is neither caprice
nor irrationalism; it is the individual’s decision to entrust herself to God where reason has
reached its own limit before the “absolute paradox,” the eternal in time—Christ (Kierkegaard,
1985, 1992).
Kierkegaard’s paradigmatic analysis of faith is the story of Abraham. Commanded to sacrifice
Isaac, Abraham faces an apparent contradiction: the divine promise that Isaac will be the son


through whom the covenant descends, and the command to slay that very son. If judged by the
universal categories of ethics, Abraham can only appear as a would-be murderer; if judged by the
calculus of reason, the promise and the command are mutually canceling. Yet Abraham proceeds
“by virtue of the absurd”: he resigns Isaac absolutely (infinite resignation) and, beyond
resignation, believes that God will nevertheless restore him (faith) (Kierkegaard, 1983). In this
moment Abraham undergoes what de Silentio calls the teleological suspension of the ethical: the
ethical, as the universal, cannot mediate the singular individual’s absolute duty to God. The point
is not that ethics is false or dispensable, but that in this extremity the single individual stands
immediately before the Absolute in a way that the universal cannot comprehend or authorize
(Kierkegaard, 1983).
This is the setting for Kierkegaard’s “knight of faith” (often, in casual usage, heard as “night of
faith”). The knight of faith resembles any moral person outwardly—he returns to the finite, loves
spouse and child, works, buys provisions—yet inwardly he lives in absolute dependence upon
God, continually performing the double movement of resignation and trust. He is not a visionary
who escapes the ethical but the one who, having passed through the ethical’s highest seriousness,
receives it back on new terms, “by virtue of the absurd.” The contrast with the tragic hero is
decisive: Agamemnon sacrifices Iphigenia for the sake of a universal ethical end (the polis); the
tragic hero remains intelligible within ethical categories. Abraham cannot be rendered intelligible
in this way; his act is either madness or faith, either offense or paradox (Kierkegaard, 1983).
Hence the knight of faith is beyond the merely “moral person” not because he despises morality,
but because in a singular relation to God he enacts a form of obedience that the moral universal
cannot ratify without ceasing to be universal. This “beyond” is qualitative, not hierarchical self-
exaltation; it is marked by silence and inward dread, not by antinomian license.
For Kierkegaard, faith does not annul doubt; doubt is faith’s dialectical companion. Climacus
insists that Christian faith holds fast to objective uncertainty “with the most passionate
inwardness”—if the paradox were rationally domesticated, faith would collapse into knowledge
and the pathos of existence would be lost (Kierkegaard, 1992). In Philosophical Fragments, this
is cast as the problem of contemporaneity: no accumulation of historical evidence can make one
“contemporary” with the God-man; the relation demanded is a present decision either to believe
(and be scandalized no more) or to take offense at the paradox (Kierkegaard, 1985). Thus faith is


a continual task, not an achieved possession: a life of repetition in which the believer daily
chooses God amid anxiety, temptation, and the susceptibility to offense.
Kierkegaard’s later works clarify the existential depth of this stance. In The Sickness unto Death,
faith is the self’s resting “transparently in the power that established it,” the antithesis of
despair—the refusal either to be itself before God or to will to be itself independently of God
(Kierkegaard, 1980). In Works of Love, the ethical fruit of faith appears as neighbor-love
commanded by God; here Kierkegaard shows that Christian existence is morally fecund
precisely because it is grounded theologically, not because it is deduced from autonomous
ethical universals (Kierkegaard, 1995). Far from granting a standing exception to morality, faith
makes the individual answerable to God in a way that generates concrete, sacrificial love; but it
also preserves the boundary that, in the Abrahamic extremity, no “ethical” tribunal can cross. The
knight of faith thus stands beyond the “moral person” in the sense that his ultimate court of
appeal is not the universal ethical but the God before whom he stands as single individual; and
precisely this God-relation, in ordinary time, returns him to the finite world as a lover of
neighbor and a doer of the good.
In summary, Kierkegaard reconfigures faith as a passionate, enacted appropriation of paradox by
the single individual before God: a leap into trusting obedience that neither reason can compel
nor ethics can fully comprehend, yet which bears ethical fruit. Abraham’s situation reveals why
faith must at once transcend the moral universal and transfigure it: beyond morality in the
moment of absolute duty to God, but returning to the world as a life of love commanded by God
(Kierkegaard, 1983, 1985, 1992).
Paul Tillich and Faith
Paul Tillich construes faith as “being ultimately concerned,” a total and centered act in which the
whole person—intellect, will, affect, conscious and unconscious—stands committed to that
which unconditionally claims one’s allegiance (Tillich, 1957). As ultimate concern, faith cannot
be reduced to any single faculty (reason, will, or feeling) nor identified with “beliefs” taken as
merely propositional assent; it is an existential orientation of the self toward the unconditional,
from which beliefs, feelings, and volitions take their measure (Tillich, 1957). Because the object
of faith is the ultimate itself, any finite reality that is elevated to ultimacy—nation, success, party,
or even a religious form—produces a demonic distortion: the finite absolutizes itself, demands


total surrender, and destroys both personality and community (Tillich, 1957; 1951). This
diagnostic lets Tillich explain why modern political idolatries function “religiously” and why
their consequences are catastrophic.
Faith for Tillich is intrinsically risky and therefore intrinsically courageous. It lives with
existential doubt, not as the corrosive skepticism of method but as the inescapable mark of
finitude confronting the unconditional without the guarantee of demonstrative certainty (Tillich,
1957). Doubt belongs to faith’s very structure; where risk is abolished, faith collapses into
knowledge or fanaticism. Hence Tillich rejects three caricatures: a purely cognitive faith that
treats assent without existential surrender; a voluntarist faith, a willful decision unsupported by
the state of the self; and a merely emotive faith that evacuates cognitive and moral content.
Genuine faith is a centered act that integrates all dimensions of the person and accepts the
venture of uncertainty (Tillich, 1957).
Because the ultimate exceeds conceptual capture, faith’s expression is symbolic and mythic. A
symbol, for Tillich, does not merely point; it participates in the reality to which it refers, opens
otherwise inaccessible depths of self and world, cannot be manufactured at will, and “dies” when
it ceases to disclose the ultimate (Tillich, 1957). Accordingly, “God” functions in theology not as
a being among beings, an object alongside others, but as the ground of being and the name for
that which concerns us ultimately (Tillich, 1951). Taken literally as a supreme object, God
becomes finite and idol-like; grasped symbolically, the term breaks open the depth-dimension of
reality and the human condition. Tillich’s “Protestant principle” generalizes this iconoclasm:
every finite bearer of the holy—doctrines, institutions, leaders—must remain revisable before the
ultimate they mediate, lest faith be displaced by idolatry (Tillich, 1948).
Faith is also inseparable from freedom. As the act of the centered self, it cannot be coerced
without ceasing to be faith; compulsion produces heteronomy and, at the limit, pathology
(Tillich, 1957). Tillich’s cultural analysis contrasts autonomy (self-legislation), heteronomy
(external domination), and theonomy (a form of cultural life in which autonomy is fulfilled
rather than negated by orientation to the ultimate). In theonomous existence, faith neither
overrides reason nor retreats into private feeling; instead, through the method of correlation,
faith answers the questions posed by existence—anxiety, meaning, estrangement—with symbols
and practices that reconstitute the self (Tillich, 1951; 1952).


The courage that sustains faith is not bravado but participation in the power of being that
overcomes nonbeing’s threats—guilt, fate, and death. Tillich famously describes “the courage to
be” as the courage “to accept acceptance,” the self’s reception of grace in the face of
unacceptability (Tillich, 1952). Here faith is both healing and dangerous: healing, insofar as
ultimate concern re-centers the self in forgiving power; dangerous, insofar as disordered
ultimacies (the demonic) can seize the same totalizing structure and bend it toward destruction.
The criterion is thus twofold: the ultimacy of the concern and its power to fulfill rather than
annihilate personhood and community (Tillich, 1957).
In sum, Tillich’s analysis yields an exacting grammar: faith is the person’s centered act of being
grasped by the ultimate; it is existentially risky and therefore courageous; it lives by symbols
that participate in the depth of reality; it is ever threatened by idolatrous distortions when the
finite masquerades as the ultimate; and it orients freedom not by coercion but by theonomy. On
this account, “religious” and “secular” phenomena are judged by the same measure: what
functions with ultimacy in a life or culture, and does it humanize or demonize? Faith so
understood is neither blind nor merely rational; it is the enacted seriousness of a life ordered to
what finally matters (Tillich, 1957; 1951; 1952).
Private Language, Language-Games, and the Question of Faith in Wittgenstein
Ludwig Wittgenstein’s later philosophy clarifies why a purely private “faith” would be
conceptually incoherent and why, conversely, the sense of “faith” is anchored in publicly
teachable practices. In Philosophical Investigations he confronts the idea of a “private
language”—a putative code whose words name items knowable only to a single subject—and
argues that such a language cannot have the kind of rule-governed meaning language requires.
Naming an inner item (a sensation) is not yet to give a rule for its correct use; without publicly
surveyable criteria, there is no distinction between “seems right” and “is right,” and thus no
standard of correctness at all (Wittgenstein, 2009, §§243, 258). His well-known “beetle in a box”
thought experiment makes the point vivid: if everyone had a box with a private “beetle” that no
one else could inspect, the word “beetle” would do its work without referring to any private
object; whatever is in the box “does not belong to the language-game at all” (Wittgenstein, 2009,
§293). The moral is not that we cannot speak of pains or faith but that the meaningful use of such
words presupposes publicly learnable criteria within shared practices.


This insistence on criteria coheres with Wittgenstein’s wider account of meaning as use within
“language-games,” themselves embedded in “forms of life” (Lebensformen). The speaking of a
language is part of an activity—requesting, promising, praying, confessing—each with its own
grammar, and there is no single essence common to all uses (family resemblance rather than
definition by necessary and sufficient conditions) (Wittgenstein, 2009, §§23, 65–71). On this
view, understanding what “faith” means requires attention to the practices in which it is
employed: prayer, liturgy, vows, obedience, consolation, testimony, exhortation. These are not
mere external accompaniments; they are the arena in which the rules for the word’s correct and
intelligible use are learned and sustained. A solipsistic, incommunicable “faith” would lack such
grammar and so would be no more a concept than a private “X” for a sensation.
Wittgenstein’s early boundary-drawing in the Tractatus complements this later therapeutic
analysis. There he famously concludes, “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent”
(Wittgenstein, 1961, 7), distinguishing what can be said (logically well-formed propositions
depicting facts) from what can only be shown (ethical, aesthetic, and “metaphysical”
significance). Although the later Wittgenstein abandons picture theory, he retains a discipline
about what counts as sense: we look to use, not to metaphysical postulates, for the measure of
meaning. In religious contexts, that disciplinary turn pushes us to describe how words like
“faith,” “grace,” or “providence” figure in a form of life rather than to hunt for inner objects to
which they secretly refer.
Wittgenstein’s scattered remarks on religion underscore this grammatical approach. In his
Lectures on Religious Belief he cautions that religious utterances are not typically hypotheses
about future events or empirical explanations; “I believe in a Last Judgment” is not a historical
prediction but part of a distinctive way of acting, reacting, and assessing—“a different attitude
from one which is scientific” (Wittgenstein, 1966, pp. 53–55). Elsewhere he suggests that a
religious belief is “a passionate commitment to a system of reference,” a frame within which
certain moves make sense and others do not (Wittgenstein, 1998, p. 64e). The upshot is not
quietism but grammatical clarity: to understand “faith,” we must map the roles the word plays
across the religious language-games in which it is at home, rather than reduce it to a purely
cognitive state or a private feeling.


Applied to faith, these theses yield both constraint and illumination. Constraint: a purely private
faith, detached from shareable criteria of use, cannot amount to a concept with norms of
correctness; it would be indistinguishable from whatever its possessor takes to be right “this
time.” Illumination: within a religious form of life, “faith” is not exhausted by assent to
propositions but is shown in patterns of commitment, avowal, hope, repentance, and trust—as
much enacted grammar as belief-that. Outsiders may misunderstand because they transpose
religious uses into alien games (treating “faith” as if it were a scientific hypothesis), while
insiders display understanding by moving aptly within the rules that govern prayer, witness,
obedience, and consolation. From a Wittgensteinian perspective, then, faith is neither a private
datum nor a reducible theory; it is a family of interwoven uses whose sense is fixed by the life in
which they have their home.
Finally, it is consistent with Wittgenstein’s later epistemology to note an analogy—handled
cautiously—between faith and the “hinge” certainties that undergird inquiry (On Certainty).
Some commitments are not empirically proved at every turn but function as the normative
background of what we do (e.g., trust in testimony within a community). Without assimilating
religious faith to these hinges, the analogy helps explain why attempts to force religious
language into alien justificatory molds often miss its point: the criteria by which “I have faith” is
judged apt or inapt are internal to the religious games that give it sense (Wittgenstein, 1975,
§§94–95, 163–166).
From Degrees of Faith to a Spectrum of Belonging
The analyses developed above—philological, scriptural, and philosophical—converge on a
working claim that “faith” is not exhausted by bare cognition but is a graded, practice-bound
integration of assent, trust, and enactment. This claim was stated programmatically at the outset
and operationalized in the article’s treatment of degrees of believers and the dynamics by which
conviction deepens or wanes in lived practice. In methodological terms, the present study also
pledged a skeptical discipline about conflating doctrine, culture, and translation—requiring that
any assertion about “faith” be either argumentatively warranted or anchored in authorized textual
economies.
These theses supply the conceptual ground for, and directly feed into, my companion study,
“Thresholds of Just-Being: Deficiency, Demise, and the Ontology of Belonging.” That essay


argues that religious identity is not a binary (believer/unbeliever) but a fragile continuum—a
spectrum of belonging—structured by varying degrees of orientation, care, and world-formation.
It introduces the phenomenological marker nur noch (“only still”) to name the deficient
believer: one who remains within the symbolic order of a tradition “just still a believer,” yet no
longer discloses the world through the Revelation’s telos. Where recognition persists without
enactment, faith survives as remainder rather than projection—identity in name rather than
existential presence.
Placed alongside the present article’s graded model, the spectrum account clarifies two poles. At
one end stands a positive mode of maximal nearness in which belief becomes “excess” rather
than sufficiency—each movement of the self called into higher accountability (“the good deeds
of the righteous are the sins of those who are nigh unto God”). At the other end stands deficient
suspension, where communal markers remain but orientation has gone inert; Revelation no
longer structures worldhood. In between lies a graded field of “becoming” and “withdrawing”
that maps precisely onto our account of faith’s degrees—dispositional stability under trial,
behavioral uptake, and the tightening or loosening of trustful enactment.
The normative consequences are twofold. First, by tying īmān to assent with warrant (Ashʿarī
taṣdīq under dalīl) while distinguishing outward islām from inward faith, the present article
explains why mere performance without recognition cannot instantiate belief; it is a different
mode of being. Second, by reading “faith” as a rule-governed practice within communal
language-games (Wittgenstein), we can diagnose nur noch as a grammatical failure of
enactment rather than a sheer loss of proposition assent: the words remain, but the use no longer
lives.
In short, the present inquiry frames the metrics (assent–trust–enactment, graded over time); the
companion article maps the field (from full existential presence to residual persistence). Readers
interested in the ontological and pastoral implications—how communities might discern,
accompany, and restore those inhabiting deficient modes without reducing identity to legal
status—are invited to consult “Thresholds of Just-Being: Deficiency, Demise, and the
Ontology of Belonging.” There, the spectrum is elaborated as a movement from enacted
presence to suspended identity, with nur noch marking the unstable threshold that calls either for
reintegration or collapse.


Conclusion
Across philology, scripture, and constructive analysis, the inquiry converges on a substantive,
non-reductive profile of faith: a graded integration of assent, trust, and enactment whose degree
is indexed by dispositional stability (resilience under counter-evidence and adversity) and
behavioral uptake within a community’s authorized practices. Lexically, the core sense of ʾ-m-n
(security/assurance) and the fides tradition (trust/pledge) support this nucleus while warning
against etymological overreach (e.g., the y-m-n “right-hand” motif belongs to symbolism unless
securely sourced). Doctrinally, the Ashʿarī distinction between inward īmān as taṣdīq under dalīl
and outward islām as compliance protects the primacy of recognition while accounting for the
necessity—but non-identity—of practice. Wittgenstein’s grammar of religious language adds a
further constraint: “faith” is neither a private datum nor a free-floating theory but a family of
uses learned and sustained in communal forms of life; assessments of aptness belong to those
games, not to alien justificatory molds. Within the Bábí/Bahá’í dispensation, these generalities
are specified by recognition of the Manifestation and covenantal loyalty, by fear of God and
detachment, and by deeds that outrun words—ethical entailments that are not optional addenda
but integral to the truth-indexing of belief.
The upshot is practical as well as theoretical. First, the model yields comparative diagnostics
without erasing difference: it distinguishes warranted assent from imitation, inward conviction
from mere performance, and living grammar from residual phraseology. Second, it frames a
humane pastoral stance toward degrees of faith—encouraging patient accompaniment across a
graded field of “becoming” and “withdrawing”—while refusing to collapse faith into either bare
cognition or external conformity. As a bridge to further work, the conclusion situates this essay
alongside the companion piece, “Thresholds of Just-Being,” which develops the spectrum from
enacted presence to suspended identity (nur noch) and explores its ontological and communal
stakes; readers are invited to consult that study for the fuller phenomenology of deficiency and
the practical question of reintegration.
