domination. Legal and cultural pluralism are met with principled coexistence: Bahá’í law is not
imposed upon others; the community demonstrates its coherence by practice while honoring civil
law and contributing to public welfare. When tensions arise, the instruments are consultation,


truthful speech, and service; power is reconceived as trust, and authority is legitimated by justice
rather than by victory.
In sum, the Commonwealth does not monopolize governance; it integrates it. The state retains
indispensable functions yet ceases to be the solitary subject of the political. Under the
sovereignty of God—which relativizes all other sovereignties—associations, scholars, media,
and economic agents assume rightful responsibility within a coherent order. The pattern is
already visible wherever consultative culture, non-partisan service, and truthfulness animate
civic life; it marks the gradual entrance of a new political rationality into history (Shoghi Effendi
1991; Bahá’u’lláh 1992).
12. Language, Identity, and the Politics of Meaning
Against epistemologies that reduce language to an instrument of domination or to the play of
indeterminate signs, the Bahá’í writings advance a different grammar of the political: language is
a divine trust ordered to truth, unity, and transformation. The political subject is not primarily the
autonomous will of liberal theory nor the positional effect of discourse; it is a soul addressed by
Revelation. “The source of all learning is the knowledge of God… and this cannot be attained
save through the knowledge of His Manifestation” (Bahá’u’lláh 1978). With this claim, authority
is relocated from human construction to the Logos; identity is reconstituted as responsiveness to
a Word that summons, judges, and educates.
This relocation does not evacuate history; it transfigures it. Revelation, transcendent in origin,
enters temporal contingency to reorder it. The Word discloses ends that exceed ideological
programs—unity and justice as divine purposes—yet realizes these ends through historical
media: law, institutions, and disciplined speech. The Bahá’í Commonwealth therefore neither
fixes meaning in metaphysical stasis nor abandons it to relativism; it maintains the permanence
of essential goods (truth, justice, unity) while their expression unfolds by progressive revelation.
The implied anthropology converges with Augustinian insistence that just order descends from a
higher source and with Farabian claims about polity perfected by revealed law, yet it is distinct in
its consultative constitution, wherein authority and deliberation are internally related rather than
opposed.


Poststructuralist critiques clarify the stakes. Foucault exposes the productive operations of
discourse in forming subjects and normalizing power; Derrida thematizes deferral and the textual
conditions of meaning (Derrida 1976; Foucault 1977, 2007). The Bahá’í response neither denies
discourse’s productivity nor the historicity of interpretation; it rejects the nihilistic inference that
truth is nothing but effect. “Every word is endowed with a spirit,” Bahá’u’lláh writes; speech
bears ontological charge and moral consequence (Bahá’u’lláh 1978). Its abuse dissolves trust and
multiplies enmity; its rectitude binds persons into the possibility of a common life. Language is
thus covenantal before it is instrumental: a bond that participates in reality rather than a mere
assertion of will.
Consultation is the praxis of this redeemed speech (cf. §§4–7). Neither adversarial contest nor
masked will-to-victory, it is disciplined truth-seeking under the sign of unity. Its virtues—
humility, detachment, candor, trustworthiness—are epistemic conditions for tracking reality, not
optional courtesies. Consultation assumes the partiality of perspectives and seeks convergence
without the coercion of party or personality. In conceding to critical theory that discourse shapes
the political, the Bahá’í model denies that domination is discourse’s highest office: guided by
revealed principle and ordered to a shared telos, language becomes the medium through which
plurality fuses into insight rather than mobilizes into faction.
Because language is world-forming, the politics of meaning is also the politics of education and
communication. The summons to an auxiliary world language is not ornamental idealism but a
practical condition for planetary deliberation; without a shared medium, justice cannot be
reasoned globally nor unity juridically enacted (Bahá’u’lláh 1992). Likewise, injunctions against
calumny and idle fancies acknowledge that the public sphere can be unmade by lies as surely as
by violence (Bahá’u’lláh 1978). Media, schools, pulpits, and parliaments thus become sites of
moral accountability in speech: where truthfulness is cultivated, trust accrues; where words are
weaponized, the commonwealth decays.
This grammar reframes identity. If the political subject is constituted by responsiveness to
Revelation, then race, class, nation, and analogous markers—while historically consequential—
are not ontologically ultimate. The self is summoned out of captivity to such determinations
without denying their force; it receives a new axis—orientation to truth and service—that
relativizes ideological identity and renders it available for unity-in-diversity. The repudiation of


partisanship follows: not flight from politics, but refusal to let speech be captured by antagonism
as organizing principle. Language must enable cohabitation; conscripted to win, it ceases to
disclose.
At the same time, both rigid essentialism and radical relativism are refused. The writings hold to
a unity of truth that unfolds across dispensations: “whatsoever hath led the children of men to
shun one another… hath, through the revelation of these words, been obliterated and abolished”
(Bahá’u’lláh 1978). Historicity and permanence are not enemies. Forms of expression change as
human capacity expands; the essence—justice, unity, the acquisition of virtues—remains stable.
Classical orientations—Plato’s highest good, Aristotle’s architectonic politics, Cicero’s res
publica, and Strauss’s retrieval of enduring questions—are acknowledged as partial anticipations;
their horizons are exceeded insofar as the highest good is named by Revelation and enacted
institutionally through a consultative order that is neither secular proceduralism nor clerical fiat
(Aristotle 1998; Cicero 1999; Plato 1997; Strauss 1959).
In this light, language is the workshop of civilization. Through words, laws are promulgated,
covenants made, councils convened, wrongs rectified, and hope taught. When the Word of God
enters history, it does not merely inform; it performs. It calls a people into being, institutes a
discipline of speech, and supplies the semantics by which justice can be conceived and enacted.
The Bahá’í Commonwealth is thus not the triumph of a slogan but the maturation of a grammar:
a revealed lexicon of unity and a consultative practice that together transmute discourse from a
scene of suspicion into an instrument of shared discernment. Language does not only speak the
world; under Revelation it helps re-create it.
Conclusion: Revelation and the Vigilance of History
The Across these chapters, a single claim has been unfolded: the Bahá’í Faith does not append a
political theology to an inherited canon; it re-founds political reason upon Revelation. Order,
justice, obligation, and sovereignty are relocated from speculative construction or partisan will to
the manifest will of God disclosed in history through the institution of the Manifestation.
Politics, accordingly, is reconceived as a revealed art: not the management of interests or the
formalization of contract, but the ordered enactment of divine purpose in collective life
(Bahá’u’lláh 1992).


Revelation discloses ends as well as origins. The telos of Bahá’í political life is twofold:
unceasing recognition of the Manifestation of God as the axis of knowledge and criterion of
truth, and the progressive realization of the oneness of humankind as juridical and civilizational
form. That teleology is historically mediated. It advances through the Lesser Peace—political
concord among states—and toward the Most Great Peace, in which revealed principles,
institutions, and laws order public life at civilizational scale (Shoghi Effendi 1991). The
Administrative Order functions in this movement not as a sectarian enclave, but as “nucleus and
pattern” of an emergent commonwealth—democratically constituted, consultative, non-clerical,
and protected in its legislative remit (Bahá’u’lláh 1992; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá 2007).
Form follows from this end. Houses of Justice legislate “according to the needs and requirements
of the time” on matters not explicitly revealed; elections proceed without candidacy or
campaigning; consultation replaces adversarial contest as the ordinary method of public
deliberation; partisanship is renounced to preserve the condition of unity upon which justice
depends (Bahá’u’lláh 1992; Shoghi Effendi 1991). Procedural rectitude—reasons-giving,
transparency proportionate to function, avenues of reconsideration and appeal within the
consultative chain—becomes the ethical armature of authority. These norms are already
operative within the community domain and anticipate, without coercion, their civil-juridical
articulation in a matured commonwealth.
Rights and duties are recast within this teleology. The “rights of man” are neither pre-political
entitlements grounded in abstract autonomy nor merely contractual claims; they are the civic
grammar of justice in an order oriented to unity. Freedom of conscience is affirmed; belief
cannot be coerced; apostasy carries no civil or penal sanction; and non-Bahá’ís enjoy full civil
equality under a just order (Bahá’u’lláh 1992; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá 2007). Reciprocity governs the
whole: liberties are preserved by obedience to just law; participation is matched by service;
authority is bounded by accountability. In this horizon, negative and positive rights are
complementary—protection from domination entails education, meaningful work, and conditions
in which spiritual capacities can be exercised (Bahá’u’lláh 1978).
Political subjectivity is likewise transformed. The individual is neither the atomized bearer of
preferences nor the partisan activist of ideology, but a moral–spiritual trustee whose agency is
realized through truthfulness, rectitude, and service (cf. §§7–9). Family life becomes the first


polity of moral formation; civil society becomes a locus of governance; economic activity
acquires civic vocation; media and schools are charged with the ethics of truthful speech. Non-
state actors—associations, learned persons, communicative institutions—participate in a
distributed architecture of governance disciplined by consultation and non-partisanship. The state
retains indispensable functions without monopolizing political agency; sovereignty is relativized
before the sovereignty of God, and authority is shared across levels within a coherent
constitutional horizon (Bahá’u’lláh 1978, 1992; Shoghi Effendi 1991).
Because transformation is historical, prudence governs tempo. Gradualism, a politics of delay
where needed, and non-coercive unity mark the path from present plural orders toward a
federated commonwealth. Legal and cultural diversity are met not by imposition but by
demonstration: institutions earn legitimacy by justice, transparency, and service; Bahá’í public
action is rendered intelligible to non-adherents in public-reason terms—peace, non-domination,
equity—while remaining faithful to revealed grounds (cf. §§4–6, 11). Where resistance arises—
from entrenched interests or inherited meanings—the instruments remain persuasion, example,
and the maturation of institutions.
None of this closes the future. Fidelity to Bahá’u’lláh entails vigilance toward further Revelation:
a refusal of the religious amnesia by which communities cling to forms while failing to recognize
the One who comes. The Covenant safeguards unity and continuity without sacralizing officials;
conferred protection in the legislative sphere secures guidance without absolutizing human
judgment (Bahá’u’lláh 1992; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá 2007). The Administrative Order is thus a pedagogy
as much as a polity—training souls and structures to enact justice now while remaining alert to
the Voice that shall speak anew.
What results is a sacred realism: neither utopian abstraction nor reductive pragmatism, but the
slow transmutation of history through purified intention, institution-building, and the unification
of peoples and nations. Authority is guardianship; citizenship is covenantal participation;
sovereignty is the capacity to enact justice on behalf of all. The measure of this order will be its
fruits: the protection of conscience, the rectification of wrong, the reconciliation of estranged
communities, and the visible advance of unity and peace. In that measure, political philosophy
returns to its first principle and its last end: the truth revealed becomes order lived.

Unity-in-Diversity as Institutional Rationality: A Relational–Covenantal Model of Modern
Individuality
Abstract
Modernity’s elevation of the autonomous subject simultaneously advanced dignity and creativity
while thinning the institutional bonds that once carried meaning, relocating religion from a
civilization-building source to privatized preference. This article proposes a relational–
covenantal alternative: independent investigation of truth is internally tethered to consultation;
authority is earned procedurally through dialogue, transparency, and answerability; and faith is
“externalized” through embodied, communal practices that make agency livable and solidarity
durable. Conceptually, we integrate refined individualism–collectivism scholarship—treating
values, practices, and institutions as distinct layers and distinguishing horizontal/vertical
variants—so that “individualism” appears as both moral claim and coordination technology
rather than a single bipolar trait. Methodologically, we pair person-level measures (self-
construal; HV×IC; expressive individualism) with behavioral and institutional indicators
(household structure, mobility traces, contract-enforcement proxies, civic participation), model
multilevel structures, and treat countries as distributions, not destinies. Empirically and
normatively, we read late-modern privatization and liquidity as a mixed moral economy—
expanding choice yet burdening coherence—while showing how dialogical authority and ritual
pedagogies (music, service, study circles, feasts) recompose bonds that let people “sign and
belong, choose and endure.” A U.S. case (First Amendment voluntarism, expressive
individualism, religious economy competition) illustrates reconfigured believing/belonging
under the primacy of choice. We close by specifying testable implications: in settings where
covenant-anchored consultative networks and participatory pedagogies are established,
intersubjective trust, social resilience, and liberty/common-good balance should improve while
reliance on coercive instruments declines.
Introduction
Modernity’s enthronement of the autonomous subject unparalleledly advanced dignity and
creativity, yet by dissolving mediating orders of meaning and authority it displaced the
individual–community relation from “institutional bonds that carry meaning” to “short-lived,
liquid agreements,” and relocated religion from a civilization-building source to private


preference. This article hypothesizes that a “relational, covenantal” model can be systematically
articulated in which independent investigation of truth and freedom of conscience do not negate
community but constitute it as consultative community; authority is reconfigured from vertical
command to covenant-bound dialogical legitimacy; and unity-in-diversity functions not as a
moral slogan but as the institutional rationality of a renewed political–cultural order. First,
knowledge is situated—not in voluntarist self-assertion—but within the revealed Word and the
norms of consultation, so that truth-judgment can exceed personal taste and the market for
meanings. Second, power is translated from coercive accumulation to the circulatory
accountability of non-partisan, answerable institutions, preserving individual innovation while
enabling pursuit of the common good. Third, embodiment and ritual move from private margin
to the core of virtue-formation, such that a relational religious identity gains institutional
durability through shared practices. Our normative–empirical expectation is that wherever
covenant-anchored consultative networks and participatory pedagogies are established, indices of
intersubjective trust, social resilience, and the liberty/common-good balance measurably improve
while reliance on coercive instruments declines; in this architecture, the family, local
communities, and consultative councils are not residues of tradition but technical strategies for
realizing unity. Thus individuality is elevated from atomic consumerism to responsible
participation, and religion from privatized taste to civilization-building praxis, with the Bahá’í
grammar of covenant and consultation offering a coherent theoretical–institutional solution to the
modern individual/collective problem.
The problem pursued here is not how to reverse modernity, but how to translate its gains into
durable institutional forms without collapsing into nostalgic communitarianism or unbounded
atomism. Two temptations must be resisted: an anti-individualist reflex that underprices the
dignity and creativity of the modern subject, and a laissez-faire individualism that reduces all
general claims to private preference. The proposed path is “accountable individuality within
consultative, covenantal community”—a self that investigates truth independently yet submits its
judgment to rule-governed dialogue in answerable networks, converting conviction into
sustained collective action.
To secure conceptual traction, the introduction first clarifies the individualism/collectivism (I–C)
map beyond a crude dichotomy. Cultural psychology now widely employs a four-quadrant model


(vertical/horizontal × individualist/collectivist), which shows that valuing the person need not
negate solidarity, and vice versa, while analytic levels (person/organization/society) must be kept
distinct. We then draw on critical sociology to profile modern threats: Marcuse’s “one-
dimensional” subject shaped by instrumental reason and consumerism; Bauman’s “liquid
modernity,” in which bonds and commitments are short-lived and chronic choice breeds anxiety.
These tendencies converge with evidence of global increases in individualism and with crisis-
behavior (e.g., pandemics) that mixes normative compliance with voluntary self-regulation.
Methodologically, a systems/coevolutionary lens (psychic ↔ social systems) cautions against
reducing structure to agency or agency to structure, while methodological localism argues that
causal mechanisms should be sought at the level suited to the explanandum rather than a priori
privileging any level.
Within a Bahá’í frame, three explanatory–normative claims scaffold the proposed architecture.
First, Revelation is not merely hortatory but performative: the Word reorders language, identity,
and institution; thus “independent investigation of truth” is internally tethered to “consultation,”
lifting truth-judgment above private taste and the marketplace of meanings. Second, the
Covenant functions as the translator of spirituality into institutional durability—from family and
local community to consultative, non-partisan bodies—achieving a shift from domination to
covenant-bound dialogical legitimacy. Third, embodiment and ritual supply a pedagogical
discipline by which faith becomes a civilization-building habitus rather than an interior event;
here we braid Bahá’í praxis with interdisciplinary work on embodied learning, externalization of
faith, and relational recovery. Together these moves allow us to pass beyond simplistic
oppositions—East/West, private religion/civic secularism, individual/collective—toward an
institutional rationality in which liberty and the common good circulate in one orbit.
The article’s contribution is twofold: theoretically, it articulates a “relational, covenantal” model
grounded in Bahá’í epistemics and institutions while integrating the refined I–C literature;
empirically, it specifies how the model can be tested via four-dimensional measures, ritual
ethnography, and consultative field experiments. Our guiding questions are: How can personal
epistemic independence be institutionally embedded in consultation without sliding into
partisanship and domination? Which embodied/ritual forms can cultivate a relational religious
identity and counter privatization? Which context-sensitive indicators register improved


liberty/common-good balance and reduced reliance on coercion? The remainder proceeds from
hypothesis (above) to conceptual and methodological framing, engages rival narratives of
individualism and religion, and culminates in the institutional architecture of the proposed model
and its implications for policy, education, and Bahá’í civilization-building.
The emergence of the “I” in Modernity
Modernity begins with Descartes, whose “I think, therefore I am” seeks an indubitable
foundation for knowledge: the subject becomes the point of departure for adjudicating truth, not
a mere social artifact. Through methodical doubt—up to the hypothesis of a supremely cunning
deceiver—Descartes strips away anything even slightly dubitable to secure the cogito53 as a
thinking thing and later grounds a real distinction between mind and body. Yet this foundational
gesture risks the Cartesian circle: reliance on the clarity of ideas of an I whose relation to body,
world, and other is underdescribed. Kant relocates the subject from substantial metaphysics to a
transcendental structure: the unity of transcendental apperception54 must be able to accompany
all representations so that objectivity arises from the a priori forms of sensibility and the
categories of understanding; the subject is a formal, unifying function, not a knowable substance,
as his critique of the Paralogisms55 makes clear. The gain is emancipation from Cartesian
substance-dualism; the cost is a content-poor “I” and an epistemic gap from things-in-
themselves56. Fichte radicalizes the turn: the I self-positing (Tathandlung) posits the not-I57 and

53 Cogito: Meaning. Descartes’ foundational certainty: in the very act of doubting or thinking, the thinker’s existence
is indubitable (“I think, therefore I am”). It is not inferred from premises; it’s a self-revealing performance.Example.
Even if a super-deceiver fooled you about everything, your doubting still shows there is a “you” doing that doubting.
Pitfall. The cogito does not prove that only mind exists, nor does it by itself deliver a full metaphysics of the world
or the body.
54 Transcendental apperception: Meaning. In Kant, the a priori unity of self-consciousness that “must be able to
accompany all my representations.” It is a function of synthesis, not an inner object; it binds the manifold of sense
into one experience.
Example. Reading a long sentence as one meaningful whole rather than a jumble of words. Pitfall. Don’t treat it as a
little “self-thing”; it’s the formal condition that makes objective experience possible.
55 Paralogisms (of pure reason): Meaning. Kant’s name for illicit inferences about the “soul” drawn from the mere “I
think” (e.g., concluding that the I is a simple, immortal substance). Example. “Because I think, my soul must be
indestructible.” Kant says this overreaches what the “I think” warrants. Pitfall. Confusing the form of self-
consciousness with a substantive ontology of the self.
56 Thing-in-itself vs. Phenomenon: Meaning. “Phenomena” are things as they appear under our forms of intuition
(space/time) and categories; the “thing-in-itself” is reality as it is independently of those forms—knowable as a
limit-concept, not as positive content. Example. A map (phenomenon) is not the city itself (thing-in-itself), though
the city constrains what a good map can be. Pitfall. Equating “thing-in-itself” with a spooky hidden object we might
someday observe; in Kant it marks the boundary of possible experience.
57 Not-I (Nicht-Ich): Meaning. In Fichte, the limiting counterpart to the I’s self-positing. The I determines itself in
relation to a resistance that is “not-I.” Example. My practical freedom becomes determinate when it meets hard


encounters a limiting Anstoß58; freedom becomes norm-creative, yet voluntarist self-grounding
threatens. Hegel contests the solitary subject: self-consciousness emerges through recognition
(Anerkennung) and finds truth in the institutions of ethical life (Sittlichkeit); freedom moves
from abstract will to concrete actuality, and rationality becomes a concrete universal realized in
family, civil society, and state. Husserl retrieves the subject as transcendental ego: the epoché59
suspends the natural attitude, intentionality60 structures every act as a noesis–noema61
correlation, and time-consciousness and horizonal givenness disclose that no datum appears
without prior horizons; later, the life-world62 and transcendental intersubjectivity63 answer
charges of solipsism64. Still, a representational cast often remains, leaving a residual
subjectivism. Heidegger’s Dasein brings the tradition to a critical crest: the human being is
always already being-in-the-world, a unitary, a priori condition that displaces the subject–object
schema. Dasein is ontologically distinctive because its being is at issue for it; its “essence” lies in

reality (another will, nature, a rule) that sets boundaries. Pitfall. Treating the not-I as a ready-made external
substance; for Fichte it functions within the I’s practical self-determination.
58 Anstoß (“check,” “impetus”): Meaning. Fichte’s name for the initial “bruise” or check that summons the I from
abstract freedom into concrete self-determination. It is not a causal blow from outside, but the trigger that awakens
limitation. Example. Hitting a wall while planning freely forces you to redraw the plan—your freedom becomes
specific. Pitfall. Reading Anstoß as a physical cause; it’s a transcendental marker of limitation and orientation.
59 Epoché (bracketing): Meaning. Husserl’s methodological suspension of the “natural attitude” (the unexamined
belief in a ready-made world) to describe how things are given in experience. It is not skepticism or denial of the
world. Example. Instead of debating “Does this table exist?” you ask “How does ‘table’ show up in my experience
right now?” Pitfall. Confusing epoché with the claim that nothing exists; it’s a shift of focus, not a negation.
60 Intentionality: Meaning. Husserl’s principle that all consciousness is about something (an object, state of affairs,
number, melody). “Aboutness” is built into conscious acts. Example. Seeing a cup, remembering a friend, fearing a
storm—all are directed to something. Pitfall. Thinking intentionality requires a real external object; even illusions
and fictions are intentionally “of” something.
61 Noesis / Noema: Meaning. Correlates in Husserl: noesis is the act (perceiving, judging, imagining); noema is the
object-as-experienced, the sense or profile under which it appears (the cup-as-seen-from-here). Example. The same
tree at noon and at dusk: the physical tree may be unchanged, but its noematic appearance (color, mood, salience)
shifts with act, angle, horizon. Pitfall. Equating the noema with the physical thing itself; it’s the thing as
intended/given, not its mind-independent composition.
62 Lifeworld (Lebenswelt): Meaning. Husserl’s name for the pre-theoretical, taken-for-granted horizon of everyday
practices within which science already operates. Science abstracts from, but never replaces, the lifeworld. Example.
You can competently drive without knowing physics; driving belongs to a skill-suffused world of meanings. Pitfall.
Treating the lifeworld as mere subjective opinion; it is the shared background that makes objectivity workable.
63 Transcendental intersubjectivity: Meaning. The a priori communal structure through which objectivity and shared
meaning are possible (pairing, empathy, communication). Counters the slide into solipsism.
Example. “This is the same table for both of us” is possible because we inhabit shared horizons of sense. Pitfall.
Reducing it to sociological convention; it’s a transcendental condition for there being one world for many subjects.
64 Solipsism: Meaning. The view that only my mind is certain/real and others or the external world are doubtful or
nonexistent. Example. “Perhaps only I exist; everyone else is a projection.” Pitfall. Confusing Husserl’s epoché with
solipsism; the former suspends commitment to describe givenness, it doesn’t deny others.


existence, in its to-be (Zu-sein). Attunement65 (Befindlichkeit) shows Dasein as always already
opened in a mood; thrownness (Geworfenheit) discloses its being delivered over to language,
history, family, and world—never at a zero-point of choice; care66 (Sorge) names the total
structure unifying projection-ahead-of-itself, already-being-in-a-world, and falling into everyday
absorption with equipment and the They (das Man)67. Being-in does not mean containment but
dwelling68; the world is not res extensa but worldhood69 disclosed70 with Dasein’s existence.
Engagement with equipment is concern (Besorgen), with others solicitude (Fürsorge); the
distinction between readiness-to-hand71 (Zuhandenheit) and presence-at-hand72 (Vorhandenheit)
reorders priority toward practical coping as more primordial than theoretical representation.
Being-towards-death (Sein-zum-Tode) articulates Dasein’s ownmost, non-relational,
unsurpassable possibility; anxiety (Angst) reveals the nothing of the world and of being-in-the-
world, opening anticipatory resoluteness (Vorlaufen, Entschlossenheit) and individuating Dasein

65 Attunement (Befindlichkeit): Meaning. In Heidegger, the way the world is disclosed through moods. Moods aren’t
mere inner feelings; they are how the world shows up as cheerful, heavy, uncanny, tedious, etc.
Example. In boredom, everything seems flat and interchangeable; in joy, the same room is vivid and inviting. Pitfall.
Treating moods as subjective colorings laid on top of a neutral world; for Heidegger they first open a world at all.
66 Care (Sorge): Meaning. Heidegger’s name for the unified structure of Dasein’s being: being-ahead-of-itself
(projection), already-being-in-a-world (facticity), and being-alongside (falling/absorption). Example. Planning a
project (ahead), belonging to a family/language (already-in), getting lost in routines (falling). Pitfall. Reading “care”
as worry or melancholy; here it is an ontological structure, not a mood.
67 the They (das Man): Meaning. The anonymous, leveling normativity of everydayness (“one does this,” “people
say…”). It dilutes ownership of possibilities and encourages conformity. Example. Choosing careers, opinions, or
tastes because “that’s just what people do.” Pitfall. Demonizing social life as such; Heidegger targets unowned
conformity, not community per se.
68 Dwelling / Abiding (In-sein): Meaning. “Being-in” the world is not containment (like water in a glass) but
residing/abiding with a familiar surround. “I am” = “I dwell alongside.” Example. To live in a city is to inhabit its
habits, routes, norms, and meanings—not just occupy coordinates. Pitfall. Reverting to a container model where
mind is “inside” and world “outside.”
69 Worldhood (Weltlichkeit): Meaning. The structure of “world” as a web of significance, references, and use-
relations opened with Dasein’s existence—not a heap of extensional stuff. Example. A hammer refers to nails, wood,
building, skill, purposes—an entire practical nexus. Pitfall. Treating world as a sum of objects (the Cartesian res
extensa), missing its meaningful articulation.
70Disclosedness (Erschlossenheit): Meaning. Dasein’s basic “openness” whereby beings and possibilities can be
understood and interpreted. Not an added property but the structural condition of understanding.
Example. Having a language, skills, and practices already in place so that things make sense to you. Pitfall. Equating
disclosedness with mere explicit knowledge; much of it is tacit, practical, and pre-thematic.
71 Ready-to-hand (Zuhandenheit): Meaning. The mode in which equipment shows up in seamless use. It tends to be
transparent in action rather than thematically noticed. Example. While hammering successfully, you don’t attend to
“the hammer” as an object; you just drive the nail. Pitfall. Thinking theory is always primary; for Heidegger,
practical coping is more primordial.
72 Present-at-hand (Vorhandenheit):Meaning. The mode in which things are thematized as objects for detached
observation or when they break down. Derivative relative to readiness-to-hand. Example. The hammer as an item
measured and inspected after it snaps. Pitfall. Assuming this theoretical stance is our default access; it’s often a
secondary attitude.


against the levelling of the They. Thus Heidegger’s critique preserves modern gains—freedom,
dignity, critical self-grounding—by insisting that Dasein is “each time mine,” yet clarifies their
limits by showing that the I is from the outset disclosed within horizons of world, other, and
history and cannot appear apart from language and dwelling. The arc from Descartes, Kant,
Fichte, and Hegel to Husserl—thinking substance, transcendental unity, self-positing will, ethical
institutions, transcendental ego—is rewritten as being-in-the-world: not objects represented to a
subject, but dwelling in a nexus of meaning, work, language, and others. In this reframing, the
modern loosening of traditional bonds both enabled autonomy and exposed the self to restless
liquidity; Heidegger’s existential structures supply a grammar for translating individuality from
an isolated atom to an open, historically responsible horizon.
The Rights-Bearing “I” and Its Emergence
Modern inwardness prepares, but does not by itself deliver, the rights-bearing person. What
turns a reflective “I” into an agent who may claim is a legal–political grammar forged across
early modern and modern thought. Charles Taylor’s genealogy clarifies the background: the
first-person turn (Augustine, radicalized by Descartes) teaches us to seek moral sources from
within; the affirmation of ordinary life gives weight to work, family, and daily vocation as sites
of dignity; expressivism adds the sense that each of us carries an inner measure that should find
outward shape. Out of that background comes a shift of idiom—from natural law as a code we
must obey, to natural rights as protections we may assert. In Locke’s articulation the rights-
bearing “I” stands before the state: rational creatures under a knowable law of nature own basic
claims to life, liberty, and estate; property arises where one’s labor is mixed with things;
consent founds government for the fiduciary task of securing rights, and breach warrants
resistance. Two consequences follow for the modern image of the person: some claims are
inalienable (you may not sell your basic life or basic liberty even if you try), and political order
is pictured “from the ground up,” as the coordination of many independent agents. That image
dignifies citizens and limits rulers; it also inclines toward possessive individualism, the habit of
treating the person chiefly as the owner of self and capacities, and of modeling many freedoms
on property.


Kant keeps the critical edge while freeing the frame from theology: human dignity lies in
autonomy, the capacity to bind oneself by laws one could will for all. In public right (Recht) the
question is not private virtue but external freedom: no one may be subjected to another’s private
choice. Hence basic rights become universal constraints that protect a space of independence
for each, independent of any one vision of the good life. This universal form levels rank and
origin and travels well across plural worlds; its chronic risk is thinness—principles that convince
on paper but do little in fact unless given institutional body. Hegel’s reply is not to reject
personhood but to complete it. Freedom begins as Abstract Right—the person who may hold
property and make contracts—but must rise through Morality (intention, responsibility) to
Ethical Life (Sittlichkeit), the institutional weave of family, civil society, and state. The hinge
is recognition (Anerkennung): the bearer of right becomes real only as claims are mutually
acknowledged and dependably enforced. Property is protected, contracts adjudicated, needs
organized through associations and markets, and a public authority stabilizes expectations;
otherwise “my right” is a wish, not a shield. Hegel thereby corrects the drift toward an isolated
atom: rights live by practices that recognize persons and tie them into common structures.
Against this backdrop the catalogue of who and what counts widens. The classical circle of civil
rights (security of the person, due process, equality before the law, freedoms of speech,
conscience, association) expands with political rights (suffrage, representation), and, in modern
democracies, social rights (education, health, welfare)—a sequence often mapped as the path
from status equality to effective capacity. Twentieth- and twenty-first-century waves add labor
rights, women’s rights, children’s rights, minority and cultural–linguistic rights, then
animal and environmental protections. These are not a betrayal of universality but a thickening
of it: they redescribe who the bearer is (worker, woman, child, minority, species-neighbor) and
what counts as injury or due regard, so that equal standing becomes something people can
actually use. Three styles of argument explain the thickening without abandoning the core. First,
recognition (in a Hegelian key): persons and groups need care, respect/rights, and social
esteem; failures of recognition are lived as moral injuries and justify targeted remedies. Second,
the ethics of care reminds law that agency is relational and vulnerable; a rights idiom that
notices rules but misses dependencies risks formal fairness with material neglect. Third,
teleological/communitarian reasoning asks about the ends of institutions: admissions and


representation are not merely deserts of isolated applicants but tools of common goods (civic
formation, equitable leadership), so “neutral” metrics may give way to purpose-fit criteria,
sometimes group-sensitive, when neutral rules entrench past skew. In each case the point is not
to dilute universal rights but to place their meaning within practices and histories that make
them real.
A sociogenesis runs alongside the doctrines. As states monopolize violence and
interdependence lengthens, external compulsion is partly displaced by self-restraint; thresholds
of shame and foresight rise; citizens become fit not only to be ruled but to claim and bear rights.
The same inward tribunal that enables law-abiding conduct becomes, in another register, the
conscience or even the punitive superego of psychoanalysis. The lesson is double: the rights-
bearing “I” is neither a natural isolate nor a mere product of command; it is formed at the
crossing of inner discipline and public institutions. This double formation also clarifies a
recurrent tension in modern discourse. If we treat rights as purely abstract protections of
freestanding selves, we risk blindness to the social making of persons and to patterned
disadvantages that neutral rules perpetuate. If we treat persons as only social products, we
forfeit the very ground on which the weak speak claims against custom, market, or majority. The
durable path is to hold both: a universal floor below which no one should fall, and context-
attentive measures that bring the floor within reach.
Placed between a philosophical account of the modern subject (from cogito to being-in-the-
world) and a psychoanalytic account of the divided self (from id/ego/superego to signifier and
Other), this section works as a hinge. From first-person self-grounding we pass to public
standing—to the person who may demand reasons and redress; from rights we pivot to the
psyche where external authority is internalized as law, conscience, and guilt. The upshot for
individualism is sobriety rather than romance: individuality is not only the felt freedom of a
private core but the status of a claimant among equals, sustained by recognition and by
institutions that make equal status bite. When it works, the rights-bearing “I” guards freedom,
summons dignity, and disciplines power; when it thins into slogans, it leaves persons legally
equal and practically voiceless. The rest of the project will ask how this juridical “I” fares in
liquid modernity and whether accountable individuality can remain steady as identities loosen
and inherited authorities fade.


Freud and the Modern Psyche
This section approaches the modern subject through psychoanalysis: first with Freud’s structural
model (id/ego/superego)73 alongside the topographical scheme
(conscious/preconscious/unconscious)74, then with Lacan’s modernization of the same apparatus.
Freud’s starting point is a field of forces. The id is the reservoir of drives (Eros and Thanatos), a
source of libidinal energy operating on the pleasure principle and pressing for immediate
discharge. The ego is a coherent organization of processes that forms around the body’s surface
and the perception–consciousness system; its job is to reality-test, to hold back, bind, delay,
transform, and sublimate drive-demands, and to control motility—hence Freud’s image of a rider
who must manage a stronger horse. The superego is the inner authority constituted by early
identifications and introjections75 of parental/societal law; it judges, prohibits, and idealizes,
installing conscience and an often unconscious sense of guilt. Crucially, in Freud’s later theory
the ego is not coextensive with consciousness: portions of the ego and the superego are
themselves unconscious. Thus the old topography (Cs./Pcs./Ucs.) is revised: the unconscious
does not simply coincide with the repressed id. The ego stands between three masters—the outer
world, the id’s libido, and the superego’s severity—and is therefore “the actual seat of anxiety.”
Concepts like cathexis76 (libidinal investment) and narcissism77 clarify how energy first cathects
the ego (primary narcissism), then invests objects, and can be drawn back in crises (secondary
narcissism). Socially, this architecture translates external authority into internal authority:
civilization depends on internalization, but a hyper-severe superego can pathologize
responsibility into obsession, inhibition, or self-sabotage. On this view, responsible individuality
is not the fantasy of a transparent self; it is the ego’s capacity to take ownership of its own
unconscious conflicts and to mediate—ethically—between drive, law, and reality.
