Freud thus bequeaths a modern subject no longer transparent to itself: the ego is a conflicted
organizer, staffed by defensive bureaucracies (repression, denial, projection, regression,
identification, etc.). Drives press with repetitive insistence; unless given form in speech,
symbolization, and relation (transference), the subject either collapses into short-circuit
satisfactions or breaks under a punitive superego. Here narcissism is pivotal: the ego lives off a
primary libidinal investment in itself; in mature ties it invests objects, but under stress it recoils,
draining the bonds of reality. The payoff for political and social theory is immediate: conscience
and guilt are not mere residues of religion; they are the psychic machinery of socialization.
Responsibility, in a Freudian key, is the ego’s learned art of delaying, binding, and transforming
drive into work, play, justice—of writing a livable compromise between pleasure, prohibition,
and the world’s demands.
Yet a merely Freudian lens no longer suffices for late modernity; Lacan re-reads Freud in and
through language. For Lacan, the Freudian ego belongs largely to the Imaginary: a composite of
identifications stabilized in the mirror stage78, inherently marked by misrecognition
(méconnaissance). The subject is divided79; the unconscious is structured like a language—that
is, the Symbolic order of signifiers precedes and inscribes us, and the big Other80 (law, language,
social discourse) is where the superego’s voice issues from. Lacan’s superego is not simply
ethical command; it is the “senseless law” of enjoyment (volonté de jouissance81), a relentless
imperative that generates guilt without end—the more you obey, the guiltier you become. He
rewrites Freud’s Wo Es war, soll Ich werden82: not “the ego must conquer the id,” but “where ‘it’
was, ‘I’ should come to be”—the subject must assume a position precisely at the site of
unconscious effects, not expel them. In this grammar, cathexis yields pride of place to
signification; desire is “the desire of the Other,” drives are partial and circulate around lack or

78 Mirror stage & Méconnaissance: Ego as image-based and misrecognizing; unity is scenic, not intrinsic. Pitfall:
reducing it to a biological episode
79 Divided subject: The subject is split by language/Unconscious; analysis assumes responsibility for this division.
Pitfall: chasing a fantasy of wholeness.
80 Big Other & Name-of-the-Father: Place of law/discourse; signifier introducing prohibition and structure. Pitfall:
personalizing the Other.
81 Jouissance: Excessive, painful enjoyment beyond the pleasure principle; often commanded by superego. Pitfall:
equating with fun.
82 “Wo Es war, soll Ich werden: ” Not conquering id but coming to be at the site of unconscious effects—owning
one’s speech. Pitfall: voluntarist misreading.


structural absence, and the task of analysis is not erecting a unified ego but assuming
responsibility for division: to speak from a place that knows it is spoken by the signifier.
This Lacanian displacement explains late-modern pathologies of individuality: in a media-
saturated, market-driven world the subject is magnetized by imaginary ideals (ideal-ego, ego-
ideal), oscillating between exhibitionism and shame; conscience mutates into a superegoic over-
demand that commands impossible enjoyment while condemning failure. Responsibility here
becomes an ethical stance toward language and law: not mastery of the unconscious, but
acknowledgment of its structuring role; not evacuation of conflict, but locating oneself at the
point where desire and law intersect, and answering for one’s speech. If Freud’s clinic aimed to
strengthen the ego for “a progressive conquest of the id,” Lacan’s clinic aims to install the
subject where “it” was—at the gap opened by the signifier—so that action can be owned without
the mirage of wholeness.
Psychoanalysis models the subject as a metapsychology of conflict and signification;
Heidegger’s existential analytic models the human being as being-in-the-world. Both treat
anxiety, guilt, and decision, but differently. Freudian anxiety signals tensions between drive and
internalized law; Heideggerian Angst discloses the “nothing” of worldhood. Freudian guilt issues
from the superego’s tribunal; Heidegger’s Schuld names an ontological indebtedness bound up
with care. Psychoanalysis’ drive is the motor of psychic life; Heidegger’s care is the structural
unity of existence. These are not rivals so much as complementary lenses: psychoanalysis pulls
the modern subject out of the fantasy of transparency by staging conflict and language;
existential analysis pulls it out of atomism by staging finitude, world, and death. Together they
move the “I” beyond an isolated atom—Freud/Lacan through the Other and the law of speech;
Heidegger through dwelling, work, and being-towards-death. The shared destination is
responsible individuality: a self that can adjudicate between liberty and norm, pleasure and
prohibition, authenticity and accountability—one that owns its conflicts rather than disavowing
them, and translates that ownership into durable commitments.
From Collectivism to Individualism (Socio-Historical)
Modernity loosens the dense fabric of inherited belonging. As cities, markets, bureaucracies,
literacy, and mass media reconfigure everyday life, the subject of tribe and estate gives way to


the citizen who consents, contracts, and claims. The classic shorthand is Tönnies’s passage from
Gemeinschaft—a kin- and place-bound community of fate, thick with shared norms and face-to-
face sanction—to Gesellschaft, an association ordered by impersonal rules, mobility, and
interest. What changes is not merely feeling but form: authority ceases to look “given by nature,”
and legitimacy must be made—stated, signed, checked—inside institutions that presume an
individual capable of saying yes or no. Even the grammar of everyday life adjusts: promises
become contracts; custom becomes statute; loyalty is reinterpreted as consent.
Durkheim tracks the same shift as a structural metamorphosis from mechanical solidarity
(cohesion by likeness) to organic solidarity (cohesion by interdependence across specialized
roles). In small, similar worlds, the collective conscience is thick, expansive, and hot: to offend a
norm is to offend the whole. As the division of labor differentiates tasks, that conscience cools
and narrows; law migrates from repressive (punishing an insult to the whole) to restitutive
(repairing harms among parts). Crucially, the very content of the collective conscience changes:
it elevates the individual as a moral precept—the “sacredness of the person.” The gain is latitude:
each actor enjoys a “proper sphere” of initiative and belief. The risk is anomie—norm-drift, a
deficit of shared orientation that leaves desire unscaled and action undecided. Durkheim’s
mechanism is mundane and powerful: dynamic density (more people, more interaction)
intensifies competition, forces specialization, and demands new, finer moral regulation. When
the village’s common rhythms recede, the person can be freer and more alone at once; and when
moral regulation lags economic change, the result is restless appetite and fragile purpose.
Durkheim answers, not with nostalgia, but with associations (occupational bodies, professional
ethics) that thicken meaning without dissolving individuality.
Weber names the engine: rationalization. Formal rationality means doing things “by the rule”—
calculation, predictability, written files. Legal-rational authority becomes definitive: offices,
competencies, hierarchies, and impersonal procedure routinize decision-making. The market
hardens into a “cosmos” whose price signals discipline conduct regardless of belief: one
complies because deviation incurs cost. Even religion lends the first push: the Protestant ethic
transposes salvation anxiety into methodical worldly conduct—inner-worldly asceticism that
prizes punctuality, accounting, sober self-control. As that ethic unmoors from its source,
technique remains while transcendence fades. The world is disenchanted—less magical, more


workable. The cost is Weber’s iron cage (a steel-hard casing): a web of efficient means that no
longer carries substantively shared ends. Substantive rationalities (ends answerable to values)
retreat before instrumental rationality (what works), leaving “specialists without spirit,
sensualists without heart.” Contracts proliferate because trust is relocated from persons to forms;
dignity is promised, warmth is not. The very success of rules produces a deficit of meaning those
rules cannot themselves supply.
Simmel shows how all this feels from the pavement. The metropolis bombards the senses; to
survive, the psyche flattens impressions into the blasé attitude—a practiced indifference that
protects and impoverishes at once. Money—the pure medium of exchange—unifies value by
abstraction, privileging the quantitative over the qualitative. Life is timed, priced, and compared;
punctuality and exactness become ethical as well as practical. Culture bifurcates: objective
culture (institutions, technologies, catalogs of knowledge) swells; subjective culture (what one
can inwardly appropriate) lags. This is Simmel’s tragedy of culture: the more the world offers,
the less the self can digest. Urban liberty expands style and choice while thinning bonds; we
invent reserve to manage proximity without intimacy; we perform difference inside fashions that
standardize the performance. The stranger—simultaneously near and far—becomes a social type;
secrecy becomes a technique of self-possession; and cynicism—the sense that “everything has its
price”—shadows the promised freedom of cash and choice. Means (money) aspire to the status
of ends; evaluation colonizes valuation.
Polanyi insists the market’s dominance was not “natural.” Historically, economies were
embedded in kinship, polity, and morality; exchange was governed by reciprocity and
redistribution long before price was sovereign. The nineteenth-century “self-regulating market”
forcibly disembedded economic life—treating land, labor, and money as if they were
commodities (fictitious commodities, because human lives and ecologies are not produced for
sale). Wages are not mere prices; they are people’s subsistence. The result is a tearing of social
tissue followed by a double movement: society pushes back to re-embed markets through factory
acts, poor relief, labor law, social insurance, and public regulation. The very grammar of rights—
worker protections, social citizenship, limits on the workday—crystallizes as institutional
antidotes to purely contractual exposure. Markets remain, but consent alone cannot carry a life;
institutions must shore it up. Where orthodox economics imagines equilibrium, Polanyi hears a


counter-melody: communities democratizing risk, re-coupling price to person, and making
society visible again as the condition of any market worth having.
Elias courts the same epoch from the inside out. As states monopolize violence and chains of
interdependence lengthen, external constraint folds into self-constraint. The thresholds of shame
and embarrassment rise; bodily conduct is schooled early until restraint becomes automatized.
What begins as etiquette matures into character: foresight, affect-control, and long-range
anticipation are no longer exceptional but ordinary competencies for life among strangers. The
knife is set aside; the fork arrives; doors, tables, and words are redesigned to buffer impulses and
coordinate conduct. Freud’s terms help name the interiorization: prohibitions migrate inward as
conscience; aggression is tamed, sometimes turned against the self. The outcome is a person
capable of bearing obligations and signing—an interior architecture that makes formal freedom
livable, and also heavy. If Polanyi narrates re-embedding in law, Elias narrates re-embedding in
personality: the social order writes itself into posture and pulse.
If Polanyi maps disembedding and Elias the internalization that made distance inhabitable,
Bauman diagnoses the melting of solids—institutions, careers, neighborhoods, and life-scripts
lose viscosity. Bonds are revocable; identities are projects rather than inheritances; commitments
are “until-further-notice.” Choice expands into choice-anxiety: ends are unstable, means are
abundant, guarantees are few. The consumer’s freedom to “shop around” for jobs, partners, and
selves conceals a permanent audition staged before markets and metrics. Security and autonomy
decouple; we hold more options and fewer anchors. Mobility—once liberation from feudal
fixity—becomes a requirement to be employable, desirable, legible to systems that reward
flexibility and penalize duration. Liquid life honors agility and punishes rootedness; the question
“What do you want?” grows exhausting not because there are too few answers, but because there
are too many, each with a countdown timer.
The digital turn amplifies liquidity without restoring depth. Under networked individualism,
dense local groups give way to wide, weak-tie networks; proximity is virtual and intermittent.
Algorithms mediate visibility, making bonds efficient, brief, and often postsocial (triangulated
through platforms and metrics). The promise is reach; the price is brittleness. We coordinate by
contracts and clicks because that is what scales; we feel unseen because scaling strips context.


Context collapse turns multiple audiences into one, incentivizing a performance-self that is at
once expressive and standardized. Social capital is re-quantified into views, likes, and scores;
solidarity becomes episodic, organized around flashes of attention; communities lean toward
“while-it-lasts.” A world legible to machines is legible to law but not always to love.
Looping back through the whole arc, a picture of modern individuality comes into focus. It is
born where Durkheim’s interdependence replaces sameness, Weber’s procedures stand in for
persons, Simmel’s money rationalizes value, Polanyi’s double movement reins in exposure,
Elias’s self-control fits individuals for distance, and Bauman’s liquidity makes choice chronic
and adhesion light. The rights-bearing “I” thrives here because law can treat each of us as
addressees and authors; the same “I” is strained because the affective infrastructures that once
held us in place have thinned. Hence the recurring pathologies named along the way: anomie
(orientation deficit), iron cage (means without ends), blasé (defensive numbness), disembedded
markets (risk privatized), over-civilized selves (guilt redirected inward), liquid bonds
(commitments shy of duration). Even the public sphere—expanded by print and platforms—
finds itself saturated with opinion yet short on orientation, abundant in options yet starved for
ends.
None of this mandates a return to Gemeinschaft. The task is neither nostalgia nor surrender to
drift, but a re-composition of bonds that can carry autonomy without dissolving meaning: forms
of association that let individuals sign and belong, choose and endure. In practice this means
institutions that are rule-bound yet hospitable; markets that price things without pricing people;
bureaucracies that keep files and remember faces; networks that amplify reach and permit roots.
It also frames the debates that follow. The socialism/liberalism dyad re-opens the ledger between
solidarity and innovation, distributive justice and liberty: how much re-embedding is needed so
that contracts do not become cover for power, and how much fluidity is required so that
solidarity does not congeal into tutelage? Marcuse’s one-dimensional man will press a different
alarm: when instrumental reason and consumer integration saturate life, critique thins and
alternatives dim—even as comfort rises. Bauman’s liquidity keeps the pressure on: institutions
that cannot absorb turbulence risk irrelevance; lives that cannot afford stability pay for freedom
with worry. The modern “I” is thus not an island and not merely a node; it is a signature laid


across shifting supports. We will measure our arrangements by how well they sustain that
signature without erasing the hand that writes it.
Concepts, Measures, and Global Trends of I–C
Modern individualism–collectivism (I–C) is best understood as a layered cultural ecology that
organizes both freedom and obligation. At the level of values, individualism treats the person as
an autonomous addressee of rights and author of commitments; collectivism treats the person as
relational, obligated by ties and shared ends. At the level of practices, individualism normalizes
privacy, dissent, preference expression, and the right to “live apart,” while collectivism routinizes
fitting-in, reciprocity, deference to elders or office, and multi-generational co-residence. At the
level of institutions, individualist orders depend on general rules—contract enforcement, due
process, transparent procedures—that allow strangers to coordinate; collectivist orders lean more
on obligation, authority, and reputations within bounded networks. Keeping these layers distinct
clarifies why the same society can valorize free speech yet expect harmony at home, or
constitutionalize rights while relying on kin insurance in everyday risk.
Two strands of modern individualism run through these layers. Expressive individualism
moralizes authenticity, self-realization, and the qualitative fullness of life; instrumental
individualism moralizes rational control, calculation, and contract. These goods often collide yet
do not cancel each other: the first supplies meaning and motivation; the second supplies
reliability and reach. The pathologies are mirror images: expressive excess drifts into endless
self-curation; instrumental excess hardens into means without ends.
A more precise map adds the hierarchy/equality axis to the I–C axis. Horizontal Individualism
(HI) combines independent selves with egalitarian norms—autonomy without status play and a
taste for equality-matching in voice and reward. Vertical Individualism (VI) combines
independence with hierarchy—autonomy expressed through competition, rank, and market
pricing. Horizontal Collectivism (HC) combines interdependence with equality—need-based
sharing and communal obligation among peers. Vertical Collectivism (VC) combines
interdependence with authority ranking—loyalty upwards, care downwards, and clear status
ladders. We resist stereotyping nations as fixed dots in this grid. Every polity is a distribution
across quadrants, with subcultures, sectors, and life-stages pulling in different directions; people


“do” different quadrants in different contexts (home vs. firm, online vs. offline). Institutional
ecologies tilt the distribution: deliberative schools and egalitarian welfare nudge HI/HC;
tournament labor markets and high-stakes testing nudge VI; lineage firms and deference-heavy
bureaucracies reproduce VC. These are tendencies, not destinies.
Institutions are not neutral scenery; they make particular kinds of individuality livable. Polanyi
shows how the modern market “disembedded” economic life by treating land, labor, and money
as if they were commodities. That tear in the social fabric triggers a “double movement”: society
re-embeds protections through labor law, social insurance, consumer standards, and public
regulation. Consent alone cannot carry a life; institutional shelters must share the load. Elias
tracks a parallel interior change: as interdependence lengthens and states monopolize violence,
external constraint folds into self-constraint. Etiquette is drilled early until restraint becomes
automatic; the person learns to defer, to anticipate, to take the long view—an interior architecture
that makes formal freedom among strangers possible, and sometimes heavy.
Late modernity, Bauman argues, melts the solids that once held individuals and groups together.
Careers, neighborhoods, and life-scripts lose viscosity; commitments become “until further
notice.” Options multiply while anchors thin; “choice” becomes an ongoing audit rather than a
settled horizon. The digital turn amplifies liquidity without restoring depth: networks scale reach
but thin context; visibility is mediated by platforms and metrics; solidarity tends toward episodic
flashes of attention. Individualism under liquidity thus both extends and destabilizes the self:
more freedom, fewer guarantees; more voice, more self-doubt.
Against this backdrop, what exactly is rising when we say individualism has risen worldwide?
Across the last six decades, multiple indicators move together: smaller households and more solo
living; higher educational attainment and white-collar shares; urbanization; stronger self-
expression and autonomy items in value surveys. Read through our layered lens, these shifts
expand two capabilities at once: room to choose (expressive) and means to execute
(instrumental). Socioeconomic development is the strongest correlate and precursor—education,
occupational prestige, and income gains tend to precede shifts in practices and values—yet
causality also runs back: individualist ecologies press for rule-of-law, contract enforcement, and
participatory institutions that, in turn, support innovation and growth. Inequality complicates the
ledger. Individualism often travels with gender equality and tolerance, yet marketization and


mobility stratify access to autonomy: the mobile enjoy flexibility; the immobile live precarity
and “permanent audition.” The result is a mixed moral economy in which some carry the costs of
others’ freedom.
Trends do not advance in a straight line. Societies stage Polanyi’s double movement rather than a
one-way slide: liberalization meets counter-pressures—retrenchment, retraditionalization,
nationalist enclosure, programmatic attempts to restore family/community—for good and for ill.
The civilizing arc Elias described can enable durable cooperation at distance and also over-
tighten into guilt and burnout. In crises that demand coordination among strangers—for example,
epidemic control—more individualist settings have often displayed weaker voluntary compliance
net of state capacity and polarization; yet the same settings may excel at rapid innovation and
transparency. These tensions belong to the structure of modern individuality rather than to any
single nation.
Because the map risks becoming a scorecard, measurement must serve meaning. We therefore
anchor person-level constructs (independent/interdependent self-construal; HI/VI/HC/VC using a
parsimonious HVIC battery; expressive-individualism items on autonomy, distinctiveness,
growth, and emotion) alongside institutional and behavioral indicators (household structure,
naming diversity, mobility traces, proxies for contract enforcement and civic participation). We
read GLOBE’s collectivism as two distinct things—Institutional Collectivism vs. Family (In-
group) Collectivism—and relabel Hofstede’s pole as Self-orientation vs. Work-orientation to
match item content. Cross-language and longitudinal comparability is examined explicitly
(configural/metric/scalar invariance); acquiescence, extremity, and reference-group effects are
addressed; and models are estimated at multiple levels (individuals nested in teams/firms and
countries or cities/sectors) with group-mean centering and clear reporting of intraclass
correlations. Countries are treated as distributions with uncertainty, not destinies; within-country
variance by urbanity, class, religion, generation, race/ethnicity is documented; situational
plasticity (threat, scarcity, density, social-dilemma structures) is expected.
A compact vignette shows why level and quadrant matter for daily experience. In HI, autonomy
preferences and self-directed coping can buffer overload; in VI, competitive striving plus
blocked progress can amplify strain through self-serving attributions; in HC, expected peer
support and shared responsibility buffer demands; in VC, loyalty norms raise effort and


compliance but risk overcommitment and silent distress. At national scale, links from perceived
workload/constraints to dissatisfaction and turnover tend to be stronger in individualist contexts.
The intervention read-through is straightforward: grant autonomy and clarify accountability
where VI dominates; institutionalize peer support, co-planning, and shared rewards where HC
prevails; pair duty with safeguards and upward voice under VC; preserve egalitarian decision
rights with individual flexibility under HI. The point is not to rank cultures but to design
environments where distinct kinds of individuality can carry obligations without dissolving
meaning.
Taken together, this section relocates I–C inside the main question of the article: what kind of
individual modernity makes, how that person lives, chooses, and believes, and which
institutional arrangements amplify or restrain those possibilities. Individualism rises as both a
moral claim (the person as a bearer of dignity) and a coordination technology (rules that let
strangers cooperate). It also generates new fragilities: liquidity without depth, mobility without
belonging, contracts without ends. The rest of the paper asks how crises, faith, authority, and
embodied practices can recompose bonds that let individuals sign and belong, choose and
endure.
Religion in Late Modernity: Privatization, Liquidity, Authority — and a Relational Alternative
Modern religion unfolds within a cultural ecology transformed by individualism. Privatization—
shifting the work of meaning-making from thick, public traditions to the choosing self—
constitutes the basic move. Under privatization, persons are expected to design a life, not simply
inherit one: beliefs, moral horizons, and identities become projects. What follows is a
“marketplace of meanings”: proliferating options, low barriers to entry, and a bricolage style in
which people assemble spiritual packages from partial traditions, curated experiences, and
personal narratives. Autonomy rises, but so does responsibility for coherence; social anchorage
thins even as choice expands. A non-moralizing diagnosis must hold both truths together.
A U.S. lens makes the dynamics vivid. The First Amendment’s twin clauses—no establishment
and free exercise—institutionalize voluntarism by denying state privilege to any church while
protecting religious initiative as a civil liberty. Tocqueville already saw how Americans build
“associations” to do together what aristocratic states once imposed; in religion this yielded
congregational polities, member funding, and lay governance that tether belonging to consent.


Bellah and colleagues add the cultural script: even within institutions, Americans are authorized
to “leave home”—to renegotiate inherited loyalties and craft a direct, unmediated relation to the
sacred. Taylor’s account of expressive individualism supplies the inner grammar—authenticity,
originality, and the calling to discover a “true self”—which reframes conversion, vocation, and
worship as projects of self-articulation. On the supply side, Stark & Finke’s religious-economy
view explains why disestablished, competitive fields reward entrepreneurial ministry:
denominations segment “markets,” innovate formats (from seeker-sensitive megachurches and
multisite campuses to small-group ecologies, parachurch networks, and digital services), and
calibrate “strictness” to signal value. Casanova’s point about U.S. “public religion” fits here:
voluntarism does not privatize faith into silence; it relocates its public force into civil society—
education, welfare, advocacy—under legal neutrality. High geographic mobility,
suburbanization, and media infrastructures further lower switching costs, normalize comparative
shopping across congregations, and make affiliation a renewable contract. Immigration adds
vitality through ethnic congregations that blend social services and identity work. The result is
not simply secular decline but a reconfiguration of believing and belonging around the primacy
of choice: authority is earned (by transparency, responsiveness, performance) rather than
presumed; commitment must be narrated, measured, and periodically re-ratified; and
“membership” is sustained by experiences that feel both personally meaningful and
organizationally legible.
Liquidity deepens this pattern. Following Bauman, late-modern life “melts solids”: affiliations,
careers, neighborhoods—and confessions—become more revocable, shorter in horizon, and
mediated by platforms. Liquid faith appears as switching and churn (multi-congregation
attendance, episodic participation), DIY syncretism and bricolage across traditions, and the
growth of “nones” alongside “spiritual-but-not-religious” and app-based or influencer-led
devotionalities. Algorithms curate visibility and tempo, turning rituals into on-demand content
and communities into networks of weak ties; the upside is flexibility and reach, the downside is
choice fatigue, shallow plausibility structures, and bonds that must be constantly re-chosen and
re-performed. In this register, individualism and market logics do not abolish religion; they
render it modular, personalized, and event-like. Precisely for that reason, groups that
counterbalance liquidity with covenantal commitments, thick small-group life, embodied


calendars (music-rich worship, feasts, service cycles), and dialogical accountability often show
greater durability: they make choice livable by giving it somewhere to endure.
Authority, too, is reconfigured. Legitimacy is less about deference to inherited offices and more
about three interlocking virtues: dialogue, transparency, and answerability. Dialogue names the
expectation that reasons be shared and contestable; transparency, that procedures and criteria be
visible and intelligible; answerability, that leaders and institutions remain open to feedback and
course-correction. This triad fits a world of standing pluralism and networked publics. It also sets
a demanding bar: authority must be earned procedurally and sustained performatively. Where
these virtues are weak, suspicion grows; where they are strong, trust can scale among strangers.
If privatization pulls religion inward, communities can “externalize” faith—make it lived,
shared, and embodied—so that meaning does not dissolve into subjectivism. The research
frontier in embodied cognition and ritual pedagogy is clear: action often precedes understanding;
the body remembers when concepts fade; shared rhythms scaffold belonging. Practices that
instantiate this include music-rich worship (where voice, posture, and cadence enact common
orientation), service projects (where doctrines take form as care for neighbors and the commons),
dialogical and study gatherings (where discourse becomes a school of mutual recognition), and
feasts/holidays that punctuate time with convivial obligations. These practices do not abolish
choice; they thicken it, teaching through repetition, coordination, and joy what no manifesto can
secure.
Seen as “religion-as-culture,” the U.S. case again illustrates the mix. Protestant legacies of lay
initiative and conscience underpin expressive, self-authoring styles even outside church walls.
Catholic and Jewish organizational densities, in different ways, model how institutions can
translate private conviction into public service, education, and communal memory. The point is
not to rank traditions but to notice how distinct ecologies convert privatized faith into durable
social forms—or fail to.
A brief Bahá’í example clarifies one relational alternative without lapsing into apologetics. Its
normative center pairs a strong claim about the dignity and responsibility of the truth-seeking
individual with consultative institutions tasked to organize collective life. Consultation, explicitly
grounded in compassion, is not mere talk: it is a rule-governed practice that disciplines voice,
distributes participation, and orients decisions to shared welfare. Unity-in-diversity functions as a


moral and institutional horizon: difference is not an error to be eliminated but a resource to be
coordinated. In this configuration, “covenant” is best read analytically as commitment
architecture—freely assumed, normatively binding ties that stabilize cooperation over time—
while leaving room for personal conscience and growth. Music, service, study circles, and festive
gatherings operate as embodied carriers of this ethos, ensuring that agency is exercised with and
for others, not only before them.
This suggests a path from atomic individualism to relational individuality. Atomic individualism
treats the self as sovereign and sufficient; relational individuality understands selves as formed-
in-relation and answerable for the webs they inhabit. The test is twofold: agency kept (persons
have real authorship over life choices) and bonds thickened (commitments become durable
enough to carry meaning across setbacks). Practical levers follow directly: cultivate dialogical
authority (so dissent and loyalty coexist), design rituals and calendars that choreograph
togetherness, invest in local institutions that mediate between private conviction and public
goods, and valorize service as a primary theatre of spiritual life.
A closing normative synthesis returns to the tension that organized this chapter. Privatization and
liquidity have enlarged moral space for dignity, conscience, and innovation. They have also
shifted the burdens of coherence and care onto individuals, often beyond what solitary agents can
bear. A defensible equilibrium does not try to rewind modernity or celebrate consumer
spirituality. It balances liberty with practices and institutions that make liberty livable: dialogical
authority that earns trust; embodied rites that teach through doing; service that knits strangers
into collaborators; and commitment frameworks that convert “until-further-notice” membership
into shared endurance. On the question “Is religion for living, or is life for having religion?”, a
relational answer refuses the binary. Religion is for living—shaping persons and publics toward
justice, peace, and joy—and life is oriented to religion insofar as the highest uses of freedom are
found in devotion to truths and communities larger than oneself. The Bahá’í case, read
analytically, exemplifies this circle: independent search dignifies the person; compassionate
consultation and unity-in-diversity dignify the polis; and covenantal commitments allow both to
persist together in time.


Conclusion
This paper has argued that the way beyond both nostalgic communitarianism and laissez-faire
atomism is accountable individuality within consultative, covenantal community.
Modernity’s gains—rights, critique, creativity—are non-negotiable; the question is how to
consolidate them into durable forms that do not dissolve meaning into preference or collapse
coordination into command. Our answer reframes the person not as an isolate but as a signature
laid across shifting supports, whose freedom requires institutional grammars capable of
carrying obligation at scale.
First, we clarified the conceptual terrain. Individualism–collectivism (I–C) is a layered cultural
ecology (values, practices, institutions) in which expressive and instrumental strands of
individualism frequently collide yet also complete each other. Adding the hierarchy/equality axis
yields the HV×IC map (HI, VI, HC, VC) and discourages nation-stereotyping by treating polities
as distributions shaped by institutional ecologies. This framework let us specify how distinct
kinds of individuality can carry obligations without dissolving meaning.
Second, we located religion inside late-modern dynamics. Privatization shifts meaning-work
from thick traditions to the choosing self, generating a “marketplace of meanings” and bricolage.
Liquidity further melts solidarities, producing revocable affiliations and episodic, modular faith.
Authority therefore requires dialogical legitimacy: public reasons, transparent procedures, and
answerability that can scale trust among strangers. These same conditions burden solitary agents
with coherence work. Our proposed equilibrium is to lead with dialogue while embedding it in
procedures and feedback, so that authority is both earned and corrigible.
Third, we argued that embodied and communal practices are not decorative but constitutive.
Research frontiers in embodied cognition and ritual pedagogy show that action often precedes
understanding; the body remembers after concepts fade; rhythm and repetition scaffold
belonging. Thus music-rich worship, service projects, dialogical/study gatherings, and feasts
punctuate time with convivial obligations, converting privatized conviction into social memory
and shared stamina. These practices do not cancel freedom; they thicken it.
Fourth, our measurement architecture insists that meaning guide metrics. We combined
individual batteries (HVIC; expressive-individualism items; self-construal) with behavioral and


institutional indicators (household structure, mobility, contract enforcement proxies, civic
participation), tested invariance and multilevel structure, and reported countries as spreads with
documented within-country variance and situational plasticity. This approach resists turning
culture into a scoreboard and sets the stage for evaluating interventions without reifying
stereotypes.
Fifth, we synthesized global trends. Over six decades, individualist values and practices
generally rose (smaller households, solo living, urbanization, education, self-expression), with
socioeconomic development strongly antecedent to shifts in practices and values—even as
causality loops back via rule-of-law and innovation. Liquidity and inequality complicate the
ledger, stratifying access to autonomy into winners of flexibility and losers of precarity. Against
this background, our model seeks re-embedding without tutelage and fluidity without erosion.
The U.S. case made the mechanism vivid: voluntarism constitutionalized by the First
Amendment, expressive individualism as cultural grammar, and a competitive religious economy
together reconfigure believing and belonging around choice. Read comparatively, this is not
mere decline but restructuring; our task is to design institutions where choice can endure.
The Bahá’í example, used analytically rather than apologetically, showed one relational
alternative: independent search dignifies the person; compassion-grounded consultation
disciplines voice and distributes participation; unity-in-diversity functions as moral horizon and
institutional rationality; and covenant reads as commitment architecture that stabilizes
cooperation while preserving conscience and growth. In this ecology, music, service, study
circles, and festive gatherings act as embodied carriers of ethos, ensuring that agency is exercised
with and for others.
Policy and practice implications follow directly:
•
Organizational design: Tailor resources to quadrant dynamics—autonomy and clear
accountability where VI dominates; peer support and shared rewards for HC; duty with
safeguards and upward voice in VC; egalitarian decision rights with flexible discretion in
HI.


•
Civic architecture: Invest in local, non-partisan, consultative bodies that mediate
between private conviction and public goods; institutionalize feedback loops to keep
authority answerable.
•
Ritual calendars: Design recurring, participatory rites—musical worship, service cycles,
dialogical study, convivial feasts—to externalize commitment and build longitudinal
solidarity.
•
Measurement & evaluation: Use multilevel models with group-mean centering and
explicit invariance tests; report spreads and situational effects; triangulate self-reports
with behavioral traces and institutional proxies.
Future research should pursue (i) consultative field experiments that test whether structured
dialogue measurably increases trust, inclusion, and collective efficacy; (ii) ritual ethnography
linking embodied participation to longitudinal commitment; and (iii) migration or mover designs
that separate origin-culture from current context. The article already specifies these lines and
their associated indicators.
Finally, we can return to the animating question: Is religion for living, or is life for having
religion? A relational answer rejects the binary. Religion is for living—to shape persons and
publics toward justice, peace, and joy—and life is oriented to religion insofar as the highest uses
of freedom are found in devotion to truths and communities larger than oneself. The Bahá’í case
exemplifies this circle: agency kept (independent search) and bonds thickened (compassionate
consultation, unity-in-diversity, covenantal commitments) so that individuals can choose and
endure together. That, in the end, is the test of modern arrangements: do they raise the odds that
free persons will also belong?

The Timeless Principles of Religion: A Comparative Study Across Christian, Islamic, and Bahá’í
Thought
Abstract
This article offers a comparative theological map of nine “timeless principles” as they appear in
Christianity, Islam, and the Bahá’í Faith: the oneness of God; the unknowability of the divine
essence; creation by God’s sovereign act; the office of prophethood; the authority of revealed
law; the cardinal virtues (justice, compassion, truthfulness, love); final judgment and the
hereafter; the supremacy of revelation; and the renewal of religion across history. Using close
readings of primary scriptures and authoritative doctrinal sources, the study identifies deep
convergences on monotheism, transcendence, moral obligation, eschatological accountability,
and the primacy of revealed guidance, alongside principled differences—especially concerning
Trinitarian grammar and tawḥīd, the structure of authority after the founding revelation, and the
modality of historical renewal. Particular attention is given to the “closure” claims in Christianity
and Islam (canonical finality and khatm al-nubuwwa) and to the Bahá’í doctrine of progressive
revelation (including its thousand-year horizon), as well as to Shīʿī distinctions between
prophethood and guardianship. The result is a model of unity-in-differentiation: a shared
theological and ethical core expressed through distinct economies of law, authority, and history.
The analysis aims to sharpen confessional self-understanding while widening the basis for
principled interfaith cooperation.
Introduction
Among the most far-reaching propositions in Bahá’í theology is the assertion that all the great
religions of the world share the same essential principles. If this claim can be sustained through
careful study, it provides a compelling framework for viewing the diversity of religious
expression not as a chronicle of mutually exclusive doctrines but as the historical unfolding of a
single divine purpose. It would suggest that the apparent differences between Christianity, Islam,
and the Bahá’í Faith—differences in theology, ritual, and legal form—conceal a common
structure of spiritual and moral truth. If, however, such unity dissolves under close examination,
it would indicate that these religions articulate fundamentally different accounts of reality, with
implications for theology, interfaith dialogue, and the possibility of a shared global ethic.


This study undertakes a systematic comparative analysis of nine foundational principles that,
according to the most authoritative sources within each tradition, stand at the heart of their
theological and moral vision. These principles are drawn not from secondary summaries or
popular apologetics, but from primary texts—the Bible, the Qur’án, and the Bahá’í Writings—
together with the theological and philosophical expositions of figures whose authority is
recognized in their respective communities. The method is twofold: first, to examine each
principle within the doctrinal and historical framework of its own tradition, grounding it in
explicit authoritative statements; second, to bring these principles into comparative view,
identifying genuine convergences as well as irreducible differences.
The nine principles examined here, ordered from the most basic theological affirmations to their
social and eschatological implications, are as follows:
(1) the oneness of God, affirmed as the ultimate reality, the source of all being, and the sole
object of worship; (2) the unknowability of God’s essence, which safeguards divine
transcendence while allowing for the manifestation of divine attributes; (3) creation ex nihilo, the
belief that the universe, including matter itself, was brought into being by God out of nothing;
(4) the role of prophethood and messengers, whereby God communicates His will to humanity
through chosen intermediaries; (5) divine law and moral principles, revealed for the ordering of
human society, the realization of justice, and the fostering of spiritual growth; (6) the centrality
of moral virtues such as justice, compassion, truthfulness, and love, which form the substance of
the religious life; (7) the Day of Judgment and the hereafter, the conviction that all will be held
accountable before God and rewarded or punished accordingly; (8) the supremacy of divine
revelation, the view that the revealed word of God in each dispensation is the ultimate and
authoritative source of truth; (9) the renewal of religion through successive messengers, the
belief that divine guidance is not static but periodically renewed in forms suited to the needs and
capacities of the age.
By structuring the inquiry around these nine principles, the analysis will allow each tradition to
speak in its own voice while providing a framework for measured comparison. The aim is neither
to dissolve the distinctiveness of Christianity, Islam, and the Bahá’í Faith into an artificial
sameness nor to exaggerate their differences, but to assess whether these affirmations can be
meaningfully described as “timeless principles” shared across the three religions. In doing so,


this article seeks to clarify the theological basis—and the limits—of religious unity in the
Abrahamic tradition.
Principle 1. The Oneness of God
The unity of God stands as the bedrock of all three traditions under consideration, though
articulated in distinct theological vocabularies and historical contexts. In Christian theology, this
unity is not merely the monotheistic claim that there is only one God; it is an ontological
assertion of God’s absolute simplicity and the identity of His essence and existence. Thomas
Aquinas, drawing on Exodus 3:14 — “Ego sum qui sum” — insists that “God did not say: I am
this or that, but simply I Am. I am what? I am ‘I Am.’” This is the metaphysical declaration that
God’s essence is His existence (ipsum esse subsistens), a truth which “forms the bedrock of
Thomistic metaphysics.” Augustine’s statement, “Only those books of Scripture which are called
canonical have I learned to hold in such honor as to believe their authors have not erred in any
way in writing them,” testifies to the unassailable authority of the revelation by which this unity
is made known. The biblical witness affirms it without qualification: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD
our God, the LORD is one” (Deut. 6:4); “I am the first and I am the last; apart from me there is
no God” (Isa. 44:6); “Before me no god was formed, nor will there be one after me” (Isa. 43:10).
Christian theology thus binds divine unity to the doctrine of simplicity — “God is perfectly
simple and non-composite” — and approaches it through the via negativa, purging
anthropomorphic projections, while affirming with Paul that there is “one Lord, one faith, one
baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. 4:5–6). The New Testament crystallizes this unity not
as an abstract monad but as the living communion of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — one
Being in three Persons — integrating divine oneness with the mystery of the Trinity.
Accordingly, the Nicene–Constantinopolitan confession does not dilute Israel’s monotheism but
explicates it: God is μία οὐσία, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις—one essence in three hypostases—such that the
Son is consubstantial (homoousios) with the Father and the Holy Spirit is “the Lord and Giver of
life … who proceeds from the Father.” The personal distinctions are relations of origin
(unbegotten, begotten, proceeding), not parts or shares in deity; hence the one, simple divine
essence is numerically identical in the three Persons. There is therefore one will, one power, and
one operation toward creation (opera ad extra indivisa), with personal “appropriations” assigned
only by fittingness. Perichoresis (mutual indwelling) secures that the Persons are in one another


without composition, so that divine simplicity is not partitioned but personally subsistent. Unity,
then, is not a solitary monad but the plenitude of the one God’s undivided life in triune
communion.
Islam’s doctrine of tawḥīd presents an equally uncompromising monotheism, expressed with
unmatched concision in Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ: “Say: He is God the One, God the Eternal. He begot no
one nor was He begotten. No one is comparable to Him” (Q 112:1–4). The Qur’ān’s repeated
rejection of shirk — “Do not assign partners to Me” (Q 6:151) — positions the oneness of God
as “the very foundation of Islam” and “the most important and pivotal concept.” It declares,
“Your God is One God; there is no god but Him, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful” (Q
2:163), and, “There is no deity except Him. Everything will perish except His Face” (Q 28:88).
The Prophet Muḥammad’s summation, preserved in the ḥadīth, identifies the first clause of the
shahāda — lā ilāha illā Allāh — as the purest formulation of divine unity. Classical theology, as
reflected in commentaries on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī’s Kitāb al-Tawḥīd, insists that God’s attributes —
His Face, Hands, Eyes — “befit Allah alone” and must be affirmed “without changing them or
ignoring them completely or twisting the meanings or giving resemblance to any of the created
things,” for “there is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearer, the All-Seer” (Q 42:11). In
Shīʿī thought, tawḥīd also encompasses God’s exclusive right to legislate and guide through
divinely appointed Imāms, the “gateways to Allah” whose obedience is obedience to Him.
Whether in Qur’ānic idiom or prophetic tradition, tawḥīd is not only a theological claim but the
foundation of worship, law, and the entire moral order.
The Bahá’í writings affirm the oneness of God with equal absolutism, expanding its meaning
into a vision of divine transcendence that explicitly denies the possibility of comprehending the
divine essence. “God in His Essence and in His own Self hath ever been unseen, inaccessible,
and unknowable,” writes Bahá’u’lláh. “There is none other God but Him, the Almighty, the All-
Bounteous. We testify that He is One in His Essence, One in His attributes.” He further declares:
“Too high is the All-Merciful for the hearts of those who have recognized Him to apprehend His
true nature, or for the minds of men to hope to fathom His essence.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, citing ʿAlī
ibn Abī Ṭālib, states that “perfect belief in Divine Unity consists in the denial of all His
attributes” — not in negating God’s perfections, but in recognizing that such attributes as
conceived by the human mind are only signs, never the divine essence itself. The Qur’ānic tanzīh


(“incomparability”) is here universalized: “Exalted, immeasurably exalted, art Thou above the
strivings of mortal man to unravel Thy mystery” (Prayers and Meditations, no. 94). This
insistence on unknowability does not diminish God’s self-disclosure; rather, it heightens the
significance of the Manifestations of God, “the Bearers of the trust of God… the embodiments of
His attributes,” through whom “the Presence of God Himself is attained.” Bahá’u’lláh thus unites
metaphysical unity with the historical unity of the Prophets: “If thou wilt observe with
discriminating eyes, thou wilt behold them all abiding in the same tabernacle, soaring in the
same heaven, seated upon the same throne, uttering the same speech, and proclaiming the same
Faith.” The oneness of God is therefore inseparable from the oneness of His revelation and the
unity of humankind — “Ye are all the leaves of one tree and the drops of one ocean” — making
divine unity the organizing axis of theology, ethics, and social order alike.
When placed side by side, the doctrinal affirmations of Christianity, Islam, and the Bahá’í Faith
reveal both a shared confession and distinctive theological elaborations. Christianity integrates
unity with the mystery of triune communion, rooted in the Shema and affirmed by Christ as the
foremost commandment; Islam guards it through the absolute rejection of shirk and the Qur’ān’s
uncompromising proclamations of divine uniqueness; the Bahá’í Faith links it to the mediated
knowability of God through His Manifestations, emphasizing both the simplicity and
transcendence of the divine essence. The convergence lies not in uniform metaphysical
formulation, but in the unshakeable conviction that the One God — utterly singular, without rival
or peer — is the source, measure, and end of all reality, and the foundational principle from
which every other doctrine flows in the comparative study that follows.
Principle 2. The Unknowability of God’s Essence
The principle that God’s essence is ultimately unknowable to human beings occupies a central
place in the theological frameworks of Christianity, Islam, and the Bahá’í Faith. While each
tradition differs in its metaphysical articulation and scriptural imagery, all three converge in
affirming that no created intellect can fully comprehend the inner reality of the divine being. This
is not a mere statement of God’s greatness, but a doctrinal boundary marker: there is an absolute
qualitative gulf between Creator and creation, one that renders any direct apprehension of God’s
essence impossible. In each tradition, this conviction functions both as a safeguard against


anthropomorphism and as an invitation to seek knowledge of God through the channels He has
Himself ordained—whether through revelation, divine attributes, or theophanic manifestation.
In the Christian tradition, the biblical witness repeatedly asserts that God is beyond the reach of
human sight, concept, and comprehension. The book of Job poses the challenge: “Can you
discover the depths of God? Can you discover the limits of the Almighty? They are high as the
heavens, what can you do? Deeper than Sheol, what can you know?” (Job 11:7–8 NASB).
Proverbs affirms the same limit: “Neither have I learned wisdom, nor do I have the knowledge of
the Holy One. Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has gathered the wind in His
fists? Who has wrapped the waters in His garment? Who has established all the ends of the
earth? What is His name or His son’s name? Surely you know!” (Prov. 30:3–4 NASB). In the
New Testament, Paul exclaims, “Oh, the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge
of God! How unsearchable are His judgments and unfathomable His ways!” (Rom. 11:33), and
elsewhere concedes, “Now we see as in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).
John’s Gospel is equally clear: “No one has seen God at any time” (John 1:18). These texts
together form the scriptural bedrock for the conviction that, in this life, the divine essence
remains hidden.
Classical Christian theology developed this biblical insight into a rigorous metaphysical doctrine.
Thomas Aquinas, following the Dionysian tradition, insists that God is not a “being” (ens)
among others, but ipsum esse subsistens, the pure act of being whose essence is identical with
His existence. As Etienne Gilson observes, the “causa prima est supra ens”—God as first cause is
“above being” in the ordinary sense. This means that while human reason can demonstrate that
God exists, it cannot know what God is: esse Dei est ignotum—“the being of God is unknown.”
Aquinas holds it “impossible for the soul of man in this life to see the essence of God,” and even
with grace “we cannot know of God ‘what He is.’” The finite intellect cannot comprehend the
infinite being “as perfectly as He is capable of being seen.” Our language, too, falters: all names
for God are analogical, drawn from creaturely perfections, and “can never express his essence
fully.” Hence Aquinas embraces a “negative theology” in which the highest knowledge available
in this life is a “learned ignorance”—knowing that we do not know.
St. Bonaventure nuances this apophatic stance by distinguishing between comprehending and
apprehending God. To “comprehend” would require equality with the object, which is impossible


for creatures. Yet we may “apprehend” God insofar as His truth is manifest in creation and
revelation. “Human beings can never either totally comprehend His essence or be in total
ignorance of His existence.” Natural reason cannot reach the mysteries of faith, such as the
Trinity; “faith alone reveals to us the nature of this model.” The result is a synthesis in which
reason affirms God’s existence and certain attributes, while faith gazes toward an ungraspable
essence that lies “beyond the reach of [our] natural faculties.”
In Islam, the Qur’án and the Prophetic traditions affirm God’s incomparability and the
impossibility of comprehending His essence with equal force. “There is nothing like Him, and
He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing” (Q 42:11). “No vision can take Him in, but He takes in all
vision; He is the All-Subtle, the All-Aware” (Q 6:103). God is al-Ṣamad—absolutely self-
sufficient, without begetting or being begotten (Q 112:1–4). The reality of His “Self” (dhāt) and
attributes is “beyond our imagination, thinking, intellect, and wisdom,” and any attempt to deny,
distort, or assimilate them to creaturely forms is a deviation from the straight path. The Qur’án
underscores human limitation: “They ask you concerning the Spirit; say, ‘The Spirit is of my
Lord’s domain, and you have been given only a little knowledge’” (Q 17:85). Knowledge of the
unseen (al-ghayb) belongs exclusively to God, who discloses it only to His chosen messengers
(Q 72:26–27). Even these messengers confess their epistemic limitation: “You know what is in
my inner-self, though I do not know what is in Yours” (Q 5:116); “We have no knowledge; You
alone know the things unseen” (Q 5:109).
Islamic theology distinguishes between God’s dhāt (essence), which is utterly unknowable, and
His ṣifāt (attributes), which are truly His yet remain beyond full comprehension. The apparent
anthropomorphisms of the Qur’án—references to God’s Face, Hands, Eyes—are affirmed as real
attributes “without [asking] how” (bilā kayf), without likening them to creation, and without
negating them. God’s knowledge encompasses all: “No leaf falls without His knowledge” (Q
6:59); “He knows what is before them and behind them, but they do not comprehend Him” (Q
20:110). To speak without knowledge about God is condemned as if’tirāʾ ʿalá-llāh—fabricating
lies against God (Q 7:33). The Qur’án itself contains muḥkamāt (clear verses) and mutashābihāt
(ambiguous verses), and warns that “none knows its hidden meaning except Allah” (Q 3:7).
Thus, as in Christianity, the unknowability of God’s essence in Islam is not an admission of
agnosticism but a recognition of the Creator–creature distinction, safeguarded by revelation.


This foundational stance on divine incomprehensibility was further elaborated by diverse
intellectual currents in the Islamic world. The Muʿtazilites, committed to strict divine unity
(tawḥīd), interpreted anthropomorphic Qur’ānic expressions metaphorically to safeguard God’s
transcendence, arguing that reason can affirm His existence but cannot penetrate His essence.
The Ashʿarites, by contrast, insisted on affirming the attributes as revealed without probing their
modality (bilā kayf), holding that the essence remains utterly beyond human grasp. The Brethren
of Purity (Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ), in their philosophical epistles, wove Neoplatonic emanation theory
into Islamic cosmology, depicting God as the First Cause whose essence is ineffable. Sufi
mystics, from al-Junayd to Ibn ʿArabī, stressed that all conceptual knowledge of God is veiled,
and that only through spiritual unveiling (kashf) can the believer approach—but never fully
comprehend—the Divine. Among philosophers, Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) identified God as the
Necessary Existent (wājib al-wujūd), whose simplicity precludes any composition and whose
essence is pure existence, while al-Ghazālī affirmed the limits of reason, emphasizing
experiential knowledge through divine illumination. Later, Mullā Ṣadrā integrated Qur’ānic
theology, Sufism, and philosophy into his doctrine of the gradation of existence (tashkīk al-
wujūd), in which God’s essence is the absolute and unconditioned reality, unknowable in itself
yet the source of all knowable being. Across these schools, the consensus endured: God’s reality
transcends every conceptual category, and human knowledge of Him is mediated entirely
through His self-disclosure in revelation and creation.
In the Bahá’í writings, the unknowability of God’s essence is not only affirmed but given
systematic theological elaboration. Bahá’u’lláh declares: “Glorified be the Merciful One, unto
Whom no allusion can be made, Whom no expression can define, nor any assertion reveal, nor
any evidence describe.” Human beings, as “utter nothingness,” cannot magnify “Him Who hath
demonstrated that no description can ever express Him and no word of praise magnify His
glory.” God is “too high… for the hearts of those who have recognized Him to apprehend His
true nature, or for the minds of men to hope to fathom His essence… from all eternity…
independent of the entire creation.” What we encounter in revelation is “the effulgence of His
names and attributes, and not His exalted Essence, inasmuch as that peerless King hath ever
been… sanctified above ascent and descent.”


This apophatic theology is developed with metaphysical precision in ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s
Commentary on the Hidden Treasure. In the station of Primal Oneness (ahadiyyat), “all names
are far from the shore of Its sanctity and It is known without Name or Attribute.” The Essence is
called “the Hidden Treasure, the Absolute Unknown, the Indescribable One, the Undiscoverable
One,” and “no likeness can be made” to it. Even the divine Names and Attributes are “utterly
annihilated” in this station, and “the path to knowing the innermost Essence of the Absolute is
closed to all beings.” The Prophet Muhammad’s confession—“We have not known Thee as Thou
shouldst be known”—is cited as the apex of wisdom. Knowing God’s essence is impossible
because it requires “encompassing” Him, which no finite being can do, and because “for the
Essence of the Absolute, there is not nor ever has been any likeness or similarity.”
In Some Answered Questions, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reiterates that “the Reality of Divinity… is exempt
from all conception” and “absolutely unique… invisible, incomprehensible, inaccessible.” Even
the most advanced human intellects can only know God through His Manifestations, for “all that
the human reality knows… of the names, the attributes, and the perfections of God refer to these
Holy Manifestations. There is no access to anything else: ‘the way is closed, and seeking is
forbidden.’” The Tablet to August Forel makes the same distinction: “Man cannot grasp the
Essence of Divinity, but can… believe in God, discover the bounties of His Grace… The Divine
Essence as it is in itself is… beyond all description.” All attributes we ascribe are “only in order
to deny imperfections” rather than to define God positively.
Across all three traditions, then, the unknowability of God’s essence is upheld as a corollary of
divine transcendence. In Christianity, it guards the Creator–creature distinction while allowing
analogical knowledge through creation and revelation; in Islam, it safeguards tawḥīd against
anthropomorphism and grounds the humility of the believer before the ghayb; in the Bahá’í
Faith, it is integral to the metaphysics of God’s absolute unity, and functions to direct human
knowing toward the Manifestations as the sole locus of divine self-disclosure. This common
ground does not erase the differences in theological vocabulary and metaphysical framing, but it
does reveal a shared reverence for the mystery of God—a mystery that both humbles human
reason and orients it toward the signs by which the Unseen makes Himself known.
Principle 3. Creation Ex Nihilo


The doctrine of creation ex nihilo—that the totality of the universe, including matter itself, was
brought into existence by God without recourse to any pre-existing material—stands as a
decisive affirmation of divine sovereignty and absolute causality in Christian and Islamic
theology, and finds a nuanced but equally exalted expression in the Bahá’í Writings. While
differing in metaphysical articulation, all three traditions reject the notion that the cosmos arose
from eternal matter or as an emanation of God’s essence, and all attribute its origin wholly to the
divine will.
In the biblical witness, the creative act is portrayed as immediate, sovereign, and effectual,
accomplished solely through the divine word. “By the word of the LORD the heavens were
made, and by the breath of His mouth all their host” (Ps. 33:6); “For He spoke, and it was done;
He commanded, and it stood fast” (Ps. 33:9). This verbal fiat signifies not a shaping of pre-
existent substance, but the calling forth of being from non-being. The Second Book of
Maccabees affirms the same: “Look at the heaven and the earth and see everything that is in
them, and recognize that God did not make them out of things that existed” (2 Macc. 7:28). In
Christian philosophical theology, this is formulated as the exclusive divine prerogative to “cause
the very being (esse) of creatures” (Aquinas), a causality in which God is present to all things
“by His very essence as the cause that gives them being” (cf. Summa Theologiae I.8.1). Etienne
Gilson stresses that creation produces being “absolutely,” requiring no substrate: God alone is
eternal, “the supreme and most pure act,” whose creative will is identical with His essence.
Against Platonic and Aristotelian cosmology, which presupposed the eternality of matter, and
against pantheistic theories of creation ex Deo, Christian orthodoxy has maintained that the
Creator is distinct from the creation and under no necessity to create. The act of creation also
entails the origination of time itself, for “the world was the beginning of time” (Augustine,
Confessions XI.13); there is no “before” in which God waited to create. The International
Council on Biblical Inerrancy accordingly affirms that Genesis 1–11 records historical fact and
denies that scientific hypotheses may overturn its teaching of a divine creation in time. For many
Christian theologians, the act of bringing all things from nothing is the supreme miracle: “If God
can create the universe out of nothing, then all other biblical miracles are easy to believe”
(Geisler).


The Qur’án expresses the same sovereignty with a rhetorical simplicity that resists metaphysical
dilution: “He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, and when He decrees something, He
says only, ‘Be,’ and it is” (2:117; cf. 3:47, 3:59, 6:73, 36:82). The divine command kun fa-
yakūn—“Be! and it is”—is repeated throughout as the very form of creation, whether of the
heavens, the first human, or the resurrection of the dead (10:34; 21:30; 32:4–9; 50:38; 57:4). God
is “the Creator of all things; He has charge of everything” (39:62), the One “who created you
from nothing before” (19:67), who “created the heavens without any visible support” (31:10),
and for whom “creating and resurrecting all of you is only like creating or resurrecting a single
soul” (31:28). The Qur’án’s polemic against idolatry often takes the form of an appeal to this
exclusive creative act: “Can He who creates be compared to one who cannot create? Why do you
not take heed?” (16:17). The hadith literature amplifies this teaching: “Allah is the Creator and
Sustainer of everything in the universe… Supreme and Incomparable, has no physical form, and
no associates” (Jāmi‘ al-Tirmidhī), and “He is the Creator and the Maker, and He is not created.
And whatever exists through His Action… is something created and made” (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī).
This origin is not merely temporal but ontological: the created depends utterly on God for its
being at every moment. To the question, “Who created the heavens? Who created the earth?” the
answer is invariably “Allah” (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim), and speculative regress to “Who created your
Lord?” is rejected as incoherent, for the Creator is uncreated. The classical designation Fatir as-
samāwāt wa’l-ard (“Originator of the heavens and the earth”) itself denotes an act without
precedent or material basis, underscoring the Qur’ánic vision of creation ex nihilo.
While the Qur’án affirms creation as the sovereign act of God—instantaneous, unconditioned,
and without precedent—Islamic philosophy has probed the metaphysical structure of this act
with considerable nuance. Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) reconciles the Qur’ānic doctrine of God as Fāṭir
(Originator) with the principle of necessary causation by framing creation as an eternal, non-
temporal emanation from the Necessary Existent (wājib al-wujūd). For him, creatio ex nihilo
does not mean a transformation from absolute non-being into being, for “nothingness” has no
ontological capacity; rather, it signifies that the existence of all contingent beings flows from
God’s essence without any pre-existing matter or substrate. The created order exists by
necessity—not in itself, but through its necessary relation to the Necessary Existent, upon whom
it depends at every instant. Thus, Ibn Sīnā preserves the Qur’ānic “Be! and it is” as the
articulation, in temporal language, of a timeless ontological dependence in which God’s act of


origination is co-eternal with His essence, yet creatures remain wholly contingent and posterior
in rank of being.
Mullā Ṣadrā, integrating Avicennian metaphysics, Qur’ānic revelation, and Sufi ontology,
radicalizes this vision through his doctrine of the primacy and gradation of existence (aṣālat al-
wujūd wa-tashkīkuhu). For Ṣadrā, creatio ex nihilo is not a single past event but an ongoing,
dynamic act in which God continually bestows existence upon all contingent realities. The
Qur’ānic kun fa-yakūn is thus ontologically continuous—every moment, every particle of being
is renewed in dependence upon the Divine Will. Creation from “nothing” means creation without
a prior cause other than God Himself, and the “nothing” here is not an existent void but the sheer
absence of independent being. This perpetual creation (al-hudūth al-dā’im) preserves divine
transcendence while affirming that existence itself is theophanic, the self-disclosure of the Real
(al-Ḥaqq) in graded forms. In this perspective, the heavens and the earth are not merely once-
originated artifacts, but ceaselessly emanating signs of the One whose creative act has neither
beginning nor end.
In the Bahá’í Writings, the theme of creation from nothing is affirmed, but it is embedded within
a metaphysical framework that distinguishes absolute nothingness from the state of potential
existence. Bahá’u’lláh declares God to be “the Creator and no creator is there except Thee”
(Lawḥ-i-Ḥikmat), the “Fashioner of the heavens and the Creator of all things” (Lawḥ-i-Arḍ-i-Bá),
who “hath made being to come forth from nothingness” (Haft Vādí). Yet He also affirms that
“God’s creation hath existed from eternity, and will continue to exist forever. Its beginning hath
had no beginning, and its end knoweth no end” (Lawḥ-i-‘Abdu’r-Razzáq). This apparent paradox
is resolved by recognizing that the title “Creator” presupposes a creation: just as “Lord of Men”
presupposes the existence of a servant, so the divine attribute of creatorship implies an eternal
relationship to that which is created. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explicitly rejects the philosophical notion that
“absolute nonexistence” could become existence: “absolute nothingness cannot find existence, as
it has not the capacity of existence” (Some Answered Questions, p. 344). Creation, therefore, is
not the production of being from a sheer void, but the bringing forth into manifest reality of
forms and potentialities eternally present in the divine knowledge: “The Creator always had a
creation; the rays have always shone from the reality of the sun… The names and attributes of
God require the existence of beings, and the Eternal Bounty does not cease” (Some Answered


Questions, p. 345). These realities exist “in the mirror of the Divine Knowledge” (Commentary
on the Hidden Treasure, p. 43) in a state of absolute unity, and through God’s will they are
substantiated in the external world: “When God manifested His glory, these… which had a
virtual existence… found their existence substantiated” (Some Answered Questions, p. 357). This
is described as a dependence “of emanation—that is to say, creatures emanate from God; they do
not manifest Him” (Some Answered Questions, p. 282), akin to the way rays proceed from the
sun without diminishing its substance.
The Bahá’í teachings further clarify this by distinguishing between unoriginated, pre-existent
realities and contingent beings. The Divine Essence—“pure sanctity and absolute holiness…
invisible, incomprehensible, inaccessible”—is the Necessary Being, existing without cause and
“independent in His Essence.” God’s names and attributes, such as knowledge and power, are
identical with His essence and thus equally without beginning. The “world of existence,” in its
totality, is described as eternal, “having neither beginning nor end,” even though its individual
forms are phenomenal and transient. Central to this cosmology is the “First Will” or “First
Mind,” the first emanation from God, without temporal beginning or end, yet existing in
complete ontological dependence upon the Divine Reality. In this framework, “absolute
nothingness” is not the source of creation; rather, all things have their archetypes in the “mirror
of the Essence of the Absolute” in a state of absolute unity, receiving concrete form only through
divine volition.
Within this metaphysical order, the act of creation is continuous and relational, not a singular
event sealed in the past. The Eternal Bounty perpetually emanates existence, bringing forth
worlds and beings in correspondence with the divine purpose. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likens this to the
sun’s radiance, which has always shone and will always shine. The emergence of created things,
then, is the transition from hidden potentiality within the divine knowledge to manifested reality
within the contingent order. Even the human species, He affirms, “has existed from all eternity”
in its essential reality, though its physical forms are composed, decomposable, and bound by
temporal conditions. This vision harmonizes the eternal, unchanging reality of God with the
ceaseless renewal of creation, situating creatio ex nihilo within a doctrine of emanation that
preserves both divine transcendence and the eternal dependence of all being upon the Necessary
Existent.


All three traditions thus affirm that the universe owes its existence entirely to God, that no pre-
existent material limits His creative act, and that His will is the sufficient and sole cause of being.
Christianity and Islam articulate this as a temporal origination of the cosmos ex nihilo; the
Bahá’í Writings, while affirming the bringing-forth of being “from nothingness,” frame this
within an eternal act of emanation from divine knowledge, rejecting the possibility of absolute
nothingness and emphasizing the continuous dependence of creation on the Creator. In each case,
however, creation is not a one-time event left to run its course, but an ongoing expression of
divine will and purpose, in which every existing thing is, at each moment, held in being by the
One “in whose Hand lies control over all things” (Qur’án 36:83).
Principle 4. The Role of Prophethood and Messengers
In all three traditions under study, divine communication is not an abstract diffusion of ideas but
a concrete historical event mediated through chosen individuals—prophets and messengers—
who stand as the focal points of God’s self-disclosure to humanity. The necessity of such
intermediaries arises from the shared conviction, already examined in the doctrine of divine
unknowability, that the essence of God transcends human comprehension. It is only through
these appointed figures that the divine will is made accessible, articulated in human language,
and endowed with binding authority.
In Christian thought, the prophetic office is anchored in the conviction that “all Scripture is
inspired by God” (theopneustos) and is “profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for
training in righteousness” (2 Tim. 3:16–17). The inspiration of the sacred writings does not mean
that the prophets themselves were divinized, but rather that God “breathed” His word through
them in such a way that, without effacing their individuality or literary style, they spoke with
unerring truthfulness. The sources emphasize that in this work of inspiration, God “utilized the
distinctive personalities and literary styles of the writers whom He had chosen and prepared,”
without overriding their human faculties. Except for certain sections like the Decalogue, the
Scriptures were not verbally dictated; rather, some forty human authors composed them in
diverse literary forms—historical narrative, poetry, prophecy, personal correspondence,
theological treatise—each reflecting unique backgrounds and concerns. Yet, because “God
cannot err” (Heb. 6:18), the resulting Scriptures are “without error or fault in all their teaching,”
whether in relation to God’s saving acts, the events of world history, or the order of creation. As


St. Thomas Aquinas affirms, “our faith rests upon the revelation made to the apostles and
prophets who wrote the canonical books” (Summa Theologica, I, Q.1, A.8), a position echoed by
Augustine’s insistence that the inspired authors “have not erred in any way in writing them.”
This inerrancy is understood analogously to the Incarnation itself: “Like Christ, the Bible is
completely human, yet without error,” for God is its ultimate cause, while the prophets and
apostles are its secondary causes.
In the biblical record, the prophet is more than a predictor of future events; he is a “man of God,”
a “watchman,” and one who must declare “all the words which the LORD has spoken… not
adding to them nor taking away” (cf. Deut. 4:2). The authenticity of a prophet’s message is
confirmed by converging signs—miracles, moral integrity, and the fulfillment of predictions—so
that “when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the thing does not come about… that is
the thing which the LORD has not spoken” (Deut. 18:22). This standard of absolute truthfulness,
so central to the Old Testament office, is equally applied to the apostles of the New Testament
and supremely to Christ Himself. Jesus explicitly upheld the divine authority and inerrancy of
the Old Testament, calling it the “Word of God” (Mark 7:13), “truth” (John 17:17), and affirming
that “Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35). He endorsed the historicity of Adam and Eve,
Jonah in the great fish, and the flood of Noah, often grounding His moral teaching upon their
literal truth. He rebuked the Sadducees, “You are in error because you do not know the Scriptures
