The Possibility and Consequences of the Lack of a Final Interpretation: A Reflection on the
Openness of Interpretation after the Age of the Interpreter in the Baha'i Faith
Abstract
This article advances a precise thesis: the cessation of a living, authoritative Interpreter after
‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi does not entail hermeneutical deficit but inaugurates a
covenantally bounded openness in which truth becomes shareable procedurally. First, it
reconstructs the constitutional grammar governing post-Guardian interpretation: authoritative
interpretation now subsists as corpus (‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi), legislation belongs to
the Universal House of Justice where the Text is silent and remains revisable, and private claims
to binding authority are excluded. Second, it distinguishes plurality from polemic, grounding an
ethic of adab that prohibits contention while licensing disciplined disagreement. Third, it
proposes a tafsīr-first hermeneutic—plain sense in context, coherence across the corpus, and
boundary-checking against the Guardian’s settled determinations—explicitly resisting esoteric
shortcuts, category mistakes, and contradiction tolerance. The constructive claim is that, absent a
living Interpreter, truth “arrives” through consultation: a communal organ of cognition that
produces actionable convergence without foreclosing future insight. Dialogues with Mouffe
(articulation without agonism), Derrida (law/justice, iterability), and Gadamer (fusion of
horizons, application) clarify why decisions can bind now while remaining nonfinal. The payoffs
are twofold: a research culture that tests proposals by integrative power, fertility, and teachability
rather than victory, and a communal practice that moves in a stable loop—consult → decide →
obey → revisit—thereby preserving unity as the form of knowing rather than its enemy.
Introduction
The present essay advances a simple but consequential claim: the cessation of a living,
authoritative expounder after ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi does not mark a deficit in the
Bahá’í economy of truth; it opens a horizontal field in which meaning is pursued as a shared
practice. Before this constitutional shift, final explanation—within its rightful sphere—could be
issued by an Interpreter whose authority closed controversy. Now only their writings remain as
binding interpretation, and the Universal House of Justice legislates where the Text is silent. In
this new horizon, the locus of decisiveness is no longer a single voice but a disciplined process


among many voices. The point of our inquiry is therefore not to enthrone private opinions, nor to
deny the oneness of truth, but to recognize that in this age the truth we are charged to enact is
first of all the unity of understanding-in-diversity itself. Difference of insight is not a pathology
to be eliminated; it is the ordinary medium of approach to the Real—provided it does not harden
into contention. When a divine matter descends into disputation, “both are in error”: not because
one proposition could not be more accurate than another, but because the method has betrayed
the telos. The standard of rightness here is not merely a verdict about statements; it is an ethos of
consultation by which a community seeks, shares, and sustains insight without wounding unity.
Stated sharply: after the Age of the Interpreter, the truth that counts first is the form of our
knowing—the horizontal practice of mutual understanding—through which more determinate
truths can continue to appear.
What follows develops this thesis in six movements. First, I reconstruct the Bahá’í constitutional
grammar relevant to interpretation after the Guardian: authoritative interpretation subsists as
corpus (the writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi), legislation continues as a protected
function of the Universal House of Justice “in matters not explicitly laid down in the Text,” and
individual believers are categorically disallowed from claiming binding interpretive authority.
This establishes that our horizon is one of principled nonfinality: openness is real, yet it is
covenantally bounded. Second, I distinguish plurality from polemic. Drawing on the explicit
prohibition of conflict and contention and the ethic of adab in consultation, I argue that the error
condemned in the texts is not difference but adversarialization: the conversion of inquiry into
rivalry, partisanship, and injury to hearts. On this account, the measure of correctness is
inseparable from the manner of its pursuit. Third, I propose a hermeneutic discipline suitable to
this horizon: a tafsīr-first method that privileges the plain and contextual sense of the Word
across the whole corpus, resists esoteric shortcuts that contradict the manifest meaning, and
treats the Guardian’s settled determinations as doctrinal boundaries rather than optional
commentary. The aim is not to freeze meaning but to keep our plurality tethered to the sources
that authorize it.
Fourth, I articulate the article’s central constructive claim: in the absence of a living Interpreter,
truth arrives procedurally. Consultation becomes the organ of communal cognition. In this
frame, “unity in diversity” is not a slogan; it is a method. Participants state what they understand;


they give reasons; they listen; they refine; and if convergence sufficient for action is reached,
they act together—submitting private reservations to the unity of the whole. Where action is
required and explicit text is lacking, institutions culminate in the House of Justice, whose
enactments bind now yet remain extendable as circumstances change. Fifth, I address two
predictable worries. Against the charge of relativism, I argue that the oneness of truth is not
denied but relocated into a relational key: truth is one, but it is recognized through a practice that
is essentially interpersonal and historically extended. Against the worry about chaos, I show how
covenantal guardrails—explicit texts, the Guardian’s corpus, the legislative sphere of the House,
and the bans on backbiting and faction—stabilize the field without reinstating a personal final
arbiter. Sixth, I demonstrate the payoffs of this frame by sketching how it reframes scholarly and
community discourse. For scholars, it legitimates robust, even contradictory proposals so long as
they observe the bounds of method and ethos; the test of such proposals is not victory in debate
but their capacity to deepen shared understanding. For community life, it clarifies why
consultation can host sharp difference without breeding camps, and why obedience to
institutional decisions is not capitulation to power but a practice by which unity thinks and
moves.
Methodologically, the paper interlaces close textual reading with conceptual analysis. I treat the
relevant passages not as isolated proof-texts but as a coherent constitutional language, and I
situate key terms—unity, contention, consultation, legislation, interpretation—within that
language. At crucial junctures I adopt a phenomenological posture: describing how
understanding actually forms between persons under the discipline of consultation, rather than
presupposing an abstract, solitary knower. Throughout, I defer to the authoritative writings where
they speak definitively, and I mark my constructive claims as proposals to be tested in the very
horizon they describe—offered to the community of readers as contributions to a shared search,
not as private finalities.
The wager of this article is that the “present absence” of a living Interpreter is a divine pedagogy.
It trains us to let truth appear in the exchange itself, to honor disagreement as a genuine mode of
unity, and to preserve the hearts from the corrosion of contention. Our task, then, is not to replace
final authority with louder assertions, but to perfect a form of life—consultation—through which
the Word continues to disclose itself. If, when you finish this essay, you find that its argument


both protects the covenantal boundaries and enlarges the horizontal space for frank, generous,
disciplined plurality, then it will have accomplished precisely what it sets out to do.
Principled Nonfinality: The Constitutional Grammar of Interpretation after the Guardian
After the passing of the Guardian, the Bahá’í community inhabits a deliberately open, yet
covenantally bounded, horizon. Authoritative interpretation no longer functions as a living office;
it subsists as corpus—the written interpretations and translations of Shoghi Effendi, together
with ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s own authoritative writings. The Will and Testament had vested in the
Guardian a singular mandate—“He is the Interpreter of the Word of God”—and bound the
friends to “turn unto him and be lowly before him,” warning that to set up rival interpretive
claims would “open wide the door of false interpretation.” With the hereditary line ended, no
individual, circle, or committee can revive that office by private assertion. What remains binding
is the Interpreter’s corpus and the constitutional lines it drew. In this sense, authority is present as
text rather than person: decisiveness now arrives citationally, by appeal to what has already been
set forth, not by the pronouncement of a new living expounder.
In parallel, legislation continues as a protected, corporate function of the Universal House of
Justice “in all ordinances and regulations that are not to be found in the explicit Holy Text.” The
House is elected, acts within a defined field, and enjoys conferred guidance in that field. Its
competence is supple and time-responsive: it may enact norms for “matters not expressly
recorded in the Book,” and, as circumstances change, it may repeal or alter its own enactments,
precisely because such enactments are supplemental to the Text, not part of it. Hence the
remarkable pairing: “whatsoever they decide” in their legislative domain “has the same effect as
the Text itself,” yet these decisions remain revisable by a later House as needs evolve. This is
constitutional elasticity by design—authorized supplementation without confusion of spheres.
The immutables of explicit Revelation remain untouched; the variables of social application are
steered, prudently and provisionally, by a living legislature.
These two coordinates entail a third: individual believers are categorically disallowed from
claiming binding interpretive authority. The same charter that establishes the Guardian’s
unique mandate and the House’s corporate competence expressly forbids personal finalities: “To
none is given the right to put forth his own opinion or express his particular conviction.” The
desired ethos is frank speech without arrogation—offer what you understand, but do not seek to


bind the community to your private construal. Even the classical instruction that, when
controversy arises, “both are wrong” and the matter should be taken to the Interpreter, teaches a
lasting method: contention itself is error, and recourse must be made to recognized sources of
authority. In the present horizon, that recourse is twofold: (1) to the authoritative corpus where
meaning has already been settled; and (2) to the House of Justice where application beyond the
Text must be decided for the sake of unity in action. What is excluded is the attempt to convert
personal insight into communal law by rhetorical force or factional mobilization.
Read together, these articles of the Bahá’í constitution yield a constructive doctrine of
principled nonfinality. Openness is real: no single living person now closes meaning;
legislation adapts to time; the community is invited to think together. Yet openness is bounded:
explicit texts set outer limits; the Guardian’s settled interpretations mark doctrinal contours; the
House legislates within its sphere, with decisions that bind but can be revised as conditions
change. This covenantal form guards against two opposite errors. Against relativism, it secures a
stable center in Revelation and the Interpreter’s corpus. Against dogmatism, it refuses to
absolutize any supplemental ordinance or private reading, acknowledging that “for each day
there is a new problem and for every problem an expedient solution,” and that divine guidance in
social affairs is mediated through institutions designed to deliberate and, when necessary, to alter
their own enactments.
Finally, principled nonfinality is not only a structure; it is a pedagogy. The writings themselves
intimate a horizon in which “the Tablet is ended, but the theme is unexhausted,” in which cycles
unfold and the “flow of the grace of the All-Merciful can never cease.” The community is thus
schooled to seek truth procedurally: to consult rather than contend; to test proposals against the
corpus; to welcome plurality of understandings as the medium by which recognition deepens;
and, where action is required, to subordinate private preference to institutional decision so that
unity may “think and move.” In this frame, the absence of a living Interpreter is not a vacuum
but a disciplined opening: an ellipsis intentionally inscribed into the constitution of the Cause, so
that the Word may continue to govern without silencing inquiry, and unity may be practiced as
the very form of knowing.


Plurality without Polemic: Adab and the Error of Adversarialization
The horizon opened by the end of a living Interpreter is not a license for rivalry; it is a summons
to practice plurality without polemic. The texts distinguish, with great care, between the fact of
diversity and the vice of dissension. Diversity belongs to creation and to revelation: “the
Manifestations… have appeared clothed in divers attire,” each with a “distinct individuality” and
“a predestined Revelation,” and yet in their essential unity they “utter the same speech, and
proclaim the same Faith.” Variation in stations, languages, customs, and temperaments is not a
defect but an adornment: like “the flowers of a garden” refreshed by one spring and one sun,
“this diversity increaseth their charm, and addeth unto their beauty”; it is “perfection itself and
the cause of the appearance of Divine bounty.” That is why the Faith commands practical
instruments of unity-in-diversity—shared language and script that “thus the whole earth will
come to be regarded as one country”—and why it warns, “Let not the means of order be made
the cause of confusion and the instrument of union an occasion for discord.” The purpose of
religion itself is “to establish unity and concord amongst the peoples of the world; make it not
the cause of dissension and strife.”
Against that ontology of difference, the writings categorically forbid adversarialization—the
conversion of inquiry into rivalry, partisanship, and injury to hearts. The line is sharp: “In this
sacred Dispensation, conflict and contention are in no wise permitted”; “promiscuous talk must
not be dragged in and contention is absolutely forbidden”; “religious fanaticism and hatred are a
world-devouring fire.” The method of speech is specified: “Defile not your tongues with the
cursing and reviling of any soul… Set forth that which ye possess. If it be favourably received,
your end is attained; if not… leave that soul to himself…. Be not the cause of grief, much less of
discord and strife.” Likewise: “Revile ye not one another…. In the Book of God… ye have been
forbidden to engage in contention and conflict.” The very emblem of zeal is transfigured:
“Unsheathe the sword of your tongue from the scabbard of utterance,” for assistance to God now
consists not in “contending or disputing with any soul,” but in conquering “the cities of men’s
hearts” by “utterance, wisdom and understanding.”
This ban is not a mere etiquette; it is a safeguard for knowledge. The texts diagnose the spiritual
mechanics by which discourse decays into polemic: idle fancies and vain imaginings, lust for
leadership, pride, love and hate that blind judgment, literalism severed from spirit, and


believing the tale-bearer. These are the engines of adversarialization. “The most burning fire is
to question the signs of God” in a spirit of denial; “they speak as prompted by their own
caprices” and are “wrapped in the veils of their own selves.” Hence the repeated purifications
demanded of seekers: cleanse the heart of imitation, “regard backbiting as grievous error,” verify
reports (“Believe not the tale-bearer”), and refuse the theatrics of outrage—even when maligned.
Where these purifications fail, inquiry tilts into faction: “wolves of evil passions and desires”
tear at unity; “the widespread differences… contention, conflict and the like are the primary
factors which provoke the appearance of the satanic spirit.” History is read as a cautionary
mirror: leaders “for the lust of leadership” have “hindered their people,” turning the law of God
into “a cause and pretext for perversity and hatred.” The remedy is not counter-polemic but adab.
Adab—courtesy disciplined by tact, moderation, and truthfulness—governs both utterance and
consultation. “O people of God! I admonish you to observe courtesy, for above all else it is the
prince of virtues.” “Human utterance is an essence… its moderation… must be combined with
tact and wisdom.” “A kindly tongue is the lodestone of the hearts of men… the fountain of the
light of wisdom.” The seeker “must never seek to exalt himself,” for “the tongue is a
smouldering fire”; he “should speak with the utmost kindliness, lowliness and humility,” as if
investigating together: “Here these things are before us. Let us investigate to determine where
and in what form the truth can be found.” Consultation concretizes this ethos: “The heaven of
divine wisdom is illumined with the two luminaries of consultation and compassion. Take ye
counsel together in all matters….” In practical terms this yields a recognizable cadence: state
one’s understanding plainly; give reasons; listen; verify; and if convergence does not emerge,
“leave him unto himself, and beseech God to guide him.” The prohibition of contention protects
precisely this cadence.
Within this ethic, the measure of correctness is inseparable from the manner of its pursuit. A
reading advanced through backbiting, rancor, or deceit is self-disqualifying; a claim pressed by
humiliation or mobilized partisanship fails the standard even if the words are otherwise plausible.
Conversely, a proposal offered with fairness, verified evidence, and a kindly tongue is already
closer to truth because it is formed in the very medium through which truth becomes sharable.
That is why the text that most sharply condemns disputation—“If two souls quarrel and contend
about a question of the divine questions… both are wrong”—immediately substitutes a method:


stop the quarrel; seek authoritative guidance; preserve love. The error is not difference but
differing as warfare. As soon as discussion becomes a theater for victory, it abandons the telos
of recognition and wounds the organ of knowledge—unity itself.
Plurality, then, is not a threat to truth but its ordinary condition, provided it is held under adab.
Differences of station and perspective ensure that “each viewpoint… is perfect and complete”
relative to its horizon; differences of culture and temperament “enrich and adorn” the common
garden when governed by one Light. The community is therefore commanded to build means of
concord—shared language and script, habits of verification, consultative councils—so that
variation may be gathered rather than weaponized. This is the practical face of unity-in-diversity:
“Be united in counsel, be one in thought.” The corresponding negations are equally practical: no
reviling, no tale-bearing, no slander, no partisanship, no turning religion into a banner for enmity.
The same breath that names religion “the chief instrument… of tranquillity” warns that its
weakening leads to “chaos and confusion”—and that its misuse as polemic sets the world aflame.
In sum: plurality is a gift to be organized; polemic is a temptation to be renounced. Where
inquiry is conducted with adab—kindly tongue, moderation, verification, humility—it becomes
consultation, and consultation is the lamp by which understanding becomes common and action
becomes one. Where inquiry is seized by self, status, or spite, it becomes adversarialization; even
if the propositions asserted are accurate, the manner of assertion falsifies them as contributions
to a common life. The writings therefore do not ask for bland sameness; they ask for courageous
speech without contempt, diversity without faction, and a discipline of conversation that allows
unity to think.
A Tafsīr-First Hermeneutic: Coherence without Shortcuts
If the interpretive horizon is open yet covenantally bounded, the method that fits it must be just
as open and just as bounded. What follows is the discipline I will use throughout the paper: a
tafsīr-first approach that begins with the manifest, contextual sense of the words; consults the
whole corpus before drawing conclusions; resists esoteric shortcuts that negate the outward
sense; and treats the Guardian’s settled determinations as doctrinal boundaries rather than
optional commentary. The aim is not to freeze meaning, but to keep a living plurality moored to
the sources that authorize it—so we achieve expansion without rupture, and depth without
contradiction.


First, we acknowledge a real source hierarchy and distinct fields of competence. The explicit
Text of Bahá’u’lláh is the constitutional center. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s authoritative explanations and
Shoghi Effendi’s settled determinations do not float as “opinions”; they define doctrine, fix the
sense of key terms, and clarify institutional design. When the Text is silent or general, the
Universal House of Justice legislates for the needs of the age; its enactments bind the community
now and may be revised as conditions change, precisely because they supplement rather than
supplant the Text. Individuals—scholars and non-scholars alike—are fully free and responsible
to investigate and expound, but never to bind the community. This grammar does not constrict
inquiry; it furnishes the rails on which inquiry moves without jumping the track.
On that track, tafsīr precedes taʾwīl. We begin by reading a passage in its ordinary sense:
according to grammar, genre, speaker, addressee, occasion, and the surrounding paragraphs—
then widen the circle to the book and the broader corpus. Only after this plain-sense work do we
consider inner meanings, and never in a way that cancels a clear outward sense or contradicts
other explicit texts. There is nothing anti-spiritual about this order. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá Himself
spiritualizes “miracles,” “resurrection,” “return,” anthropomorphic language about God, and the
“ascension” in ways that illuminate the plain sense rather than war against it. Symbol and
metaphor are not escapes from the text; they are disciplined extensions cued by the text and
confirmed by the corpus.
Because revelation speaks across many Tablets, genres, and occasions, sound interpretation is
coherence-seeking. I call this the “unified theory” requirement. On any topic, we assemble all
relevant passages—direct and indirect—and we look for an interpretation that allows the greatest
number of them to stand together without strain. A reading that solves one verse by creating
frictions with five others is inferior to a reading that satisfies them all, or that at least reduces
tensions while leaving nothing contradicted. Here the principle of non-contradiction is not a
philosopher’s add-on; it is a covenantal courtesy to the Word itself: the same Revelation does not
teach opposites in the same respect. Where our favorite construal collides with an explicit text or
with a settled determination of the Guardian, we revise or relinquish the construal—not the text.
From this follow rules of evidence that keep us honest. We read words by their ordinary usage
unless the corpus indicates metaphor or technical sense. We check parallel loci: how does the
Revelation itself use “world,” “knowledge,” “return,” “resurrection,” “infallibility,” “House of


Justice,” “conferred infallibility,” and so on? We distinguish domains—worship fixed by Text
versus social questions open to legislation; essential spiritual verities that do not change versus
time-bound applications that can. We verify reports, shunning tale-bearing and rumor. And we
advance our readings with the adab of consultation: a kindly tongue, moderation, fairness, and a
standing willingness to amend when better reasons or overlooked texts appear.
Because the mind loves shortcuts, we name and refuse the typical fallacies. The esoteric
override imports a mystical gloss that erases a clear outward sense; the literalist dissonance
insists on a surface reading where the authoritative corpus marks symbol or parable; cherry-
picking builds doctrine from congenial quotations while ignoring contrary evidence or genre
signals; category mistakes treat legislative enactments as scripture or, conversely, treat explicit
scripture as if it were merely local policy; private finality smuggles binding force into personal
insight under the banner of “inner meaning”; equivocation slides the sense of key terms mid-
argument; and contradiction tolerance waves away logical collisions in the name of “plurality.”
Plurality describes perspectives; it does not license incoherence.
To make this less abstract, here is the cadence I will actually follow when treating a contested
question, without chopping it into steps. I gather the textual field and classify it by authority
(Text/‘Abdu’l-Bahá/Guardian/House) and genre (law, theology, counsel, parable, prayer). I read
each item for its apparent sense in context, noting where the writings themselves authorize
symbolic construal. I then harmonize: I look for an account that lets the whole set stand
together. If two prima facie readings clash, I prefer the one that preserves more texts and is
elsewhere affirmed by the authoritative corpus. I boundary-check against the Guardian’s
determinations so I don’t “solve” a problem by trespassing a doctrinal line. If the issue is
practical and the Text is general or silent, I identify what belongs to the legislative lane—the
House’s sphere—separating timeless principle from time-bound application. Before sharing, I
perform quality control: does this require imputing error to clear texts? does it lean on
speculation rather than converging reasons? does it keep faith with non-contradiction? And then I
publish with adab—as a proposal offered to the community, not as a private decree.
None of this excludes inner meanings; it domesticates them. Where the corpus spiritualizes, we
spiritualize; where the corpus guards transcendence (“the way is closed, and seeking is
forbidden”), we avoid anthropomorphism and respect the limits of discourse about the Divine


Essence. The touchstone for every inner reading is the corpus itself, not ingenuity. When an
allegorical insight truly comes from the text and fits the whole, it clarifies; when it arrives as a
flourish that asks the community to forget what the words say elsewhere, it is not insight but
license.
Because the writings insist that genuine knowledge is as much moral as intellectual,
hermeneutics includes purification. Detachment from idle fancies, freedom from rancor and the
lust for leadership, the refusal to revile, vigilance about tale-bearing, the kindly tongue—these
are not pieties pasted onto scholarship; they are conditions for seeing. The texts distinguish light
poured by the Holy Spirit from “satanic learning” that is clever, contentious, and self-regarding.
Cleansing the mirror of the heart is how symbol becomes luminous instead of becoming a mirror
for our own desires.
In this same spirit, independent investigation does not mean isolation. It means seeing with
one’s own eyes—free of blind imitation and party spirit—within the covenantal grammar. It
means reading widely in the corpus, consulting those illumined in heart, weighing claims
methodically, and gladly accepting correction from the Text and from the authorized boundaries.
Its fruit is not a private throne but a contribution that others can test and share in consultation.
When this discipline succeeds, it looks and feels a certain way. It honors the plain sense and
literary form of passages; integrates all relevant texts into a stable, non-contradictory whole;
respects the Guardian’s determinations and the House’s sphere; travels well—teachable
without special pleading or insider gnosis; and serves action—clarifying what belongs to
principle, what to legislation, and what to the tact and wisdom of local consultation. Above all, it
keeps plurality tethered: letting meanings deepen and diversify without being torn into rival
finalities. In short, tafsīr before taʾwīl, coherence before cleverness, and adab before
adversariality—so that the Word can continue to govern a diverse community without being
broken apart by the very hands that seek to understand it.
Truth Arrives Procedurally: Consultation as the Organ of Communal Cognition
Here is the article’s central constructive claim: once there is no living Interpreter, truth does not
disappear; it arrives procedurally. The community thinks by consultation. In this register,
“unity in diversity” is not a slogan of manners but a method of knowing. Participants state what


they understand, give reasons, listen, and refine; when convergence sufficient for action emerges,
they act together—submitting private reservations to the unity of the whole. Where action is
required and explicit text is lacking, the path culminates institutionally in the Universal House of
Justice, whose enactments bind now and remain extendable as circumstances change. The point
is epistemic as well as ethical: the procedure is how truth, enough for faithful action, becomes
shareable.
This horizon is providential rather than a deficit because it trains core virtues that a
permanent, living interpreter can inadvertently blunt. First, perpetual deference risks epistemic
outsourcing, weakening the duty of independent investigation (ʻAbduʼl-Bahá, 2014; 2007).
Second, it nourishes taqlīd—habits of heteronomous deference that displace reflective judgment
and patient examination of evidence (ʻAbduʼl-Bahá, 2014). Third, it suppresses the pedagogical
function of tests (ibtilāʾ): only through trial, error, and the communal sifting of arguments do
we separate “ore” from “gold,” clarifying both intention and reality (Baháʼuʼlláh, 1990; 2003).
The post-Interpreter order, on this reading, is a tutelary arrangement that trains spiritual and
intellectual adulthood under covenantal constraints.
Placed alongside contemporary theory, this looks less like concession and more like advance.
Chantal Mouffe shows how hegemonic articulations assemble a provisional “we”; because no
articulation is final, the field remains contestable. Her normative move turns antagonism into
agonism—enemies into adversaries constrained by common rules, with a constitutive outside
(what a discourse excludes to define itself). The Bahá’í grammar both agrees and disagrees. It
agrees that unity is produced by discourse and institution and that no articulation is immune to
revision. But where Mouffe preserves adversarial contest as democracy’s lifeblood, the Bahá’í
writings ban adversarialization. The energy she would sublimate into contest we transmute
into consultation: the same plural claims come to speech, but the rules of engagement oblige a
kindly tongue, verification, humility, and an explicit refusal of polemic. In Mouffe’s terms,
consultation “articulates” a people by installing nodal points—revealed principles, the
Guardian’s settled determinations, and the House’s enactments—that organize meaning without
foreclosing future re-articulation. The difference is that the Bahá’í chain of equivalence is
covenantally anchored: “unity” cannot be captured by partisan desire because textual and
institutional brakes check its drift.


If Mouffe clarifies how discourses produce unity, Derrida helps explain why unity must remain
nonfinal. He distinguishes law (determinate, enforceable) from justice (“to come,” exceeding
any code). Decisions are necessary, but every real decision crosses an aporia; it cannot be
deduced from rules alone. That is precisely how Bahá’í procedure lives: consultation seeks the
best recognition now, then hands time-sensitive questions to the House of Justice, whose laws
are valid and binding yet revisable. The distance between present law and justice “to come” is
not failure; it is the moral space that keeps the community mobile, corrigible, awake. Derrida’s
iterability—meaning’s travel through repeated citation without a single sovereign voice—also
maps here: after the Interpreter, meaning circulates through the authoritative corpus and
institutional pronouncements. “Unity in diversity” thus names not an achieved synthesis but a
disciplined openness: a readiness to revisit, to listen again, to let new circumstances call forth
new applications. If deconstruction is vigilance against premature closure, consultation is that
vigilance made communal—adab as ethic, legislation as instrument.
Gadamer, finally, gives the phenomenology. Understanding happens as conversation in which
horizons fuse; we never start from nowhere but from prejudgments—not vices to erase but
starting points to test. Application (Anwendung) is intrinsic to understanding itself. This is
consultation’s everyday texture. Participants bring their horizons—languages, experiences,
competences, temperaments—into a shared inquiry shaped by tradition (the texts and corpus)
and oriented to application (what shall we do?). The conversation “has a subject” that claims us;
it is not a technique we control. Out of that play, a phronetic result emerges: not a proof that
compels every mind, but a judgment that is good enough, now, for unified action—subject to
further light. Gadamer’s point that authority is not coercion but the earned credibility of what
has shown itself true also clarifies why the Guardian’s corpus and the House’s enactments
“weigh” in discourse without silencing it.
These interlocutors also illuminate how discourses are produced and maintained so that
plurality yields unity rather than faction. Mouffe alerts us to the pragmatics: unity is reproduced
by practices—shared vocabularies, citation habits, rituals of speech, calendars of decision, and
institutional forms. The Bahá’í community has them: norms against backbiting and tale-bearing;
expectations of verification; the rhetoric of a “kindly tongue”; habits of beginning with prayer
and a statement of principle; nonpartisan elections; bodies designated to consult at local,


national, global levels. Derrida reminds us that each practice excludes possibilities; hence the
need for humility and structured revisability lest today’s unity become tomorrow’s injustice.
Gadamer shows why these practices must be lived as genuine conversation rather than as
technique: only then do prejudgments become productive and tradition stay alive. In this way,
discourse is not just what we say but what we do to keep the space of saying hospitable.
Two clarifications forestall confusion. First, consultation is not liberal interest aggregation: it
does not count preferences; it seeks recognition of what is true and fitting under Revelation and
reason, and only then counts votes if needed to settle action. Second, consultation is not
technocratic expertism: expertise is welcomed, but it must speak in the common tongue and
submit to the same discipline of reasons and adab. The measure of success is not intellectual
victory but actionable convergence that preserves hearts.
What results is a distinctive picture of communal cognition. Truth here is neither the decree of a
solitary Interpreter nor the outcome of rhetorical combat. It is the product of a practice:
disciplined speech under covenantal constraints, oriented to shared action, and institutionally
capable of deciding now while remaining open to “what comes.” The Universal House of Justice
is the hinge that turns discourse into decision and keeps decision revisable; consultation is the
muscle that moves the hinge without tearing the door from its frame. In such a polity, “unity in
diversity” is not the end of thinking but its very method: we come to know together by learning
how to stay together while we know.

difference is that the Bahá’í “chain of equivalence” is covenantally anchored: the signifier
“unity” cannot be captured by partisan desire because there are textual and institutional brakes on
its drift. In short, where agonism wagers on domesticating conflict, consultation wagers on
disarming it—without suppressing difference.

is the moral space that keeps the community mobile, corrigible, awake. Derrida’s insight into

revisit, to listen again, to let new circumstances call forth new applications. If deconstruction is


vigilance against premature closure, consultation is that vigilance made communal, with adab as
its ethic and legislation as its instrument.

The Payoffs: How This Frame Rewrites Scholarship and Community Life
What changes when we take seriously that, after the Interpreter, truth arrives procedurally and
consultation is the organ of communal cognition? Two domains feel the difference at once:
scholarly work and the everyday discourse of the community. In both, the aim is no longer to win
but to deepen recognition; unity becomes not a mood but the form in which knowledge travels.
For scholars, this frame legitimates robust—and even contradictory—proposals so long as
they observe the bounds of method and ethos. “Tafsīr first” and “coherence across the whole
corpus” are not gatekeeping slogans; they are the shared rules that make proposals
commensurable. A thesis is sound insofar as it (i) respects the manifest sense and genre of texts,
(ii) integrates all relevant passages without contradiction, (iii) stays within the doctrinal
boundaries fixed by the Guardian’s determinations, and (iv) is offered with adab: a kindly
tongue, fair citation, verification, and a readiness to revise. Under these terms, two rival readings
need not be treated as enemies at law; they can coexist as live hypotheses in a common
workspace, each tested by its integrative power (how many texts and experiences it harmonizes),
fertility (the new questions it opens and resolves), and teachability (whether others can reproduce
the moves from sources to conclusions). The “result” of scholarship is thus not a knockout but an
increase in shared intelligibility—more people able to see more of the same thing together.
This also recalibrates scholarly genre. Articles become offers rather than edicts: they state
claims, show their textual dataset, narrate the constraints, and mark what is inference versus what


is explicit. Replies become acts of repair—adding overlooked texts, tightening logic, or
softening rhetoric—rather than performances of superiority. Retractions and revisions are not
embarrassments; they are virtues internal to a method that prizes coherence over cleverness. And
because private finality is out of bounds, scholars practice citational accountability: anchoring
arguments in the authoritative corpus and distinguishing clearly between doctrine, legislative
application, and personal theological construction. The long arc of such work is cumulative: rival
proposals sharpen one another until a pattern emerges that the community can actually use.
For community life, the same grammar explains how consultation can host sharp difference
without breeding camps. The bans on backbiting, tale-bearing, and contention, coupled with
non-partisan elections and a kindly tongue, remove the oxygen from faction. Disagreement gets
routed through reasons rather than loyalties; persons are honored while proposals are tested.
Meetings themselves shift tone: participants name the problem, state what they understand, give
reasons anchored in text and experience, ask clarifying questions, and listen for convergences.
Minutes capture reasons and constraints (not just outcomes), so future consultations can learn
rather than relitigate. When disagreement persists and action is still required, institutions decide;
the friends then act together, submitting private reservations to the unity of the whole.
Because obedience follows consultation, it is not capitulation to power; it is the way unity thinks
and moves.
This yields a practical rhythm that is the opposite of chaos. Where the Text is explicit, we
conform. Where it is general or silent and practice is needed, we consult toward actionable
convergence; when convergence is insufficient, competent institutions decide. Those decisions
bind now yet remain extendable—revisited as conditions change and understanding grows. The
loop is stable without being static: consult → decide → obey → revisit. Ethically, this loop
protects hearts; epistemically, it preserves learning. It is how a diverse body walks in step
without pretending that inquiry has ended.
Seen together, the scholarly and communal payoffs reinforce each other. Scholarship supplies
carefully bounded hypotheses and harmonizations that consultation can actually use;
consultation supplies feedback from life—what clarifies, what confuses, what heals—which in
turn refines scholarship. In both spaces, the measure of success is the same: not victory in debate,
but greater shareability of truth. The result is a culture that neither fears strong claims nor


tolerates strong-arm tactics; that invites daring proposals yet binds them to the sources; that
moves as one without a personal final arbiter because its very movement is how it comes to
know.
Conclusion: Openness with Order, and How Unity Thinks
This article has argued that the end of a living Interpreter widens, rather than weakens, the space
of faithful understanding—provided we inhabit it with a constitutional grammar and an ethic
suited to its scale. Authoritative interpretation now subsists as corpus; legislation continues in the
House’s protected sphere; and individuals are categorically disallowed from claiming binding
authority. Within that horizon, plurality is distinguished from polemic: difference is not the
problem—adversarialization is. A tafsīr-first hermeneutic that privileges the plain and contextual
sense across the whole corpus, resists esoteric shortcuts, and treats the Guardian’s settled
determinations as doctrinal boundaries, keeps inquiry open while keeping it tethered.
On that basis, the article’s constructive claim is that truth now arrives procedurally.
Consultation becomes the organ of communal cognition. “Unity in diversity” is not a slogan but
a method: we state what we understand, give reasons, listen, refine, and act together when
convergence sufficient for action appears—submitting private reservations to the unity of the
whole. When action is required and the Text is not explicit, the process culminates institutionally
in the Universal House of Justice, whose enactments bind now yet remain extendable as
circumstances change. In dialogue with Mouffe, Derrida, and Gadamer, this yields a picture of
discourses that produce unity without enmity, decisions that are binding without being final, and
conversations in which horizons fuse without coercion.
Two predictable worries do not stick. The charge of relativism fails because the oneness of truth
is not denied but relocated into a relational key: truth is one, but is recognized through practices
that are interpersonal and historically extended, answerable to sources, reasons, fruits, and one
another. The fear of chaos fails because covenantal guardrails—explicit texts, the Guardian’s
corpus, the legislative lane of the House, and the bans on backbiting and faction—stabilize the
field without reinstalling a personal final arbiter. Order and learning coexist in a reliable loop:
consult → decide → obey → revisit.


The payoffs are practical. In scholarship, strong and even contradictory proposals are legitimate
when they honor method and adab; the test is not victory but added shareability of truth. In
community life, consultation can host sharp differences without breeding camps, and obedience
to institutional decisions is not capitulation to power but the way unity thinks and moves.
If there is a single discipline to carry forward, it is this: tafsīr before taʾwīl, coherence before
cleverness, and adab before adversariality. In the absence of a living Interpreter, this is how a
diverse community remains intelligent, and how intelligence remains united—how we keep
openness from dissolving into relativism and order from hardening into absolutism, so that the
Word continues to govern a people capable of understanding together, acting together, and
learning together.
