elaborating the constitutional ethos of the Order, repeatedly underscores its non-clerical
character and warns against any confusion of administration with sacral office: “the
administration of the Cause is an instrument and not a substitute for the Faith,” a means to
channel spiritual aims without generating caste or hierarchy (The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh;
Bahá’í Administration). Practically, the electoral norms—no candidacy or solicitation, secret
ballot, election by the prayerful conscience of the community—are designed to suppress status-
seeking and to reinforce the understanding of office as self-effacing service (Shoghi Effendi,
Bahá’í Administration; Universal House of Justice, messages on Bahá’í elections).
Within this frame, the symbolic inference “male-only membership implies male spiritual
superiority” misfires. The texts deny any such implication: there is “no distinction as to male and
female” before God; membership neither elevates an ontological station nor creates priesthood
(’Abdu’l-Bahá, The Promulgation of Universal Peace; Shoghi Effendi, The World Order of
Bahá’u’lláh). What the clause effects is a narrowly drawn eligibility rule for a legislative service
body, not a ladder of holiness or rights. That said, one may still assess perceived signaling effects


(addressed elsewhere in the article), but those perceptions cannot be grounded in the doctrinal
architecture itself, which consistently construes office as service within a rigorously non-clerical
order.
Argument 11 — Complementarity (“Two Wings”)
P1. A system can assign some differentiated roles while upholding equal dignity and reciprocal
dependence.
P2. Bahá’í teachings frame men and women as “two wings,” emphasizing complementarity for
collective flight.
∴ C. The UHJ clause can be viewed as a (bounded) role differentiation consistent with equality.
Analysis
This argument maps role differentiation to an established theological motif: masculine and
feminine as complementary, co-equal forces required for human “flight.” It is textually grounded
in ubiquitous exhortations to equal dignity and mutuality. As analysis, it is normatively coherent
(difference ≠ inferiority) but vulnerable to overuse: absent a limiting principle,
“complementarity” can rationalize virtually any asymmetry. Within equality/equity, it legitimates
differentiated roles only where text clearly warrants and where non-diminution of opportunity is
demonstrable.
The textual thrust of the “two wings” image is elevation of women to parity, not their restriction:
“The world of humanity has two wings—one is women and the other men. Not until both wings
are equally developed can the bird fly” (‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Tablet to The Hague). This is paired with
categorical assertions that before God there is “no distinction as to male and female,” and with
public commitments to women’s full participation—“their rights with men are equal in degree,”
they “will enter all the administrative branches of politics,” and they “go neck and neck with the
men” (Promulgation 133–35; Paris Talks 182–84). Read closely, then, complementarity is non-
hierarchical interdependence: it seeks equal capacity and co-service, not a theory of separate
spheres.
Applied to the membership clause, complementarity clarifies but does not enlarge it. First, it
explains how a single, explicit differentiation of eligibility can be accommodated within a system
whose normative baseline is equal worth and equal rights: distinct roles can be ordered toward a


common end without degrading either “wing.” Second, it sets guardrails: because the texts
themselves ground equality and restrict the differentiation to one office, “complementarity”
cannot be invoked to generalize further exclusions or to supply speculative rationales the texts
withhold. Indeed, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explicitly characterizes remaining sex-based differences in this
age as “negligible,” a warning against inflating complementarity into essentialism (Universal
House of Justice, 8 Jan. 1981, on behalf of the House). Finally, the broader legal-moral pattern
corroborates the non-hierarchical reading: Bahá’í law includes both gender-neutral obligations
and a few gender-specific assignments (e.g., the husband’s capped dowry obligation; exemptions
for women in pilgrimage and in fasting during pregnancy and nursing), none of which are treated
as statements of superior rank (Bahá’u’lláh, Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶¶16, 32, 66; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Paris
Talks 182–84). In sum, the “two wings” principle supports a model of cooperative
complementarity in which equality of station and rights is primary, and a lone, text-delimited
functional differentiation is received as part of a just institutional design—not as a license to
reintroduce hierarchy.
Argument 12 — Pragmatism of Institutional Design
P1. The UHJ’s remit is to legislate on matters not explicitly recorded; explicit provisions set
constitutional boundaries.
P2. The membership clause is treated as explicit text; changing explicit text is outside UHJ
authority.
∴ C. Maintaining the clause expresses constitutional prudence, not policy preference.
Analysis
Formally, it claims institutional prudence: some constitutional features need not be axiologically
loaded if they stabilize global governance under textual constraints (legislation on non-textual
matters, protection/promotion, stewardship). It positions the clause within a larger design that
prioritizes unity and functionality. The strength is systemic coherence; the weakness is relevance
drift—unless one shows how this particular differentiation uniquely serves those ends (which the
texts do not state). Equity lens: helps explain how the system functions well; does not convert the
clause into a utilitarian policy.
Bahá’u’lláh depicts governance as dealing with “new problem[s]” requiring “expedient


solution[s]” referred to the House of Justice, which is to act according to the needs of the time
(Tablets—“Bishárát,” “Ishráqát”). ‘Abdu’l-Bahá constitutionally assigns the Universal House of
Justice authority over matters “not explicitly recorded” in the Texts (Will and Testament), while
also stating—without giving a reason—that “the House of Justice … is confined to men,” and
that its wisdom will become manifest (Selections 79–80). Shoghi Effendi characterizes the
Administrative Order as an instrument to secure unity and preserve identity while avoiding
rigidity (World Order). Put together, a single text-fixed eligibility rule (male-only at the apex)
can be viewed as a prudential anchor that reduces contestation at the center, enabling broad
legislative flexibility and full female leadership across every other sphere (Local and National
Spiritual Assemblies, the Counsellors’ ranks, agencies, public representation). This is a
coherence claim, not a causal explanation: it does not say why the text set this rule; it shows how
the rule can serve the Order’s pragmatic design while the equality principle is realized elsewhere.
Argument 13 — Contradiction Claim
P1. If a community proclaims full equality but excludes women from its apex body, principle and
structure are in tension.
P2. The UHJ is the apex and excludes women.
∴ C. The system materially and symbolically contradicts its equality principle.
Analysis
The critique is axiological: a male-only apex body undercuts equality symbolically and
materially, regardless of breadth of female participation elsewhere. It treats “apex” as meaning-
rich (final court, ultimate authority) and so reads any exclusion there as paradigmatic. Its force
lies in semiotics and role-model effects; its limit is constitutional context—apex membership is
service without clergy, and equality is realized widely in other nodes. In equality/equity terms, it
presses the hardest on symbolic coherence; responses must engage symbols, not only rules.
The force of the objection is real: representation at the center carries symbolic weight, and
communities must reckon with the social meanings of their structures. Two clarifications,
however, are required by the texts and the constitutional design of the Bahá’í Administrative
Order. First, the membership rule is treated inside the canon as explicit text, not as a policy
judgment: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that “the House of Justice … is confined to men,” adding that the


wisdom of this will “erelong be made manifest as clearly as the sun at high noon” (Selections
from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá 79–80). Letters written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi reiterate
the point while refusing speculative rationales (28 July 1936; 15 July 1947). Within Bahá’í
constitutional theology, the Universal House of Justice legislates “all matters not explicitly
recorded” in scripture; it does not alter what the texts themselves fix (‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Will and
Testament). Thus the question is not whether a policy inconsistent with equality should be
amended; it is whether a community constituted by a textually bounded order can coherently
affirm comprehensive equality of worth while accepting a single text-grounded eligibility rule.
Second, “apex” must be described accurately. The Bahá’í Order is non-clerical; membership is
construed as service rather than rank, and there is no priesthood. The Universal House of Justice
exercises conferred infallibility in its legislative sphere (Some Answered Questions 256), but
authoritative interpretation ended with Shoghi Effendi; decision-making elsewhere is
deliberately diffuse: Local and National Spiritual Assemblies, the institution of the Counsellors,
and a broad ecology of committees and agencies. In this ecology, the writings repeatedly and
programmatically insist on women’s full participation—“neck and neck with the men,” with an
“inalienable” right to vote and entry “into all the administrative branches of politics” (Paris Talks
182–84); “in the sight of God there is no distinction as to male and female … God does not
inquire, ‘Art thou woman or art thou man?’” (The Promulgation of Universal Peace 133–35).
The record of practice—from Ṭáhirih and Bahíyyih Khánum to women Hands of the Cause (e.g.,
Martha Root, Dorothy Beecher Baker, Amatu’l-Bahá Rúḥíyyih Khánum) and contemporary
leadership as Continental Counsellors, Assembly members, and international spokespersons—
confirms that the exception has not generalized into wider exclusion (Shoghi Effendi, God
Passes By 309–12; Messages to the Bahá’í World; Bahá’í International Community statements).
Where, then, does the critique still bite? Symbolically, the optics of a male-only apex can jar
with modern expectations of parity; that tension cannot be erased by fiat. Materially, one must
ask whether legislative outcomes reflect gender bias. Here, the corpus points the other way:
central guidance has consistently advanced women’s equality and leadership—e.g., urging “first
priority to the education of women and girls” and identifying the emancipation of women as a
prerequisite of peace (Universal House of Justice, Oct. 1985). Within the equality/equity frame
used throughout this article, the relevant distinction is between equality of worth/rights—which


the texts make emphatic and which practice widely realizes—and equity of institutional roles,
which in a text-constituted community may admit a single, bounded differentiation where an
explicit text so directs (Selections 79–80; Paris Talks 182–84). The contradiction claim therefore
highlights a genuine symbolic cost; the counter-case is that, given the canonical status of the rule
and the demonstrated breadth of women’s authority elsewhere, the community’s doctrinal
coherence and its material commitments to equality remain intact even as one eligibility clause
stands as a textually disciplined exception.
Argument 14 — Semantic Challenge to rijāl
P1. In Semitic usage, masculine plurals can be generic (“people”).
P2. If rijāl is generic in the relevant loci, the text need not entail sex exclusivity.
∴ C. The rule may be a misreading; membership need not be male-exclusive.
Analysis
The logic is philological: rijāl may function generically in Semitic vocatives; therefore, the verse
need not be sex-exclusive. As method, it is valuable to test range of meaning and internal usage;
its constraint is authoritative closure—‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s explicit construal fixes membership as
male, and Shoghi Effendi’s correspondence operationalizes that construal. Equity frame:
philology alone cannot overturn binding interpretation; the equality project must proceed within
that settled reading.
The philological premise—that masculine forms may be generic—is sound in principle, and the
Bahá’í corpus recognizes generic usage in English renderings (Promulgation 74–77). However,
three features of the Bahá’í textual record close this particular ambiguity.
1. Internal usage patterns. In multiple passages Bahá’u’lláh speaks of “the men of God’s
House of Justice” (Ishrāqāt: “It is incumbent upon the men of God’s House of Justice
…”; Bishārāt: “the men of God’s House of Justice have been charged with the affairs of
the people”), and in the Aqdas He twice links the institution to explicitly male diction
around stewardship and fiduciary duty (“We admonish its men … O ye Men of
Justice!”, ¶52). While masculine plurals can be inclusive in Arabic, the specific lexical
choice rijāl (plural of rajul, adult male) ordinarily denotes males rather than a mixed
group; when a genuinely generic human collective is intended, terms like nās (people) or


role nouns (e.g., ahl, dhawū) are common. The repeated pairing of the institution with
rijāl establishes a male-referential register rather than a neutral role noun (Aqdas ¶52;
Ishrāqāt; Bishārāt).
2. Authoritative interpretation. Whatever residual ambiguity a purely lexical reading
might leave is resolved by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s explicit gloss: “The House of Justice,
however, according to the explicit text of the Law of God, is confined to men; this for a
wisdom of the Lord God’s which will erelong be made manifest as clearly as the sun at
high noon” (Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá 79–80). Letters written on
behalf of Shoghi Effendi reiterate the same construction—“women are not eligible to the
International [Universal] House of Justice” (15 July 1947); “its membership is
exclusively reserved to men” (28 July 1936)—while declining any speculative rationale
beyond the Master’s assurance. In Bahá’í hermeneutics, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s and the
Guardian’s authoritative guidance norm how potentially ambiguous diction is to be read.
3. Doctrinal delimitation. The same sources that fix male-only eligibility at the universal
level simultaneously affirm women’s full eligibility at the local and national levels and
their comprehensive spiritual equality (Selections 79–80; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Paris Talks 182–
84; Promulgation 133–35). Thus the semantic field is not left to inference: the canon
itself draws the boundary—universal level male-only; all other levels and spheres
inclusive—thereby confirming that rijāl here is not merely generic.
Provisional verdict.
As a linguistic proposal, the “generic rijāl” reading is intelligible; as a Bahá’í doctrinal reading it
is overridden by repeated textual specification and by authoritative interpretation. The
equality/equity frame adopted in this article preserves what the semantic challenge rightly
highlights (the danger of over-reading grammatical gender) while locating the decisive
constraint: where the texts and authorized interpreters treat the clause as “explicit,” rijāl
functions sex-specifically for this single institution, even as the wider corpus secures women’s
equal station and broad eligibility elsewhere (Aqdas ¶52; Ishrāqāt; Bishārāt; Selections 79–80;
letters on behalf of Shoghi Effendi, 28 July 1936 and 15 July 1947).


Argument 14 — Deferral as Rationalization
P1. Deferring reasons for an apparent exception can mask inconsistency and foreclose
accountability.
P2. The UHJ clause is justified by an appeal to “wisdom deferred.”
∴ C. The appeal functions as an ad-hoc shield over contradiction.
Analysis
Two concessions are in order. First, an indefinitely deferred rationale can, in principle, be
misused rhetorically; the 1947 phrasing reads dismissively to some contemporary ears (letter on
behalf of Shoghi Effendi, 15 July 1947). Second, the discomfort is philosophically intelligible:
when a community affirms equality yet upholds a sex-specific rule at its apex, it reasonably
invites questions of coherence.
Yet, measured against the textual dossier and the community’s constitutional logic, the charge of
ad-hoc rationalization overstates its case. (1) The deferral is not a post hoc invention to fend off
modern critique; it is embedded in the authoritative texts that themselves state the rule. ‘Abdu’l-
Bahá both affirms women’s full spiritual equality and declares that “the House of Justice… is
confined to men; this for a wisdom of the Lord God’s which will erelong be made manifest as
clearly as the sun at high noon” (Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá 79–80). The same
passage is the source of the deferral; it is part of the primary statement, not an auxiliary excuse.
(2) The scope is uniquely bounded. The corpus links male-referential diction to this single
institution (e.g., “O ye Men of Justice!” in The Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶52; repeated references to “the
men of God’s House of Justice” in Ishrāqāt and Bishārāt), while explicitly affirming women’s
equal station and broad eligibility elsewhere (Selections 79–80; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Paris Talks 182–
84; The Promulgation of Universal Peace 133–35). Letters written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi
confirm the construction—“its membership is exclusively reserved to men”—and likewise
refrain from supplying a rationale (28 July 1936; 15 July 1947). (3) Accountability is not evaded
but re-located. By design, the Universal House of Justice legislates on matters “not explicitly
recorded” in the holy texts; it does not possess authority to reinterpret explicit provisions
(‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Will and Testament). The community’s responsibility, therefore, is twofold: to
uphold the explicit clause, and simultaneously to implement—vigorously and measurably—the
Faith’s comprehensive commitments to the equality and advancement of women across every


other sphere of life and administration (Selections 79–80; Paris Talks 182–84; Promulgation
166, 175).
Within the article’s equality/equity frame, “deferred wisdom” operates as a hermeneutic
guardrail: it bars speculative just-so stories (essentialist, paternalist, or sociological) precisely
because the texts themselves withhold reasons; it keeps the exception singular; and it sustains
evaluation where reasons are available—namely, in the clarity of the textual rule, the
constitutional limits of institutional authority, and the empirical record of women’s leadership
throughout the Administrative Order. The critique rightly flags an unresolved tension—the
reason remains unstated—but mischaracterizes the deferral as an evasive maneuver. In the
Bahá’í sources, deferral is integral to the revealed statement of the rule and coexists with robust
textual and practical commitments to equality (Bahá’u’lláh, The Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶52; Bahá’u’lláh,
Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh—Ishrāqāt, Bishārāt; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Selections 79–80; letters on behalf of
Shoghi Effendi, 28 July 1936 and 15 July 1947; Universal House of Justice, letter to an
individual believer, 26 May 1971).
Argument 15 — Pragmatic Harms & Equity Counter-claim
P1. Male-only apex bodies signal a “glass ceiling,” harming aspirations and perceived fairness.
P2. Equity norms favor inclusive apex representation to avoid these harms.
∴ C. Justice requires women’s inclusion on the UHJ.
Analysis
Two strands: (i) pragmatic harm: a male apex signals a glass ceiling, dampens aspirations, and
communicates misfit with contemporary equity norms; (ii) equity imperative: inclusion at the
highest level is a fairness requirement, not optional symbolism. These arguments are strongest on
sociological signaling and normative coherence with modern inclusion ethics; they are limited by
the community’s text-bounded constitution and by counter-signals from pervasive women’s
leadership elsewhere. In the equality/equity frame, they identify real risks of discouragement and
reputational cost; any faithful response must weigh those risks while honoring the textual
boundary.
The signaling concern has philosophical bite, and Bahá’í sources themselves insist on the full
equality of women and men in station and rights (ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Selections from the Writings of


ʿAbdu’l-Bahá 79–80; Paris Talks 182–84; The Promulgation of Universal Peace 133–35, 166,
175). Two features of Bahá’í constitutionalism, however, complicate a straightforward
transposition of modern equity norms. First, the membership rule is treated as explicit text—
rooted in Bahá’u’lláh’s address to the “Men of Justice” (Arabic vocative rijāl al-ʿadl) in The
Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶52 and authoritatively clarified by ʿAbdu’l-Bahá: “the House of Justice… is
confined to men; this for a wisdom… which will erelong be made manifest” (Selections 79–80).
Because the Universal House of Justice legislates only “all matters not explicitly recorded” in the
Sacred Texts, it has no mandate to revise an explicit provision (ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Will and
Testament). Second, the Bahá’í Administrative Order is non-clerical and treats office as service
rather than status; membership in the UHJ confers neither priestly rank nor spiritual superiority
(Shoghi Effendi, The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh; see also Shoghi Effendi, God Passes By).
These constraints do not dissolve the equity critique; they relocate it. The appropriate test
becomes whether the singular eligibility rule has, in practice, generalized into broader exclusion.
The record points the other way. From Ṭáhirih Qurratu’l-ʿAyn’s juristic and public leadership in
the Bábí era (Nabíl-i-Aʿẓam, The Dawn-Breakers), to Bahíyyih Khánum’s stewardship of the
worldwide community during ʿAbdu’l-Bahá’s travels and the succession interval (Balyuzi,
Bahíyyih Khánum 168–211; Shoghi Effendi, God Passes By 309–12), to multiple women
appointed Hands of the Cause—Keith Ransom-Kehler, Martha Root, Dorothy Beecher Baker,
Amelia Collins, Amatu’l-Bahá Rúḥíyyih Khánum, Clara Dunn, Corinne Knight True, Agnes
Baldwin Alexander—women have borne some of the heaviest global responsibilities of the Faith
(Shoghi Effendi, Messages to the Bahá’í World: 1950–1957; The Ministry of the Custodians;
The Bahá’í World memorials). In the contemporary period, women routinely serve as
Counsellors and Auxiliary Board members, are elected to Local and National Spiritual
Assemblies, direct agencies and institutes, and represent the community before the United
Nations—e.g., Bani Dugal, Simin Fahandej, and Diane Alai (Bahá’í International Community,
UN Office releases; Universal House of Justice, The Promise of World Peace). This broad
participation operationalizes the Faith’s teaching that women and men are the “two wings” of
humanity (ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Paris Talks 182–84) and its policy priority for girls’ and women’s
education (Universal House of Justice, The Promise of World Peace).


Thus, while a male-only UHJ can generate adverse external signals, the internal design and
practice mitigate the “glass ceiling” inference in three ways: (1) the rule’s source and
immutability lie in explicit text rather than policy preference (Bahá’u’lláh, The Kitáb-i-Aqdas
¶52; ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Selections 79–80); (2) the apex office carries service, not sacerdotal status
(Shoghi Effendi, World Order); and (3) women’s leadership is pervasive, authoritative, and
publicly visible across every other institutional rung. Seen through the article’s equality/equity
frame, the critique rightly alerts us to reputational and motivational risks; the Bahá’í response,
bounded by its hermeneutic commitments, is to maximize women’s substantive authority and
visibility everywhere the texts permit—and the historical and contemporary record shows
precisely that trend.
Argument 16 — Patriarchy/Disciplinary Reading
P1. Systems that centralize authority in male bodies often encode patriarchal discipline.
P2. The UHJ is all-male and supreme.
∴ C. The clause reproduces patriarchal power under a sacral veneer.
Analysis
Here the lens is power/discipline: a male apex encodes patriarchal authority within a panoptic
administrative rationality. It usefully interrogates organization, surveillance, and symbolic
authority; yet it risks mischaracterization by importing clerical paradigms into a non-priestly
order and by overlooking counter-evidence (women’s leadership breadth; anti-clerical design). In
equity terms, it sharpens attention to power effects, but a full account must integrate
constitutional features (service posture, no clergy, elective/consultative ethos) that complicate the
label.
Two constitutional features blunt the inference from “male apex” to “patriarchal regime.” First,
the membership rule is treated within Bahá’í hermeneutics as explicit text rather than policy:
Bahá’u’lláh’s address to the “Men of Justice” in The Kitáb-i-Aqdas (¶52) is authoritatively
glossed by ʿAbdu’l-Bahá—“the House of Justice… is confined to men; this for a wisdom…
which will erelong be made manifest” (Selections from the Writings of ʿAbdu’l-Bahá 79–80).
Because the UHJ legislates only “all matters not explicitly recorded” in the Sacred Texts, it lacks
mandate to alter an explicit provision (ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Will and Testament). The critique therefore
targets a textual settlement more than a discretionary design choice. Second, the Administrative


Order is structurally non-clerical; it repudiates priesthood and construes office as service, not
rank (Shoghi Effendi, The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh). UHJ membership confers neither
sacerdotal status nor superior spiritual station; authority is functional and bounded.
Where the critique does have traction is in optics and in the sociology of signaling: a male-only
apex can read, externally, as patriarchal even if internally justified textually. The appropriate
question, then, is whether the single eligibility rule has generalized into broader patterns of male
monopoly and disciplinary exclusion. The historical record points the other way. Women have
exercised consequential authority across the system—from Ṭáhirih Qurratu’l-ʿAyn’s juristic and
public leadership in the Bábí era, to Bahíyyih Khánum’s stewardship of the worldwide
community during ʿAbdu’l-Bahá’s travels and the succession interval, to multiple women
appointed Hands of the Cause (Keith Ransom-Kehler, Martha Root, Dorothy Beecher Baker,
Amelia Collins, Amatu’l-Bahá Rúḥíyyih Khánum, Clara Dunn, Corinne Knight True, Agnes
Baldwin Alexander)—and in contemporary roles as Continental Counsellors, Auxiliary Board
members, and international spokespersons (e.g., Bani Dugal, Simin Fahandej, Diane Alai). This
sustained participation operationalizes the principle of equality and undercuts the claim that a
male-only apex has produced a system-wide disciplinary patriarchy (ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Paris Talks
182–84; ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, The Promulgation of Universal Peace 133–35, 166, 175).
Finally, the “panopticon” analogy overreaches. Bahá’í administration lacks coercive apparatus
and state jurisdiction; its instruments are persuasion, consultation, election without candidacy,
and voluntary compliance under religious commitment, not surveillance backed by sanction
(Shoghi Effendi, The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh; Universal House of Justice, letters of 26 May
1971 and related guidance). That said, the critique helpfully alerts Bahá’ís to reputational risks:
within the fixed textual boundary, the community’s task is to maximize women’s substantive
authority and public visibility everywhere the texts permit—precisely the trend the record
already exhibits (Bahá’u’lláh, The Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶52; ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Selections 79–80; Cole,
Modernity and the Millennium; Cole, “Panopticon”).
Argument 17 — Sex/Gender Ambiguity: Who counts as “men”?
P1. If “men” is undefined across sex/gender complexities (e.g., intersex, transgender), eligibility
becomes indeterminate or exclusionary.


P2. Modern psychology distinguishes sex (biological) and gender (identity/role); Bahá’í law
recognizes male/female and proscribes homosexual acts.
∴ C. The clause invites unresolved boundary cases under contemporary frameworks.
Analysis
In the Bahá’í legal vocabulary, the norm is binary—male and female—and the restriction is
framed in those terms. The primary texts speak of “men” (rijál) in addressing the House of
Justice (Bahá’u’lláh, The Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶52) and, in ʿAbdu’l-Bahá’s authoritative gloss, state
that “the House of Justice… is confined to men” (Selections from the Writings of ʿAbdu’l-Bahá
79–80). Elsewhere the law presupposes a male/female framework in regulating marriage and
sexual ethics; permissible sexual relations are confined to “a man and the woman to whom he is
married” (Universal House of Justice, note to Aqdas no. 134). The same note explains that
Bahá’u’lláh’s condemnation in Aqdas ¶107 (including the phrase “We shrink, for very shame,
from treating of the subject of boys”) has been interpreted by Shoghi Effendi as a prohibition of
homosexual relations (Bahá’u’lláh, The Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶107; UHJ, note no. 134). On this basis,
Bahá’í law recognizes two sexes/genders for juridical purposes—male and female—and orders
marriage, chastity, and eligibility within that binary.
Orientation is not an eligibility category. Letters explain that homosexual acts are forbidden
while acknowledging medical aspects and urging compassion, effort, and recourse to
professional care; but they do not imply a third gender or a redefinition of “man/woman”
(Universal House of Justice, letter to an individual believer, 12 Jan. 1973; letter, 14 Mar. 1973;
letter, 9 Jan. 1977; letter on behalf of Shoghi Effendi, 26 Mar. 1950). In this framework, a gay or
bisexual male remains, legally, a “man”; moral standing (chastity, obedience to law), not
orientation per se, governs administrative good standing.
Edge cases (e.g., intersex conditions or requests arising from gender dysphoria) are recognized in
principle as having medical dimensions (Universal House of Justice, 12 Jan. 1973). Because the
Sacred Texts do not specify criteria for such cases, they fall—like other questions “not explicitly
recorded”—within the legislative/executive competence of the Universal House of Justice to
handle pastorally and case-by-case (ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Will and Testament). What can be said
doctrinally is limited but clear: (1) the operative legal categories in the texts are male/female; (2)


the UHJ eligibility clause uses “men” in that binary register; (3) sexual orientation does not
redefine one’s sex category; and (4) medically complex cases are addressed through institutional
guidance rather than by re-reading the textual term “men” as a fluid gender identity.
What “Eligibility” Entails: The Remit of the Universal House of Justice (descriptive)
To make the stakes transparent, this section sets out—without advocacy—the functions and
limits of the Universal House of Justice (UHJ) as defined in the primary texts, and then states
precisely what the eligibility rule forecloses (and what it does not).
The House of Justice is ordained by Bahá’u’lláh in the Kitáb-i-Aqdas and styled by Shoghi
Effendi “the ‘House of Justice,’ … the ‘Men of Justice,’ the ‘Deputies of God,’ the ‘Trustees of
the All-Merciful’” (God Passes By 214). It is described by the Guardian and by the House itself
as the “apex” of the Administrative Order and “the supreme organ of the Bahá’í
Commonwealth”; in the Guardian’s absence it is “the last refuge of a tottering civilization,” the
sole infallibly guided institution to which all must turn within its ordained sphere (Universal
House of Justice, 27 May 1966). Beyond legislation, it bears continuing responsibilities of
administering, protecting, adjudicating, and coordinating the affairs of the Faith worldwide
(UHJ, 19 May 1985; Constitution, Declaration of Trust; powers & duties).
Core remit (functions). The primary sources assign to the UHJ: (1) legislation on matters “not
expressly recorded” in the Sacred Texts, including the power to abrogate its own enactments as
conditions change; (2) stewardship of global plans for teaching and consolidation; (3) protection
and promotion of the Cause; (4) administration of the world community; (5) elucidation of
obscure questions and decision upon matters that have caused difference; (6) preservation and
classification of the Writings; (7) receipt and disposition of Ḥuqúqu’lláh; and (8) adjudication of
disputes within its purview and the pronouncement of sanctions for violations of Bahá’í law
(ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Some Answered Questions 172–73; UHJ, 9 Mar. 1965; 27 May 1966; 7 Dec.
1969; Constitution, powers & duties; Star of the West VII.15, 138–39).
Method and conferred infallibility. Decisions of the UHJ are “guarded from mistake” within
its sphere of legislation on non-textual matters—what ʿAbdu’l-Bahá terms “conferred
infallibility” of the body, not of individuals (Some Answered Questions 172–73). Before
legislating, the House “studies carefully and exhaustively both the Sacred Texts and the writings


of Shoghi Effendi,” consults at length, drafts and redrafts—and often refrains from legislation if
timing or competence is not clear (UHJ, 9 Mar. 1965; 27 May 1966; 7 Dec. 1969). Unity of
doctrine is safeguarded by the Text and by the authorized interpretations of ʿAbdu’l-Bahá and
Shoghi Effendi; unity of administration is assured by the authority of the UHJ (UHJ, 9 Mar.
1965).
Boundaries (what the House is not). Authoritative interpretation of Scripture belongs to the
Guardian; the UHJ “cannot undertake any function which exclusively appertained to the
Guardian,” nor can it legislate to create a successor to Shoghi Effendi or appoint additional
Hands of the Cause (UHJ, 27 May 1966). Although it bears legislative, administrative, and
judicial functions for the community, the House is not a state and does not exercise coercive
sovereignty; its Constitution frames its remit as the governance of Bahá’í affairs and service to
wider peace and comity (Constitution, Preamble; Declaration of Trust; powers & duties). In
Shoghi Effendi’s own balance, the Guardianship and the UHJ are “complementary in their aim
and purpose… [to] ensure the continuity of… authority…, safeguard the unity of its followers
and maintain the integrity and flexibility of its teachings” (UHJ, 27 May 1966).
Election, composition, and internal procedure (how it is formed and acts). The UHJ “shall
consist of nine men” elected by secret ballot by all members of the National Spiritual Assemblies
at the International Bahá’í Convention, ordinarily every five years (Constitution, By-Laws V; cf.
ʿAbdu’l-Bahá, Will and Testament). There are no nominations, no campaigning, and the electoral
atmosphere is to be silent and prayerful (Constitution, By-Laws VI). Provision exists for
absentee balloting by NSA members; tie votes are resolved by additional ballots among those
tied; vacancies are ordinarily filled by by-election unless the House defers to the next regular
election (By-Laws V). The House has no officers; it organizes its own work, may establish
quorums for specified classes of business, authorizes its formal signature (“The Universal House
of Justice” / “Baytu’l-ʿAdl-i-Aʿẓam”), affixes its Seal, and provides for the recording and
verification of decisions (By-Laws V).
Oversight, review, and appeals (how its authority relates to other bodies). The
Administrative Order comprises elected councils at local, national, and universal levels, and
appointed institutions for protection and propagation (Constitution, Preamble; By-Laws II–III,
IX–X). Local Spiritual Assemblies govern local Bahá’í affairs; National Spiritual Assemblies


exercise exclusive jurisdiction within their country or region. The UHJ has the right of review
over any decision of an LSA or NSA and may approve, modify, reverse, or intervene if an
Assembly fails to act (By-Laws VII). Appeals proceed from believer to LSA to NSA, and from
NSA to the UHJ, which decides whether to take jurisdiction; inter-Assembly disputes follow a
similar chain, with provision for direct appeal to a higher body if a lower one refuses to forward
the case (By-Laws VIII). The Boards of Counsellors—appointed by the UHJ—extend into the
future the Hands’ specific functions; Auxiliary Boards serve under the Counsellors. A
Counsellor’s rank renders him or her ineligible for LSA/NSA service; if elected to the UHJ, a
Counsellor (or Auxiliary Board member) ceases to hold that appointment (By-Laws IX–X).
What the eligibility rule actually forecloses—and what it does not. The Constitution codifies
that only men may be elected as one of the nine members of the UHJ (By-Laws V). That single
rule forecloses one thing only: service as a member of the Universal House of Justice. It does not
bar women from: (a) voting in all Bahá’í elections; (b) serving on Local and National Spiritual
Assemblies (from which the electors of the UHJ are drawn); (c) taking part—through NSA
membership—in the International Convention that elects the House; (d) appointment as
Counsellors and Auxiliary Board members; (e) directing agencies and institutes; (f) representing
the community before the United Nations and in other public fora (Constitution, By-Laws II–III,
V, IX–X; Paris Talks 182–84). Membership in Bahá’í institutions is construed as service, not
status or rank; the members of the House “are not… responsible to those whom they represent,”
nor governed by popular feeling, but must decide “in a prayerful attitude” and with an
“unfettered decision,” confident that “God will verily inspire them with whatsoever He willeth”
(Shoghi Effendi, quoted in Constitution, Declaration of Trust).
Why this descriptive map matters for the debate. Read together, these provisions define a
text-bounded apex institution whose core authority is legislative (on non-textual matters) and
administrative/judicial for the Bahá’í community, operating by disciplined consultation under
conferred infallibility, clearly demarcated from authoritative interpretation and from state
sovereignty. In this architecture, the membership clause narrows eligibility for one body without
diminishing women’s voting rights, service at local and national levels, appointment to high-trust
global offices, or participation—through NSA service—in the five-yearly electoral process that
constitutes the House itself. The descriptive picture thus clarifies exactly what women do not


stand for (membership among the nine) and how that differs from every other arena of
governance and leadership in which they do.
Hermeneutic Hypotheses as Theology, Not Doctrine
Any constructive reading of Bahá’í Scripture must keep sharply in view the line that separates
binding text from private exegesis. Binding authority for belief and practice rests in the explicit
Word of Bahá’u’lláh, the authorized interpretations of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi, and the
decisions of the Universal House of Justice within its legislative sphere over matters “not
expressly recorded” in the Text. Unity of doctrine is preserved by the authentic texts and those
authorized interpretations; no individual may propound “authoritative” or “inspired” readings,
and the House of Justice does not interpret but legislates in its clearly defined orbit (Universal
House of Justice, Wellspring of Guidance 52–53, 84; Messages 1968–1973 38–40). Within these
boundaries, theological hypotheses may be offered—provided they are explicitly marked as
reflection (not teaching), rigorously text-attentive, non-contradictory to explicit rulings, and
undertaken in a spirit of scholarly humility and devotional purpose.
Read in that disciplined way, the Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih (“Tablet of the Houri”) is a particularly
suggestive—yet deliberately veiled—mystical drama. The Tablet stages the advent of a celestial
feminine figure, “the Houri,” who emerges from “the pavilions of holiness, preservation, and
majesty” with an identity inscribed upon her brow: “By God! This is the Houri whom none has
beheld save God” (Bahá’u’lláh, “Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih,” unofficial trans., user-provided). Her descent
is cosmogenic: when she turns her gaze heavenward, the dwellers of the heavens are
thunderstruck; when she looks to earth, the earth is irradiated by her beauty. The narrative is
saturated with multi-layered imagery: her hair’s movement perfumes the worlds and sets “the
animal spirit” quivering in the core of beings; her voice is “like the heavenly dove,” yet “new
and fresh… beyond letter, word, and sound,” as though all books reduced to a mere gloss on her
melodies; at one moment she is a “sweet, living water” coursing through the realities of
existence; at another, a “fire… kindled in a divine tree,” from whose spark the element of fire
itself was created (Bahá’u’lláh, “Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih”). The metaphysical horizon is explicit: the
Tablet names the gradated worlds—Lāhūt (divine realm), Jabarūt (might), Malakūt (kingdom),
Mulk (dominion)—and maps the Houri’s passage across them in a rhetoric of sovereignty (royal


pavilions, tents of purity and might), epiphany (inscription by the “Most Exalted Pen”), and
audition (a “novel mode” of speech that exceeds phoneme and lexeme). Such diction signals that
we are in the register of theophanic symbolism, not institutional instruction.
Two narrative axes anchor the drama. First, the Houri’s initial unknowing and progressive
recognition. She does not, at first, “know the conditions of this world,” nor even recognize the
One she addresses, asking Bahá’u’lláh “Who are you?” and inquiring after familial protectors
who might console Him. Receiving only restrained replies—“A servant of God and the son of
His handmaiden”; “Do not ask me… for you will not be able to hear… even a letter”—she
listens at His breast and liver, searches His limbs “as though she had lost something,” and finds
no human organ by which to take His measure. Perplexity mounts to lament—“You have
bewildered me in your affair”—until, overcome by recognition, she cries out and “falls upon her
face” lifeless; Bahá’u’lláh then washes her with His tears, shrouds her, breathes into her, and,
after giving “glad-tidings of what no one could hear,” returns her to her pre-ordained pavilion
(Bahá’u’lláh, “Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih”). Second, the Tablet repeatedly frames her affect as cosmically
consequential: at the “quivering of her heart” the earth shakes; at her weeping “heaven and earth
split asunder,” mountains are rent. In Bahá’í idiom, these are signs of Resurrection—
dispensational rupture—transposed from geology to inward topography: the “earth” as human
hearts convulsed by the tests of Revelation; the “mountains” as prior proofs leveled so that a new
horizon may be seen.
On a close, symbolically disciplined reading, many elements support a theologically fruitful—
yet non-doctrinal—hypothesis. The Houri’s sovereign provenance and liminal agency (at once
supernal and affective) cohere with personifications of the revealed Word in Bahá’u’lláh’s
corpus; the “dove” voice recalls the idiom of revelation, while the twin modalities of “water” and
“fire” align with Scriptural tropes for life-giving knowledge and purifying judgement. The
unveiling of “one of her two breasts” from which innumerable suns shine is startling but
intelligible within classical semantic fields: the breast as the locus of nourishment and gnosis—
here metaphorized as the radiant effulgence of meanings that engender “suns” (new cycles of
insight) in “heavens without beginning or end.” Her hair—braided, perfumed, cascading—
functions as the sensuous synecdoche for the multiplicity of the Word’s signs: the slightest
motion diffuses fragrances (intimations) that make “the animal spirit” quiver, i.e., awaken the


life-principle across beings (Bahá’u’lláh, “Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih”). Her interrogative catechesis,
ignorance, and death-by-recognition dramatize the overwhelming alterity of the Manifestation:
even a hypostatic feminine wisdom, drawn from pavilions of glory, cannot grasp Him by
terrestrial measures; when she does recognize, her annihilation (fanāʾ) and revivification model
the movement by which created realities die to their limitations and are quickened by the Word.
Placed beside Bahá’u’lláh’s clear teaching that Revelation is progressive and millennial in
rhythm—“Whoso layeth claim to a Revelation direct from God, ere the expiration of a full
thousand years, such a man is assuredly a lying impostor” (Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶37)—the Tablet’s
insistently feminine theophanic register becomes theologically suggestive. Without asserting
more than the text warrants, one may responsibly entertain a hypothesis that the Houri functions
as an archetype of unveiled Wisdom whose feminine profile widens the symbolic horizon within
which future Revelation can be imagined. That hypothesis does not identify the Houri as a
Manifestation; the text never does so, and it pointedly withholds “a secret… which it is not meet
that I should mention.” Nor does it forecast historical particulars. Rather, it intimates—through
sovereign, inscribed identity; mediatory descent and ascent; cosmogenic speech; and world-
convulsing affect—that the revealed Word’s plenitude includes feminine imagery of sovereignty
and pedagogy, consonant with a religion that enshrines the equality of women and men and
repeatedly depicts humanity as “two wings of one bird” (‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Selections 79–80;
Promulgation 133–35, 166).
Two clarifications are essential if this hypothesis is to remain theologically sound. First, nothing
in the Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih—a mystical Tablet in a consciously symbolic key—bears on, let alone
alters, the explicit, interpreted eligibility clause for membership on the Universal House of
Justice. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s ruling is categorical and paired with deferral of rationale: “the House of
Justice… is confined to men; this for a wisdom… which will erelong be made manifest as clearly
as the sun at high noon” (Selections 79–80). Shoghi Effendi’s correspondence preserves
precisely that stance of acceptance without speculative rationale (28 July 1936; 15 July 1947).
Because authoritative interpretation ended with the Guardian, and because the House of Justice
legislates only on matters “not expressly recorded,” private exegesis of a mystical Tablet cannot
be deployed to adjudicate, dilute, or re-read that clause (Universal House of Justice, Wellspring
of Guidance 52–53, 84). Second, the Tablet’s tremors and “rending of mountains” dramatize the


pedagogy of divine tests—“veils of glory”—not the polemics of institutional reform. Their force
is purgative and confirmatory, aimed at hearts rather than bylaws (cf. Bahá’u’lláh, Kitáb-i-Íqán
§53 on the function of symbolic terms to “test and prove the peoples of the world”).
The hypothesis advanced here is that Bahá’u’lláh’s Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih (Tablet of the Houri)
functions as a symbolic prefiguration of a future feminine Manifestation of God, and that the
present, text-fixed limitation of membership on the Universal House of Justice to men is (part of)
the hidden “wisdom” deferred by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá: it preserves a space for a severe divine test at
the next theophany, when believers must recognize and submit to a woman Manifestation
unshielded by prior institutional habit (ʻAbdu’l-Bahá, Selections 79–80). On this reading, the
Tablet’s sovereign Maiden—radiant, world-shaking, yet initially “unaware” of earthly conditions
until addressed and revived by the Beloved—allegorizes a future feminine theophany whose
appearance overturns inherited measures and demands a purified recognition (Bahá’u’lláh,
Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih, unofficial trans.). The “earth’s quaking” and “rending of mountains” are read
as eschatological signals of dispensation-break, fitting Bahá’u’lláh’s doctrine that “symbolic
terms and abstruse allusions” are intended “to test and prove the peoples of the world”
(Bahá’u’lláh, Kitáb-i-Íqán §53).
A chain of theological reasons makes this conjecture intelligible within Bahá’í categories. First,
progressive revelation forecloses finality and sets only a temporal guardrail: “Whoso layeth
claim to a Revelation… ere the expiration of a full thousand years… is assuredly a lying
impostor” (Bahá’u’lláh, Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶37). Second, the distinction between essential
infallibility (proper to a Manifestation) and conferred infallibility (proper to the House of Justice
within its sphere) implies that, at the next advent, the Manifestation’s authority supersedes all
derivative authorities (ʻAbdu’l-Bahá, Some Answered Questions 172–73). Third, because
authoritative interpretation has ended with the Guardian and the House legislates only on matters
“not expressly recorded,” the male-only eligibility stands as an explicit, non-legislable rule in
this dispensation—one that, precisely by not institutionalizing women at the apex now, heightens
the future test: believers must pass from institutional symbolism to spiritual recognition when a
woman bears essential authority (Universal House of Justice, Wellspring of Guidance 52–53,
84). In this sense, the “wisdom” deferred may be eschatological and pedagogical: a divinely
arranged discrepancy that purifies motives, exposes residual patriarchy, and compels allegiance


to the Word itself rather than to familiar administrative signs (Bahá’u’lláh, Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih;
Kitáb-i-Íqán §53).
Methodologically, this remains theology, not doctrine. It proposes a coherent, text-attentive
hypothesis that honors progressive revelation, the Houri’s feminine symbolism, the pedagogy of
tests, and the constitutional architecture of the Order; yet it neither claims to unveil the deferred
“wisdom” with certainty nor licenses any present-tense alteration of the explicit rule (ʻAbdu’l-
Bahá, Selections 79–80; Universal House of Justice, Wellspring of Guidance 52–53, 84). Its
proper use is devotional and pedagogical: to enlarge the community’s symbolic horizon, to ready
hearts for a future theophany that could be feminine, and to interpret the present limitation as a
possible divine proving-ground—without converting a mystical exegesis into legislative
argument or counter-textual advocacy.
There is another Tablet, “Ḥúr-i-ʿUjāb” (“The Wondrous Maiden”), whose idiom and dramaturgy
closely parallel the Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih and that, read alongside it, sharpens the same eschatological
horizon. Here again Revelation is personified as a sovereign Maiden who “lifted the veil from
her face” and disclosed a “novel, wondrous beauty.” Her epiphany is world-disruptive: with a
glance she “shot as meteors are cast,” with the fire of her countenance she “burned all names and
titles,” and at her manifestation “the frames of existence quaked; then she vanished.” The
imagery then turns sacramental and judicial: she passes “the wine of life” and a “morsel of
roast,” her palm “reddened…with the blood of lovers,” she sings to the Beloved with lute and
rebāb, melts “the inmost hearts,” and draws “the sword of her sidelong glance.” The coda is
explicitly polemical and apocalyptic: she reproaches “the People of the Book” for denial,
announces that certain “secrets of God” are deliberately veiled “from the pages and the Book—
save when the Promised One appears on the Day of Return,” and then withdraws. the repeated
wordʿujāb refrain (“verily this is a wondrous…”), which functions like a liturgical hammer-
stroke, accumulating signs that together stage revelation as shock, consolation, testing, and
concealment.
Placed in dialogue with the Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih, this Tablet confirms four through-lines relevant to
my hypothesis. First, both Maids are agents of upheaval: their appearance shakes earth and sky,
rending inherited stabilizers (“mountains” in the Húríyyih; “frames of existence” in the Ḥúr-i-


ʿUjāb). Second, both annul and re-signify social markers: the Houri makes “all books… a
single exegesis” of a “new and fresh” song; the Wondrous Maiden “burned all names and titles,”
a striking trope for the obsolescence of prior taxonomies—including those that believers may be
tempted to absolutize. Third, both encode pedagogy by concealment: Bahá’u’lláh’s reticence
before the Houri’s direct questions, and the Wondrous Maiden’s declaration that divine “secrets”
are intentionally veiled “save when the Promised One appears,” converge with the Íqán’s rule
that “symbolic terms and abstruse allusions” are designed “to test and prove the peoples of the
world.” Fourth, both foretell denial and selection: the Houri’s death and revivification cipher
the annihilation of inherited measures and the gift of new life through the Beloved’s speech; the
Wondrous Maiden’s reproach to the “People of the Book” prefigures the recognitional crisis that
greets every advent.
The feminine theophany dramatized in these Tablets can be read as a symbolic prefiguration of a
future feminine Manifestation of God; and the present, explicit limitation of Universal House of
Justice membership to men can be understood as part of the deferred “wisdom” that prepares a
severe divine test at that future advent. The test would be twofold. Negatively, it would expose
any residual habit of treating an all-male apex as a metaphysical constant rather than a
dispensational eligibility rule bounded by text. Positively, it would compel the community to
pass from institutional symbolism to essential recognition—to “burned names and titles”—
when a woman bears the innate, essential authority of God’s Manifestation. Read this way, “we
veil the secrets of God from the pages and the Book—save when the Promised One appears on
the Day of Return” aligns with ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s assurance that the rationale for the present clause
“will erelong be made manifest,” suggests that the disclosure is eschatological rather than
analytic, and situates the community’s current obedience within a pedagogy of veils of glory:
fidelity under partial understanding, so that the next unveiling can sift hearts rather than
vindicate a prior theory.
Two methodological guardrails remain crucial. First, neither Tablet furnishes a juridical warrant
to alter what the explicit texts and authorized interpretation already fix for this dispensation; by
Bahá’í constitutional design, authoritative interpretation has ended with the Guardian and the
Universal House of Justice legislates only on matters “not expressly recorded.” These visionary
scenes therefore belong to theology and devotion, not to legislation or counter-legislation.


Second, precisely because the Wondrous Maiden “burns names and titles,” any theological use
of these Tablets should discipline our imagination away from essentialist rationales (about
“female nature” or paternal “exemption”) and toward the recognitional stakes the texts
themselves underline: denial by “People of the Book,” the veiling and unveiling of secrets, the
quake of old measures, the wine that both wounds and heals. Kept within these limits, Ḥúr-i-
ʿUjāb and Lawḥ-i-Ḥúríyyih together offer a robust symbolic horizon within which my hypothesis
is both intelligible and spiritually fruitful: the present male-only eligibility can be received as a
divinely arranged proving-ground that preserves, for the Day of Return, the freedom and severity
of a recognition that may arrive in a woman’s voice.
Situated Engagement with the Literature
This section situates the article’s claims amid the main scholarly and para-scholarly
conversations that readers are most likely to consult. I present each contribution in its best form
and then indicate where our equality/equity framework concurs, qualifies, or departs.
Karen Bacquet (2006)
Bacquet’s core claim is that a standing contradiction exists between the Bahá’í principle of the
equality of women and men and the exclusion of women from the Universal House of Justice
(UHJ); when this tension arises, the community has largely prioritized loyalty to institutional
authority over reform. She frames this as a collision of “principle and authority,” documents how
the exclusion was historically articulated, outlines liberal Bahá’í arguments for change, and then
narrates the administrative and social responses that keep the status quo in place.
Key planks (steel-manned):
•
Doctrinal tension. Equality is a fundamental, widely taught Bahá’í principle, and women
already vote and serve widely across the administration, yet are excluded from the
highest elected body. This juxtaposition is not incidental but structural.
•
Textual/semantic ambiguity. Liberals point to confusions in the early record:
Bahá’u’lláh uses rijál (“men”) for both local and universal houses; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s
1902/1909 letters are read variously (with the Arabic ‘umúmí possibly meaning “general”


rather than “universal”), and in 1912 He called for a mixed-gender council in Chicago—
facts that, taken together, make the present reading look non-obvious and historically
contingent.
•
Authority & legislation. Because the dossier appears inconsistent, liberals argue the
UHJ sits precisely where Bahá’í scripture assigns the task of resolving “obscure
questions,” and could legislate to include women—legislation being changeable and thus
not a threat to scripture.
•
Communal dynamics. Bacquet’s online content analysis found >17% of posters openly
rejecting the permanent exclusion; however, the dominant pattern in the rank-and-file is
deference to authority, reinforced by pre-publication review and, in some cases,
sanctions—producing a chilling effect on reform discourse.
•
Signaling & the Covenant. Drawing on Mark Chaves, she argues that refusing women
at the apex signals resistance to outside pressures; in the Bahá’í case the signal is inward-
facing: the exclusion is cast as irrevocable and attempts to alter it as covenantal
disloyalty.
Response
1) Text vs. eligibility. I agree with Bacquet that equality is axiomatic in the Bahá’í corpus and
that the UHJ clause is explicitly text-based. Where I part ways is in category: the rule defines
eligibility for one office, not a judgment about worth or a general civil right—an internal
distinction evidenced by the same article’s acknowledgment that women already “serve in
powerful positions at all levels.” Treating eligibility as if it were equality-of-station is a category
mistake that blunts analytic precision even before we address wisdom-deferred.
2) Semantics and scope. Bacquet fairly notes the terminological flux (rijál; baytu’l-‘adl;
‘umúmí) and the 1912 Chicago precedent; that’s the strongest part of her paper. But she stops
short of a full accounting of how later, authoritative guidance has read those same items,
including explicit statements that the 1902/1909 letters were not intended to govern local
practice and that women’s exclusion applies uniquely to the Universal House of Justice, even
while women serve everywhere else. (She cites the House’s clarifications but treats them as
merely administrative positioning.)


3) “UHJ can fix it”. Bacquet reports the liberal thesis that the UHJ could legislate women’s
inclusion to resolve an “obscure question.” That accurately reflects a view in the discourse—but
it collides with the UHJ’s own stated reading of its remit, which (as she herself notes) rejects the
idea that it can overturn this particular eligibility rule. In other words, the locus of ambiguity
claimed by liberals is denied by the very institution scripture authorizes to rule on such
ambiguities. Analytically, that undercuts the move from “confusing record” → “therefore
legislative latitude.”
4) “Deferral = rationalization”. Bacquet’s strongest rhetorical charge is that “wisdom deferred”
functions as an authority shield. Our analysis distinguishes two layers: (a) hermeneutic deference
to explicit text (which any text-bound community will maintain), and (b) sociological effects
(how deference plays out in communities). She compellingly documents the latter—sanctions,
review, chilling effects—but those data don’t convert the former into contradiction; they show
the costs of maintaining a text-bounded rule in a modern equality frame. That’s an important, but
different, conclusion.
5) Practice and “glass-ceiling” signaling. Bacquet opens by acknowledging that women vote
and “serve in powerful positions at all levels,” which weakens any claim that the clause has
generalized into broader exclusion in practice; the lived pattern is mixed—symbolically jarring
to some, yet institutionally porous everywhere except the single office. My earlier “lived
practice” argument doesn’t solve the symbolism, but it does bound the sociological inference.
6) Sample & inference. Her >17% figure comes from posters in an online forum—useful for
mapping discursive diversity, but not a representative sample. Even so, it supports a fair
descriptive point: significant dissent exists alongside majority deference. The paper is strongest
as a sociology-of-knowledge snapshot; it is less decisive when it ventures into what the UHJ
could do textually.
Bottom line. Bacquet convincingly documents tension management (deference mechanisms;
chilled reform discourse) and fairly surfaces the best liberal arguments from ambiguity
(rijál/‘umúmí; 1912). Where our analysis lands differently is on doctrinal mechanics: the same
sources she cites depict the UHJ as denying legislative latitude on this specific point, keeping the


clause in the “explicit-text/deferral” box rather than the “obscure-question/legislate” box. That
doesn’t dissolve symbolic objections, but it clarifies why—within a text-bounded system—the
rule stands as an eligibility clause while women’s leadership remains otherwise pervasive in
practice.
Cole (works): Where the disciplinary / theocracy lenses illuminate vs. mischaracterize
Across Modernity and the Millennium and “The Bahá’í Faith in America as Panopticon,” Cole
advances two linked theses. First, he reads Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá as articulating a
liberal, non-theocratic social vision—religion–state disentanglement, representative government,
nation-state formation, internationalism, and women’s emancipation—with a House of Justice
whose remit is intra-community rather than over the state. Second, he contends that late-20th-
century American Bahá’í administration employs “disciplinary” techniques (pre-publication
review, informal reporting, blackballing/shunning) that constrain internal discourse even as the
movement projects a liberal public image. In short: the textual horizon is liberal-pluralist; some
contemporary practices trend theocratic/disciplinary.
Response
1) Theocracy vs. revealed constitutionalism.
My position (developed in “Toward a Bahá’í Political Philosophy: Manifestation, Authority, and
the Form of Civilizational Unity”) is that the Bahá’í order institutes a revealed constitutionalism:
divinely authorized legislation by elected Houses of Justice; consultation in lieu of priesthood;
and the rule of law rather than sacral despotism. This rejects “theocracy” in the pejorative sense
while also resisting an exclusively intra-community construal. The textual telos is the Bahá’í
Commonwealth—a constitutional, non-clerical public order, coming by stages, in which the
Universal House of Justice is the constitutional apex legislating on matters not explicitly
revealed and coordinating executive and judicial functions. Thus “apex” names a constitutional
function oriented to the unity of humankind, not clerical sovereignty; and a permanently
privatized, voluntary-association reading underdescribes the public horizon explicitly envisaged
for mature stages of the World Order.


2) Discipline, due process, and the “panopticon” claim.
In “Managing the Fold: Punishment, Marginality, and Apostasy as Tools of Communal
Governance,” I map the Bahá’í sanction repertoire as administrative, minimal, and restorative.
The heaviest ordinary measure—loss of administrative rights—is exceptional, reversible, and
nested within due process (notice, warnings, individualized inquiry, appeal), while the
designation of covenant-breaking is narrowly centralized and protective rather than a generalized
culture of shunning. I propose a graded typology (peripheral → marginal → reformist →
dissenter → whistle-blower → apostate, alongside a non-pejorative “unenrolled believer” lane)
precisely to avoid the rhetorical flattening that powers panopticon narratives. None of this denies
frictions documented in the U.S. field site; it does argue that a totalizing “disciplinary state”
frame fails to capture an explicit jurisprudence of restraint and reintegration, and that U.S.
anecdotes should not be universalized across diverse national cultures and administrative
practices.
3) Teleology of modernity: equality, unity, institutions.
Where Cole emphasizes a liberal/anti-theocratic reading of the nineteenth-century texts, my
account situates politics in the Bahá’í teleology of recognition and unity—equality of women
and men, religion–state disentanglement, peace, and global cooperation—institutionally realized
through education, consultation, and elected Houses of Justice. The equality/eligibility tension
analyzed in this article belongs inside that constitutional architecture: equal spiritual station and
equal civic dignity alongside one explicit, text-delimited eligibility rule—without collapsing
either pole.
Bottom line.
Cole’s work usefully cautions against sacral despotism and assembles U.S. administrative
frictions that deserve attention. My reading departs on two points: (i) the Bahá’í texts envisage a
staged, constitutional public horizon beyond a permanently intra-community remit; and (ii) the
administrative corpus embodies a discipline of mercy—procedurally bounded, restorative, and
exceptional—that the “panopticon” frame overgeneralizes.


Wendi Momen (2023), The Bahá’í Faith and the Equality, Rights, and Advancement of Women:
A Survey of Principles, Praxis, and Discourse
what the piece contributes at its strongest:
Momen offers a comprehensive survey showing that equality of women and men is a
foundational Bahá’í teaching with practical outworkings in education, leadership/participation,
and the prevention of violence—areas where Bahá’í institutions and communities have pursued
measurable initiatives in both internal life and public discourse. The article’s scope spans core
texts and decades of BIC advocacy, underscoring a through-line from doctrine to
implementation. It highlights leadership and participation explicitly, indicating that inclusion in
decision-making is a live axis of practice and policy in the community’s evolution, even as it
acknowledges the Universal House of Justice within the keyword frame of the discussion
(signaling the sensitivity of that locus while keeping the focus on broader equity gains).
The survey also points to empirical inputs—e.g., BIC’s 1994 global survey on women in the
Bahá’í community—which documented strengths and gaps and then fed into programmatic
statements and initiatives, evidencing a data-informed posture rather than anecdote.
Response (what changes, after my paired analyses):
My equality/eligibility frame affirms Momen’s central arc: the Faith’s doctrine of equality and
its institutionalization through education and participation are real, sustained trends. That
empirical record materially supports the argument titled “Lived Practice Demonstrates Non-
Generalization”: it is difficult to maintain that the Universal House of Justice eligibility clause
has metastasized into broader exclusion when wide swaths of decision-making and
representation have, in fact, included women (Momen, “The Bahá’í Faith and the Equality,
Rights, and Advancement of Women”). Momen’s use of Bahá’í International Community survey
work strengthens this shift from symbolism to outcomes—i.e., are women present, resourced,
and leading across the system? —which is the right evidentiary test for that claim.
At the same time, the survey genre does not settle either the “Contradiction Claim” (that a
male-only apex symbolically undercuts equality) or the “Pragmatic Harms & Equity Counter-
claim” (that a male-only apex signals a glass ceiling). Momen’s article is not designed to
adjudicate the eligibility clause; it catalogs principle-to-practice linkages at scale. Read alongside


my paired analyses, his findings therefore calibrate these objections: yes, an apex-level signal
remains; but system-level evidence of women’s authority and participation complicates any
thesis that exclusion is pervasive or programmatic. The result is a narrower, evidence-
constrained critique rather than a wholesale indictment.
Baharieh Rouhání Ma‘aní, Clustered contributions
1. “The Effect of Philosophical and Linguistic Gender Biases on the Degradation of
Women’s Status in Religion” (JBS, 1998)
2. “Preparing Bahá’í Communities in the East and West to Embrace Gender Equality”
(Lights of Irfan)
What these pieces contribute at their strongest:
Across these essays Rouhání Ma‘aní distinguishes revelation from reception: she traces how
philosophical premises and gendered language (including translation choices and generic
masculines) have historically skewed interpretation against women, degrading their status in
religious traditions. She urges method awareness—watching for linguistic and conceptual bias—
while insisting that the Bahá’í scriptural core is explicitly egalitarian and that remediation
involves education, careful exegesis, and institutional learning.
She then turns to context: many Bahá’í communities, especially in the Middle East and parts of
South Asia, face stubborn cultural headwinds even when doctrine is clear. Her East/West paper
identifies typical resistances (e.g., customary norms about leadership, family roles), and counsels
strategies: persistent education, building capacities, and applying authoritative guidance with
cultural intelligence rather than confrontation—an incremental path that moves practice toward
principle.
Response (what changes, after our paired analyses):
Rouhání Ma‘aní’s Rouhání Ma‘aní’s bias-diagnosis sharpens the handling of the argument titled
“Semantic Challenge to rijál.” It shows why masculine lexemes in Semitic and Persianate
scripture cannot be assumed to encode exclusion, and why disciplined philology and intratextual
usage must be weighed before importing contemporary cultural intuitions. That supports the
method rule we adopt throughout: binding doctrine rests on authoritative texts and their
interpretive corpus, not on modern presumptions about gendered language. Her context-mapping


also calibrates empirical claims on both sides. For defenders, it explains why equality advances
unevenly—culture is stubborn—without imputing doctrinal deficiency. For critics, it foregrounds
lived effects: where cultural inertia persists, women can face material inequities despite
egalitarian doctrine. That nuance dovetails with the argument “Lived Practice Demonstrates
Non-Generalization,” while also giving traction to “Contradiction Claim” and “Pragmatic Harms
& Equity Counter-claim” at the level of symbol and signal: the apex exception has not cascaded
into wholesale exclusion, yet the signaling harms critics identify require attention precisely
because bias is real. Her practical remedies—education, capacity-building, and disciplined
hermeneutics—fit the equality/equity synthesis we advance: pursue full inclusion across all
eligible spheres while recognizing one text-delimited rule whose rationale is expressly deferred.
Read together with Momen’s contribution, the division of labor is clear. Momen supplies the
system-level “what”—principle-to-practice linkages, data points, and institutional actions that
evidence women’s leadership across the Order—thereby materially underpinning “Lived Practice
Demonstrates Non-Generalization.” Rouhání Ma‘aní supplies the analytic “why/how”—how
linguistic and cultural bias can distort reception, and how communities actually move toward
principle—thereby constraining over-extension of the “Semantic Challenge to rijál” and
clarifying where critiques about symbolism and equity have purchase. Taken together, and in
light of our paired analyses, these works do not “solve” the eligibility question; they discipline it:
semantic claims must be tested against philology and authoritative interpretation, and equity
claims must be tested against practice and context, with ongoing attention to signaling effects
even where inclusion is substantively achieved.
Conclusion
The analysis has aimed to replace speculation with clarity by keeping three lines straight: (1)
what the texts say and do not say; (2) what the UHJ actually is empowered to do; and (3) what,
in practice, the eligibility clause does and does not foreclose.
First, the binding sources establish a single, explicit eligibility rule alongside an architecture that
assigns interpretation to ʻAbdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi, and legislation on non-textual matters
to the Universal House of Justice. The House’s conferred infallibility operates corporately within
that legislative sphere, and the institution preserves doctrinal unity not by interpreting texts but
by acting where the texts are silent . This boundary is decisive: neither private exegesis nor


mystical symbolism can adjudicate, dilute, or re-read the explicit clause; authoritative
interpretation ended with the Guardian, and the House legislates only where the Text is not
expressed .
Second, the remit map shows the real stakes. “Apex” in Bahá’í usage marks the headship of a
text-bounded, intra-community institution whose core authorities are legislative (on non-textual
matters) and administrative/judicial—not sovereignty over non-Bahá’ís, and not a clerical caste.
Within this order, the membership clause narrows one eligibility only; it does not limit women’s
right to vote, to serve in elected bodies at local and national levels, to be appointed to high-trust
offices, or to participate—through National Spiritual Assemblies—in constituting the UHJ itself
every five years . Service posture (not status) further reframes symbolism: members decide in a
prayerful conscience and are “not… responsible to those whom they represent,” confident that
“God will verily inspire them,” which reduces the plausibility of reading the clause as a rank or
dignity denial .
Third, the paired debates clarify both force and limit. The “explicit text & singularity” claim
holds: the rule is text-grounded and singular; it has not generalized to wider exclusion in lived
practice, where women routinely bear decision-making and representational authority across the
system (as documented in the remit/Constitutional sections and in the paper’s practice analyses).
At the same time, the “apex signal” is not imaginary; readers concerned about symbolic harms
are right to name the tension, but wrong to infer a programmatic subordination when the rest of
the order structurally includes and depends upon women’s leadership. Our equality/equity
synthesis therefore directs energy to maximizing inclusion and resourcing across all eligible
spheres while receiving one explicit exception whose reason is, by text, deferred .
Within that horizon, the paper’s theological proposal locates the “deferred wisdom” in an
eschatological pedagogy: the feminine theophany of the Lawḥ-i-Ḥūriyyih—and its reinforcement
in the Ḥūr-i-ʿUjāb’s world-convulsing drama—can be read as widening the symbolic field within
which a future Manifestation might be recognized as feminine, thereby testing residual
patriarchies in the community of the faithful. The tremors, the rending of mountains, the death-
by-recognition and revivification, the reproach to “People of the Book,” and the veiling of
“secrets” until the “Day of Return” together stage Revelation as ordeal and consolation—a
proving-ground for allegiance to the Word rather than to familiar institutional signs . Kept within


methodological bounds, this is theology, not doctrine: it readies hearts for possibilities the Text
itself leaves open, even as it refuses to legislate from allegory or to trespass on an explicit,
interpreted ruling .
Finally, the paper’s descriptive clarity invites practical commitments. If the one explicit
exception is to remain singular in scope, communities must continue to pursue measurable
inclusion, leadership pipelines, and public representation for women across all other rungs of the
Administrative Order; to engage edge cases with pastoral competence inside the House’s lawful
sphere; and to resist both protective paternalism and reductive symbolics. The covenantal stance
is thus twofold: order communal life by the clear texts that bind us, and let the “new and fresh”
song of the Word enlarge the heart’s horizon as we await the wisdom promised to appear “as
clearly as the sun at high noon”

A Review of Recent Views of Atheists and Religion-Critics
Abstract
This article surveys, organizes, and evaluates leading contemporary critiques of theism alongside
the most defensible theist replies, with an eye to common standards of evidence and theory
choice. Rather than adjudicating piecemeal arguments in isolation, the paper compares “big
pictures”—naturalism and theism—using familiar theoretical virtues: evidential fit, explanatory
power and depth, coherence, simplicity properly understood, and modal clarity. The discussion
first anchors empirical dependencies (e.g., systematic covariation between consciousness and
brain states) without inferring reductive metaphysics, then reformulates the evidential problem of
evil and divine hiddenness in likelihood terms, clarifying what would count for or against theism
given background knowledge. It recasts design reasoning from Paley’s contrivance to present-
day fine-tuning claims, separating biological sub-optimality from cosmological boundary
conditions. It contrasts secular moral non-naturalism and Singer’s impartialism with theistic
groundings that aim to explain objectivity, authority, motivation, and modal necessity in one
place. It reframes “religious violence” as a problem of mechanisms—sacred values, identity
fusion, outbidding, organizational entrepreneurship—rather than essences, showing how
religious repertoires can both amplify conflict and enable peace. Throughout, Oppy’s meta-
strategy (burden of proof, priors, parsimony) and Carroll’s physics-first minimalism serve as the
naturalist benchmark; the paper argues that neither side enjoys a knock-down case and that
assessment turns on total-evidence comparisons rather than slogans. A Bahá’í perspective is used
heuristically to illustrate a non-fundamentalist theistic stance that (i) accepts discipline from the
sciences, (ii) centers moral formation and unity, and (iii) rejects violence as a betrayal of
religion’s point. The conclusion identifies research frontiers in cosmology, consciousness, and
normativity where developments are most likely to shift the comparative balance.
Belief in God as a “Skyhook” (method, explanation, reduction)
Belief in God as a “skyhook” means that: that appealing to God functions as an illegitimate
explanatory shortcut, a top-down “lift” that suspends the normal demand for stepwise,
mechanism-showing accounts. By contrast with “cranes” (explanations that build complexity
from simpler processes), a skyhook merely relabels the puzzle—“an intelligence did it”—and


thereby halts inquiry. On this critique, theistic appeals are said to operate like “God-of-the-gaps”
moves or intelligent-design insertions: they add an unanalyzed agent where our science is thin.
The section that follows accepts this warning against skyhooks and rejects such moves; but it
also argues that classical theism is not offering a rival mechanism within nature. Rather than
