hoisting where physics or biology falter, it proposes an ultimate ground for there being any law-
governed order, intelligibility, and normative standards by which cranes themselves are
evaluated.
Daniel Dennett’s crane/skyhook contrast is a lucid methodological warning: whenever a putative
explanation merely relabels a difficulty or inserts an unanalyzed intelligence at the top of the
story, we have a “skyhook”; when an account shows, step by disciplined step, how complex
forms emerge from simpler processes, we have a “crane.” Darwin’s “dangerous idea,” on
Dennett’s telling, is exactly the discovery of a crane—algorithmic selection over heritable
variation—capable of generating the living world’s apparent design without positing prior Mind
(Dennett 1995, 2006). That much is correct; hence intelligent-design and ‘God-of-the-gaps’
strategies are methodologically defective. they terminate inquiry prematurely and confuse
ignorance with explanation (cf. Dawkins 2006). Good theism should not need such skyhooks—
and this essay rejects them.
The question is whether God, as theism conceives Him, is the kind of posit that crane/skyhook
rhetoric targets. Classical theism says no. The skyhook metaphor presumes that “God” is being
offered as a peer-level cause inside nature’s web, as if God were an item alongside other items—
a late-arriving device to hoist matter where physics and biology cannot. But on the classical
account, God is not a rival crane. God is the unrestricted, noncomposite, necessary act that gives
rise to there being any ordered field within which cranes can operate. Put differently: cranes
explain within the order; God explains why there is an order—why laws obtain, why there are
modal structures fit for lawfulness, and why reason tracks those structures at all. Treating such a
ground-of-being claim as a “skyhook” is a category mistake. It misreads theism as a pseudo-
mechanism when it is a thesis about the metaphysical conditions under which mechanisms,
explanations, and explanatory norms are possible (Plantinga 2011; cf. Lewis 1947; Searle 1983).
A two-level account follows. On the proximate level the present article accepts cranes: natural
selection, gene–culture coevolution, cognitive heuristics, learning dynamics, institutional


incentives. They do real explanatory work within their proper domains. On the ultimate level we
ask three questions cranes do not even purport to answer. First, why these laws? A physics-first
picture can of course adopt brute regularities or spread them across multiversal ensembles; but if
lawfulness fine-grained enough to permit chemistry, biology, and minds is treated as a stopping
point, the “simplicity” of naturalism is purchased at the price of unexplained nomic structure.
Theism says: such lawfulness is not surprising—order reflects an ordering source (Collins 2009;
Barnes & Lewis 2016). Put more sharply: Humean “best-system” views make laws elegant
summaries of what just so happens; non-Humean primitivism takes laws as irreducible features
of reality; multiverse models relocate the puzzle to the meta-laws that specify the ensemble and
its measure. None of these, by themselves, explains why there is any stable, mathematically
tractable, life-enabling order at all—or why reason should fit it so well. The theistic proposal is a
different kind of explanation: laws are contingent expressions of a rational will, so we should
antecedently expect a world with deep regularities, elegant mathematics, and intelligible
structure, even if we cannot deduce exact constants. That yields a modest prediction profile
(lawfulness and intelligibility rather than parameter values), but it trades brute nomic facts for
grounding: the de facto regularities of physics are not ultimate; they flow from a unifying source
whose nature makes such order unsurprising. On this framing, appeals to multiverse or brute law
are not errors but alternative stopping points; the comparative question is which stopping point
does more explanatory work—unifying “why any laws,” “why these kinds of laws,” and “why
minds can know them”—without ad hoc additions. Second, why does reason fit the world? If
our cognitive systems are shaped exclusively by selection for fitness, global trust in truth-
tracking—especially in abstract, nonlocal domains—looks epistemically lucky. Theism grounds
that fit in prior Logos; reason is not a happy accident but a participation in intelligibility
(Plantinga 2011; Lewis 1947). A helpful analogue is Hegel’s provocative dictum—“what is
rational is actual, and what is actual is rational”—often misread as mere conservatism. Its deeper
claim is that actuality is intelligibly structured, not brute. The theistic stance agrees on
intelligibility’s primacy while avoiding Hegel’s metaphysical identity of thought and being: the
world’s rational order reflects, without exhausting, a rational source. Thus the prediction is
modest but real: expect pervasive lawlikeness, mathematical aptness, and a cognitive apparatus
oriented to truth, not just to fitness. By contrast, a fitness-only story owes bridge principles from
survival success to reliability across far-flung truth domains—principles it does not obviously


possess. Third, whence normativity and intentionality? If all causation is blind and
nonintentional, aboutness and categorical oughts cannot be derived, only redescribed. Naturalist
“identifications” of normativity with social function or projection may model use, but they
undercut the very standards by which we call an explanation better or worse. The theistic picture
makes rational normativity and intentional directedness primitive at the source (Searle 1983;
Adams 1999). To sharpen the point: there are two jobs any theory must do—(i) explain why
there are stance-independent reasons and correctness conditions at all (why some beliefs and acts
are right/wrong, apt/inapt, independent of what we prefer), and (ii) explain why such reasons
bear on us with authority and can criticize prevailing practices. Functional or genealogical stories
can illuminate how we came to deploy “ought” and “about,” but unless they recover objective
standards they risk collapsing normativity into mere convention and “aboutness” into
correlational bookkeeping. By contrast, on theistic grounding, value is anchored in a necessarily
good personal reality; obligations flow from that reality’s authoritative will; and intentionality
reflects participation in a prior Logos, yielding genuine direction-of-fit and the possibility of
misrepresentation (not just dysfunction). Epistemically, this allows ordinary routes—conscience,
rational reflection, experience—to track reasons without magic, since minds are fitted to a
normative order they did not invent. Modally, it explains why core norms (e.g., prohibitions on
cruelty, requirements of honesty) present as exceptionless and not merely local equilibria. And
motivationally, it clarifies why reasons can bind against interest: they answer to a good that is not
reducible to our desires yet is constitutive of our flourishing.
Graham Oppy presses that the best total theory is the one with the leanest ontology consistent
with the data; by that metric, adding God is a gratuitous posit (Oppy 2018, 2024). Parsimony,
however, is not sovereign among theoretical virtues. Depth, unity, modal reach, and explanatory
grounding matter as much as head-counts of kinds. An account that leaves laws, modal structure,
reason’s reliability, and normativity as irreducible brute features of reality is not obviously
simpler in any explanatorily valuable sense. It is simply thinner. Theism introduces one
primitive—God—but does distinctive work with it: it unifies otherwise brute explananda under a
single, principled ground. When the full array of theoretical virtues is weighed—explanatory
power and scope, coherence, illumination of practice—parsimony no longer adjudicates on its
own (Swinburne 2004; Oppy 2013; cf. Rea 2018). It is true that a scientific theory must be
consistent with current data; equally, honest theories say “these data so far support this


conclusion,” and then expose their local commitments to severe tests and progressive problem-
solving rather than shelter behind elastic auxiliaries. The push for the “least costly” view often
mistakes Occam’s razor for a command to minimize ontology full stop; properly used, the razor is
a ceteris paribus penalty after fit, coherence, and explanatory reach are assessed. A picture that
shaves primitives but pays with a warehouse of brute facts is not obviously simpler in any
explanatorily valuable sense. The question about God is not a bolt-on fix inside physics; it is
about foundation—the beginning/source that could unify laws, rational fit, and normativity
without multiplying ad hoc respects. Here your rule of one is apt: if a single, undivided ground
plus lawful bridges (e.g., from Logos to intelligibility; from perfect goodness to categorical
normativity) compresses the total theory while illuminating practice, it earns its ontological keep;
if it cannot, parsimony rightly dismisses it as a skyhook. In short, severe testing disciplines
method, the razor trims after other virtues are tallied, and foundational posits should be judged
by whether one primitive delivers genuine unification rather than a thinner list of unexplained.
Sean Carroll’s “poetic naturalism” artfully clarifies how many vocabularies can be legitimate for
a single world: physics gives the base description; higher-level talk—agents, meanings, values—
tracks stable patterns at useful scales (Carroll 2016). For method, that is salutary. But at the limit,
poetic naturalism is candid: the universe may “simply be”; value is a human construction; some
questions of “why” have no deeper layer. That candid restraint is compatible with science; it is
not, by itself, a reason to prefer naturalism as a metaphysics. To say “there is no deeper answer”
is not to show that a deeper answer is illicit, only that one is not available inside a physics-only
register. The theistic claim is precisely that the deeper answer belongs to a different level of
explanation, not a different object inside the same level.
Finally, nothing in this reply requires us to deny cultural or cognitive explanations of religious
phenomena. Memetics and norm psychology are excellent cranes for modeling diffusion,
coordination, costly signaling, and prosocial surveillance; they tell us how religious complexes
spread and stabilize (Dawkins 1976; Norenzayan 2013; Henrich 2015). But they do not
adjudicate truth or ought. A belief’s epidemiology is not its epistemology. Research on the
cultural evolution of prosocial cooperation shows that religious traditions can cultivate durable
norms of trust, charity, and restraint, without that sociological fact either debunking or
confirming their metaphysical claims. The right inference is modest: explanation of transmission


is orthogonal to evaluation of content. Cranes belong in the story; skyhooks do not. And God is
neither.
Conclusion. Dennett is right to prize cranes and to scorn skyhooks where they paper over
ignorance. But “God as skyhook” misfires against classical theism. The theistic claim is not that
God props up failing mechanisms inside nature; it is that the intelligible order in which
mechanisms work, and the rational norms by which we judge explanations, have an ultimate
ground. On the proximate register, Darwinian and cultural cranes do the lifting. On the ultimate
register, theism answers why there is any lifting—any order, any law, any grip of reason on the
real—at all. Once the registers are distinguished, the skyhook critique loses its target, and the
contest with naturalism must be decided not by parsimony alone but by the full suite of
theoretical virtues, where grounding and total fit count.
Evolutionary / Memetic Accounts of Religion
A mature naturalistic research program now models religion as a suite of ordinary human
phenomena: beliefs, rituals, institutions, narratives, and artifacts that emerge from domain-
general cognition and spread through cultural evolutionary dynamics. Explanations here are
resolutely bottom-up—tracking diffusion, coordination, enforcement, and learning—without
antecedent metaphysical commitments. This section synthesizes the main strands (memetics,
cognitive by-products, and adaptationist cultural evolution), marks their limits, and states the
crucial guardrail for our overall project: explaining spread and function does not settle truth
or normativity.
Dennett sets the frame: religion belongs to the catalog of “unquestionably natural phenomena,”
apt for the same empirical scrutiny we apply elsewhere (Dennett 2006). On his memetic
extension of Darwinian thinking, religious complexes are shaped by differential replication of
culturally transmitted items (“memes”) whose success often turns on transmissibility rather than
truth. In this sense, ritual forms, doctrinal packages, and institutional roles can be analyzed as
memeplexes with design-like organization but no top-down designer (Dennett 2006; Dawkins
1976). Still, the strongest versions of memetics overreach if they demand high-fidelity copying
on the gene model: as Sperber, Boyer, and Atran emphasize, cultural transmission is frequently
reconstructive rather than copying-like, so memetics works best as a heuristic integrated with


cognitive and social-learning mechanisms, not as a stand-alone theory of culture (Dennett 2006,
app. C).
Carroll’s “poetic naturalism” provides a helpful register discipline: there is one physical world
governed by lawlike regularities, yet many legitimate vocabularies for describing stable higher-
level patterns—agents, meanings, values, institutions—within it (Carroll 2016). That pluralism
allows social-scientific talk about norms and purposes without positing new substances. It also
counsels humility: on naturalism some “why” questions (e.g., why these laws?) may simply
bottom out. Either way, this register distinction inoculates against a common mistake—confusing
an account of how religious representations travel with a verdict on whether any are true or any
norms binding.
Adaptationist cultural evolution
On the adaptationist side, Big Gods theory holds that beliefs in powerful, knowledgeable,
morally concerned deities—supernatural monitors who reward compliance and punish
violations—reduce enforcement costs and help scale cooperation in large groups (Norenzayan
2013). A meta-analysis across 25 studies (N ≈ 4,825) finds that religious priming tends to
increase prosocial behavior, with effects concentrated among believers and negligible among
nonbelievers; laboratory findings further suggest that endorsing punitive God concepts is
associated with lower cheating, whereas purely benevolent concepts can show the opposite
association. Cross-cultural and historical patterns converge: the prevalence of moralizing,
surveillance-capable deities rises with societal size and complexity; early China’s Heaven (天)
and Imperial Roman oath regimes exemplify supra-human monitoring used to regulate markets,
promises, and public morality.
Henrich generalizes the mechanism via cumulative culture: prestige and conformist biases,
payoff-based learning, and CREDs (credibility-enhancing displays) assemble costly, public
signals—fasts, abstinences, painful rites—that are hard to fake and thereby stabilize
cooperation while hardening group boundaries (Henrich 2015). Over time, cultural selection
stitches together ritual–doctrine packages that better solve free-rider and scaling problems.
Ethnographic trajectories (e.g., New Guinea highlands ritual-belief complexes) illustrate how


standardized transmission, supernatural enforcement, and reputational regimes can converge to
produce durable prosocial orders.
Fine-grained historical comparisons support the “cost → commitment → cooperation” channel.
In a 120-year dataset, religious communes outlasted secular communes by roughly fourfold on
average; across 83 communes, the number of behavioral restrictions (fasts, food taboos, sexual
limits, constraints on possessions and outside contact) predicted longevity (R² ≈ 0.38) net of size,
income, and founding cohort (Sosis & Bressler 2003). The logic is straightforward: cost screens
for commitment and deters free-riding.
Yet none of this warrants triumphalism. Norenzayan himself stresses that prosocial religions are
one cause among many in a larger network that includes third-party institutions, the rule of law,
markets, moral emotions, and social safety nets; secular mechanisms can substitute for, or
supplant, religious ones as societies change. The empirical base is mixed in places: some
commune studies report no religiosity advantage; some ritual-trust results are fragile; and several
critics warn that “Big God” datasets overweight Abrahamic cases. Adaptationist inferences
should therefore be treated as domain-sensitive and provisional.
By-product cognition
By-product models explain religion as recruiting ordinary cognitive architecture—no dedicated
“religion module” required (Atran 2002; Barrett 2012). Humans exhibit hyperactive agency
detection, a teleology bias, intuitive mind–body dualism, and a taste for minimally
counterintuitive representations; these features make gods, spirits, and purposive cosmologies
intuitive, memorable, and culturally portable. Coalition psychology and affect supply adhesive
force; ritual synchrony, awe, and costly displays deepen commitment. Methodologically, the line
here is cautious: laboratory tasks do not automatically generalize to field settings; and a purely
scientific perspective may be incomplete with respect to adherents’ lived evidential bases. Still,
the by-product program robustly explains why certain religious ideas are “easy to think” and
“easy to spread.”
Memetics as tool, not tribunal
A broad cross-disciplinary literature underscores a crucial guardrail: memetics and cultural
evolution are excellent cranes for epidemiology and coordination—but they are not courts of last


resort on truth or normativity. A belief’s route of transmission is not its reason to believe; the
evolutionary function of a norm does not determine its moral authority. We therefore adopt these
models in full as explanatory tools, while insisting on their adjudicative modesty.
Box 1 — Explaining Spread ≠ Explaining Truth
Cultural-evolutionary models (memes, prestige/conformist bias, CREDs) explain how religious
representations diffuse, persist, and solve cooperation problems. These are epidemiologies of
representation, not epistemologies of truth or metaethics of normativity. Diffusion dynamics
cannot, by themselves, license conclusions about truth-value or moral authority. (Dennett
2006; Dawkins 1976; Atran 2002; Barrett 2012; Henrich 2015; Norenzayan 2013.)
Sidebar — Adaptationist vs By-Product (and a synthesis)
•
Adaptationist (Norenzayan; Henrich; Sosis & Bressler).
Moralizing high gods, supernatural monitoring, and costly signals reduce enforcement
costs and scale cooperation; cultural selection assembles ritual–doctrine packages that
outperform rivals in intergroup competition.
•
By-product (Atran; Barrett).
Religion rides on ordinary cognition—agency detection, teleology, dualism, minimally
counterintuitive concepts—without a specialized “religion module”; coalition psychology
and affect supply the glue.
•
Synthesis for this article.
By-product mechanisms supply the materials (what is salient, sticky, memorable);
adaptationist dynamics select and shape those materials into durable prosocial
complexes that travel and scale. Either way, see Box 1: scope of spread ≠ status of truth.
Critical note — Natural explanation ≠ anti-religious result
Of course the rise and spread of religions are natural phenomena in the sense that they unfold
within the ordinary causal fabric of the world. No serious theism requires that belief’s
transmission be “supernatural” in its mechanisms any more than it requires crops to grow by
miracle rather than photosynthesis. Expecting supernatural propagation dynamics is a category


mistake—and then congratulating oneself for finding natural mechanisms is to knock down a
straw man. On classical theism, God is the ground of nature’s order; secondary causes are the
norm. So memetic, cognitive, and cultural-evolutionary accounts rightly show how religious
representations travel, scale, and stabilize; they do not, without further argument, show whether
any of those representations are true or any norms authoritative. Confusing etiology with
evaluation is the genetic fallacy. The real philosophical work remains: adjudicating truth and
normativity on independent grounds, while welcoming the cranes that explain cultural spread as
part of the story rather than as verdicts on its ultimate warrant.
Conclusion. Evolutionary and memetic approaches have moved the study of religion from
armchair speculation to testable models. Properly bounded, they illuminate how religions emerge
and endure without “explaining away.” They sharpen—rather than settle—the distinct questions
of metaphysical truth and moral realism. On any fair view, these accounts furnish indispensable
cranes in the story of religion; they are not tribunals of ultimate warrant.
Religion-as-Natural vs Reductionism (What “Natural” Should Mean)
Much of the present debate turns on an equivocation. Sometimes natural names a method—
explain by disciplined appeal to law-governed processes and public evidence. Sometimes it
names a metaphysics—the physical is all there is. Sometimes it names a social imaginary—the
background picture that renders certain reasons salient and others inert. Clarifying these senses
matters. “Naturalizing” religion in the methodological sense does not, by itself, license reduction
in the metaphysical sense, nor does it settle the evaluative standing of religious claims. The
cognitive-scientific “naturalness” thesis is descriptive and probabilistic: religious representations
are likely outputs of ordinary minds in ordinary environments, not thereby adjudicated true or
false (Geertz & Markússon 2010). Likewise, methodological naturalism in science properly
brackets appeals to transcendence; it does not thereby establish metaphysical naturalism.
Within its proper register, explanatory sufficiency can be real. Dennett is right to demand cranes
rather than skyhooks: stepwise, bottom-up, algorithmic accounts that build complexity from
simpler processes (Dennett 1995, 2006). Darwinian selection is a paradigm crane; at the cultural
scale, differential retention and transmission model the spread of doctrines and rites without
positing a prior Mind. At the same time, Dennett legitimates higher-level description via the


intentional stance—useful as an emergent vocabulary, not as a fundamental ontology. Carroll’s
poetic naturalism complements this discipline: there is one physical world, but many legitimate
ways of talking about it—microphysical description at the base; agents, meanings, values, and
institutions at stable higher levels (Carroll 2016). Those stories are real as patterns, not as
additions to physics’ furniture. Yet Carroll is candid at the limit: some “why” questions may
bottom out in brute facts; value is constructed rather than discovered outside ourselves. Grayling
presses the further thesis that once naturalistic cranes suffice within their domains, religious
explanation is redundant, and humanism can furnish meaning and ethics without metaphysical
remainder (Grayling 2013). That is a substantive claim of explanatory sufficiency—and it marks
the true fault line.
Oppy urges methodological conservatism: prefer “big pictures” that minimize posits while
maximizing explanatory breadth and depth; by that metric, naturalism is simpler than theism by
one entity (God) and so presumptively better (Oppy 2018, 2024). But parsimony is not sovereign
among theoretical virtues. Depth, modal reach, unification, and—crucially—explanatory
grounding matter. If a view treats lawfulness, modal structure, the fit between reason and world,
and normativity as irreducible brute features, it is lean but shallow. A rival that introduces a
single primitive—God—to do unifying work across these explananda may be less sparse yet
more powerful. The contest cannot be decided by head-count simplicity alone.
Three resources clarify how to keep “natural” without collapse into reduction. First, Plantinga’s
compatibilist thesis—“superficial conflict, deep concord” between science and theism;
“superficial concord, deep conflict” between science and naturalism—locates the pressure point
in epistemology (Plantinga 2011). His Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism contends that
if our cognitive faculties are products solely of unguided selection for fitness, global trust in
truth-tracking—especially in abstract, nonlocal domains—is precarious. Cranes may explain how
we reason; they do not on their own ground the normativity of reason. Plantinga also
underscores the category mistake at issue: methodological naturalism is apt for science;
metaphysical naturalism is not licensed by science. Second, Taylor reframes secularization as a
transformation in the conditions of belief, not merely a decline in practice (Taylor 2007).
Modern life is conducted within an immanent frame, which can be inhabited as closed (only the
natural counts) or open (transcendence is thinkable). Cross-pressures and a “nova effect” of


proliferating options fragilize both belief and unbelief. What registers as “natural” is historically
constructed; it is not fixed by physics alone. That genealogy blocks any inference from
methodological success to metaphysical closure. Third, Cottingham’s distinction between
weak/methodological and strong/ontological naturalism resists scientistic overreach
(Cottingham 2005). The former is an open research program; the latter is a metaphysical thesis
that outruns science. Moral and aesthetic experience—“traces” of overwhelming goodness and
beauty—are not candidates for quantitative capture yet are not thereby epistemically idle; to
exclude them a priori is arbitrary. A humanly adequate naturalism must make conceptual space
for value, meaning, and spiritual experience without reducing them to “nothing but” their
enabling mechanisms.
The upshot is straightforward. Naturalizing religion in method does not entail reducing religion
in metaphysics. Explanations of origin and function are not verdicts on truth or normative
authority. Methodological naturalism is compatible with both naturalist and theist ontologies; it
alone does not adjudicate between them. A credible philosophy of religion should therefore be
maximally natural in method and minimally reductive in metaphysics. Dennett’s cranes and
Carroll’s model pluralism rightly discipline inquiry within the world. Oppy’s parsimony
matters—but it is not decisive where questions of grounding arise. Plantinga’s epistemic caution,
Taylor’s genealogy of the immanent frame, and Cottingham’s resistance to scientistic overreach
together articulate a non-reductive sense of “natural.” On this view, religion can be fully natural
in origin and operation without being explained away; the live philosophical work concerns
whether the best total picture of reality is the leanest or the deepest—the one that spares posits,
or the one that grounds law, intelligibility, and normativity in a unified way.
Critical excursus — What “natural” forgot (Heidegger on physis)
When we say “natural,” we usually smuggle in a modern picture of natura: a stock of
measurable stuff governed by universal laws and available for calculation and control.
Heidegger’s historical-ontological reminder is that this is not how the Greeks first understood
physis. For the early thinkers, physis named the self-blossoming emergence of what is—the
dynamic, self-showing sway (Walten) of beings into presence—intimately bound up with
aletheia, unconcealment. The point is not philological trivia; it is about the background ontology
our methods presuppose. If “natural” tacitly means only “what fits a pre-laid grid of calculation,”


then “naturalizing religion” will be read as reducing it to mechanisms by fiat. But if “natural” is
allowed to echo physis—emergence, revealing, abiding—then disciplined explanation of origins
and functions need not foreclose questions of meaning, truth, or disclosure.
Heidegger’s rereading of Heraclitus’ fragment—physis kryptesthai philei—captures the dialectic:
not “nature loves to hide,” as if a capricious realm were playing games with us, but “emergence
tends toward self-concealment.” Every act of showing is at once a veiling; beings come forth,
and in that very coming-forth the “whole” that lets them appear recedes. On this view, the later
“forgetting of Being” (Seinsvergessenheit) is not a mere intellectual lapse but an intrinsic risk of
revealing itself: what is present stands out; the enabling background falls from view. That risk
becomes a historical trajectory.
Aristotle marks the decisive turn. He formalizes physis as an internal principle of movement
(kinēsis) and articulates the passage from dynamis (potentiality) to energeia (being-at-work). But
to make this intelligible he repeatedly reaches for the analogy of technē: the craftsperson
imposes form (eidos) on matter (hylē) to produce a finished product. This analogy, Heidegger
argues, subtly reorients us from emergence to production: Being is grasped as something like a
made thing, present-at-hand, available to reason’s handling. It is a brilliant advance—and the
first conceptual slide toward reduction: what once named a living unfolding becomes thinkable
in terms of externally intelligible structure and completion.
The Roman translation completes the slide. Physis (from phyein, to grow) becomes natura (from
nasci, to be born): the dynamic event of coming-into-presence is flattened into a static given,
“that which has been born.” Modern science then lays a “mathematical” grid (in Heidegger’s
special sense) over what is: reality is revealed, in advance, as homogeneous, quantifiable, and
lawlike. In The Question Concerning Technology, this culminates in Gestell (enframing), a mode
of revealing that “challenges-forth” beings as standing reserve (Bestand): resources on call for
use. Hence the eerie literalness of “human resources.” The danger is not the machines but the
ontology: when enframing becomes dominant, all revealing looks like inventorying; whatever
cannot be tallied seems unreal.
Placed against this genealogy, the live methodological project—memetics, cognitive by-
products, cultural evolution—is not thereby suspect. It is precisely the kind of technē-inflected,
stepwise “crane” work that deserves pride of place in explanation. The caution is different: don’t


let a historically contingent ontology of natura dictate your metaphysics. Explaining how
religious representations arise, spread, and scaffold cooperation does not settle whether any of
them participate in truth or disclose aspects of Being. A ritual can be both a CRED (a credibility-
enhancing display) in the cultural-evolutionary sense and a mode of revealing in the Greek
sense—questions of warrant and meaning are not answered by epidemiology alone.
This also reframes “methodological vs. metaphysical” naturalism. Methodologically, we should
bracket transcendence and insist on public, law-governed accounts: that is the proper humility of
inquiry. Metaphysically, however, it is a further—non-compulsory—step to claim that only what
fits the grid of Gestell is real or authoritative. Heidegger’s point dovetails with our earlier
guardrail: let cranes do their explanatory work without turning them into tribunals of last resort
on truth and value. Otherwise we mistake the success of a revealing for the exhaustiveness of
reality.
Finally, this genealogy clarifies the real philosophical choice. One can inhabit the modern
immanent frame (to use Taylor’s term) as closed: all that counts is the calculable. Or one can
inhabit it as open: committed to crane-like explanations while remaining alive to disclosures that
may not reduce to inventory. On the “open” reading, to call religion “natural” is to say that it
arises within physis—the shared field of emergence and unconcealment—not to decree that it is
nothing but its mechanisms. That is the sense of “natural” we should keep: maximally empirical
in method, non-reductive in metaphysics, and alert to the risk that our very success at explaining
can blind us to what makes explaining possible.
Belief in belief, enculturation, and indoctrination
Dennett’s notion of “belief in belief” names a social-psychological posture in which the act of
believing—especially believing that others should believe—gets prized apart from the truth of
what is believed. He observes that many “believe in God,” but “many more believe in belief in
God,” and that this valuation often motivates protective strategies that shield creed from serious
scrutiny (Dennett 2006). On his analysis, what is commonly called “religious belief” frequently
functions as professing: public avowal and ritual performance that sustain communal goods even
where inner conviction is thin, and that are reinforced by taboos on criticism, threats of sanction,
and daily liturgies of belonging (Dennett 2006; cf. Dawkins 2006). The upshot is a cultural
economy that can stabilize adherence independently of evidential warrant.


Dawkins presses the point where it concerns children. He objects to labeling minors
“Catholic/Muslim/Christian children,” insisting the honest description is “a child of
Catholic/Muslim/Christian parents.” For him, fear-laden doctrines (e.g., eternal hell) and
authority-shielded curricula exemplify indoctrination: early enculturation that privileges
credulity over inquiry and discourages comparative evaluation of rival claims (Dawkins 2006).
His prescriptive contrast is straightforward: teach about religions—comparatively, historically,
critically—rather than teach that any one religion is true. Harris generalizes this critique to the
public square, arguing that norms which exempt “faith-claims” from evidential accountability
create permission structures for dogmatism; the corrective, he contends, is unapologetic
epistemic scrutiny applied even-handedly to all comprehensive doctrines (Harris 2004; 2006).
Ethnography complicates simple “indoctrination” stories in salutary ways. Luhrmann’s fieldwork
shows that many congregations train experience—teaching novices to attend to inner imagery
and to interpret certain thoughts as “God’s voice,” and cultivating skills that reliably yield
experiences adherents take as divine encounter (Luhrmann 2012). Her participants, by ordinary
clinical measures, are typically well-adjusted; what distinguishes them is learned practice within
a meaning-making community, not pathology. That finding dovetails with clinical guardrails: the
DSM-5-TR defines delusion as a fixed false belief not ordinarily accepted by one’s culture or
subculture, and it cautions clinicians not to pathologize culturally normative religious beliefs or
practices (APA 2022). Put bluntly: speaking in tongues, possession states, disciplined prayer
journals, or “hearing from God” are not ipso facto symptoms of disorder; they must be assessed
against communal norms, functional impact, and the person’s broader cognitive-affective profile.
A constructive vocabulary for education and civic discourse falls out of these distinctions. First,
belief-in-belief is a real phenomenon worth naming wherever social reward structures prize
profession and deference over examination. Second, indoctrination is best reserved for
pedagogies that present claims as immune to evidence, suppress higher-order critique, and
enforce deference to authority; by contrast, enculturation can transmit identities and practices
while still cultivating reflective agency. Third, comparative, context-rich instruction about
religions—including their internal disagreements and mutual incompatibilities—supports
informed consent in the sense Dennett borrows from Humphrey: what would these children
choose later, once equipped with the information and skills needed to decide? (Dennett 2006).


Finally, public-facing philosophy has a role in modeling epistemic hygiene. The most fruitful
interlocutors in the contemporary media sphere exhibit a steelmanning, long-form style—
probing claims without caricature, distinguishing description from evaluation, and making space
for lived experience alongside evidential demands. That posture matters here: it allows one to
take seriously the ways communities teach people to experience and profess, to acknowledge the
social functions those practices can serve, and yet to keep sharply in view the difference between
routes of transmission and reasons for assent. Explanations of how beliefs spread and stick—
memetic, cognitive, pedagogical—do indispensable descriptive work; they do not, by
themselves, adjudicate truth or normativity. On that boundary, both scholarship and civic
education should be unembarrassedly clear.
A Bahá’í rejoinder: enculturation without indoctrination, and a symmetry requirement
A useful counterexample to the “indoctrination” diagnosis comes from Bahá’í pedagogy. Core
principles explicitly enjoin the independent investigation of truth, forbid taqlīd (blind imitation),
and require that religious commitment cohere with science and reason (Bahá’u’lláh, Kitáb-i-
Íqán; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Some Answered Questions). Institutionally, children participate in classes
and community life, but are not counted as adherents by default; at the age of maturity (fifteen)
they are expected to decide for themselves. The educational aim is therefore not the insulation of
creed from criticism but the cultivation of reflective agency—comparative study, consultation
(deliberation in common), exposure to rival outlooks, and explicit permission to revise. By the
standards operative in the “belief-in-belief/indoctrination” critique, this looks like enculturation
under the discipline of inquiry, not opacity or coercion.
A second consideration is sociological rather than doctrinal. No one raises children in a vacuum;
absent parental formation, horizons are set by peers, platforms, and the most persuasive voice in
the feed. The live policy choice is not between “neutral childhood” and “religious upbringing,”
but between opaque inculcation (any content presented as immune to evidence or exit) and
transparent formation (parents present what they judge true, teach how to test it, and protect the
adolescent’s right to conscientious dissent). Framed this way, the ethical criticism properly
targets methods—fear appeals, information control, taboo enforcement—rather than the mere
fact of transmission.


A third point concerns normative parity. Prominent critics of religion (Dawkins, Dennett, Harris)
object to organized efforts to transmit religious convictions while simultaneously authoring trade
books, designing curricula, touring, and debating with the explicit aim of spreading secular
humanism or atheism. There is nothing objectionable per se about such advocacy; the problem is
the tacit asymmetry it sometimes presupposes: that religious transmission is “proselytizing”
while secular transmission is “education.” A fair standard requires content-neutral constraints on
pedagogy: prohibit coercive tactics and insulation from counter-evidence for everyone; require
comparative instruction, genuine encounter with objections, and meaningful freedom of exit for
everyone. Applied even-handedly, this standard vindicates Bahá’í practice as a model of non-
coercive enculturation and binds secular advocacy to the same constraints it urges on religious
communities.
The upshot for the larger argument is straightforward. “Belief in belief” names a real pathology
where public profession is rewarded and critical scrutiny punished; “indoctrination” properly
names methods that foreclose higher-order evaluation and enforce deference to authority. But
these are methodological vices, not content markers. Where a tradition (as in the Bahá’í case)
institutionally mandates inquiry, prohibits blind imitation, and places religion under the
discipline of reason and science, the charge of indoctrination misses its target. And where secular
movements propagate their convictions, they stand under the same ethical discipline they
commend to others. The appropriate remedy, accordingly, is not to curtail parental formation but
to entrench a symmetry requirement in civic and educational practice: persuasion for all,
coercion for none.
Religion and Science: Conflict, Complementarity, or Compartmentalization?
Debate about the proper relation between religion and science typically clusters around three
stances: principled conflict, cautious complementarity, and negotiated compartmentalization.
Advocates of conflict insist that religious claims, insofar as they purport to explain reality,
compete head-to-head with scientific hypotheses and should be judged by the same evidential
standards. Richard Dawkins makes the point starkly: either treat “God” as a bona fide
explanatory hypothesis and submit it to empirical adjudication, or concede that its status is no
higher than other untestable posits (Dawkins 2006). Sam Harris ties this to public risk, arguing
that faith’s insulation from evidence fosters dangerous social dynamics; beliefs held immune to


rational scrutiny are, on his view, a recurrent source of sectarian harm (Harris 2004). On the
conflict picture, then, the epistemic norms of science apply across the board; where religions
make claims about the world—creation, miracles, answered prayer—they enter the scientific
arena and must accept scientific verdicts.
Stephen Jay Gould’s “non-overlapping magisteria” (NOMA) proposes a truce by redrawing the
map. “The magisterium of science covers the empirical realm: what the universe is made of
(fact) and why it works this way (theory). The magisterium of religion extends over questions of
ultimate meaning and moral value.” The two, he contends, “do not overlap.” In this register,
science neither affirms nor denies divine “superintendence” because such questions lie beyond
its legitimate methods (Gould 1997/1999). The peace, however, is normative and fragile: once
religions stake claims on science’s turf—young-earth chronologies, publicly testable miracles—
Gould’s amicabilis concordia collapses, because those are empirical assertions. Critics respond
that the “miracle-free” religion shielded by NOMA does not match lived theologies on the
ground; but Gould’s point is not descriptive sociology. It is a boundary proposal: if we wish to
avoid epistemic entanglement and culture-war stalemates, do not confuse fact-finding with
value-making.
A complementarity program seeks something more integrative than a détente without collapsing
domains. John Polkinghorne’s version is “critical realism” across both science and theology:
each is truth-aimed, fallibilist, and inferential, but they address differently scaled questions. He
treats cosmic intelligibility and the anthropic “fit” as theistically suggestive (not probative) signs
that the universe is hospitable to mind and value (Polkinghorne 1998). On divine action, he
rejects both deistic distance and law-breaking interventionism, arguing instead for providence
working through the openness of physical processes (e.g., quantum indeterminacy, chaotic
sensitivity) in ways that do not violate regularities. Evolution is fully accepted as the physical
story of life’s history; “intelligent design” is, on this account, a category mistake about causation.
Science offers the “horizontal” story of processes; theology adds a “vertical” story of purpose
and ultimate destiny—two eyes, one world.
Sean Carroll’s physics-first “poetic naturalism” presses the conflict pole from the other side by
insisting that the domain already covered by our best physics is vast and explanatorily sufficient
for ordinary life. His treatment of quantum foundations (Carroll 2016, 2019) is explicit: in the


Everettian picture there is one universal wavefunction evolving unitarily by the Schrödinger
equation—no collapses, no special role for observation, no need for extra ontological furniture.
Many-Worlds is “lean and mean”: just the quantum state and its single evolution law. Within this
frame the Core Theory governing everyday phenomena leaves “no room”—as a matter of
explanatory need—for telekinesis, astrology, or survival of the soul; and gesturing to gaps
(origins, consciousness) is dismissed as “God-of-the-gaps” maneuvering. Carroll does offer
methodological humility about open problems, but as a metaphysics his stance is physics-first
minimalism.
Graham Oppy turns that minimalism into a comparative method. On his view, the better “big
picture” is the one that minimizes unmotivated commitments while maximizing explanatory
breadth and depth. Naturalistic pictures, he argues, tend to do more with less: adding God is a
substantive ontological expansion that frequently yields no compensating gain in testable
predictions or explanatory score. When theistic proposals simply relocate brute facts to divine
intention, he contends, parsimony and methodological conservatism advise sticking with the
leaner view (Oppy 2013, 2018, 2024). The theist’s rejoinder—that one primitive (God) can unify
many explananda (laws, reason’s reliability, normativity)—appeals to depth rather than
spareness, but Oppy’s challenge keeps the burden squarely on whether the addition does real
explanatory work.
These three stances are often conflated with sociological findings about religion’s correlates,
which is a category mistake. Consider national variation in mortality from heart disease.
Whatever the sign and size of associations between religiosity and health, they turn on
confounds—socioeconomic status, healthcare access, regional culture, diet, stress ecology—that
are orthogonal to the metaphysical question. Correlation does not adjudicate whether science and
religion conflict or complement each other; it instead warns against over-interpreting social data
as if they settled philosophical stakes. By the same token, the empirical study of religion as a
cultural phenomenon—belief transmission, cooperative payoffs, identity effects—has genuine
scientific interest yet remains neutral on truth claims and on the NOMA boundary.
What follows from this mapping? First, the conflict position is strongest where religions present
publicly checkable claims about natural history and present mechanics; there, scientific
adjudication is appropriate and NOMA’s non-overlap dissolves. Second, compartmentalization


can reduce friction in plural societies by clarifying that “what is” questions and “what matters”
questions are not the same—but it will disappoint traditions whose core affirmations include
claims about events in the world. Third, complementarity offers a constructive research posture
for those who accept the scientific image while insisting that questions of meaning, value, and
purposive order are not exhausted by physics. Finally, method matters: if one prizes ontological
economy above all, Carroll’s and Oppy’s minimalism will look decisive; if one prizes unifying
depth and ultimate grounding, Polkinghorne-style theism will look rationally attractive even as it
forgoes “gaps.”
In short, there is no single lever that settles the relationship between science and religion.
Conflict emerges where empirical claims collide; compartmentalization manages boundaries;
complementarity explores layered descriptions of a common world. Each stance carries costs and
benefits—epistemic, practical, and cultural—and the live philosophical work is to make those
trade-offs explicit rather than smuggling them in under the banner of “science” or “faith.”
A Bahá’í Epistemic Contribution to the Map
On the Bahá’í account, the conflict/complementarity/compartmentalization trichotomy is
reframed by a prior thesis about knowledge itself. The Writings present a structured typology—
material, conceptual, existential, moral, divine, intrinsic divine, culminating in “true knowledge
in conformity with reality”—and insist that distinct domains of inquiry ultimately cohere within
a unified, teleological framework ordered to justice, unity, and spiritual growth.
Methodologically, this carries two immediate commitments for science–religion debates:
independent investigation of truth (no deference to imitation or superstition) and an explicit
principle of the harmony of science and religion as a regulative ideal.
First, where conflict rightly obtains—i.e., when religious claims trespass on publicly checkable
matters—the Bahá’í standard is crisp: “Any religious belief which is not conformable to
scientific proof and investigation is superstition,” so claims that contradict established science
must be revised or relinquished. That stance rejects khurāfāt not as a culture-war posture but as
an epistemic failure to integrate the levels of knowing; the unity of truth forbids appeal to
unverifiable occult causalities or authority-shielded taboos.


Second, complementarity is strengthened—not weakened—by this unity thesis. “Knowledge in
conformity with reality” functions as both criterion and goal, integrating empirical precision,
conceptual rigor, existential self-knowledge, moral practice, and revealed guidance into a single
truth-aimed enterprise. On this view, science and theology are not sealed magisteria but
differentiated lenses—“two eyes”—within a coordinated pursuit whose telos is civilizational and
moral as well as cognitive.
Third, against strict compartmentalization (NOMA), your framework argues for unity-in-
diversity rather than non-overlap: diverse methods and perspectives are welcome insofar as they
converge on a single reality and serve common goods. Diversity of discourse is not relativism; it
is an enriching plurality ordered to eventual concordance in judgment and action.
Finally, the superstition file gives you a normative edge in public reasoning: to exempt “faith-
claims” from evidential accountability is not piety but epistemic deviation. Superstition
fragments the unity of knowledge, misplaces causality, and degrades agency; the remedy is a
disciplined ascent through the epistemic hierarchy—observation, reason, moral action—under
revelation’s guidance. Thus your position can endorse rigorous scientific adjudication of
empirical claims, reject “God-of-the-gaps” strategies, and still defend a teleological, integrative
account of meaning and value that science alone does not supply.
In short: your contribution neither capitulates to conflict nor retreats to compartmentalization. It
proposes a complementary unity in which science retains adjudicative authority over empirical
questions, religion supplies teleological integration and moral orientation, and both are
constrained by a single norm—conformity to reality across the material, rational, and spiritual
registers.
Heidegger on Modern Science: Calculative Power, Missing Foundations
Heidegger’s criticism is not that modern science is false, but that it is self-limiting by design and
prone to forget the ground that makes its success possible. Modern natural science is a regional
enterprise: it investigates beings under a prior projection that renders them as measurable, law-
governed, and manipulable. This prior projection is what he calls the “mathematical”—not
arithmetic, but the a priori schematizing that lets nature show up as quantity, function, and law.
Hence the deliberately provocative claim that “science does not think”: scientific method


explains within an already-posited framework; it does not ground that framework, nor does it
address the question of Being that first opened the region to inquiry.
Two clarifications follow. First, the gain: modern science achieves unprecedented exactness and
control precisely by narrowing the field—phenomena are set up to appear as what can be
measured, modeled, predicted, and reproduced. Technology consummates this stance: Gestell
(Enframing) “challenges forth” the real as Bestand (standing-reserve), a stock of resources pre-
ordered for use. Second, the cost: because this stance works by bracketing grounds, it tempts a
slide from method to metaphysics—what appears under the experimental–mathematical
projection is taken as the whole of the real. That slide is scientism: the elevation of one
legitimate mode of disclosure to the measure of Being as such. Modern science explains
brilliantly; it does not (and by its own lights cannot) supply the foundations of its explaining—
why there are laws, why order is projectable, why truth matters, what beings are beyond being
measurable.
This diagnosis bears directly on boundary questions. What is “science,” and what are its limits?
Science is inquiry into beings under a guiding projection that renders them accessible to lawlike,
public investigation; its limits are internal to that projection. It yields no verdict on its own
presuppositions (e.g., the intelligibility of the world, the status of value), because asking those
questions would require stepping outside the regional frame that makes scientific explanations
possible. Science versus knowledge. “Knowledge” is broader than empirical science:
mathematics knows by proof; history by critical reconstruction of singular pasts; philosophy by
concept formation and argument; ethics by practical reason; theology (if true) by revelation
scrutinized by reason. These are distinct modes of disclosure with their own validity-conditions,
not ersatz sciences. Are God or soul scientific objects? Not as “science” defines its region. If
science means the experimental study of entities within the causal nexus, then God—conceived
as unrestricted, necessary ground of that nexus—is not an item among items; likewise, the soul
qua simple subject is not investigable by the same instruments that map contingent processes.
Neuroscience can chart fine-grained dependence; the ontological status of subjectivity
(reduction, realization, emergence, form/substance) is adjudicated where grounding questions
live—by metaphysical argument constrained by, but not identical with, empirical finding.
Modern reductionism. Reduction is constitutive of the scientific stance; the danger is forgetting


that the projection is a choice of disclosure, not an ultimate ontology. When the projection
hardens into a worldview, everything—including persons—tends to appear as programmable
resource (“human resources”), and questions of meaning, value, and purpose are displaced as
non-questions.
Read through the lens of a Bahá’í epistemic architecture, this Heideggerian boundary-setting
locates science and religion within a larger, ordered map of knowing. The Bahá’í Writings
present a structured typology—material, conceptual, existential, moral, divine, intrinsic-divine—
culminating in “knowledge in conformity with reality,” and insist that distinct domains
ultimately cohere within a unified, teleological framework oriented to justice, unity, and spiritual
growth. Two methodological commitments follow. Independent investigation of truth rejects
imitation and khurāfāt (superstition) as epistemic failures; claims that contradict established
science are to be revised or relinquished. Harmony of science and religion functions as a
regulative ideal: empirical precision, conceptual rigor, existential self-knowledge, moral practice,
and revealed guidance are to be integrated into a single truth-aimed enterprise. On this view,
science and theology are not sealed magisteria but differentiated lenses—“two eyes”—brought to
bear on a common reality.
Consequently, the trichotomy of conflict, complementarity, and compartmentalization can be
reframed. Conflict rightly obtains where religious assertions trespass on publicly checkable
matters; complementarity is strengthened by the unity-of-truth thesis, which seeks concordance
across levels rather than truce by segregation; strict compartmentalization gives way to unity-in-
diversity, permitting multiple methods and perspectives insofar as they converge on reality and
serve common goods. The superstition critique supplies a public norm: exempting “faith-claims”
from evidential accountability fragments the unity of knowledge, misplaces causality, and
degrades agency; the corrective is a disciplined ascent through the epistemic hierarchy—
observation, reason, moral action—under revelation’s guidance.
In sum, modern science should be kept at full strength inside its proper region; its success does
not license reductivism in principle. Foundational questions—law, intelligibility, normativity—
belong to metaphysics and, in a Bahá’í register, to revelation, under the common norm of
conformity to reality. This posture neither capitulates to conflict nor retreats to non-overlap; it
proposes an integrative unity in which science retains adjudicative authority over empirical


claims, religion supplies teleological and moral orientation, and both are coordinated within a
single, non-reductive account of truth.
Consciousness and Mind–Brain Dependence
This section argues three points. First, the scientific record shows a strong, law-like dependence
of conscious life on the brain: change the brain in specific ways and you predictably change both
the level (awake, asleep, anesthetized) and the contents (what it’s like) of experience. Second,
those dependence facts do not, by themselves, decide the big metaphysical question of what
consciousness is. They underdetermine whether mind just is brain activity, is realized by it, is a
form structuring it, or is a distinct emergent subject that arises with it. Third, within the
constraints set by successful physics, there remain live, theist-compatible views of mind—
nonreductive physicalism, hylomorphism, and emergent dualism—that deserve comparative
evaluation rather than premature dismissal.
Begin with the empirical anchor. Classic lesion and intervention studies map mind to brain with
impressive precision. Damage to orbitofrontal and broader prefrontal circuits is reliably linked to
disinhibition and difficulty acquiring new behavioral rules (Bechara, Damasio, & Damasio
2000). Occipital lesions can yield “blindsight”: subjects deny seeing yet discriminate above
chance (Weiskrantz, Warrington, Saunders, & Marshall 1974). Split-brain commissurotomy can
produce partially independent streams of awareness in the two hemispheres (Sperry 1996). More
recent “perturb-and-measure” work during anesthesia goes beyond case reports: when people are
conscious, a magnetic “poke” to cortex spreads as a rich, long-range wave; under general
anesthesia, the same poke fizzles locally (Casali et al. 2013). These findings justify a modest but
strong conclusion: conscious states covary in fine detail with brain states and dynamics. They do
not yet tell us what consciousness is.
Why not? Because dependence data are compatible with multiple metaphysical models. Even
materialists often admit an “explanatory gap”: a complete physical description seems to leave
open why and how it feels like anything at all (Levine 1983; see Papineau 2002 on Levine). So,
while neuroscience narrows the field—it rightly rules out airy dualisms that ignore biology—it
does not, on its own, adjudicate between identity (mind just is brain activity), realization (mental


properties are higher-level features instantiated by the physical), form-in-matter accounts, or
emergent-substance views.
Here is where a familiar piece of physics-based pressure shows up, now spelled out with care. It
is often said that physics is causally closed. In ordinary terms, this is a bookkeeping claim: for
the energies and scales that matter to everyday life (brains, bodies, tables), every physical event
already has a sufficient physical cause according to our best laws. If a neuron fires, the physical
story—ion flows, membrane potentials, neurotransmitters—fully explains why it fired. If we
then add, on top of that sufficient physical cause, a second and distinct mental cause, we risk
systematic overdetermination—two independent causes doing the very same job on every
occasion (Papineau 2002). One-off overdetermination is possible (two bullets arrive at once), but
building it into every bodily movement makes the theory ad hoc. Jaegwon Kim sharpened this
into the exclusion worry: if physical causes suffice, then irreducible mental causes look idle
unless we can show how they do genuine work without simply duplicating the physical story
(Kim 2005). From the physics side, Sean Carroll articulates a matching concern: the Core
Theory—the successful quantum field theories plus the regime-appropriate treatment of
gravity—is a rigid mathematical system that leaves “no wiggle room for intervention by
nonmaterial influences,” and it posits “no particles or fields” capable of carrying personal
information beyond death (Carroll 2016, 189, 214, 218, 372). Taken at face value, that can sound
definitive.
Yet even Carroll concedes that consciousness is the central pressure point for a purely physicalist
picture and that we currently lack a complete theory of it (2016, 320). That concession matters.
The moral to draw is narrow but important: the empirical success of the Core Theory strongly
constrains appeals to extra forces or energies; it does not, by itself, decide whether
consciousness is identical to, realized by, or metaphysically distinct from physical states. Those
are thesis-level commitments that go beyond low-energy physics.
Within those constraints, three theist-compatible positions remain live. I summarize each with its
intuitive picture, its advertised strengths, and its costs.


1. Nonreductive physicalism. On this view (e.g., Murphy 2006), human persons are wholly
physical organisms. Mental life—including reason, normativity, and religious
awareness—arises from neurobiological complexity shaped by culture and (for a theist)
in relation to God, without positing a separable immaterial substance. Think of the mental
as higher-level features that come into being when matter is organized in the right way.
Strengths: honors causal closure; integrates smoothly with scientific psychology;
preserves talk of reasons and norms without treating them as mere fictions. Cost: must
meet Kim-style exclusion head-on—showing how mental properties have genuine causal
relevance rather than mere covariance—without collapsing into straight reduction.
2. Hylomorphism. In the Aristotelian–Thomistic tradition (Aquinas, ST I q. 75; modern
development in Jaworski 2016), the “soul” is the body’s form: the organizing principle
that makes this parcel of matter one living person. Causation is not only pushes and pulls;
it also includes formal/organizational causes that constrain lower-level processes
without adding new forces. Think of the difference between a random pile of parts and a
functioning watch: same matter, different organization, different powers. Strengths:
avoids the “two-thing” picture of a ghost in a machine and offers a principled account of
multi-level causation consistent with physical laws. Cost: must say, with precision, how
formal causation relates to the quantitative language of physics, lest it degenerate into
decorative “pattern talk.”
3. Emergent dualism. On this family of views (Hasker 1999; with nearby non-Cartesian
dualisms like Swinburne 2013), when brain organization hits the right threshold, a new
simple subject emerges—the self—with its own persistence conditions and top-down
causal powers. Think of a genuinely new locus of agency riding on but not identical to
the brain. Strengths: gives a robust place to first-person agency and a natural route to
personal survival. Cost: bears the heaviest closure/exclusion burden and inherits
integration puzzles (how does the emergent subject pair with the right body? how do its
influences respect conservation laws?) that must be met without ad hoc “gaps.”
Two framing pressures keep the debate open and honest. First is the hard problem (Chalmers
1996): even perfect correlations do not explain why physical processing is accompanied by
subjective experience at all—why there is something it is like. That challenge presses especially


on identity theses. Second is Searle’s “biological naturalism” (1992): consciousness is a real,
irreducible biological feature caused by brain activity—monist in ontology, anti-reductive in
explanation. That challenge presses on reductive moves that erase first-person reality.
It is useful, at this point, to clarify some terms often used without definition—now with concrete
examples. The Core Theory is physicists’ shorthand for the empirically confirmed low-energy
package: the Standard Model’s quantum fields for matter and forces, plus general relativity
wherever spacetime curvature matters and quantum gravity can be ignored; it is the toolkit
behind semiconductors and MRI scanners. Causal closure says: within that regime, physical
effects have sufficient physical causes described by those laws—no “missing entries” are needed
in the causal ledger. Realization means a higher-level property (say, being in pain) is
instantiated by lower-level physical states without being identical to any single micro-
description: many different neural microstates can realize the same pain, much as the same
melody can be realized by different instruments. Overdetermination is when one effect would
have two distinct sufficient causes of the same kind “stacked”; acceptable in rare coincidences, it
becomes theoretically suspicious if posited for every action. Formal causation (in hylomorphic
talk) is the way organization makes new powers available without adding energy—like software
enabling new functions on the same hardware, or a watch’s assembly enabling timekeeping
given the very same parts.
Where does this leave the theist? Not with license to smuggle in new forces; the Core Theory’s
success blocks that. But neither with a forced march to identity-theory materialism. The
dependence findings and closure arguments restrict the option space; they do not collapse it. A
theist can coherently adopt (i) a nonreductive physicalism in which God creates and sustains an
ordered world whose forms of organization give rise to minded life and normativity; (ii) a
hylomorphic account in which the soul as form grounds the unity and causal powers of the
person without violating physics; or (iii) an emergent dualism that posits a genuine subject
arising with, and acting through, the brain, while undertaking the serious work of meeting
conservation and pairing challenges.
Interim verdict for the larger project. Grant the science: consciousness depends on the brain in
fine detail. Be exact about the physics: its triumph strongly discourages appeals to extra energies


or “interventions.” But do not pretend the science has solved the metaphysics. It has not.
Nonreductive physicalism, hylomorphism, and emergent dualism each respect current physics
while making different trade-offs about causal efficacy, the unity of the person, and the prospects
for survival. The rational task is comparative: weigh which package best explains the data
(including first-person data), offers clear modal commitments, avoids ad hoc moves, and keeps
faith with what our best physics actually says—and does not say—about mind.
The problem of evil (evidential arguments; pain/pleasure data)
The evidential problem of evil does not claim that God and suffering cannot logically coexist. It
asks a comparative question that can be put in plain terms: when we look carefully at the world’s
actual pattern of pain and pleasure—who suffers, how often, how intensely, and to what apparent
purpose—does that pattern fit better with the idea of a perfectly good God governing reality, or
with the idea that nature is not being guided for moral ends at all? Paul Draper frames the
contrast by setting theism against what he calls a hypothesis of indifference: on indifference, the
nature and condition of sentient life are not the result of benevolent or malevolent agency by
nonhuman persons; the world is not morally “aimed” (Draper 1989). If we then attend to
ordinary, public facts about pain and pleasure, a striking regularity appears. Across human beings
and many animals, pains and pleasures function as biologically useful signals: pains push
organisms away from threats, while pleasures pull them toward opportunities, in ways that
reliably track survival and reproduction. Alongside this, the world contains large amounts of
suffering whose usefulness to the sufferer is obscure: predation and parasitism, “play” that
maims in some species, diseases that corrode and kill, lingering and unattended deaths. That
overall profile is exactly what indifference would lead us to expect. It is not what a morally
perfect governor would most naturally be expected to arrange, unless further explanations are
introduced.
Bringing evolutionary history into view strengthens the initial impression. Deep time is filled
with morally perplexing “waste”: mass extinctions, vast die-offs, and ages of nonmoral animal
suffering that unfold with no human observers and with no evident contribution to the growth of
virtue or to the exercise of human freedom. None of this logically refutes theism; the question is
not deductive but evidential. The point is that, prior to special-purpose explanations, a world


with exactly these features sits comfortably within an indifferent picture and sits uncomfortably
within a theistic picture that posits perfect goodness at the helm.
Michael Tooley develops this evidential pressure in a systematic way without relying on
technical symbolism. He distinguishes kinds of evils—those arising from human agency, those
arising from nature, patterns of distribution that seem unfair, and the most severe “horrendous”
cases—and then asks what we should initially expect to find if theism were true. As cases
accumulate—pediatric cancers, unseen agonies of animals in wildfires, and countless other
instances—the claim that none of this should surprise a theist grows demanding unless we
multiply appeals to reasons that are, for now, hidden from us (Tooley, Elements). A familiar
theistic reply, often called skeptical theism, cautions that our cognitive limitations make it
unsurprising that we cannot see God’s justifying reasons in specific cases; failing to see a reason
is not evidence that there is none. Tooley raises two sober cautions about leaning too heavily on
this move. First, if we license a very broad skepticism about our ability to judge whether reasons
exist, we risk undermining ordinary inductive practices we rely on in science and daily life,
where carefully not-finding something after extensive search is some evidence that it is not there.
Second, even if some unknown goods exist, the cumulative, fine-grained profile of suffering still
looks, on its face, more like what we would expect in an indifferent or naturalistic world than in
one providentially ordered by perfect goodness. That is, as an initial reading of the data,
indifference appears to fit more simply and directly.
David Hume anticipated this posture with disarming clarity. In the Dialogues Concerning Natural
Religion, after surveying the mixed phenomena of good and ill within a law-governed world,
Philo advises that we should proportion causes to effects: mixed effects do not warrant the leap
to an unmixed, perfectly good cause, and the uniformity of natural law undercuts a “mixed
principles” story that toggles between benevolence and malice. The modest stance left standing
is indifference. Contemporary reconstructions (for example, Pitson) simply translate Hume’s
counsel into the now-familiar language of comparative explanation: the hypothesis of
indifference better fits the observed facts about pain and pleasure than theism.
The theistic literature has not been idle in the face of these pressures. Its responses fall, roughly,
into two kinds: calibrated humility about our limits, and constructive accounts of why a good
God might permissibly allow a world like ours. On the first front, skeptical theism argues that,


given the gulf between divine wisdom and human understanding, it would not be surprising if we
could not discern God’s reasons in many particular cases; therefore, “we see no justifying
reason” is not strong evidence that there is none. This caution has real bite, but it must be
carefully constrained lest it spill over into a general skepticism that disables ordinary moral
judgment and empirical inquiry. Much of the post-Rowe discussion (see Howard-Snyder 1996)
asks whether skeptical theism can be articulated precisely enough to block rash “no-see-um”
inferences without corroding the everyday inferences we need to live and to do science.
On the constructive front, several models shift attention from species-level bookkeeping to what
happens in the life of the sufferer. John Hick’s Irenaean “soul-making” proposal maintains that a
stable, law-like world kept at some epistemic distance from God is exactly the sort of setting in
which distinctively personal goods—courage, compassion, steadfastness—can take root. A
pleasure-maximized environment would stunt moral growth. Hick does not deny the hardest
data: the intensity and distribution of suffering, especially among children and nonhuman
animals, often seem to outstrip any plausible contribution to the sufferer’s flourishing. His reply
is eschatological: the goods that justify divine permission need not all be realized within a single
finite life, and the created order as a whole may be the best available stage for the end God seeks.
Critics counter that this risks treating some persons as instruments for others and insist on a
patient-centered constraint: if a good God permits a child’s anguish, the justifying good must in
some way accrue to that very child.
Marilyn McCord Adams makes that constraint explicit. She isolates “horrendous evils,” by
which she means sufferings so extreme that, considered by themselves, they threaten to engulf
the positive meaning of a person’s life. In such cases, mere “outweighing” on a cosmic ledger is
not enough. Divine goodness would need to defeat the horror in the sufferer’s own life,
integrating even what is appalling into an organic unity that renders the whole, for that person, a
great good. Adams’s strategy is unapologetically theocentric and future-oriented (and, in her
preferred form, Christological): only intimate participation in the infinite good of God can effect
the kind of person-relative transformation that defeats horrors, and successful defeat is
inconsistent with everlasting ruin. This is a powerful, patient-centered reply, but it openly relies
on robust theological commitments—incarnation, universal restoration—that go beyond the thin
content of “bare” theism.


Eleonore Stump complements this with a narrative, second-personal approach. She argues that
what is most destructive about suffering is the way it can fracture a person’s inner life—
disintegrating the will’s integrity and the “desires of the heart.” If that diagnosis is right, an
adequate theodicy often cannot be given in abstract, third-person survey terms. It must show,
case by case, how God could permissibly allow particular sufferings as a kind of severe medicine
aimed at the sufferer’s own healing and union with God, and it must do so while respecting
freedom. Through close readings of individual lives, Stump contends that divine providence can
be personally justifying in precisely this way, even when the world’s aggregate statistics still
look bleak from a distance. The methodological lesson is as important as the metaphysical one:
some explanations belong essentially to the second-person register of relationship and repair.
Where does this leave a fair-minded evaluator? As a matter of initial evidence, the familiar
features of pain and pleasure in living systems—and the long evolutionary record of apparently
pointless animal suffering—do support an indifferent reading of the world more directly than
they support bare theism. Hume’s advice to proportion causes to effects remains apt. At the same
time, the most serious theistic responses do not rest on vague appeals to “greater goods” tallied at
the level of the species. They concentrate instead on person-centered goods: the cultivation of
virtue under stable law (Hick), the defeat of life-engulfing horrors in the sufferer’s own good
(Adams), and second-personal healing that can justify permissions in the only register where
they could be justifiable—namely, in the lived relationship between God and the sufferer
(Stump)—supplemented by a carefully limited skepticism about our capacity to survey divine
reasons. These responses do not erase the initial evidential tilt toward indifference; rather, they
offer a thicker explanatory package whose credibility must be judged holistically. The famous
case of the fawn that dies unseen in a forest fire (Rowe) makes the dialectic vivid: taken in
isolation, such a tragedy looks exactly like what an indifferent world would produce; the theist’s
best reply is not to deny the look of things but to argue that, within a larger and person-centered
story about goods and destiny, there may be justifications we are not presently positioned to see.
The rational task, therefore, is not to declare victory from a single datum but to compare whole
views—asking which account best fits the full spread of facts, maintains coherence without ad
hoc patches, and avoids levels of skepticism that would undermine ordinary reasoning.


My response adopts a privation-and-finitude strategy. If God is perfect and absolute good, then
whatever proceeds from God is not identical with God but is other than God; creation, as created,
is finite. On the classical causal principle that an effect receives its actuality from its cause only
in a limited, participated way, what is caused is less perfect than the uncaused source. It follows
that imperfection is not an accident tacked onto an otherwise perfect cosmos but a necessary
consequence of there being anything other than God at all. Evil, on this picture, is not a positive
“stuff” that God makes; it is a lack—privation—of a due perfection in a finite subject, just as
ignorance is the absence of knowledge. Because creatures exist along a spectrum of capacities
and forms, privations likewise come in degrees. Inanimate things lack powers that plants
possess; plants lack the sensory and locomotive powers of animals; animals lack the rational and
moral powers characteristic of human persons. Each higher level includes, in a transformed way,
many of the perfections of the levels below, and each lower level, by comparison, exhibits more
extensive absences. What we call “natural evils” arise from these built-in limitations of finite
natures: the further a being stands, by kind and capacity, from the fullness of divine perfection,
the more room there is for the sorts of lacks that register to us as harms.
This framework also explains why many goods and evils are relational rather than absolute when
assessed within the created order. A single event can be good relative to one set of capacities and
aims and bad relative to another. Predation is harmful to the gazelle but life-sustaining for the
lion; the same process can sustain the integrity of a species while destroying an individual
organism. Even large-scale geophysical processes that we experience as devastating—
earthquakes, for example—are not merely destructive forces. They belong to the lawful
dynamics by which a living planet regulates energy, recycles crustal material, shapes mountains
