and basins, creates aquifers, and supports biodiversity. At the scale of human habitation, such
events can be grave evils because they frustrate goods proper to our form of life; at the scale of
the Earth system, they serve ends without which the very conditions for those human goods
would not obtain. The point is not to deny the reality of local harms, but to situate them within a
world whose interlocking processes trade off benefits and costs across levels. Once creation is
understood as a hierarchy of finite forms coordinated by stable laws, it is neither surprising nor
gratuitous that some goods for wholes are secured through losses to parts, and that what counts
as a loss or a benefit is indexed to the nature and interests of the creature in question.


Two clarifications guard against common confusions. First, to say that evil is a privation is not to
trivialize suffering; it is to locate its metaphysical source in limits and lacks rather than in a rival
positive principle. On this view, greater participation in perfections—truth, life, order,
consciousness, virtue—reduces privation; distance in kind or defect in development increases it.
Second, we should resist unreflective anthropomorphism when we extend human predicates to
nonhuman nature. It is a natural habit of understanding to ascribe loyalty to dogs, cunning to
foxes, or pride to lions, and that habit can help us navigate a complex world; but without care it
also blurs important differences among kinds of beings and leads us to treat nonmoral processes
as if they were moral agents.
This matters especially for the case of animal suffering. Nonhuman animals plainly feel pain and
act to avoid it; what they lack, so far as our best accounts indicate, is the distinctively human
capacity to conceptualize their suffering in a second-order way, to narrate it, to evaluate it under
a moral description, or to reorient their lives by reflective choice. Their behavior is largely
governed by instinct and environmental constraint; “ought” and “blame” are out of place here.
Predation, competition, injury, and death in the nonhuman world are tragic within their sphere,
but they are not moral evils in the sense that presupposes responsible agency. They are
manifestations of finite forms interacting under law in a dynamic order whose very stability and
fecundity depend on processes that, when viewed narrowly, can be harsh.
Taken together, these claims yield a theistic explanation that reshapes the evidential landscape. If
creation necessarily introduces finitude, if kinds of creatures differ by real degrees of perfection,
if many goods and harms are relational within a law-governed whole, and if much of what
troubles us in nature lacks the conditions of moral agency, then a significant portion of the
world’s “evil” is precisely what a theist should antecedently expect from a cosmos that is other
than God yet ordered to host layered forms of life. The data that initially seem to favor
indifference—systematic ties between pain/pleasure and biological functioning, ecological trade-
offs, deep-time “waste”—are, on this metaphysical package, not anomalies but the predictable
signatures of created finitude under stable law. This does not remove the need to address
distinctively moral evils among human persons, nor does it deny the existential weight of
suffering; it does, however, show why a world containing privations of many kinds is not an
awkward afterthought for theism but a structural feature of any creation that is not itself the


Absolute. Thus, ‘good’ and ‘evil’ are evaluative predicates applied by rational agents; many
natural processes are nonmoral in themselves, though they can be harmful or beneficial relative
to particular kinds.
Divine Attributes and Soteriological Severity
Three classical pressure points naturally follow the problem of evil: whether divine omniscience
(specifically, foreknowledge) can be reconciled with libertarian freedom; what “omnipotence”
coherently amounts to; and whether severe soteriological outcomes—traditionally, “hell”—can
be squared with perfect goodness. The aim here is cartographic rather than polemical: to map the
principal options, give their best-case rationale, and register the costs a rigorous reader will (and
should) press.
On foreknowledge and freedom, the Boethian line holds that God’s cognition is not earlier-than
but outside time: God possesses life “all at once,” so what we call past/present/future are
presented to the divine intellect in a single, atemporal “now.” Consequently, God’s knowing a
future free choice does not fore-fix it; God knows the contingent as contingent and the free as
free. The familiar modal distinction helps: it is necessary that if God knows that p, then p; it does
not follow that p is necessary (Law 2019, 177–78). Contemporary expositions keep the core
claim: eternity is the “whole, simultaneous” possession of life, and atemporal cognition need not
impose antecedent causal determination on temporal acts (Stump & Kretzmann 1981). Two
worries remain. First, some fear that infallible certainty—atemporal or not—undercuts
alternative possibilities; the Boethian replies that certainty tracks truth, not modality, and the
act’s being free is part of what is known. Second, doubts about the coherence of atemporality
(and about petition, response, and providence across the temporal/eternal divide) are not
frivolous; they are costs to be noted rather than knock-down objections.
Ockhamism takes a different tack, distinguishing hard past facts (wholly about the past) from
soft past facts (about the past in virtue of future contingents). God’s past belief that you will
freely do A at t is a soft fact; had you freely done ¬A, the past fact would (counterfactually) have
been different. On this view, foreknowledge does not render the future accidentally necessary,
because the past truth is “about” the future choice (Wainwright 2007, 31–32). The cost is
metaphysical: the hard/soft boundary is contentious, and relocating counterfactual dependence to
the past may not rescue the sort of freedom that insists on the “fixity” of the past.


Molinism posits middle knowledge: prior to any creative decree, God knows not only what will
be freely done but what any free creature would do under any admissible circumstances
(counterfactuals of freedom). On that basis, God orders providence by actualizing a world in
which his ends are achieved via foreknown free choices (Wainwright 2007, 28; Flint 1998). The
decisive challenge is the grounding objection: what makes such counterfactuals true (or false)
prior to decree? If nothing grounds them, how can God know them? Molinists offer replies
(primitive truths about creaturely essences; God’s cognitive access to creaturely acts in logically
possible circumstances), but the metaphysical bill is not trivial (Wainwright 2007, 28; Flint
1998). A nearby backstop, should one relax libertarianism, is semi-compatibilism: Fischer &
Ravizza argue that moral responsibility requires guidance control rather than alternative
possibilities, preserving responsibility even under determinism (Fischer & Ravizza 1998).
Independent of which reconciliation one prefers, Plantinga’s free-will defense answers the
logical problem of evil: it may be that significantly free creatures suffer transworld depravity, so
that in any feasible world at least some free agent goes wrong; thus it is possible (and hence not
contradictory) that God could not actualize a world with free moral good and no moral evil
(Plantinga 1977). Interim verdict: between Boethian timelessness, Ockhamism, and Molinism
(with compatibilist resources in reserve), omniscience and creaturely freedom can be rendered
coherent in more than one way; each incurs costs corresponding to its central move.
On omnipotence, Aquinas’s classical analysis remains the standard: omnipotence is the power to
do all things that are possible; contradictions are not “things” and so fall outside the scope of
power (ST I, q.25, a.3–a.4). Hence the “stone so heavy God cannot lift it” is a pseudo-task, an
incoherent description rather than an object of power (Mavrodes 1963). Contemporary
formulations keep the extension of power to the broadly logically possible (Plantinga 1974/1977;
Swinburne 1993/2016). This restriction is not an ad hoc retreat but a conceptual cleanup that
blocks category mistakes like “create a round square” or “make p ∧ ¬p true.” Harder
curiosities—e.g., whether an omnipotent being could change the past—are best handled by
analyzing the modal profile of time, not by inflating the notion of power beyond coherence.
On soteriological severity, the tradition contains more than one coherent model of post-mortem
loss, and mapping them matters for the moral assessment of theism. One family construes hell as
eternal separation by self-exclusion: the “doors locked from the inside” picture on which some


persons freely and finally refuse participation in the divine life, and divine goodness honors that
freedom even at tragic cost (Walls 1992). Proportionality is addressed not by tallying discrete
transgressions but by life-shape: trajectories of settled refusal fix one’s stance toward the good;
eternal loss reflects that stance rather than a crude retribution schedule. The strength (respect for
freedom) is also the hardest question: why is post-mortem resistance irrevocable, how is divine
love not finally defeated by creaturely refusal, and why does permanent loss not impugn perfect
goodness? A second family—annihilationism or conditional immortality—holds that the finally
impenitent do not persist in endless misery but ultimately cease to exist; “eternal punishment”
names the permanence of death, not everlasting torment (Fudge 2011). This reduces the moral
tension of perpetual suffering and aligns with texts that take death as the “wages of sin,” but
invites worries about retributive justice, the respect due to an agent’s continuing agency if the
agent is extinguished, and the handling of passages that suggest ongoing post-mortem states. A
third family—hopeful or patristic universalism—maintains that perfect goodness and perfect
power ultimately reconcile all persons without overriding freedom; judgment is remedial and
every will is eventually healed, not coerced (Talbott 1999). Here the stress points are freedom
(how universal reconciliation avoids determinist pressure), justice (whether the moral
seriousness of evil is sufficiently registered without permanent loss), and text (whether
universalist readings can bear the exegetical load). The upshot for the global assessment is
modest but important: theistic commitment does not force a single, morally maximalist severity
picture; principled options exist that many analytic theists find coherent, each with transparent
trade-offs.
Taken together, these treatments show that the apparent collisions—foreknowledge versus
freedom, omnipotence versus coherence, hell versus goodness—are not conceptual dead-ends.
There are multiple, well-developed routes through each; choosing among them turns on familiar
theory virtues (explanatory power, fidelity to data—philosophical and textual—modal clarity,
and parsimony) rather than on any single knock-down consideration.
The Bahá’í writings address the trio of pressure points—foreknowledge and freedom, the
coherence of omnipotence, and soteriological severity—by reframing each in light of divine
perfections and the economy of creation disclosed by Revelation. On foreknowledge, the core
claim is that God’s knowledge is comprehensive and unerring but non-causal. God’s “essential


knowledge” surrounds the realities of things “before as well as after their existence”; it is a
perfection of God, not an efficient cause of creaturely acts. Knowing is not making. The familiar
analogies make the point plain: the general foreknowledge that the sun will rise, or a
mathematician’s prediction of an eclipse, does not bring these events about; likewise, prophetic
foretelling (for instance, of Christ’s martyrdom) registers what will occur without producing it.
Within that framework, human beings truly possess freedom in matters of good and evil—justice
and tyranny, equity and injustice—and are answerable for their choices. Divine assistance is
necessary for any human action as such, but assistance is not compulsion. The classical image is
nautical: the wind or steam that moves the ship corresponds to God’s sustaining help, while the
rudder corresponds to human will; the power to move is from God, the direction—east or west—
is set by the creature. That same pattern governs the Bahá’í treatment of “fate.” There is an
unalterable decree (like oil that will, in due course, be consumed in a lamp), but there is also a
conditional, impending fate that can be averted (like a sudden wind that snuffs the lamp before
the oil is spent). Wisdom, foresight, and moral effort operate precisely in this sphere of the
conditional, and the distinction preserves both divine justice and genuine human agency. Hence
predestination understood as compulsion is rejected: God creates in a manner “consistent with
[creatures’] potentialities,” not by pre-assigning some to felicity and others to loss.
Omnipotence, in this corpus, is not arbitrary might but wise sovereignty: the Ever-Living and
All-Powerful One originates and sustains all things, ruling nature by “accurate regulations and
laws.” The power by which God “doeth whatsoever He willeth” is inseparable from all-
encompassing wisdom; the order, necessity-relations, and intelligible properties of the world are
signs of that wisdom, not constraints upon it. Creation is by fiat—being called forth from
nothingness—yet the created order is not capricious; it is law-governed precisely so that moral
and spiritual life can unfold within it. In this setting, the divine Manifestations—Prophets and
Messengers—are “centers of the light of reality,” uniquely transparent to and authorized by the
omnipotence of God. What emanates from them is “identical with the truth” and “conformable to
reality.” Their world-renewing efficacy—the power to quicken souls, order communities, and
transform civilizations across millennia—functions as an evidential marker of Revelation rather
than as an exception to coherent omnipotence.


The moral meaning of severe soteriological outcomes is likewise recast. “Hell” is not a cosmic
torture chamber maintained by a perfectly good God; it is the soul’s state of self-incurred
distance from the Source of its life, the inward combustion of unbelief and vice, the deprivation
that follows from turning away. Evil, on this account, is a privation—a want of a due
perfection—rather than a positive substance God creates. Just as ignorance is the absence of
knowledge and blindness the absence of sight, so moral and spiritual evils name lacks and
distortions in finite subjects. Paradise and hell, accordingly, are primarily conditions of proximity
and estrangement: “reunion with Me” versus bondage to one’s lower self. This does not evacuate
justice. The world is “established upon the foundations of reward and punishment”; actions have
real consequences, and accountability is integral to the education of souls and the maintenance of
order. But the moral architecture is tempered by mercy. Because existence is capacious and
oriented to growth, there remains the possibility of advancement after death through God’s
bounty—by the soul’s own supplication, by the prayers of others, and by the intercession of the
Holy Manifestations. This prospect does not trivialize wrongdoing or dissolve responsibility; it
locates divine judgment within a teleology of healing rather than a regime of interminable
retribution and thereby aligns severity with perfect goodness.
Taken together, these teachings yield a coherent package. God’s foreknowledge is exhaustive yet
non-coercive; human beings act with real freedom in the arena that matters morally, supported
but not forced by divine aid; and whatever in the created order looks like fixity of outcome is
either a necessary feature of law-governed nature or a conditional horizon within which prudence
and virtue operate. Omnipotence is unrestricted power conjoined to wisdom, manifest in a
universe whose stable order makes responsibility and virtue possible and in the revelation of
Manifestations whose authority is itself a sign of that power. Final loss, where it occurs, is
intelligible as self-chosen separation, not as a divine delight in punishment; and the same
goodness that secures justice opens paths of post-mortem healing under the sovereignty of grace.
In this way, the Bahá’í perspective preserves robust libertarian agency under divine omniscience,
gives a coherent content to omnipotence without collapsing into arbitrariness, and reinterprets
“hell” in a manner that upholds both the seriousness of moral life and the supremacy of mercy.


Divine hiddenness
Divine hiddenness names a pattern that many find existentially forceful and evidentially
probative: even among open, conscientious inquirers there are cases of persistent, nonresistant
nonbelief; if God is perfectly loving, why isn’t a relationship with God unavoidably available to
such persons? J. L. Schellenberg’s argument can be stated explicitly as follows: (1) if a perfectly
loving God exists, then for any finite person who is capable of a personal relationship with God,
God is “always open” to relationship with that person; (2) if God is always open to relationship
with a person S and S is capable of such relationship, God would ensure that S is in a position to
enter it—minimally, S would have the nonresistant belief that God exists, since such belief is a
necessary precondition of mutual relationship; (3) therefore, if a perfectly loving God exists,
there would be no cases (among the capable) of nonresistant nonbelief; (4) yet some humans are
in fact nonresistant nonbelievers—agents who are open to relating to God and do not “aim to
shut the door,” yet lack belief through no fault of their own (Schellenberg 2015: 54–55, 103).
From (1)–(4) Schellenberg infers that no perfectly loving God exists, and thus that God does not
exist (2015: 103). On his own pastoral gloss, a perfectly loving God would not defer availability
for relationship until a late stage of life or the hereafter; rather, like a good parent, God would
disclose early and steadily so that filial relationship may develop “from youth” (2015: 194–95).
Schellenberg anticipates familiar replies. Appeal to soul-making or other outweighing goods is
answered with the thought that omnipotence could jointly secure those goods and the availability
of reciprocal relationship now. Skeptical-theist appeals to unknown reasons are pressed likewise:
if the conjunction of perfect love and present nonresistant nonbelief is incoherent, then “there’s
no adequate reason for God to allow non‐resistant non‐belief” ([379, p. 111]). The argumentative
pressure therefore falls on either rejecting the existence of nonresistant nonbelief, disputing the
inference from perfect love to pervasive availability, or reinterpreting what “availability” must be
like for a transcendent agent.
One crucial clause in such formulations is the claim that there is “no adequate reason for God
to allow nonresistant nonbelief.” Here, nonbelief simply means lacking the belief that God
exists; nonresistant designates agents who are sincerely open to the evidence and would accept
belief were God to disclose Himself in ways appropriate to their cognitive and moral situation
(that is, their nonbelief is not due to culpable indifference, hostility, or self-deception). To allow


such nonbelief is for God—who could, consistently with respect for freedom and epistemic
integrity, make relationship-enabling awareness available—to refrain from doing so. Adequate
reason means a reason that is morally sufficient, theologically fitting, and prudentially weighty.
The force of the clause, then, is not that God should coerce belief, but that when a person is
genuinely receptive and capable of relationship, a perfectly loving God would at least ensure
access to noncoercive, person-directed grounds for belief; continued hiddenness in such a case
would be morally puzzling unless some countervailing reason—one that preserves goods like
freedom, moral growth, or non-manipulative relating—obtains.
The 2002 Howard-Snyder & Moser collection maps the main strategies. Some essays develop
skeptical-theist lines, urging that our grasp of the value-structure relevant to divine self-
disclosure is too thin to underwrite the strong modal judgment Schellenberg requires. Others
pursue transformative theism: on Moser’s proposal, divine self-manifestation aims at moral
transformation rather than mere spectacle, so selective “divine hiding” can be redemptive—“God
thus would be selective at times in self-manifestation…for redemptive purposes,” withholding
disclosure where reception would not yet be cooperative ([Moser in 2002 volume], quoted in the
provided sources). Wainwright’s Edwardsian theme pushes in the same direction: perceiving the
divine may be partly conditioned by the agent’s dispositional posture, such that evidential uptake
is bound up with the formation of the heart. By contrast, analytic clarifiers (e.g., van Inwagen)
anatomize the structure of the hiddenness inference itself, probing whether “nonresistance” is
evidentially accessible in the strong sense the argument presupposes. Across these approaches
runs a concession of sorts: even if hiddenness is not probative against theism, it is at least
expectation-revising—any viable theism must say more about the aims and modes of divine
self-presentation.
Michael Rea shifts the frame by insisting that most classical talk of “hiddenness” primarily
names divine transcendence—God’s incomprehensibility—rather than a strategic silence that
invites easy probabilistic assessment. Hence his counsel of humility about expectations: when
we project from our “non-revealed” concepts of divine attributes to predictions about how God
would manifest, violations of those predictions do not by themselves show that the
corresponding predications are false ([Rea 2018: 56]; [378, p. 56]). Rea also queries the pivotal
link in Schellenberg’s argument—that perfect love straightforwardly entails standing


relationship-availability of the sort at issue—warning that this imports a specifically modern,
parental model of love that may not be apt for divine agape. “Perfect-love doesn’t necessarily
translate into wanting a relationship” in the assumed way; our grip on what perfect love would
require for a transcendent agent is tenuous ([338, p. 17]). On this account, hiddenness is not
primarily absence but the “darkness” that attends creaturely encounter with the incomprehensible
God ([264, p. 13]). The pastoral payoff is a chastened stance: faithful inquiry can remain
intellectually and spiritually serious without demanding that God become an object among
objects on our timetable; “humility about expectations” is itself part of fitting responsiveness to
the divine (Rea 2018: 56).
On the conflict pole, Sam Harris treats silence and non-intervention as strong disconfirmation of
a loving personal deity. In a maximally perfect God, persistent horrors and unanswered cries
imply either impotence or indifference—“If God exists, either He can do nothing to stop the
most egregious calamities, or He does not care to. God, therefore, is either impotent or evil”
(Harris, cited in the provided sources). He generalizes: a world authored by a loving revealer
should contain clear, peace-promoting revelation; instead, the textual record is morally mixed
and often combustible. The upshot is ethical: do not let “pious hope” outrun evidence; public
reason must anchor conviction if cooperation is to be secured (Harris, quoted as supplied).
Paul Draper supplies an evidential template into which hiddenness naturally fits. His likelihood
method compares how expected a datum is on rival hypotheses given background knowledge.
Just as the observed distribution of suffering is, on his view, antecedently more probable on a
Hypothesis of Indifference than on theism, so too the widespread absence of belief—
especially among epistemically conscientious inquirers—is claimed to have very low probability
on theism and higher probability on indifference: P(nonbelief | theism & k) ≪ P(nonbelief |
indifference & k) (Draper, as summarized in the sources). Draper’s own framework is holistic,
however: hiddenness would be one line in a ledger that also includes putative theistic
confirmations (e.g., moral awareness, religious experience) and defeaters; the verdict turns on
total evidence.
Where does this leave the dialectic? First, hiddenness raises the evidential bar for any theism
that treats divine love as readily analogized to ideal human parenting; on that picture,
Schellenberg’s expectation of unambiguous availability has bite (Schellenberg 2015: 103; [380,


pp. 54–55]; [136, 194–195]). Second, hiddenness presses conceptual work on divine love and
presence: if divine love is not best modeled on constant overt availability, the burden is to
articulate a theologically serious why—whether in terms of redemptive transformation (Moser),
the dispositional conditions of perception (Wainwright), the limits of creaturely cognition
(skeptical theism), or the transcendence-first stance (Rea [2018: 56]; [264, p. 13]). Third,
hiddenness invites epistemic modesty about our ability to verify “nonresistance” in the robust
sense needed to close the argument; discerning motivational posture from the outside is fraught,
and even first-person reports are contestable. None of these moves dissolves the experiential
sting of absence, but together they undercut the claim that hiddenness straightforwardly entails
atheism.
Two guardrails follow. (i) Evidential modesty. Hiddenness is powerful pro tanto evidence
against certain models of theism; it is not a knockdown proof in light of live undercutters and
alternative construals of love, presence, and evidence (Draper; Rea 2018). (ii) Category
discipline. Treating God as an item within the field that ought to meet our baseline canons of
third-person availability misreads classical theism’s metaphysical claim about a transcendent
agent whose self-manifestation is purposive and not beholden to our testing regimes (Rea 2018:
56; Moser 2002). Within those guardrails, the argument’s existential force remains: for many, the
silence of heaven is not merely an explanatory datum but a wound. A satisfactory theism must
not explain that wound away; it must show how love, transcendence, and redemptive intent could
coexist with it—without special pleading, and with the moral seriousness that hiddenness itself
demands.
My own reply rejects what I will call the theatrical-demand standard that tacitly underwrites
many hiddenness complaints. On that standard, if a perfectly loving God existed, He would
disclose Himself by overt spectacle—an audible voice from the sky, writing on the clouds, public
miracles on demand—such that disbelief would be virtually impossible for any minimally
attentive observer. But this expectation commits a category mistake about the object of inquiry
and the appropriate modes of evidence. On classical theism and on Bahá’í teaching alike, the
divine Essence is not an item within space-time to be inspected alongside other objects; it is
“immensely exalted” beyond direct comprehension. God is known mediately—through the
Manifestations who mirror the divine perfections, through a law-governed creation saturated


with intelligible signs, and through the moral-spiritual transformations their teachings reliably
produce. To fault God for not appearing as a stage effect is therefore akin to faulting
mathematics for not presenting its truths to the senses: number and justice are not seen as lamps
are seen; they are apprehended by their structures, entailments, and fruits. Love, too, can be
known by its operations—formation of character, reconciliation of enemies, regeneration of
communities—without theatrics.
Once the metaphysical category is right, the evidential standard shifts from coercive spectacle to
person-directed disclosure. The point of revelation, on this picture, is not to overrun freedom but
to elicit it; not to win assent to a display, but to effect transformation of will and heart. Hence the
Bahá’í emphasis on independent investigation of truth: seekers are summoned to exercise
judgment, detach from prejudice, and respond to reasons and exemplars proportioned to their
actual capacities. Miracles and public wonders are explicitly down-ranked as decisive proofs
(they convince only eyewitnesses and are easily recast as “enchantments”); the durable, world-
addressed “proofs” are the enduring efficacy of the Manifestations and the civilizational
fruitfulness of the laws they promulgate. In that light, an insistence that perfect love must take
the form of constant, unmistakable third-person availability is unwarranted. Non-manipulative
self-manifestation protects freedom and epistemic integrity; it honors the fact that recognizing a
transcendent God cannot be the same kind of thing as confirming a laboratory regularity.
This framework also reframes the appeal to nonresistant nonbelief. The simple assertion that
there are many whose nonbelief is wholly nonresistant is hard to verify in the robust sense the
argument requires, not because sincerity is denied but because uptake is shaped by “veils” that
are themselves ethically salient: entrenched imitation, ideological and economic attachments,
resentments, the subtle pride of intellect, and the long shadows cast by corrupt religious
leadership. Bahá’í sources treat such veils, together with tests that separate “light from
darkness,” as standing features of moral life, not ad hoc patches. They both explain differential
reception and preserve accountability without collapsing belief into compulsion. Moreover, the
tradition’s distinction between decreed and conditional fate clarifies how divine providence can
set stable conditions for inquiry (law-governed nature, real freedom, authentic opportunities for
encounter) while leaving room for prudence, effort, and growth to affect outcomes. A loving
God can therefore have adequate reasons to allow some instances of sincere, persistent


nonbelief within time: to safeguard freedom from coercion; to prevent idolatry of the divine
Essence; to calibrate disclosure to the graded capacities of agents and eras; and to orient
knowledge of God to the transformative ends for which it matters.
Finally, worries about justice lose much of their force once hiddenness is seen through this lens.
The gravest loss is not a divine refusal to speak but separation—a privation of the goods for
which the soul is made. Accountability, then, tracks one’s response to the Manifestation and to
the signs already given, not success in compelling God to meet a theatrical standard of evidence.
And the architecture is tempered by mercy: because existence is ordered to growth, post-
mortem progress and pardon remain possible by divine bounty. Hiddenness retains its
existential sting and ought not be explained away; but it no longer functions as a straightforward
defeater of perfect love. Rather, it becomes part of the grammar of relating to a transcendent God
who aims, not at provoking gasps in a theater, but at making lovers—persons whose recognition
is free, morally serious, and fitted to the kind of reality God is.
Hiddenness, evil, and speculative realism (Meillassoux lane)
The evidential pressure on theism from evil and hiddenness is by now familiar. Paul Draper’s
likelihood frame sets the baseline: let T be theism, HI the “Hypothesis of Indifference,” and O
the conjunction of facts about pleasure and pain. Draper argues that, given background
knowledge, the biological role of both states in goal-directed organisms makes O antecedently
far more likely on HI than on T—“I will argue that it is the biological role played by both pain
and pleasure in goal-directed organic systems that renders this claim true” (Draper 1989: 334).
His canonical inequality reads: P(O | HI & k) ≫ P(O | T & k) (1989: 334). Importantly, Draper
insists this is a pro tanto result: to judge theism’s overall probability one must weigh all relevant
data with a sound method of appraisal, including putative confirmations for theism as well as
defeaters (cf. Draper 1989).
J. L. Schellenberg supplies the complementary pressure from divine hiddenness. His 2015
statement is crisp: (1) If a perfectly loving God exists, God is always open to personal
relationship with every finite person; (2) such openness requires acting so as to make relationship
participation possible; hence (3) if God exists, God always so acts; but (4) some finite persons
are (or have been) nonresistant nonbelievers; therefore (5) no perfectly loving God exists,


and thus (6–7) God does not exist (Schellenberg 2015: 103). Here nonresistant nonbelief
names those who lack belief without “shutting the door,” and who would believe were God to
make himself known (2015: 54–55, 103). Read together, Draper and Schellenberg supply a two-
pronged evidential challenge: the world’s affective economy fits indifference better than love,
and God—if perfectly loving—would remove nonresistant nonbelief.
Speculative realism—in particular Quentin Meillassoux—offers an unorthodox “lane” into this
terrain by redrawing what counts as necessity, law, and even divinity. In After Finitude (UK:
Edinburgh University Press, trans. Brassier, 2005), Meillassoux targets correlationism—the
thesis that we only ever have access to the correlation between thought and world—and seeks a
rational route to an absolute that is not mind-indexed. His signature wedge is the ancestral or
arche-fossil datum (statements about events prior to life or thought), which, he argues, can be
known as such and so already exceed correlationist confines. From there he develops the
principle of factiality: the necessity of contingency. On this picture, nothing about what exists or
how laws hold is necessary; only contingency is necessary. The modal upshot is “hyper-chaos”:
time without reason, in which laws could change without cause or ground, and the Principle of
Sufficient Reason fails in the strongest sense. While we lack a compact verbatim line here, the
governing theses can be put this way (paraphrasing AF): the world is necessarily contingent;
there is no contradiction in claiming that what happens today need not happen tomorrow even if
it happened yesterday (cf. Meillassoux 2005).
That modal revolution has two striking consequences for our topic. First, if nothing necessary
exists except contingency itself, then a necessary God—the classical theistic absolute—cannot
exist. Second, precisely because all determinate states of affairs are contingent, we can entertain
the possibility of radical breaks within reality without invoking miracle in the traditional sense of
law-violation—law itself is not necessary. It is along this path that Meillassoux’s later, more
overtly “religious” speculation proceeds.
In the lectures and fragments grouped under “The Divine Inexistence” (DI), Meillassoux
proposes a position he calls divine inexistence: God does not (now) exist, but could come to
exist. The move “unknots the atheo-religious link between God and necessity (God must or must
not exist) and reattaches it to the virtual (God could exist)”—a formula Meillassoux states
explicitly (as cited from “Spectral Dilemma,” 269). DI’s moral engine is not metaphysical


tidiness but justice: only the advent of a God-to-come could rectify the injustices of the dead
by universal resurrection: “the only way to rectify unjust deaths is by giving the dead a chance
to re-live their unjustly terminated lives…. ‘we owe the dead nothing less’,” and “the negative
knowledge of our mortality thus refers to the positive knowledge of our possible rebirth”
(Meillassoux, DI: 189, as cited; see also Mangion’s summary, pp. 125–26). Crucially, the “God-
to-come” is not necessary, is not the hidden transcendent of classical theism, and does not name
a human becoming-god; rather, the hoped-for mediator appears contingently and (on
Meillassoux’s own constraints) relinquishes power once justice is accomplished (“the mediator
actually and definitively abolishes their own power once the rebirth occurs”—DI: 224, as cited).
Two bridges matter for the present dialectic. First, DI depends on AF’s modal base: only if
absolute contingency is true can we coherently hold that no necessary God exists now and yet
God could come to exist. Hence Meillassoux’s own explicit link: we must detach divinity from
necessity and attach it to the virtual (“Spectral Dilemma,” 269). Second, DI reframes the
problem of evil and hiddenness. There is no present God to hide and no present providence
to indict. Theodicy becomes a hope rather than a defense: because contingency is absolute, one
may hope for a future rectification (universal resurrection and justice) grounded not in current
governance but in the possible advent of a redeemer-God.
How should this “contingency lane” be assessed against the Draper/Schellenberg baseline?
1. Likelihoods and evil. DI disarms the demand for a theodicy now by denying a present
God. That bluntly undercuts Draper’s target hypothesis T. On the other hand, DI does not
thereby explain O on HI; it introduces a new modal backdrop (AF) and a future-oriented
eschatology without current governance. In evidential terms, DI concedes Draper’s claim
that our observed affective economy fits indifference better than love for the present
world; its distinctive wager is that absolute contingency keeps open the possibility of a
future that retrofits justice.
2. Hiddenness. As with evil, hiddenness dissolves as an argument against a perfectly
loving present God, because DI negates that antecedent: there is none. But
Schellenberg’s argument can be reloaded as a comparative: if theism means perfect love
now, DI is not theism. If “religion” is allowed to include Meillassoux’s post-theistic


hope, the dialectic shifts from whether God hides to whether hope for a God-to-come is
rationally permissible on AF.
3. Normative motivation and grief. DI’s strongest intuitive pull is ethical-existential: the
dead. Radical contingency is conscripted not to license arbitrariness but to legitimate
mourning-grounded hope: “we owe the dead nothing less.” This makes DI responsive
to the pathos behind the problem of evil without claiming that present horrors are
somehow permitted for higher goods.
There are, however, serious pressures on the Meillassoux lane.
•
Self-reference/coherence. Critics ask whether the “necessity of contingency” is itself
necessary; if so, we have a brute necessity that looks oxymoronic, and if not,
contingency might itself contingently fail, re-admitting necessity (raising a stability
problem for the view). The worry is not scholastic nit-picking: AF’s work is to underwrite
a robust absolute; if its absoluteness is only contingent, the rational “purchase” on the
absolute seems jeopardized.
•
Esoteric eschatology. Even sympathetic commentators note tensions when DI is cashed
out: What guarantees that the God-to-come would be good rather than demonic? As
Gratton remarks, the progressivism implicit in DI “sits uncomfortably with the contingent
world to which it is applied,” including the possibility that the emergent “fourth-world
being” might be malign rather than the hoped-for child-Messiah (Gratton 2014: 84). In
AF-terms, nothing guarantees the value-profile of the advent.
•
Comparative metaphysics. By rejecting a necessary good, DI purchases room for
justice-hope at the cost of present normative governance. The classical theist will say:
the price is too high; the modal ground for universal moral truths and obligations is
firmer on a necessary good than on hyper-chaos plus hope. The naturalist will say: if we
are already conceding HI for the present, better to keep the ontology lean and treat DI’s
eschatology as a beautiful—but untethered—wish.
Where does this leave a neutral evaluator? Three guardrails:


(i) Distinguish targets. Draper/Schellenberg pressure classical theism; DI is not that target. It
should be assessed as a post-theistic or para-religious stance anchored in AF’s modal
revolution.
(ii) Keep the modal cost ledger clear. AF’s denial of PSR and law-necessity pays for DI’s hope
with hyper-chaos. That buys conceptual space for a just advent, but also for demonic ones—
and undercuts familiar expectations about explanation and stability.
(iii) Respect the ethical ache. DI’s power is ethical-existential: it refuses to explain away horror
and instead reorients rational hope toward resurrectional justice. Even if one ultimately prefers
a classical theist or a minimalist naturalist picture, the DI proposal marks an intellectually serious
attempt to re-specify the field where hiddenness and evil press hardest: the graves.
Design arguments: from Paley to fine-tuning (and Priestley)
The design tradition in philosophy of religion moves from everyday intuition to frontier physics.
Its core thought is simple: some patterns look purpose-shaped rather than merely accidental, and
such patterns seem to call for an explanation. William Paley gave the classic expression. If you
pick up a stone on a heath, nothing about it forces you to posit a maker. But if you pick up a
watch, with springs and gears proportioned and arranged so as to mark the hours, you naturally
infer an artificer. The point is not perfection—an imperfect watch is still a watch—but purposive
organization: parts fitted to ends (Paley 1809). Paley then extended the thought to living systems,
especially the eye, arguing that their function-serving organization warrants a design inference.
Even if we bracket specific biological examples, Paley’s deeper claim survives: purposive
structure is a distinctive kind of order that presses the “why this, rather than a shapeless
aggregate?” question.
Modern discussions keep Paley’s intuition but shift scale. Instead of arguing from particular
organs, they ask about the preconditions for any life at all. Contemporary cosmology and
particle physics suggest that many basic features of our universe—initial conditions and
“fundamental constants”—sit in narrow ranges that allow chemistry, long-lived stars, and stable
planets. Vary them modestly and you get universes with no heavy elements, no galaxies, or only
black holes. A few standard illustrations convey the flavor. The amplitude of primordial
density fluctuations (often labeled Q) measures how lumpy the early universe was. Make Q


much smaller and matter never condenses into galaxies; make it much larger and structure
formation runs away into violent clumping that disrupts stable planetary systems. Small
fractional changes in the strong nuclear interaction skew the delicate balance by which stars
forge carbon and oxygen; skew it enough and the nuclear “recipe” for life’s building blocks fails.
Alter the masses of the light quarks or the electron too far and ordinary chemistry collapses.
At early times (around a nanosecond after the Big Bang), the mean density must be exquisitely
close to a critical value for later structure to emerge. And the initial low-entropy state—the
extraordinarily smooth, uniform beginning out of which structure slowly formed—occupies, by
Roger Penrose’s estimate, an unimaginably tiny region of the space of possibilities; he calls it
“absurdly small,” the sort of target a designer would have to “aim for” with fantastic precision
(Penrose 1989; see also Barnes & Lewis 2016 for a survey). These are descriptive claims—maps
of “life-friendly” windows—not yet conclusions. The argumentative step asks what best explains
the fact that the basic fabric of reality happens to land in such windows.
One influential way to turn the description into an argument comes from Robin Collins. He
recommends keeping the logic modest and comparative. Treat “our universe is life-permitting”
as the datum. Then compare how expectable that datum is on two broad pictures: theism (there is
a purposeful mind behind the universe) and a naturalistic single-universe picture (no such mind;
the constants and initial conditions are just what they are). If life-permitting ranges are tiny on
the naturalistic picture but not tiny on the theistic picture, then—other things equal—the datum
tilts toward theism. Collins also addresses two common worries. First, when ranges are
unbounded or hard to measure, focus on the epistemically illuminated range, i.e., the portion
we can actually evaluate for life-permitting status, rather than speculating beyond our lights.
Second, even if a multiverse exists in which “somewhere or other” life is likely, we still face an
indexical fact: this universe—the one we observe—has these life-friendly values. A successful
explanation must connect to those specific values, not only to the claim that “some universe or
other” would host observers (Collins 2012).
Naturalistic replies divide by domain. In biology, Charles Darwin’s great insight—evolution by
natural selection—shows how functional complexity can arise cumulatively without foresight.
Richard Dawkins captured this with the image of the “blind watchmaker”: the appearance of
design in the biosphere can be produced by a mindless filtering process acting over deep time.


That seriously undercuts Paley-style arguments from particular organs (Dawkins 1986, 2006). In
fundamental physics, Sean Carroll urges a science-first strategy: treat apparent fine-tuning as a
prompt to look for deeper dynamical laws, inflationary mechanisms, or multiverse models, and
discard proposals that generate internal pathologies. One such pathology is Boltzmann-brain
domination: if a theory makes it overwhelmingly likely that “you” are a fleeting thermal
fluctuation with illusory memories, it is cognitively unstable and should be rejected. The
methodological moral is cautious: push physics forward; don’t plug explanatory gaps with the
supernatural where disciplined theory might do the work (Carroll 2016). Graham Oppy
generalizes this caution into a comparative maxim: choose the best total picture—the one that
explains the most with the fewest unmotivated assumptions. On his assessment, adding God to
handle fine-tuning increases ontology without delivering commensurate predictive or
explanatory gain over naturalism constrained by standard scientific virtues (Oppy 2018).
Two clarifications keep the conversation from talking past itself. First, biological sub-
optimality is orthogonal to cosmological fine-tuning. Biologists rightly point to “revealing
flaws”—the detoured recurrent laryngeal nerve in the giraffe, human pelvic and spinal
compromises—as evidence that organisms bear the marks of history, trade-offs, and
developmental constraints. Those cases do genuine work against an “artisan tinkerer” hypothesis
within biology. But they do not touch the cosmological question. Fine-tuning claims concern the
backdrop that makes any chemistry and any evolution possible. One can fully accept
evolutionary contingency and still press the question, “Why is the backdrop so hospitable in the
first place?” Second, the anthropic principle is not a universal solvent. It answers an
observational selection effect—of course observers find themselves in a life-friendly
environment; otherwise they wouldn’t be around to notice—but it does not by itself explain why
the underlying generator (single-universe laws or multiverse measure) places non-negligible
probability on life-friendly regimes rather than almost none. Put non-technically: “we observe a
habitable universe because we are here” is true but incomplete; what still calls for explanation is
why there are habitable universes to be observed at all, given the apparent narrowness of the
habitable range.
Dawkins raises a further objection meant to block any move back to theism from fine-tuning.
Even if the universe is strikingly special, appealing to a designer simply relocates the


improbability. A mind capable of choosing constants looks, on the face of it, at least as complex
as the order to be explained—the “Ultimate Boeing 747” objection. Classical theists respond that
this misconstrues what “God” is supposed to be. The point is not to posit a very complicated
mechanism inside the world whose many parts require assembly. It is to posit a necessary, non-
composite ground of being and intelligibility, not made out of parts at all. On that
understanding, a regress-stopping explanation is exactly what is being offered; to demand a
further designer of the Designer is to mistake categories. Some theists add a simplicity claim: a
single, unbounded personal cause may be simpler—more unified—than a mosaic of brute,
unrelated initial conditions. Others dispute that this notion of “simplicity” tracks genuine
theoretical virtue (Aquinas, ST I q.3; Swinburne 2004; Oppy 2018). However that dispute goes,
it is worth noting that fine-tuning arguments are not meant to be deductive proofs. They are
likelihood comparisons in the spirit summarized by Elliott Sober: evidence favors the
hypothesis on which it was more to be expected. If the evidence in question is the existence of
life-permitting structure at the foundations, then the relevant comparison is between
foundational-level hypotheses (theism, deeper-law naturalism, multiverse naturalism), not
between an artisan-designer of organisms and Darwinian “cranes” within the biosphere (Sober
2008; Collins 2012).
Some historical perspective helps. Before Darwin supplied a naturalistic engine for biological
complexity, Joseph Priestley gave crisp voice to the design impulse: wherever there is a fit of
one thing to another—means suited to ends—there must be a cause that grasped and intended
that fit (quoted in Tapper 2020). Contemporary physics does not settle Priestley’s instinct; it
relocates it to the ground floor. The modern question is not “Is the eye a telescope?” but “Why is
there a universe with the capacity for telescopes and eyes at all?”
How, then, should a neutral reader assess the field? A balanced, academically cautious verdict
has several parts. First, Paley’s core intuition—that purposive organization is a distinctive
pattern—remains philosophically live. The physics catalogue, taken at face value, really does
identify narrow, multi-parameter windows that enable long-lived, chemistry-friendly worlds; that
mapping gives the design intuition a clean evidential shape. Second, the comparative form of
modern arguments (à la Collins) is the right one: if a single unguided universe would very
probably have been sterile, while a theistic universe would not, then the datum of a life-friendly


cosmos prima facie tilts toward theism—unless naturalistic stories (deeper laws, well-behaved
multiverse measures) can remove the surprise without introducing worse problems (e.g.,
Boltzmann-brain domination, measure pathologies). Third, naturalistic rejoinders are
substantial, not stopgaps. Evolution explains away much of the biological case, and live
programs in cosmology explore concrete, test-constrained mechanisms that might underwrite the
cosmological case. Fourth, parsimony is a real theory virtue but not a trump. If a single
primitive (God) unifies explanatory domains—laws of nature, rational normativity, teleology—
some will judge the extra ontology worth its keep; others will side with Oppy’s leaner picture
and insist the unification is illusory or redundant. Finally, both sides face ongoing work:
physicists continue to refine the map of life-relevant parameters and to test speculative
mechanisms; philosophers continue to argue about what, if anything, the map means for our best
“big pictures.”
In short, the design debate today is neither a museum piece nor a knock-down proof. It is a
comparative, cumulative contest among large-scale pictures of reality. Paley’s intuition still
motivates the question; the physics has raised the stakes; and the live options—purposive mind,
deeper law, multiverse—remain in play, each with clear explanatory ambitions and recognizable
costs.
Secular ethics vs theistic grounding (Singer/Grayling; moral non-naturalism)
A clear secular benchmark is Peter Singer’s program. In Animal Liberation and Practical Ethics,
he rejects species membership as morally special and insists on the equal consideration of
interests: like suffering counts alike wherever it occurs, so sentience, not “being human,” marks
the boundary of concern (Singer 1975/2011; 2011). From that starting point follow two well-
known edges. First, duties of beneficence become demanding. Singer’s shallow-pond thought
experiment fixes the intuition: if you can wade into a shallow pond to save a drowning child at
the mere cost of muddying your shoes, you are obligated to do so. Distance and numbers do not
matter in themselves; if we can prevent something very bad from happening without sacrificing
anything of comparable moral importance, we should do it. Singer’s conclusion is that
relatively small sacrifices (luxuries, discretionary consumption) are morally negligible compared
with the preventable harms of global poverty, so those with means have stringent duties to aid
effective relief. Second, early-life ethics receives unsettling verdicts. Because personhood—


capacities for self-awareness, rationality, future-directedness—rather than mere biological life
carries the decisive weight, some choices about abortion and neonatal care are assessed more
permissively than many theists would allow (Singer 2011).
Singer also explains why our moral circle often lags behind our principles and how it can widen.
Evolution has equipped us with partialities that favor kin and tribe; these are adaptive biases.
But they can be chastened by reflection. Reason allows us to recognize that many of our gut
reactions have no independent moral warrant. As we deliberate, we learn to widen sympathy
beyond kin and tribe, aiming at what he calls an objective point of view of the universe—a
standpoint from which each interest counts once and only once (Singer 1981/2011). In later work
with de Lazari-Radek, Singer defends this Sidgwickian impartialism against evolutionary
“debunking” arguments: even if some of our dispositions are adaptive, the normative force of
equal concern does not evaporate merely because we can tell an origin story about it (de Lazari-
Radek & Singer 2014).
A nearby secular voice, A. C. Grayling, locates ethics in human flourishing under conditions of
freedom, sympathy, and public reason. On this broadly humanist view, what makes actions right
or wrong is their relation to human (and sentient) well-being and to the virtues that sustain it;
obligations are justified by reasons accessible to any reasonable inquirer, without appeal to
divine command. The method is deliberately this-worldly and cumulative: refine norms by
reflection, experience, and dialogue rather than by deference to alleged revelation.
A second secular strand is moral non-naturalism. Its core claims can be made precise.
Objective moral truths are real in the strong sense that propositions such as “gratuitous cruelty
is wrong” are truth-apt and not mere expressions of feeling. They are stance-independent: their
truth does not depend on what anyone (or any culture) happens to approve. And they are
irreducible to natural facts: moral properties (wrongness, fairness, virtue) are not identical to,
or definable in terms of, physical, biological, or psychological properties. Derek Parfit argues
that there are such irreducibly normative truths, graspable by rational reflection rather than by
microscope or survey; some principles are self-evident upon sufficient understanding (Parfit
2011). Russ Shafer-Landau’s robust realism adds an important structural claim: moral
properties supervene on the natural “without reduction.” Wherever the natural facts are fully
fixed—say, the deliberate infliction of severe pain on a child for fun—the moral status is thereby


fixed (it is wrong), yet the moral property is not identical with, or analyzable into, those natural
facts. Supervenience secures reliability (no moral “flip” without some underlying change) while
preserving irreducibility (Shafer-Landau 2003). David Enoch’s deliberative indispensability
argument pushes from practice to ontology. Deliberation is constitutive of agency for creatures
like us: we cannot help but ask what we ought to do. And “oughts” are irreducibly normative;
they are not just predictions or preferences. Since we cannot opt out of agency (“shmagency” is
no real option), we are entitled to believe in the kind of objective normativity our deliberation
presupposes (Enoch 2011). On the naturalist side, Graham Oppy keeps the metaphysics lean. He
argues that naturalism can house a wide range of metaethical views—from quasi-realism to
robust realism—without invoking anything supernatural; adding God typically increases
commitments without delivering commensurate explanatory gain (Oppy 2018, 2019).
Our theistic critique does not dismiss these secular achievements; it asks whether a theistic
grounding offers a more integrated explanation of the very features secular theorists prize—
objectivity, authority, motivation, and necessity. Four pressure points bring the contrast into
focus.
First, epistemic access. If moral facts are sui generis and non-natural, by what faculty do we
know them? Replies that appeal to “rational insight” and “self-evidence” are intelligible but can
look like the queerness John Mackie warned about. A theistic alternative relocates access: if the
same personal Good who grounds normativity also creates rational agents in that Good’s image,
then moral cognition is neither occult nor lucky. It is a designed fit between finite minds and the
normative structure of reality—on Robert Adams’s view, the excellence of God’s character is the
supreme standard, and our capacity to apprehend reasons is part of the imago Dei (Adams 1999).
Second, motivation. Robust secular realism typically treats motivation as external to
recognition: apprehending a non-natural fact does not by itself move the will. That sits uneasily
with the strenuous impartial demands in Singer’s framework (e.g., routing significant
discretionary income to effective aid). Theistic accounts tie obligation to a law-like authority
(the will or commands of a necessarily good God) and motivation to love of the Good—an
affective-volitional link that helps explain why reasons rightly bind against interest and why
failures to respond are not just errors but faults (Evans 2013; Murphy 2002).


Third, explanatory role and parsimony. Non-naturalism posits a dualism—natural facts here,
non-natural moral facts there—connected by supervenience but not explained by it. A theistic
moral non-naturalism is monistic in ground: both the natural order and the moral order depend
on one necessarily good, personal reality. The same source that makes there be laws of nature
also makes there be laws of rightness and equips us to recognize them. That promises
explanatory unity rather than a mere conjunction of two independent ontologies (Adams 1999).
Oppy’s challenge about parsimony remains: if secular robust realism can live with brute
normativity, why not stop there? Our answer is that theism is not an extra wheel bolted onto
ethics; it is a common-source account that simultaneously explains cosmic order, normative
order, and our apt access to both. Whether that integrative gain is worth the cost is exactly the
comparative question.
Fourth, modal robustness. Secular robust realists rightly say that some things are necessarily
wrong (“in all possible worlds”). But necessity can start to look like a brute stopping point:
necessary—full stop. On a theistic grounding, by contrast, necessity is not freestanding; it traces
to the necessary character of God. The de dicto stability of moral truths is anchored in the de re
stability of the Good itself (Adams 1999; Evans 2013). That does not change everyday verdicts;
it deepens their modal basis.
Two test cases illustrate the contrast in use. Consider genocide. Every serious view condemns it.
A secular non-naturalist can say: given the natural facts (systematic extermination), the non-
natural property of grievous wrongness is instantiated—full stop. The theistic account adds why
this must be so: persons bear the divine image; their good participates (derivatively) in the Good;
to annihilate a people is to assault something sacred by relation. The verdict is the same, but the
depth of explanation differs. Consider demanding impartial reasons. Parfit and Singer are right
that trivial self-interest cannot outweigh catastrophic harms to others; robust realism affirms
categorical reasons to sacrifice. A theistic account retains the same impartial “ought,” while also
explaining its authority (law-relation to a perfect legislator) and its motivational grip
(conformity to the personal Good whose love is the archetype of impartial concern). The result is
not stricter ethics—Singer already sets a high bar—but a thicker story of why the bar binds and
why we should expect frail agents to need transformation, communities, and liturgies of love to
live up to it.


Several clarifications and guardrails matter. First, secular non-naturalism secures objectivity
without scientism and deserves its due. It blocks relativism and underwrites categorical
reasons; Enoch’s point about the inescapability of deliberation is especially forceful. Second,
Singer’s equal consideration has been among the most morally fruitful ideas in contemporary
ethics; the expansion of concern to nonhuman animals and to distant strangers stands as a major
achievement. Third, the naturalist’s parsimony objection is serious. If one judges that the secular
package already explains the phenomena at acceptable cost—epistemic access via reflection,
motivation via cultivated sympathies and institutions, necessity via brute modal facts—then
adding God can look gratuitous. Fourth, by the same token, if one prizes integration—a single
source for the being of things, the normativity of reasons, and the mind’s fit to both—then the
theistic package may earn its keep.
In sum, the live dispute is not between morality and amorality, nor between reasons and mere
feelings. It is a comparative question about foundations. Singer and Grayling sketch a secular
ethic that is impartial, humane, and publicly shareable. Robust non-naturalists give it
metaphysical spine. Our claim is comparative, not dismissive: when one weighs epistemic
access, motivational depth, explanatory unity, and modal grounding together, theistic moral
non-naturalism offers a more integrated basis for the very features secular theorists rightly
prize—even while acknowledging that secular theories can capture much of our everyday moral
landscape and have spurred some of its most admirable reforms.
Science, Well-Being, and Normativity (Harris)
Harris contends that moral questions are, at bottom, empirical questions about the well-being of
conscious creatures and that a mature science of the mind could, in principle, determine correct
answers to them (Harris 2010). He argues that the customary firewall between facts and values is
illusory: because well-being supervenes on brain states and worldly conditions, there are
scientific truths to be known about it; further, a “moral landscape” of peaks (maxima of
flourishing) and valleys (depths of suffering) provides a representational space in which
competing norms can be adjudicated empirically (Harris 2010). He grants pluralism—there may
be multiple, incompatible yet roughly equivalent “peaks”—but insists the possibility of several
peaks does not render morality subjective; rather, cross-cultural differences in flourishing are


themselves facts about the brain and social organization that science can, in principle, measure
and compare (Harris 2010).
Treating these claims as a research program rather than a conclusion, several questions arise.
First, the is/ought transition: even if science maps correlations between practices and well-
being, the claim that we ought to promote well-being is not itself a descriptive deliverance.
Harris often replies that the “ought” talk is a misleading artifact and that, once we focus on
conscious experience, the only non-question-begging terminal value available is well-being
(Harris 2010). But that reply simply re-asserts a substantive normative commitment: that well-
being is objectively choice-worthy as such. It does not follow from neuropsychology that we are
categorically bound to maximize well-being; at best, the science identifies means to
independently chosen ends. Thus, Harris’s view presupposes a form of value realism—that well-
being is genuinely good—and the burden is not discharged by showing that well-being is widely
desired or that it reliably subserves other aims. In short, science can illuminate what promotes a
value, not why that value is authoritative.
Second, the measurement problem is nontrivial. Harris allows that “well-being,” like “health,”
is open-textured and revisable (Harris 2010). That concession protects the view from easy
counterexamples but weakens its claim to provide categorical, action-guiding reasons now.
Scientific operationalizations (self-reports, psychometrics, neuroimaging proxies) are defeasible
and often incommensurable across persons and cultures. To be clear: this is not an argument for
relativism; it is the more modest point that epistemic access to moral facts—even if they are facts
about flourishing—is often underdetermined by currently available measures, and thus cannot
alone bear the justificatory weight Harris wants them to carry in live disputes (e.g., corporal
punishment, gender practices, honor norms).
Third, dissenters and normativity. Harris’s handling of dissenters (e.g., the psychopath who
“prefers” domination or cruelty) implies that such preferences simply misapprehend their own
good. Perhaps; but that is a normative thesis about what counts as one’s good, not a
neuroscientific discovery. The view therefore tacitly trades on a standard moral-realist structure:
there exist stance-independent reasons that correct or trump first-person desire sets. If so, the
crucial work is being done by a metaethical grounding of normativity, not by the empirical
sciences as such.


A theistic account can be staged as a competitor explanation precisely at this grounding level. On
the Adams/Evans family of views, moral value is not an emergent descriptive property but is
anchored in the necessary character of a perfectly good God. On Adams’s “modified divine
nature/command” theory, the good is identified by resemblance to God’s nature, while moral
obligations are constituted by the commands of a loving Deity (Adams 1999, ch. 11; 231–248).
This avoids both reduction (values are not mere natural facts) and arbitrariness (commands
express, rather than create, the good). Evans makes the structure explicit: only the commands of
a necessarily good and loving God could generate moral obligations; a “supernatural evil being”
could not (Evans 2013, 90, 92), and our epistemic access can be mediated by conscience as a
natural capacity (v, 42, 26). The contrast with Harris is sharp. Harris offers a promissory
epistemology of morality (more measurement will eventually constrain disagreement) while
presupposing the normative authority of well-being; the theistic view offers a metaphysical
ground for that authority and then welcomes the sciences instrumentally to guide application. Put
differently: science may well improve our map of the moral landscape, but it does not supply the
north.
Bridge. The foregoing raises the classic arbitrariness challenge: if normativity depends on God,
are the goods good because God commands them, or does God command them because they are
good? The next subsection addresses this Euthyphro problem directly.
Resolving Euthyphro: Divine Nature and Command
Socrates frames the dilemma crisply: is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or is it
pious because the gods love it? Read as a challenge to theistic metaethics, the horns are familiar:
arbitrariness (if divine will makes values, anything could be good) versus independence (if
values are independent, God is normatively redundant). Contemporary theists resolve the
dilemma by rejecting its forced disjunction. On Adams’s view, goodness is grounded in God’s
necessary character, not in unconstrained fiat; divine commands then specify obligations for
creatures in ways that express that character (Adams 1999, ch. 11; 231–248). This two-level
structure allows both modal depth and normative content: God’s perfect goodness is necessary
(hence not contingent or arbitrary), while the applications of obligation can vary with created
natures and circumstances (Adams 1999, 255–256). It also secures an important distinction


Adams presses: an act can be good without being obligatory; obligation has a “social” or
authoritative dimension that commands uniquely supply (231–248).
Evans articulates the arbitrariness block more directly. On the form of divine command theory he
defends, only the commands of a God who is necessarily good and loving can generate
obligations; by design, this excludes “commands” to do what is intrinsically vicious (Evans
2013, 90, 92). The dependence relation is thus preserved (obligations depend on divine
commands), while arbitrariness is denied (commands flow from and aim at the good). Nor does
this render moral praise of God empty: God is praiseworthy, inter alia, in virtue of how His
commands further the good (Evans 2013, 90). Epistemically, the view does not require constant
special revelation: conscience is among the ordinary means by which divine requirements can be
known, even by non-theists (Evans 2013, v, 42, 26).
Two standard objections can be met briskly. First, vacuity (“good = God’s nature” reduces to a
label). The reply is that the theory is not a mere stipulation; it attributes to God a rich cluster of
evaluative perfections (e.g., lovingkindness, justice, faithfulness) that structure the content of
goodness and constrain what could be commanded. Second, normative autonomy (“then we
need an independent criterion to identify those perfections”). Here the theist embraces a familiar
stance: evaluative knowledge is partially basic—grasped in conscience and practical reason—but
metaphysically grounded in God. That is, epistemic routes to moral knowledge can be shared
with non-theists, while the explanatory ground of normativity is theistic.
This resolution also clarifies the dialectic with Harris. If Harris’s project presupposes that well-
being is objectively to-be-promoted, then he tacitly relies on a non-descriptive normative fact.
The Euthyphro-responsive account supplies precisely what Harris lacks: a ground for such
categorical reasons (God’s necessary goodness) that is neither arbitrary will nor independent
Platonic moralism—and then treats the empirical sciences as crucial, but instrumental, guides to
the specification of those reasons in complex circumstances.
Popular atheism & public discourse (O’Connor & Hitchens)
Christopher Hitchens gave the “conflict” template its most potent public rhetoric. In the set-piece
chapter “Religion Kills,” he strings cases (Ireland, Lebanon, India, Pakistan, Israel/Palestine) to


argue that when identity is sacralized, ordinary political grievance hardens into absolutism: “In
Northern Ireland I have seen whole communities wall themselves off from one another and
refuse to speak the ordinary language of daily life,” and in Beirut the same pattern metastasized
into militias and massacre (his essayed excerpt juxtaposes Belfast sectarianism with a Beirut
descending into fratricide). The through-line is simple: creeds that claim divine warrant
supercharge tribal enmity, and claims to revelation license coercion where argument fails.
Hitchens’s register is maximalist, but the evidential punch is anecdotal and journalistic; its force
rests less on tidy inference than on the cumulative effect of scenes of sectarian ruin.
Hitchens’s polemical style also trades on stark contrasts between scientific fallibilism and
confessional certainty. In the excerpted material he frames religious authority as structurally
disposed to suppress inquiry and to “impose” its will once it can marshal force—a move that
buttresses the book’s subtitle (“How Religion Poisons Everything”) but invites the standard
rejoinder that political and ethnic dynamics are doing much of the causal work in the very cases
he canvasses. What Hitchens indisputably achieved, however, was to fix a public baseline: when
religious identity goes hot, violence is not an accident but a predictable downstream effect of
absolutist meaning-systems.
Alex O’Connor (Cosmic Skeptic) represents a different idiom of public atheism: long-form,
dialed-down, and relentlessly comparative. His Within Reason podcast is a forum more than a
pulpit, hosting both critics and sympathizers—among them Richard Dawkins and Slavoj
Žižek—with topic lists that run from divine hiddenness to ethical objectivity and scriptural
ethics. The format signals a meta-point: the case for naturalism should be made where the best
counterarguments are given time to breathe, not merely scored by rhetorical flourish. (For
orientation to the series and guests, see catalogues and profiles that list O’Connor’s regular work
and interlocutors.)
That tonal and methodological shift matters. Where Hitchens leans on morally charged reportage
to claim that “religion kills,” O’Connor’s interviews and debates aim to locate which claims
(hiddenness, miracles, moral realism, scriptural violence) actually move the comparative ledger
between theism and naturalism—and which do not. The result is a public-facing version of the
academic posture taken by Draper and Oppy: parse evidence by likelihoods and theory-virtues


rather than by invective, and concede ground where one’s side lacks advantage. The audience
takeaway is less a rallying-cry than a research program.
For contrast on the broader culture of public meaning, James A. Herrick’s The Making of the
New Spirituality: The Eclipse of the Western Religious Tradition anatomizes a parallel
rhetorical current: a diffuse “new religious synthesis” that challenges each major tenet of the
Judeo-Christian frame and supplies alternative idioms—holism, immanentism, therapeutic
teleology—for moral and existential talk in the public square. Herrick’s diagnostic thesis is that
this synthesis functions rhetorically as a replacement metaphysic in late-modern discourse rather
than a mere private piety; that is why it shapes media and politics even as formal church
affiliation wanes.
Put together, these three strands map the contemporary field. Hitchens supplies the polemical
north star for conflict-framings; O’Connor models adversarial yet charitable comparison that
trades heat for light; Herrick charts an adjacent, less combative replacement of traditional
religion by a “new spirituality” that nevertheless continues to do thick worldview work in public.
The upshot for readers of this volume is methodological: if we are going to assess the standing of
“religion” in public life, we should separate (i) the rhetorical force of Hitchens-style indictment,
(ii) the comparative evidential work that actually shifts priors in public debates (O’Connor’s
lane), and (iii) the cultural uptake of spirituality as a meaning-system that competes with both
confessional theism and hard naturalism (Herrick’s terrain). Only then do we see clearly where
disagreements are empirical, where they are about theory-choice, and where they are about the
stories a culture is willing to live by.
Religious violence, extremism, and causal mechanisms
Is religion uniquely violent—or is “religious violence” a misleading category that hides the real
engines of conflict? New Atheist polemics answer the first way: Sam Harris and Christopher
Hitchens press a simple causal story in which doctrinal certainty, eschatological rewards, and
immunity from evidential checks make religion a standing danger to civil peace (Harris 2004,
2006; Hitchens 2007). That rhetoric is forceful as diagnosis and galvanizing as exhortation. But
it is not where the best explanation lives.


William Cavanaugh’s Myth of Religious Violence disrupts the starting point. There is, he
argues, no stable, transhistorical essence called “religion” to which a peculiar propensity to
violence can be attached; the very religious/secular split is a modern, political construction that
legitimates state coercion and “other-izes” non-liberal publics (Cavanaugh 2009). On his
reconstruction of the so-called Wars of Religion, the relevant cleavages were dynastic, fiscal, and
jurisdictional as much as doctrinal; the wars look less like eruptions of ungovernable piety than
like state-building by other means. The policy moral follows: if we cannot coherently isolate
“religious” violence from “secular” violence, then treating religion as a primitive explanatory
variable is a category mistake.
R. Scott Appleby reframes rather than rejects religion’s causal relevance. In The Ambivalence of
the Sacred (2000), religion is “powerful medicine”: the same encounter with the sacred that can
sacralize out-group enmity and mobilize sacrificial militancy can also empower peacemaking,
mediation, and restraint. Outcomes turn on mechanisms and contexts—leadership cues,
institutional discipline, grievance construction, the sacralization of ethnic and national identities,
and the availability of nonviolent repertoires. Appleby’s point is not ecumenical sentiment; it is
mechanism-sensitivity.
Mark Juergensmeyer’s Terror in the Mind of God (2000/2003) adds a grammar of cosmic war.
When worldly disputes are narratively lifted into an absolute struggle between good and evil,
three things follow: stakes become uncompromisable; enemies are demonized (“satanized”); and
violence is staged as sacred performance—symbolic, exemplary, ritualized. Time is apocalyptic
(patience can be measured in centuries, or transposed to a transtemporal register), and space is
sacral (land becomes covenantal). Crucially, Juergensmeyer insists that most such conflicts do
not begin as religious; they are “religionized” at points of frustration and escalation, after which
the repertoire and motivational structure change.
Taken together, these strands recommend re-specification: stop asking whether “religion causes
violence” and ask how religious ideas, institutions, and identities interact with more general
causal machinery. Four recurrent mechanisms are particularly useful:
•
Sacred values. When objects, norms, or places are protected against trade-offs, standard
cost–benefit bargaining collapses; affronts motivate outrage, not compromise (Appleby
2000).


•
Identity fusion. A visceral “oneness” with the group can make extreme self-sacrifice feel
self-expressive; martyrdom becomes psychologically intelligible within a sacralized
collective self (Juergensmeyer 2000).
•
Outbidding and spoiler dynamics. In competitive fields, actors can escalate to more
absolutist, purity-signaling positions to outflank rivals and block settlements
(comparative politics literatures on religious outbidding).
•
Organizational entrepreneurship and provocation cycles. Movements leverage legal
and institutional niches to grow; repression (or anticipated repression) is framed as
persecution, which then justifies tactical escalation.
