A brief case registers these dynamics outside stereotyped theaters. The Rajneeshpuram
movement in Oregon (1980s) began as a charismatic commune and, under Ma Anand Sheela,
routinized into a centralized organization that sought municipal incorporation to secure
autonomy. Land-use fights and church–state litigation were narrated internally as existential
threats to a sacred project. Escalation followed: internal coercion, immigration fraud, a bioterror
attack, and plots against public officials. Nothing in the story is explained by a generic “religion
makes people violent” trope; much is explained by entrepreneurial institution-hacking, sacred-
value entrenchment, leadership radicalization, and a provocation–repression spiral (Wright 2023;
Religious Violence without Religion).
Public conversations have begun to catch up to this shift in emphasis. In debates and long-form
interviews, Alex O’Connor (Cosmic Skeptic) often presses the comparative question
Harris/Hitchens sidestep: is the explanandum religion per se or dogmatic certainty under
conditions that amplify sacred values, fuse identities, and reward outbidding? Framed that way,
the empirical task is not to tot up “religious wars,” but to map when and how religious
repertoires supercharge dynamics that also appear in avowedly secular movements.
Two guardrails, then:
1. Category discipline. Claims that religion is uniquely violent do not survive definitional
scrutiny (Cavanaugh) or cross-case comparison (Appleby; Juergensmeyer). Religion is
best treated as a force multiplier whose effects are conditional on institutional, narrative,
and incentive structures.


2. Mechanism literacy. Explaining and mitigating violence require attention to sacred-
value triggers, fusion pathways, organizational incentives, and competitive fields. That is
where policy and prevention belong—not in generic prescriptions to privatize religion,
but in concrete work on de-escalation frames, leadership selection and accountability,
institutional channeling of grievance, and settlement designs that respect non-fungible
commitments.
Harris and Hitchens were right about one thing: ideas matter. But the live philosophical and
social-scientific work is to specify which ideas, in which settings, through which mechanisms,
and under which constraints. On that score, the best explanation is neither denunciation nor
exoneration of “religion,” but a granular account of how sacred meanings, organizational forms,
and political opportunity structures interact to make some paths to violence salient—and others
to peace practicable.
From a Bahá’í vantage point, “religious violence” is a misleading category if it is taken to
ascribe a distinctive homicidal tendency to religion as such. What needs explaining in empirical
cases is not the bare presence of religious language but the activation of familiar causal
machinery—sacred-value hardening, identity fusion, outbidding, and entrepreneurial
leadership—often under conditions of grievance and competition. Normatively, the Bahá’í
writings insist that authentic religion is ordered to unity and concord; descriptively, they locate
the proximate engines of conflict in “self and passion,” the lust for leadership, blind imitation,
and fanaticism that attach themselves to religious identities and institutions once those identities
and institutions are conscripted into worldly contests. On this view, scripture and history should
not be read as a ledger of faith’s inherent violence but as a contrast between religion’s telos (to
“safeguard the interests and promote the unity of the human race” and to “foster the spirit of love
and fellowship”) and the recurrent perversions of that telos when spiritual authority is
instrumentalized for partisan ends. Hence the striking internal constraint: the “law of holy war”
is abrogated; enmity, reviling, and sectarian rancor are proscribed; believers are enjoined to
“consort with the followers of all religions in a spirit of friendliness and fellowship.” Those are
not merely pious slogans. They are design-features aimed at disabling the very mechanisms by
which sacred repertoires are commonly weaponized.


Notice how the Bahá’í analysis maps onto the mechanisms canvassed in the contemporary
literature. Sacred values: the writings repeatedly warn that fanatical absolutization—“religious
hatred is a world-devouring fire”—turns non-fungible commitments into occasions for rage
rather than reconciliation. The remedy is re-sacralization of universals (the oneness of
humankind, justice, truthfulness) and the de-sacralization of markers that fuel sectarian
bargaining failures (ethnicity, party, confessional supremacy). Identity fusion: rather than fusing
the self with a militant subgroup, the Bahá’í ideal seeks to expand identity to a planetary “we,”
making it psychologically harder to construe outsiders as enemies and easier to internalize loss-
minimizing compromises as self-expressive. Outbidding: where religious marketplaces reward
purity signaling and maximalism, the Bahá’í emphasis on consultation, obedience to law, and
Covenant aims to remove reputational returns to ever-more absolutist postures and to discipline
leadership incentives away from spoiler behavior. Organizational entrepreneurship: because
movements scale through niches, legal gray zones, and repertoires of provocation and
victimhood, the writings press two counter-moves: (i) an uncompromising critique of clericalism
and the “lust of leadership” that turns spiritual capital into political patronage; and (ii) non-
violent repertoires of action (education, service, interfaith fellowship) that absorb grievance into
constructive projects rather than into cycles of retaliatory escalation.
The Bahá’í corpus is also explicit about misattribution. When religions descend into internecine
rancor or become pretexts for conquest, the texts diagnose not a property of revelation but a loss
of spiritual essence—“a body without a soul.” Over time, truth is eclipsed by blind imitation,
“idle fancies,” and the hardening of metaphors into shibboleths; leaders “worship no god but
their desires” and protect position by mobilizing followers against convenient outsiders. In that
register, episodes often labeled “religious violence” look, on closer inspection, like the
politicization of religion under familiar incentives: status threats, rent extraction, authoritarian
legitimation, and outgroup blame. Read this way, the Bahá’í perspective converges with
Cavanaugh’s category discipline and Appleby’s “ambivalence of the sacred”: sacred vocabularies
are force multipliers whose direction—toward blood or peace—depends on how institutions,
narratives, and incentives are configured.
Because the diagnosis is not merely conceptual but institutional, the remedies are institutional
too. Beyond the injunctions to personal virtue (truthfulness, justice, temperance, patience) and


the categorical ban on vilification and sectarian contempt, the writings propose architectures of
peace designed to channel conflict away from violence: a Supreme Tribunal to arbitrate
interstate disputes, consultative governance to reduce zero-sum factionalism, and educational
projects that attack the root stock of violence—prejudice in its religious, racial, political, and
economic forms. Far from privatizing religion, the program treats religion as a public good when
rightly practiced: a reservoir of motivation for costly cooperation, a narrative frame that renders
restraint honorable, and an authority structure that can delegitimate spoiler tactics even when
they carry short-term reputational benefits.
This does not romanticize religious history. The Bahá’í sources are sober about persecution,
Covenant-breaking, and the ease with which communities fracture under the blows of ambition
and fear. They register how prophets and reformers have been exiled, imprisoned, and killed at
the instigation of religious and political elites whose interests were threatened. But that record is
folded back into the same analysis: the atrocities are explained by human failings and
institutional incentives, not by anything demanded by authentic religion; and the appropriate
response is to strengthen the norms and structures that prevent the religionization of grievance in
the first place.
Set against the mechanism-literacy proposed earlier, the Bahá’í perspective can be summarized
in two theses. Analytically, it endorses re-specification: religion is not a primitive causal
variable but a repertoire that interacts with grievances, leadership incentives, and organizational
opportunities. The question is never “Does religion cause violence?” but “Which religious ideas
and institutions, under which incentives and narratives, accelerate or dampen known pathways to
violence?” Normatively, it claims that genuine religion contains internal resources—doctrinal,
ethical, and institutional—that lower the temperature of those pathways: it forbids the rhetoric
that sacralizes enmity, erodes the payoffs to outbidding, enlarges the circle of identity, supplies
non-violent repertoires, and builds adjudicative fora capable of handling non-tradeable claims
with dignity. If public debate continues to ask whether “religion is uniquely violent,” the Bahá’í
answer is a principled no; if it asks how to reduce the probability of violence in worlds where
sacred meanings matter, the answer is: get the mechanisms and the moral architecture right,
and insist—by precept and by institution—that the name of God is never a license for the works
of hate.


Oppy’s meta-strategy: burden of proof, priors, and theoretical virtues
Graham Oppy does not try to swat down theistic arguments one by one. He asks a bigger
question: if we step back and compare two whole pictures of reality—theism (“there is a
personal God who creates and sustains everything”) and naturalism (“the natural world is all
there is”)—which picture is the better overall theory of the world? To answer that, he uses the
same “theory virtues” scientists and philosophers use in other domains: be as simple as you can
(don’t multiply assumptions without need), explain a lot (breadth), explain it well (depth), fit the
evidence, cohere with what we already have good reason to accept, and avoid ad hoc patches.
Burden of proof, as Oppy sees it. On this way of proceeding, there is no courtroom asymmetry
where one side bears a special burden while the other gets a free ride. Both sides must put a total
package on the table and show why it wins on the standard virtues. Oppy’s recurring claim is
straightforward: theism adds a very large commitment—an ultimate, maximally powerful
mind—on top of what naturalism already posits. Unless adding God buys clear, compensating
explanatory gains (better predictions, tighter unification, fewer brute facts overall), the addition
counts against the theistic package on grounds of simplicity.
Why Oppy is wary of “cumulative cases.” Many theists present a “rope, not chain” approach:
even if no single argument is decisive (cosmological, moral, fine-tuning, religious experience,
etc.), together they become strong. Oppy’s reply is methodological. If each strand has weak
premises, hidden assumptions, or shifts the question elsewhere, bundling them does not
magically improve them. A long argument that depends on many questionable steps is not
stronger because it is longer. What matters is whether any single, non-defective argument carries
real weight; if not, a bundle of light straws does not become a beam.
What are “priors,” and why Oppy won’t front-load them? In Bayesian language, a prior is
your starting credence before you look at the evidence. Some theists (notably Richard
Swinburne) argue that theism is, by its very form, a simple hypothesis—“one person without a
body, unlimited in power, knowledge, and goodness”—and that genuine simplicity should raise
its prior. Oppy is skeptical of playing this game at the outset. He thinks we have no non-
question-begging way to assign a precise starting probability to “God exists.” If we can’t
responsibly fix priors, then the debate should shift from massaging the start line to comparing
how well each big picture handles the evidence and earns the standard theory virtues overall.


From priors to evidential fit (likelihoods) and total theory. If you set priors aside, what
matters is how much the data we actually have would surprise you on each view. Paul Draper’s
way of putting this has become standard: take a piece of evidence (call it E), and ask, “Is E more
to be expected if theism is true, or if naturalism is true, given our shared background?” Draper
applies this to pain and pleasure, arguing the biological role and distribution of suffering look
antecedently more like what an indifferent world would produce than what a perfectly good God
would orchestrate. Oppy adopts this style of assessment: when a side has to add many auxiliary
assumptions to make the evidence unsurprising (“God has reasons we cannot see,” “there are
many universes somewhere,” “fine-tuning will dissolve under deeper physics,” etc.), those
auxiliaries are not free—they count against simplicity or independently demand support. The
better picture is the one that fits the data without a growing list of unearned extras.
Parsimony, stated plainly. Parsimony is not “prefer the shallow view.” It is “do not pay for
entities you don’t need.” Oppy’s headline claim is blunt: atheism is simpler than theism
because it razors away an ultimate personal being. So long as naturalism can match theism’s
explanatory reach—accounts of cosmology, consciousness, morality, meaning—without
invoking a transcendent mind, the leaner package wins by default. If theism is to overcome that
default, it must earn its keep by delivering genuine explanatory leverage that naturalism lacks.
How this plays out on familiar fronts.
•
A-priori proofs (ontological/cosmological by pure reason): Oppy thinks they stumble on
familiar hurdles. Arguments that try to get existence from concepts, or a necessary being
from very general premises, either embed controversial assumptions or leave a gap from
“some necessary being exists” to “the God of theism.” Even sympathetic philosophers
rarely expect an a-priori route to succeed.
•
Fine-tuning/design: Oppy’s mature view is that invoking God does not improve the total
ledger. The naturalist can pursue deeper laws, selection effects, or (speculatively)
multiverse models—and these avenues are continuous with scientific practice. Unless
theism predicts or explains something here that naturalism cannot (without equal
speculative cost), the net gain is unclear.


•
“Cumulative case” revisited: Moving from design to morality to religious experience
does not help if each individual move is equivocal and the theist keeps paying with new
assumptions. Longer is not better when what gets longer is the tab.
Swinburne’s counter-move, and Oppy’s reply. Swinburne argues that theism is, in fact, the
simplest ultimate theory: one ultimate principle (a personal God) explains why there are laws at
all, why there are moral truths, why minds exist, and so on. For Swinburne, that kind of
unification should raise the prior for theism and then allow a cumulative case to push it higher
still. Oppy pushes back on both steps. First, he doubts we can responsibly say, in advance, that “a
single infinite mind” is objectively simpler than a sparse, impersonal base with laws—especially
when the theistic attributes (omniscience, omnipotence, perfect goodness) are rich and multiply
theorized. Second, if we move off priors to global comparison, he thinks naturalism still does
at least as well on breadth, depth, and fit without adding a maximally puissant hypothesis. In
short: the promised simplicity dividend is, to him, unproven; the parsimony debit remains.
Carroll’s “poetic naturalism” as a feel for the default. Sean Carroll offers an attitude that
helps explain Oppy’s pull toward parsimony. There is one physical world, governed (at
everyday energies) by well-confirmed physics; on top of that world we can legitimately speak
many “poetic” languages—about meanings, morals, choices—without positing extra layers of
metaphysical furniture. If the Core Theory suffices as a base layer for what we observe, and if
higher-level talk can be understood as useful descriptions rather than as additional entities, then
the bar for adding a God-level posit remains very high.
What “burden of proof” becomes on this view. It’s not that theism must “prove God” in a
strict sense, or that naturalism must “disprove God.” Rather: given contested starting points,
which package makes the world less puzzling at a lower cost? Whenever a side shores up its
picture by tacking on special-purpose clauses (“God has inscrutable reasons here,” “the
universe-generator has just the right measure there”), Oppy totals that on the cost side of the
ledger. Draper’s likelihoods supply the meter for evidential fit; parsimony and coherence price
the assumptions; and the more auxiliaries a view needs, the more its simplicity advantage
erodes.
Where this leaves a fair-minded reader. Oppy’s meta-strategy relocates the debate’s center of
gravity. Instead of asking, one by one, whether the Kalam premise holds, whether this fine-


tuning ratio is tiny, or whether this experience is veridical, he asks: Does adding God, all-things-
considered, improve our best theory of reality once we price in simplicity, coherence,
conservatism, and fit with the total evidence? His answer—for now—is no: the ledger still favors
the lean side. A theist can answer in kind—by arguing that theism really does buy unification
worth paying for (about laws, consciousness, normativity, meaning) and that its added
assumptions are fewer than the many brute posits naturalism must accept. But Oppy has made
the terms of trade clear: no free priors, no magic from piling up weak arguments, and no
exemptions from the ordinary standards by which we compare big theories everywhere else.
Conclusion
The foregoing review does not vindicate a verdict by slogan—neither “science has refuted God”
nor “atheism collapses under reason.” What it does is narrow the field and clarify how the
contest should be run. First, the right level of analysis matters. Treating neural dependence as a
reductive proof of materialism, or treating evolutionary/memetic accounts of religion as verdicts
on truth, confuses mapping with metaphysics. Conscious states covary with brain states in fine
detail, but that underdetermines identity claims; evolutionary explanations of transmission
underdetermine questions of warrant. Getting the explanandum right prevents category mistakes
that inflate modest data into grand conclusions.
Second, method disciplines substance. Hiddenness and evil have evidential bite only when
framed as comparative likelihoods against live alternatives on shared background knowledge.
Likewise, design arguments clarify considerably once we distinguish organismic sub-optimality
(where Darwinian explanation excels) from cosmological preconditions for any life (where low-
entropy initials, parameter sensitivity, and measure problems do real work). In each arena,
theism gains ground only by earning it—by raising the probability of the relevant data without ad
hoc auxiliaries; naturalism gains ground by explaining as much with fewer commitments without
hand-waving away unsolved anomalies.
Third, the moral ledger divides labor. Secular robust realism secures objectivity without
scientism and rightly emphasizes impartial reasons (as in Singer’s “shallow pond” line of
thought). Yet it leaves open questions about epistemic access, authority, and motivational grip.
Theistic groundings that tie normativity to a necessarily good personal source aim to unify


objectivity, bindingness, and motive in one place; whether that unification is worth the
ontological cost is precisely the comparative question, not something to be settled by definitional
fiat.
Fourth, physics constrains without closing the case. Successes of the Core Theory make appeals
to extra forces or energies illicit, but they do not decide whether consciousness is identical to,
realized by, or metaphysically distinct from physical states, nor do they settle whether life-
permitting boundary conditions are brute, multiversal, law-entailing, or teleological. Live science
circumscribes metaphysics without dictating it.
Fifth, classical theism is not a monolith on its hardest edges. There are coherent routes through
foreknowledge and freedom (Boethian timelessness, Ockhamism, Molinism), through
omnipotence (power over the logically possible), and through soteriological severity (self-
exclusion models, annihilationism, hopeful universalism). Adopting any route incurs transparent
costs; denying this plurality stacks the deck.
A recurring lesson from the violence debate is likewise diagnostic. “Religious violence” is a poor
primitive. Mechanisms—sacred values, identity fusion, outbidding, provocation–repression
spirals—do the explanatory work and show why religious repertoires can intensify conflict and,
under different leadership and institutional designs, anchor peace. This is where policy belongs:
de-escalation frames, accountability for gatekeepers, settlement designs that respect non-fungible
commitments.
What should a neutral evaluator conclude? That the ledger is mixed and dynamic. Naturalism
retains a parsimony advantage so long as it can continue to address fine-tuning pathologies,
avoid Boltzmann-brain absurdities, and offer credible bridges for consciousness and normativity.
Theism retains a unification advantage where it can illuminate cosmic order, mind, and morality
together without contrivance and where its lived expressions demonstrably promote the goods it
names. On either side, progress is likeliest where research is hottest: (i) cosmology (measures
over multiverse space, the structure of low-entropy initials, selection effects), (ii) consciousness
(whether a satisfying explanatory bridge from the physical/functional to the phenomenal is


possible), and (iii) normativity (accounts that explain objectivity, authority, and motivation
together, and that earn their ontological keep).
The paper’s constructive proposal is modest but non-trivial. Comparative evaluation should
proceed under shared virtues—evidential fit, explanatory depth, coherence, and simplicity rightly
construed—while refusing category errors (methodological successes overread as metaphysical
closure) and straw opponents (caricatures of either side’s best versions). The Bahá’í materials,
used here heuristically, exemplify a theistic stance that accepts empirical discipline, rejects
violence as a betrayal of religion’s point, and centers moral and civic formation—showing that
“religion” in the analysis must be specified by doctrines, institutions, and practices rather than by
essence-talk. On this framing, neither dismissal nor deference is in order. There is substantive
work to do—and, crucially, there are common standards by which to do it.
